\(\Pi = (\text{Id}, Z)\) being the period matrix for \(C\) satisfies \(Z = Z^T\), which means, \[\int_{\gamma_{g+j}}\omega_i = \int_{\gamma_{g+i}}\omega_j\]

and thus, \[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\int_{q_j}^{p_j}\omega_i = m_i + \sum_{j=1}^{g} m_{g+j}\int_{\gamma_{g+i}}\omega_j\]

By \((\dagger)\) we get, \[\pi_{g+i}(\phi') = m_i + \sum_{j=1}^{g} m_{g+j}\int_{\gamma_{g+i}}\omega_j (\dagger\dagger)\]

Now let, \[\widetilde{\phi}:= \phi' - \sum_{j=1}^{g} m_{g+j}\omega_j\]

and note that as \(\pi_j(\omega_i) = \delta_{ij}\) for \(i,j = 1, \ldots, g\), we have,

\[\int_{\gamma_i}\widetilde{\phi} = \int_{\gamma_i}\phi' - \sum_{j=1}^{g} m_{g+j}\omega_j = -m_{g+i} \in \mathbb{Z}\]

and by \((\dagger\dagger)\), \[\int_{\gamma_{g+i}}\widetilde{\phi} = \pi_{g+i}(\phi') - \sum_{j=1}^{g} m_{g+j}\int_{\gamma_{g+i}}\omega_j = m_i \in \mathbb{Z}\]

In conclusion, \(\widetilde{\phi}\) is the differential that would make our construction work and settle the proof of (ii) once and for all. 0◻

Remark. The relevance of Abel’s Theorem to the existence of meromorphic functions is that the Abel-Jacobi map is surjective (which is often referred to as Jacobi’s Inversion Theorem).

title: Orientation and Covering Maps
html:
S. Viswanathan

Here is an intuition illustrating the need for orientability of a manifold. Suppose you want to measure the volume of a Möbius band or a cylinder, that is, the set \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) with \((0,t)\sim(1,1-t)\), or with \((0,t)\sim(1,t)\), respectively. In the absence of an ambient manifold such as \(\mathbb R^3\), these surfaces, as abstract objects, do not have faces. Thus the volume of a page, as a manifold with boundary in its own right, does not have to account for the two sides. It is essentially the area of a page as a whole. To measure the volume of a cylinder, draw a loop around it and measure how much area you sweep as you traverse it. To keep track of the area you have already swept, flag it.

But if your manifold is such that, even when you end back where you started, you do not see your flag, as would happen for the Möbius band, you would end up overcounting. More precisely, the amount you overcount will depend on the charts you choose. Therefore, having a consistent sense of direction is crucial to being able to integrate on a manifold.

In this exposition we shall see some covering-space-theoretic implications of orientability. We have seen covering space theory in calculating fundamental groups, lifting holomorphic branches, studying covering spaces, classifying manifolds, and pushing certain invariant metrics. We shall now see yet another application: the Orientation Covering Theorem.

Given a covering map \(\pi\colon E\to M\), there are fundamentally three objects associated to it: \(\pi_1(M)\), the fundamental group; \(\Aut_\pi(E)\), the group of deck transformations; and \(E\), the covering space. Let us see what these objects have to say about the orientability of \(M\).

Theorem 14

Let \(\pi\colon E\to M\) be a smooth normal covering map, where \(E\) is a connected, oriented smooth manifold and \(M\) is a smooth manifold. Then \(M\) is orientable if and only if the action of \(\Aut_\pi(E)\) on \(E\) is orientation-preserving.

Proof. Since \(E\) is connected, \(M\) is connected. Let \(O_E\) be the orientation on \(E\). Since \(M\) is connected, there are exactly two orientations of \(M\). Fix \(q\in E\). One of the orientations of \(M\) is such that \(d\pi_q\colon T_qE\to T_{\pi(q)}M\) is orientation-preserving.

Let \(O_M\) be that orientation. We have \(\pi^*O_M=O_E\) at \(q\); since \(E\) is connected, \(\pi^*O_M=O_E\). For \(\varphi\in\Aut_\pi(E)\), we have \(\pi\circ\varphi=\pi\), so \[\varphi^*O_E=\varphi^*(\pi^*O_M) =(\pi\circ\varphi)^*O_M=\pi^*O_M=O_E.\] Thus \(\varphi\) is orientation-preserving.

Conversely, suppose \(\Aut_\pi(E)\) is orientation-preserving. Fix \(p\in M\), and let \(U\) be an evenly covered neighbourhood of \(p\). Let \(\sigma\colon U\to E\) be a smooth section, and induce the orientation \(\sigma^*O_E\). If we prove that this is a well-defined way of orienting \(M\), we are done. Let \(\sigma_1\colon U\to E\) be another smooth section. Since \(\pi\) is normal, there is a \(\varphi\in\Aut_\pi(E)\) such that \(\sigma_1(p)=\varphi(\sigma(p))\) and \(\sigma_1=\varphi\circ\sigma\). The latter follows from uniqueness of local sections of smooth covering maps, that is, inverses of \(\pi|_{\sigma(U)}\). Since \(\varphi\) is orientation-preserving, \(\sigma_1^*O_E=\sigma^*\varphi^*O_E=\sigma^*O_E\). Hence the orientation is well-defined.

From the action of \(\Aut_\pi(E)\), a Lie group in its own right, one can determine the orientability of \(M\). But one can do better by considering a particular covering space. Before we do that, here is an example.

Example 6

The map \(q\colon S^n\to\mathbb{RP}^n\) is a covering map. For \(n>1\), \(S^n\) is simply connected, and \(\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^n)=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\cong\Aut_q(S^n)\). The nontrivial element of \(\Aut_q(S^n)\) is \(\alpha(x)=-x\), the antipodal map. The map \(\alpha\) is orientation-preserving if and only if \(2\nmid n\). Therefore \(\mathbb{RP}^n\) is orientable if and only if \(2\nmid n\). Also, \(\mathbb{RP}^1\) is orientable.

Orientation Covering

We are now going to construct a particular covering map for \(M\) to help us analyse its orientability. Define \[\widehat M:=\{(p,O_p):p\in M,\ O_p\text{ is an orientation of }T_pM\}, \qquad \widehat\pi\colon\widehat M\to M,\quad\widehat\pi(p,O_p):=p.\] This is called the orientation covering of \(M\).

Proposition 15

Given the orientation covering \(\widehat\pi\colon\widehat M\to M\), one can give \(\widehat M\) a smooth structure such that:

(a)

\(\widehat\pi\colon\widehat M\to M\) is a smooth covering map.

(b)

A connected open set \(U\subset M\) is evenly covered by \(\widehat\pi\) if and only if \(U\) is orientable.

Proof. Let \(U\subset M\) be an orientable open set with orientation \(O\). Set \[\widehat U_O:= \{(p,O_p)\in\widehat M:p\in U,\ O_p\text{ orients }T_pM \text{ and is determined by }O\}, \qquad O|_p=O_p.\] We show that \(\{\widehat U_O\}_{(U,O)}\) forms a basis for \(\widehat M\). Let \((p,O_p)\in\widehat M\). One can find a chart at \(p\), which by default has an orientation induced from a domain in \(\mathbb R^n\). Thus there is a pair \((U,O)\) with \(O|_p=O_p\). Consequently \((p,O_p)\in\widehat U_O\), so \(\bigcup_{(U,O)}\widehat U_O=\widehat M\).

Let \((p,O_p)\in\widehat U_O\cap\widehat U'_{O'}\). Then \(O|_p=O'|_p=O_p\). Let \(V\) be the component of \(U\cap U'\) containing \(p\). The orientations \(O|_V\) and \(O'|_V\) agree at \(p\), so \(O|_V=O'|_V\). Hence \(\widehat V_{O|_V}\subset\widehat U_O\cap\widehat U'_{O'}\). The restriction \(\widehat\pi|_{\widehat U_O}\) is bijective onto \(U\), and \(\{\widehat U_O\}_{(U,O)}\) forms a

basis for \(\widehat M\), while these \(U\) form a basis for \(M\), since charts are orientable. Therefore \(\widehat\pi\) is a local homeomorphism.

Let \((U,O)\) be such that \(U\) is connected. Then \(U\) can have only two orientations, and \(\widehat\pi^{-1}(U)=\widehat U_O\sqcup\widehat U_{-O}\). Both restrictions \(\widehat\pi|_{\widehat U_O}\colon\widehat U_O\cong U\) and \(\widehat\pi|_{\widehat U_{-O}}\colon\widehat U_{-O}\cong U\) are homeomorphisms. Thus \(\widehat\pi\) is a covering map, and an orientable connected open set is evenly covered. There is a unique smooth structure on \(\widehat M\) for which \(\widehat\pi\colon\widehat M\to M\) is a smooth covering map. The space \(\widehat M\) can further be given a unique orientation, called the pullback orientation, since \(\widehat\pi\) is a local diffeomorphism.

To prove (b), it remains to show that if \(U\subset M\) is an evenly covered domain, then \(U\) is orientable. Indeed, let \(\sigma\colon U\to\widehat M\) be an injective smooth local section. Then \(U\) can be endowed with the pullback orientation.

We now state our main theorem, the reason for studying these orientation covers. Since \(\widehat\pi\) is a covering map, its restriction \(\widehat\pi|_W\) to a component \(W\) of \(\widehat M\) is surjective. The fibres of \(\widehat\pi\) have cardinality \(2\), so \(\widehat M\) is either connected or has two components.

Theorem 16 — Orientation Covering Theorem

Let \(M\) be a connected smooth manifold and \(\widehat\pi\colon\widehat M\to M\) its orientation covering. If \(M\) is orientable, then \(\widehat M\) has two components. If \(M\) is not orientable, then \(\widehat M\) is connected.

Proof. If \(M\) is orientable, then, being connected and open, it is evenly covered by Proposition 15. Since \(|\widehat\pi^{-1}(\{p\})|=2\), we have \[\widehat\pi^{-1}(M)=M^+\sqcup M^-=\widehat M,\qquad \widehat\pi|_{M^\pm}\colon M^\pm\cong M.\] If \(M\) is not orientable, let \(W\) be a component of \(\widehat M\). The restriction \(\widehat\pi|_W\) is a covering map. Since \(W\) is connected, the degree of \(\widehat\pi|_W\) is invariant on \(W\), so its fibres have cardinality either \(1\) or \(2\). If their cardinality were \(1\), then \(\widehat\pi|_W\colon W\to M\) would be a diffeomorphism, making \(M\) orientable. Therefore their cardinality is \(2\), and surjectivity of \(\widehat\pi|_W\) implies \(W=\widehat M\), which is connected.

In hindsight, \(\widehat M\) may seem tailor-made to capture orientability by merely restating it in a different form on a made-up space \(\widehat M\). But that is not the

case. The right way to think about it intuitively is via an ambient manifold. Consider surfaces in \(\mathbb R^3\), say a page. The space \(\widehat M\) is basically what you get after slicing the surface along its extra dimension, which in \(\mathbb R^3\) would be its thickness.

You will not obtain something similar if you slice a Möbius band. There, after slicing, the orientation cover \(\widehat M\) remains connected. Beyond offering this geometric insight into orientability, there are mathematical reasons substantiating the Orientation Covering Theorem.

Proposition 17

Let \(M\) be a connected smooth manifold. If \(\pi_1(M)\) has no subgroup of index \(2\), then \(M\) is orientable. In particular, all simply connected smooth manifolds are orientable.

Remark

If \(M\) were simply connected and covered something orientable, say \(\pi\colon M\to M/{\sim}\) with \(M/{\sim}\) orientable, then \(\pi\), being a smooth covering map, is a local diffeomorphism. Hence \(M\) is orientable.

Proof. Suppose \(M\) is not orientable. Then \(\widehat M\) is connected. Let \(\widehat\pi\colon\widehat M\to M\) be its orientation cover. Choose \(q\in\widehat M\), and let \(p=\widehat\pi(q)\in M\). Let \(\alpha\colon\widehat M\to\widehat M\) interchange points in the same fibre: if \(\widehat\pi(q)=\widehat\pi(r)=p\), then \(\alpha(q)=r\) and \(\alpha(r)=q\).

Note that \(\alpha\) is smooth. Let \(U\) be evenly covered, with \(\widehat\pi^{-1}(U)=U_0\sqcup U_1\). Then \[\alpha|_{U_0}=(\widehat\pi|_{U_1})^{-1}\circ(\widehat\pi|_{U_0}), \qquad \alpha|_{U_1}=(\widehat\pi|_{U_0})^{-1}\circ(\widehat\pi|_{U_1}).\] Such \(U_i\) cover \(\widehat M\), so \(\alpha\) is smooth on \(M\), and \(\widehat\pi\circ\alpha=\widehat\pi\). By definition, \(\alpha\in\Aut_{\widehat\pi}(\widehat M)\). If \(\beta\in\Aut_{\widehat\pi}(\widehat M)\), then \(\beta\) separates \(\widehat M\) into points that \(\alpha\) swaps fibrewise and points that \(\alpha\) does not.

But \(\widehat M\) is connected, so \(\Aut_{\widehat\pi}(\widehat M)=\{\id_{\widehat M},\alpha\}\). Since the action of \(\Aut_{\widehat\pi}(\widehat M)\) is transitive, \(\widehat\pi\) is a normal covering, and \[\pi_1(M)/\widehat\pi_*(\pi_1(\widehat M)) \cong\Aut_{\widehat\pi}(\widehat M).\] Thus \(\widehat\pi_*(\pi_1(\widehat M))\) is an index-\(2\) subgroup of \(\pi_1(M)\).

With this, we conclude.

title: Smooth Covering Manifolds
html:
Coverings and smooth structures

Covering maps and covers are studied for a wide range of reasons. Of them all, one that is fundamental is the problem of classifying topological manifolds. Taking our cue from invariance of domain, which states that, given a Euclidean space \(X\), there is a unique \(n\) such that \(X\cong\mathbb R^n\), we ask: is there a list of all possible \(n\)-manifolds, up to homeomorphism?

Covering-space theory aids us in answering this question because manifolds are semilocally simply connected and locally path connected. Thus, if \(M\) is a manifold, for every subgroup \(H<\pi_1(M,m)\) it provides a covering map \(p:E\to M\) such that \(p_*(\pi_1(E,e))=H\). Set \(H=\{1\}\). The way \(E\) is constructed for this \(H\) forces \(E\) to be simply connected. Regardless, \(p:E\to M\) would be a normal covering, so \(M\cong E/G\), where \(G<\Aut(E)\) is a subgroup acting properly discontinuously.

Therefore, covering-space theory has helped us reduce the classification problem for arbitrary topological manifolds to that of classifying simply connected manifolds. What happens when we give this story a smooth structure? Let’s begin with two questions:

Q1.

When is a topological covering map between smooth manifolds a smooth covering map?

Q2.

When is a smooth map between manifolds a covering map?

The lifted smooth structure

Definition 1 — Smooth covering

A topological covering map \(p:E\to M\) is said to be a smooth covering map if, for every \(x\in M\), there is an evenly covered neighbourhood \(U_x\) of \(x\) with \[p^{-1}(U_x)=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha, \qquad p|_{V_\alpha}:V_\alpha\longrightarrow U_x \quad\text{a diffeomorphism for every }\alpha\in I.\]

Proposition 1 — Answer to Q1

Let \(M\) be a smooth \(n\)-manifold, \(E\) a connected topological space, and \(p:E\to M\) a topological covering map. Then \(E\) admits a unique smooth structure which makes it a smooth \(n\)-manifold and makes \(p\) a smooth covering map.

Proof. Hausdorffness. It is easy to see that \(E\) is Hausdorff. Let \(e_1,e_2\in E\). If \(p(e_1)\ne p(e_2)\), then the Hausdorff property of \(M\) separates \(p(e_1)\) and \(p(e_2)\) by neighbourhoods which can be pulled back to \(E\). If \(p(e_1)=p(e_2)\), then the covering-map definition separates \(e_1\) and \(e_2\): let \(\widetilde p=p(e_1)=p(e_2)\) and let \(U_{\widetilde p}\) be an evenly covered neighbourhood of \(\widetilde p\). Then \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) must belong to different slices of \(p^{-1}(U_{\widetilde p})\). Hence \(E\) is Hausdorff.

Forget second countability for the time being.

Compatible charts.

Now let us dress \(E\) with a smooth structure. Let \(y\in E\), put \(x=p(y)\), and let \(U_x\) be an evenly covered neighbourhood of \(x\). Let \((\varphi,U'_x)\) be a chart containing \(x\), so \(x\in U'_x\). Shrink \(U_x\) (or \(U'_x\)) to \(U_x\cap U'_x=U\). Then \((\varphi,U)\) is still a chart, and \(U\) is still an evenly covered neighbourhood of \(x\).

Write \(p^{-1}(U)=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\). Say \(y\in V_\alpha\); then \((V_\alpha,\varphi\circ p|_{V_\alpha})\) is a chart for \(E\). These charts are compatible. Let \((\widetilde V,\widetilde\varphi)\) and \((\widetilde W,\widetilde\psi)\) be two such charts for \(E\). The transition map is \[\widetilde\psi\circ\widetilde\varphi^{-1}: \widetilde\varphi(\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W) \longrightarrow\widetilde\psi(\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W).\] Here \(\widetilde\psi=\psi\circ p|_{\widetilde W}\) and \(\widetilde\varphi=\varphi\circ p|_{\widetilde V}\), where \((p(\widetilde W),\psi)\) and \((p(\widetilde V),\varphi)\) are charts of \(M\).

Consequently, \[\begin{align*} \widetilde\psi\circ\widetilde\varphi^{-1} &=\left(\widetilde\psi|_{\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W}\right) \circ\widetilde\varphi^{-1}|_{\widetilde\varphi(\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W)}\\ &=\left(\psi\circ p|_{\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W}\right) \circ\left(\varphi\circ p|_{\widetilde V}\right)^{-1} |_{\widetilde\varphi(\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W)}\\ &=\left(\psi\circ p|_{\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W}\right) \circ\left(\varphi\circ p|_{\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W}\right)^{-1}\\ &=\psi\circ p|_{\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W} \circ\left(p|_{\widetilde V\cap\widetilde W}\right)^{-1}\circ\varphi^{-1} =\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}. \end{align*}\]

Smoothness of the covering map.

Another immediate fact is that, with this smooth structure, \(p\) is a smooth map. Let \(y\in E\) and \(x=p(y)\), let \((\varphi,U)\) be the evenly covered chart of \(M\), and let \((\widetilde\varphi,V)\) be the corresponding chart of \(E\), as constructed before. Then \(p(V)\subseteq U\); in fact, \(p(V)=U\). We have \[\varphi\circ p\circ\widetilde\varphi^{-1} =\varphi\circ p\circ(\varphi\circ p)^{-1}=\id,\] which is smooth from \(\widetilde\varphi(V)\) to \(\varphi(U)\). Thus \(p\) is a smooth covering map. What we have in particular managed to prove here is that \(p|_V:V\to U\) is smooth; one can similarly prove that the inverse branch \(p^{-1}|_U:U\to V\) is smooth.

Therefore, \(p\) is a smooth covering map, and \(E\) a smooth manifold of dimension \(n\)?

Uniqueness.

Now let us see why this smooth structure is unique. For that, one needs to shave off a bunch of open sets. Let \(E\) and \(E'\) denote the topological space \(E\) with two smooth structures, of which \(E\) is the one we constructed. In order to show \(E\sim E'\), meaning that these two structures are the same, one must show that charts of \(E'\) and charts of \(E\) are compatible.

Let us now consider the following diagram. Here \(E\) and \(E'\) denote the same topological space \(E\), but with different smooth structures.

Let \(E'\) be the manifold we constructed. There is a continuous lift \(\widetilde p\) of \(p\), since \(E=E'\) as topological manifolds and \(\pi_1(E)=\pi_1(E')\).

We shall first show that \(\widetilde p\) is smooth. Let \((\psi,V)\) be a chart at \(x\in M\) such that \(V\) is an evenly covered neighbourhood of \(x\), and let \(U\) be such that \(p'|_U:U\to V\) is a diffeomorphism. Let \((\sigma,W)\) be a chart at \(y\in E\) such that \(\widetilde p(W)\subseteq U\). Then \[\psi\circ(p'\circ\widetilde p)\circ\sigma^{-1} \text{ is smooth} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\psi\circ p')\circ\widetilde p\circ\sigma^{-1} \text{ is smooth}.\] Hence \(\widetilde p\) is smooth, using the charts \((\sigma,W)\) and \((\psi\circ p',U)\).

Now fix a point \(m\in M\), and let \(e,e'\) lie in the corresponding fibres of \(m\), that is, \(e\in p^{-1}(m)\) and \(e'\in(p')^{-1}(m)\). Let \(\widetilde p\) be the unique lift sending \(e\) to \(e'\). One can similarly construct a lift of \(p'\) such that \(\widetilde p'(e')=e\). Notice that \(\id_E\) and \(\widetilde p'\circ\widetilde p\) are both lifts of \(p\), and they agree at a fixed basepoint.

It follows that \(\id_E=\widetilde p'\circ\widetilde p\) and \(\id_{E'}=\widetilde p\circ\widetilde p'\). Therefore \(\widetilde p\) is a diffeomorphism. Further, \(\widetilde p=\id_E\), since \(p'=p\) as topological maps. Thus the smooth structures of \(E\) and \(E'\) are compatible.

Second countability.

Now let us show that \(E\) is a topological manifold. The thing left to prove is that \(E\) is second countable. Notice that second countability is what allowed us a countable partition of unity, with which we constructed smooth exhaustion functions and level sets, which became the backbone of a lot of submanifold theory. Here is how we shall prove that \(E\) is second countable.

Consider the monodromy action of \(\pi_1(M,q)\) on the fibre \(p^{-1}(q)\), given by \(P_0\mapsto f\cdot P_0=\widetilde f(1)\), where \(\widetilde f(0)=P_0\). Fix \(P_0\in p^{-1}(q)\) and define \[\Phi:\pi_1(M,q)\longrightarrow p^{-1}(q), \qquad \Phi([f])=f\cdot P_0.\] If \(E\) is connected, it is path connected, so \(\Phi\) is surjective. Now, if we prove that \(\pi_1(M,q)\) is countable, then the rest follows. Since \(M\) is second countable, it is Lindelöf. If \(\{U_x\}_{x\in M}\) is the cover of \(M\) by evenly covered neighbourhoods, a countable subcover \(\{U_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}\) exists. Countability of \(\pi_1(M,q)\) implies that \(p^{-1}(q)\) is countable. Consequently, \(p^{-1}(U_i)\) has countably many slices, and each slice, being diffeomorphic to \(U_i\), is second countable.

Thus, by merging all the countable bases of \(\{p^{-1}(U_i)\}_{i=1}^{\infty}\), one obtains a countable basis of \(E\). The following lemma will finish our proof.

Countability of the fundamental group

Lemma 2 — Countability of the fundamental group

Let \(M\) be a topological manifold. Then \(\pi_1(M,P)\) is countable for every \(P\in M\).

Proof. Let \(\{B_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}\) be a countable basis of coordinate balls. Since \(M\) is second countable, each \(B_i\cap B_j\) has only countably many components. Pick a point \(x_i\in\widehat{B_j\cap B_k}\), where \(\widehat{B_j\cap B_k}\) varies over all components of all intersections \(B_j\cap B_k\), and let \(X=\{x_i\}\). Notice that \(P\in M\) belongs to a component of some \(B_j\cap B_k\), so we may assume that \(P\in X\).

Let \([f]\in\pi_1(M,P)\), with \(f\colon[0,1]\to M\). By the Lebesgue number lemma, there is a partition \(0<a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_n<1\) of \([0,1]\) such that \(f([a_i,a_{i+1}])\subseteq B_{i+1}\) for suitable basis elements. Notice that \(f(a_i)\in B_i\cap B_{i+1}\); let \(x_i\) and \(f(a_i)\) lie in the same component. Thus \(f=f_1*f_2*\cdots*f_n\), where \(f_i=f|_{[a_{i-1},a_i]}\), \(a_0=0\), and \(*\) denotes the usual concatenation.

Let \(g_i\) be a path from \(x_i\) to \(f(a_i)\). We can then factor \(f\) as follows: \[\begin{aligned} f&=\underbrace{g_0*f_1*g_1^{-1}}_{h_1} *\underbrace{g_1*f_2*g_2^{-1}}_{h_2} *\cdots*\underbrace{g_{n-1}*f_n*g_n^{-1}}_{h_n}\\ &=h_1*h_2*\cdots*h_n. \end{aligned}\]

A loop based at \(P\) has been transformed as shown in Figure SC6.

Thus every \(f\) can be factored using paths \(h_{x_i x_{i+1}}\) from \(x_i\) to \(x_{i+1}\). Notice that both \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) belong to \(B_i\). Hence any two paths \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) between them satisfy \(\gamma_1\simeq\gamma_2\). It follows that \[[f]=\mathop{*}_{i=1}^{n}[h_{x_{i-1}x_i}].\] Every \([f]\in\pi_1(M,P)\) is therefore a finite product of elements from the countable set \(\{[h_{x_{i-1}x_i}]\}_{n,i}\). Consequently, \(\pi_1(M,P)\) is countable.

Proper local diffeomorphisms

Proposition 3 — Answer to Q2

Let \(M\) be a connected smooth manifold and let \(p\colon E\to M\) be a proper local diffeomorphism. Then \(p\) is a covering map.

Proof. The image \(p(E)\) is open because \(p\) is a local diffeomorphism. It is also closed because \(p\) is proper and \(M\) is locally compact and Hausdorff. Since \(M\) is connected, \(p\) is surjective.

Since \(p\) is a local diffeomorphism, \(p^{-1}(\{q\})\) is discrete. It is also compact, because \(p\) is proper, and hence is finite. Write \(p^{-1}(q)=\{p_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\). For each pair \(p_i,q\), there are open neighbourhoods \(V_i\) and \(U_i\) of \(p_i\) and \(q\), respectively, such that \(p|_{V_i}\colon V_i\to U_i\) is a diffeomorphism.

Since \(E\) is Hausdorff, there are neighbourhoods \(W_i\) of \(p_i\) such that \(W_i\cap W_j=\varnothing\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Replace \(V_i\) by \(V_i\cap W_i\) and \(U_i\) by \(p|_{V_i}(V_i\cap W_i)\). The restriction \(p|_{V_i}\colon V_i\to U_i\) is again a diffeomorphism.

Now replace each \(U_i\) by \(U=\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}U_i\) and each \(V_i\) by \(V_i\cap(p|_{V_i})^{-1}(U)\). Then \(p|_{V_i}\colon V_i\to U\) is a diffeomorphism for every \(i\), and \(V_i\cap V_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\).

The set \(K=\bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}V_i\bigr)^c\) is closed in \(E\), so \(p(K)\) is closed. Replace \(U\) by \(U\setminus p(K)\).

Then \(p^{-1}(U)\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}V_i\). Finally, replace \(V_i\) by \(V_i\cap p^{-1}(U)\). After these shavings, we have \[p^{-1}(U)=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}V_i, \qquad p|_{V_i}\colon V_i\longrightarrow U \quad\text{a diffeomorphism}.\] Thus \(p\) is a smooth covering map.

Covering Lie groups

Now let us impose further structures on our original setting and see where it leads us. We saw before that covering space theory helped reduce the classification problem by a lot. We then saw how the structure was still preserved once we shifted our course to the category of smooth manifolds. More precisely, we saw that a topological cover of a manifold also preserves the smooth structure. If we now lift this to the category of Lie groups and ask whether smooth covering maps preserve the group structure, the following proposition answers this in its full glory!

Proposition 4 — Yes, group structure is preserved!

Let \(G\) be a connected Lie group, and let \(\pi\colon\widetilde{G}\to G\) be a smooth covering map with \(\widetilde{G}\) simply connected. Then one can endow \(\widetilde{G}\) with a Lie group structure for which \(\pi\) is a Lie group homomorphism. Furthermore, \(\widetilde{G}\) is unique up to Lie group isomorphism.

Proof. Consider \(\widetilde G\), the universal cover of \(G\). Then \(\pi\colon\widetilde G\to G\) is a smooth covering map. Therefore, \(\pi\times\pi\colon\widetilde G\times\widetilde G\to G\times G\) is also a smooth covering map: one can evenly cover \(G\times G\) componentwise. There is a multiplication map on \(G\times G\); let’s lift it.

The diagram gives \(\pi\circ\widetilde m=m\circ(\pi\times\pi)\), or \(\pi(\widetilde m(x,y))=\pi(x)\cdot\pi(y)\). Let \(\widetilde m\) be the lift of \(m\circ(\pi\times\pi)\). For \(x,y\in\widetilde G\), define \(x\cdot y:=\widetilde m(x,y)\). Notice now that \(\pi\) preserves multiplication. We know that \(m\circ(\pi\times\pi)\) is continuous, hence so is its lift. Also, \(\pi\circ\widetilde m\), being equal to \(m\circ(\pi\times\pi)\), is smooth; thus \(\widetilde m\) is smooth.

(Indeed, \(\pi\) is a local diffeomorphism. Let \(\pi\colon V_p\to U_{\pi(p)}\) be the diffeomorphism between neighbourhoods of \(p\) and \(\pi(p)\). Since \(\pi\circ\widetilde m\) is smooth, there are neighbourhood charts \((W,\varphi)\) at \(q\in\widetilde m^{-1}(p)\) and \((U_{\pi(p)},\psi)\) at \(\pi(p)\) such that \(\psi\circ(\pi\circ\widetilde m)\circ\varphi^{-1}\) is smooth. One can arrange \(U_{\pi(p)}\) so that \(\pi\colon V_p\to U_{\pi(p)}\) is a local diffeomorphism. Then \((W,\varphi)\) and \((V_p,\psi\circ\pi)\) are charts such that \((\psi\circ\pi)\circ\widetilde m\circ\varphi^{-1}\) is smooth. This can be done for every \(q\) and \(\pi(p)\).

Therefore, \(\widetilde m\) is smooth.) Thus one has a smooth multiplication function.

Similarly, by lifting \(i\circ\pi\), where \(i\) is the inverse map on \(G\), one gets a smooth inverse map \(\widetilde i\) on \(\widetilde G\). Now it remains to check that \(\widetilde G\) indeed forms a group with \(\widetilde m\) and \(\widetilde i\) as its operations.

Pick \(\widetilde e\in\pi^{-1}(e)\). One can arrange \(\widetilde m\) and \(\widetilde i\) so that \(\widetilde m(\widetilde e,\widetilde e)=\widetilde e\) and \(\widetilde i(\widetilde e)=\widetilde e\). Now these \(\widetilde m\) and \(\widetilde i\) are unique. Let \(f\colon\widetilde G\to\widetilde G\) be defined by \(f(x)=\widetilde e\cdot x\). Then \[(\pi\circ f)(x)=\pi(\widetilde e\cdot x) =\pi(\widetilde e)\cdot\pi(x)=\pi(x).\] Now \(f\) and \(\operatorname{Id}_{\widetilde G}\) are both lifts of \(\pi\), and \(f(\widetilde e)=\widetilde e\cdot\widetilde e=\widetilde e =\operatorname{Id}_{\widetilde G}(\widetilde e)\). Hence \(f=\operatorname{Id}_{\widetilde G}\), so \(x\cdot\widetilde e=\widetilde e\cdot x=x\).

Now let’s move on to associativity. Define \(\alpha_L,\alpha_R\colon\widetilde G\times\widetilde G\times\widetilde G \to\widetilde G\) by \[\alpha_L(x,y,z):=(x\cdot y)\cdot z, \qquad \alpha_R(x,y,z):=x\cdot(y\cdot z).\] Note that \((\pi\circ\alpha_L)(x,y,z)=(\pi\circ\alpha_R)(x,y,z) =\pi(x)\pi(y)\pi(z)\). Thus \(\alpha_L\) and \(\alpha_R\) are lifts of \(\pi(x)\pi(y)\pi(z)\), and they agree at the base point \((\widetilde e,\widetilde e,\widetilde e)\). Therefore one can borrow associativity from \(G\) by claiming that the lifts must be unique.

One can similarly show that \(x\cdot x^{-1}=x^{-1}\cdot x=\widetilde e\). Therefore \((\widetilde G,\cdot)\) is a Lie group and \(\pi\colon\widetilde G\to G\) is a Lie group homomorphism.

Remark

Notice that the demand that \(\widetilde G\) be simply connected was crucial: it helped us literally lift the group structure on \(G\). Such a lift might not be possible for some other smooth covers of \(G\).

Uniqueness across the categories

Now let’s briefly talk about the uniqueness of \(\widetilde G\), to see how the structures are lifted from one category to another. If \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) are two simply connected Lie groups with smooth coverings \(p_1\colon G_1\to G\) and \(p_2\colon G_2\to G\) that are also Lie group homomorphisms, then we have the following.

There are continuous lifts \(\widetilde p_1\) and \(\widetilde p_2\) of \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) such that the diagram commutes. Thus \(\widetilde p_2\) is a homeomorphism. Next, \(p_1\circ\widetilde p_2\) is smooth and \(\widetilde p_2\) is continuous, with \(p_1\) a local diffeomorphism. Hence \(\widetilde p_2\) is smooth, and therefore a diffeomorphism. Finally, \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) are covering maps, so \(\widetilde p_2\) is a covering map that is smooth; hence \(\widetilde p_2\) is a group homomorphism.

All three versions of \(\widetilde p_2\) coincide. It is not difficult to see that the group structure with respect to which \(\widetilde p_2\) is a Lie group homomorphism coincides with that of \(G_2\). The reason that \(\widetilde p_2\) as a diffeomorphism coincides with \(\widetilde p_2\) as a homeomorphism is clear. The only issue is the last \(\widetilde p_2\); let us resolve that.

Notice that \[\begin{align*} p_1\bigl(\widetilde p_2(xy)\bigr) &=p_2(xy)=p_2(x)\cdot p_2(y)\\ &=p_1\bigl(\widetilde p_2(x)\bigr)\cdot p_1\bigl(\widetilde p_2(y)\bigr) =p_1\bigl(\widetilde p_2(x)\cdot\widetilde p_2(y)\bigr). \end{align*}\] Hence \(\widetilde p_2\circ m_2\) and \(m_1\circ(\widetilde p_2\times\widetilde p_2)\) are lifts of the same map \(m\circ(p_2\times p_2)\). Here \(m_2\) and \(m_1\) denote the multiplication maps of \(G_2\) and \(G_1\), respectively. If we show that \(\widetilde p_2\circ m_2\) and \(m_1\circ(\widetilde p_2\times\widetilde p_2)\) agree at a base point, say \((e_2,e_2)\), where \(e_2\) is the identity of \(G_2\), then uniqueness of lifts would tell us that \(\widetilde p_2(xy)=\widetilde p_2(x)\widetilde p_2(y)\).

Now one can choose \(\widetilde p_2\) from the group of deck transformations so that \(\widetilde p_2(e_2)=e_1\), with \(e_1\in p_1^{-1}(e_1)\). For that \(\widetilde p_2\), one can similarly prove \(\widetilde p_2(x^{-1})=(\widetilde p_2(x))^{-1}\). Thus \(\widetilde p_2\) is a group homomorphism, hence a group isomorphism, and therefore, of course, a covering map.

Thus all the \(\widetilde p_2\) coincide, and the respective structures fall into place.

Classification and complex structures

We didn’t impose the Lie group structure simply to poke around and see. It turns out that the initial simplification of classifying topological manifolds, when translated to the category of smooth manifolds, would pertain to classifying all simply connected smooth manifolds and their groups of automorphisms. One finds that \(G<\operatorname{Aut}(E)\), acting properly discontinuously on \(E\) to yield all manifolds, itself takes up a discrete Lie group structure. Most often, for some specific \(E\), the group \(\operatorname{Aut}(E)\) is a Lie group. Thus our original classification problem boils down to classifying all discrete Lie subgroups of a given Lie group, which is itself a field of study. Therefore, Lie groups enter into this story quite naturally!

One sees the full strength of this simplification the moment one gives this a complex structure. Firstly, one can translate this simplification word for word. So, given the following:

When we make the identification \(E/G\cong M\), where \(E\) is a universal cover of \(M\), one can forget \(M\): given a smooth structure on \(M\), there is a unique smooth structure on \(E\), and hence a unique smooth structure on \(E/G\).

Now consider complex \(1\)-manifolds, that is, Riemann surfaces. Simply connected Riemann surfaces are classified.

Theorem 5 — Uniformisation theorem

Given a simply connected Riemann surface \(S\), we have \(S\cong\mathbb C\), \(\mathbb P_1\), or \(\mathbb D\).

If \(G<\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb P_1)\) acts properly discontinuously on \(S\), then \(G=\{0\}\). In the case of \(\mathbb C\), \(G\cong\mathbb Z\) or \(\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z\). These are easy consequences of elementary theorems taught in a complex analysis or topology course.

Now it merely remains to classify the discrete subgroups of the Lie group \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\). Therefore, the story we have told so far is not a mere tell-tale heart!
excerptHtml: Covering maps and covers are studied for a wide range of reasons. Of them all, one that is fundamental is the problem of classifying topological manifolds. Taking our cue from invariance of domain, which states that, given a Euclidean space \(X\), there is a unique \(n\) such that \(X\cong\mathbb R^n\), we ask: is there a list of all possible \(n\)-manifolds, up to homeomorphism?

title: Flat Structures and Teichmüller Curves
html:
Teichmüller Curves

Let \(T_g\) denote the Teichmüller space of closed genus-\(g\) surfaces. We have the well-known identification \(M_g\approx T_g/\MCG(g)\). The action \(\MCG(g)\curvearrowright T_g\) is properly discontinuous. Consequently \(M_g\) is a complex orbifold of dimension \(3g-3\).

Definition 4 — Teichmüller curve

We say that \(V\subset M_g\) is a Teichmüller curve if the inclusion \((V\cong\mathbb H/\Gamma)\hookrightarrow M_g\) is an isometry. The inclusion is assumed to be in the regular set. On \(V\) we have the usual hyperbolic metric coming from a torsion-free discrete subgroup \(\Gamma\subset\PSL_2(\mathbb R)\).

Question

How do we get a metric on \(M_g\)?

Here \(\sigma\in\Deck(\mathbb H/S)<\Aut(\mathbb H)\).

One obtains a metric on \(M_g\) in a similar fashion.

Here \(\sigma\in\MCG(g)\); the fibre should be discrete. On \(T_g\) one has the Weil–Petersson metric \(\omega_{\mathrm{WP}}\).

1.

The symplectic form is \(\operatorname{Im}(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}}) =\sum_{i=1}^{3g-3}d\ell_i\wedge d\theta_i\).

2.

\(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}}\) is a Hermitian form on \(T_g\). We have \(T_X(T_g)\approx\mathbb C^{3g-3}\) and \(T_g\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^{3g-3}\ (Q^2(S_g))\). Set \[\langle q_1,q_2\rangle:=\int_X\frac{q_1\overline{q_2}}{\lambda^2},\] where \(\lambda\) is the hyperbolic metric on \(X\).

The real part \(\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}})\) is a Riemannian metric on \(T_g\), and its imaginary part is a symplectic form on \(T_g\). Together they give a Kähler structure on \(T_g\).

Theorem 7 — Ivanov, H. Masur, M. Wolf

\(\operatorname{Isom}_{\mathrm{WP}}(T_{g,n})=\MCG(g,n)\). For \(n=0\), this was Royden’s work.

We do not need the full power of the theorem above to get a metric on \(M_g\). Let \(\sigma\in\MCG(g)\). For \(x=(S,f_1)\) and \(y=(S,f_2)\), we have \[d(\sigma\cdot x,\sigma\cdot y)=d(x,y) =\inf_{f\in[(f_2\circ\sigma)\circ(f_1\circ\sigma)^{-1}]}\ln K(f) =\inf_{f\in[f_2\circ f_1^{-1}]}\ln K(f).\]

Thus \(\sigma\) is distance-preserving and bijective. By the Myers–Steenrod theorem, \(\sigma\) preserves \(\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}})\). Here \(d\) is the distance induced by \(\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}})\) on \(T_g\).

Definition 5 — Complex geodesic

If \(f\colon\mathbb H\to M_g\) is an isometry, then \(f\), or \(f(\mathbb H)\), is called a complex geodesic in \(M_g\).

Translation Structure

Let \(X\in M_g\) be a Riemann surface and \(\omega\in\Omega X\) a holomorphic \(1\)-form. Set \(D=(\omega)\); then \((\omega)=D+0\). By Brill–Noether duality, \[L(D)=\{f\in R(X):(f)+D\ge0\}\approx I(0),\qquad I(D)=\{\eta\in M(X):(\eta)\ge D\}\approx L(0),\] with the pairing \((\eta,f)\). By Riemann–Roch, \[\dim L(D)-\dim I(D)=\deg D+1-g,\qquad \underbrace{\dim I(0)}_{g}-\underbrace{\dim L(0)}_{1} =\deg D+1-g.\] Therefore \(\deg(\omega)=2g-2\). Let \(\Sigma\) be the zeros of \(\omega\); then \(|\Sigma|=2g-2\).

Let \(p\in X\setminus\Sigma\). There is a chart \((U_p,x_p)\) such that \(U_p\cap\Sigma=\varnothing\) and \(\omega\ne0\) on \(U_p\). If \(\omega=\phi_{x_p}\,dx_p\), define, for \(q\in U_p\), \[z_p[x_p(q)]:=\int_0^{x_p(q)} \phi_{x_p}\bigl(x_p(\gamma(t))\bigr)\,dx_p(\gamma(t)).\] Since \(\pi_1(U_p)=0\), the map \(z_p\circ x_p\) is well-defined.

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\frac{dz_p}{dx_p}(x_p(q))=\phi_p(x_p(q))\). Define \(\widetilde z_p:=z_p\circ x_p\). Then \(\omega=d\widetilde z_p\). This is an elaborate way of saying: work with \(\phi_{x_p}\circ x_p\). But we notice that \[\frac{d\widetilde z_p}{d\widetilde z_q}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \widetilde z_p=\widetilde z_q+c \qquad\text{(translation charts).}\] Let \(p\in\Sigma\). Locally in \((U_p,x_p)\), write \(\omega=\phi_{x_p}\,dx_p\). If \(\phi_{x_p}(p)=0\) of order \(n\), then \(\phi_{x_p}\equiv z^nh(z)\,dz\). Again, since \(U_p\) is simply connected, one can find \(h(z)^{1/n}\). Modify \(x_p\) to \(\widetilde z_p:=\bigl(zh(z)^{1/n}\bigr)\circ x_p\). Then \(\omega=(\widetilde z_p)^n\,d\widetilde z_p\).

The map \(\phi\colon(\text{sector},\widetilde z_p^n\,d\widetilde z_p) \longrightarrow(\mathbb H,dz)\) is an isometry, where \[\phi(\widetilde z_p)=\frac1{n+1}(\widetilde z_p)^{n+1}, \qquad dz=d\phi=\frac d{d\widetilde z_p} \left(\frac1{n+1}(\widetilde z_p)^{n+1}\right)d\widetilde z_p.\] We have thus obtained a flat metric \(dz\) on \(X\), with cone singularities of angle \(2(n+1)\pi\) at points of \(\Sigma\).

We have \(\phi_3=\phi_2\circ\phi_1\) and \(\phi_3'=\phi_2'(\phi_1)\cdot\phi_1'=0\). By the Identity Theorem, \(\phi_1,\phi_2\) are also translations.

Thus \((X,\omega)\) gives \((U_p,\widetilde z_p)\), a translation structure; in the reverse direction, pull back \(d\widetilde z_p\) by \(\widetilde z_p^*\).

Now consider the space \(\Omega M_g:=\{(X,\omega):\omega\in\Omega X,\ \omega\ne0\}\). The projection \(\Omega M_g\xrightarrow{\pi}M_g\) is a holomorphic vector bundle of rank \(g\), since \(\operatorname{rank}(\Omega X)=g\), with its zero section removed. A stratum is \[\Omega M_g(p_1,\ldots,p_n) :=\{(X,\omega):(\omega)=p_ix_i,\ x_i\in X,\ p_i\ge0\} \subset\Omega M_g.\]

\(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\) Action

Let \((X,\omega)\in\Omega M_g\). We have a translation structure \((U_p,\widetilde z_p)\) on \(X\). For \(A\in\SL_2(\mathbb R)\), define \(A\cdot(X,\omega):=(U_p,A\circ\widetilde z_p)\). Then \[\begin{aligned} (A\circ\widetilde z_q)\circ(A\circ\widetilde z_p)^{-1}(z) &=A\circ(\widetilde z_q\circ\widetilde z_p^{-1})(A^{-1}(z))\\ &=A(A^{-1}(z)+c)=z+A(c). \end{aligned}\] Thus \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\curvearrowright\Omega M_g\) by stretching and rotating the translation structure.

Remark

\((M_g,\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}}))\) is a highly inhomogeneous space: \((T_XM_g,|\cdot|_{\mathrm{WP}})\not\cong(T_YM_g,|\cdot|_{\mathrm{WP}})\) for \(X\ne Y\). Hence we built a bundle of forms on \(M_g\). The space \(\Omega M_g\) admits an \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\) action and is therefore highly homogeneous. One can easily observe that \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\) preserves \(\Omega M_g(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\).

If \(A\in\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\), that is, a rotation, then \(A\cdot(X,\omega)\) is just \((X,e^{i\theta}\omega)\). We thus have

Here \(F(A):=A\cdot(X,\omega)\) for some fixed \((X,\omega)\in\Omega M_g\). The map \(\pi\circ F\) factors through \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\). The action \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\curvearrowright\mathbb H\) is by fractional linear transformations, with \(\operatorname{Stab}(i)=\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\) and \(\operatorname{Orb}(i)=\mathbb H\).

Theorem 8

The map \(f\colon\mathbb H\to M_g\) is a complex geodesic.

We shall defer the proof to the end. Here are a few consequences.

Geodesic rays in \(M_g\).

Every point has a real geodesic through it. For fixed \((X,\omega)\), set \[\gamma\colon[0,\infty)\to M_g,\qquad \gamma(t):=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-t}&0\\0&e^t\end{pmatrix}\cdot(X,\omega).\]

Teichmüller curves in \(M_g\).

Let \(\operatorname{Stab}(X,\omega)=:\SL(X,\omega)\), the Veech group. Then \[\SL(X,\omega)\curvearrowright \SL_2(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\cong\mathbb H.\] If \(\SL(X,\omega)\) were a lattice in \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\), then the normalisation map \(V\cong\mathbb H/\SL(X,\omega)\longrightarrow M_g\) would give examples of Teichmüller curves in \(M_g\), generated by \((X,\omega)\).

Proof of Theorem 8. Let \(x,y\in\mathbb H\), with \(x=i\) and \(y=it\). Then \(f(i)=X\), since \(\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Stab}(i)\) fixes the complex structure on \(X\). Let us first compute the coset of \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\) that sends \(i\mapsto it\). We have \[\frac{ai+b}{ci+d}=it \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=dt,\quad b=-ct,\qquad t=u^2>0.\] Thus \[A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}a/u&b/u\\-bu&au\end{pmatrix}\colon i\mapsto it, \qquad a^2+b^2=1,\quad(a,b)\in S^1.\] We have \(f(it)=(U_p,A(t)\circ\widetilde z_p)\). Finally, \[d_{M_g}(f(i),f(it))=\log(\text{dilatation of }A(t)),\qquad d_{\mathbb H}(i,it)=\log t=\int_1^t\frac{dy}{y}.\] For general \(x,y\in\mathbb H\), use a Möbius map \(\varphi\in\PSL_2(\mathbb R)\) sending \(x\mapsto i\) and \(y\mapsto it\) for some \(t\). The map \(A(t)\) is linear, and computing its dilatation is standard.

Proposition 9

\(\SL(X,\omega)\) is a discrete subgroup of \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\), and the quotient is never compact.

We shall see the proof later.

Remarks.
1.

If \(\omega\in\Omega X\), then in a chart \((U_p,x_p)_p\), \(\omega=\phi_{x_p}\,dx_p\). Hence \(\phi_{x_p}\frac{dx_p}{dx_q}=\phi_{x_q}\). In \((U_p,\widetilde z_p)\), we have \(\phi_{x_p}\equiv1\) for \(p\in X\setminus\Sigma\). Thus \(\frac{d\widetilde z_p}{d\widetilde z_q}=1\), so \(\widetilde z_p=\widetilde z_q+c\).

2.

If \(p\in\Sigma\), look at the chart \((U_p,x_p)\): \(\omega=\phi_{x_p}\,dx_p=x_p^ng(x_p)\,dx_p\). Define \[h(x_p(q)):=\int_0^{x_p(q)} x_p^n(\gamma(t))g(x_p(\gamma(t)))\,dx_p(\gamma(t)).\] Then \(\frac{dh}{dx_p}(x_p(q))=x_p^n(q)g(x_p(q))\). Thus \(h\) has a zero at \(0\) of order \(n+1\), so one can take an \((n+1)\)st root.

Set \(\widetilde w(x_p(q)):=(k+1)^{1/(k+1)}h(x_p(q))^{1/(k+1)}\). Then \[\begin{aligned} \frac{d\widetilde w}{dx_p}(x_p(q)) &=\frac1{k+1}(k+1)^{1/(k+1)} h(x_p(q))^{-k/(k+1)}\frac{dh}{dx_p}(x_p(q))\\ &=\widetilde w(x_p(q))^{-k}\phi_{x_p}. \end{aligned}\] We have \(\phi_{x_p}=x_p^ng(x_p)\) and \(\widetilde w(x_p)=(k+1)^{1/(k+1)}h(x_p)^{1/(k+1)}\). Therefore \[\begin{aligned} \widetilde w(x_p(q))^{-k}\phi_{x_p} &=x_p^ng(x_p)(k+1)^{-k/(k+1)}h(x_p)^{-k/(k+1)}\\ &=\frac1{k+1}(k+1)^{1/(k+1)} h(x_p)^{-k/(k+1)}\frac{dh}{dx_p}(x_p) =\frac{d\widetilde w}{dx_p}. \end{aligned}\] Replace \(x_p\) by \(\widetilde w\circ x_p=:\widetilde z_p\). Then \(\omega=\widetilde w^n\,d\widetilde w\).

The map \[\phi:=\frac1{n+1}(\widetilde w)^{n+1} \colon U_p\cap\widetilde w^{-1}(\text{sector})\longrightarrow\mathbb H\] satisfies \(\omega=d\phi\). There are \(2(n+1)\) sectors.

We have \(\frac{d\phi}{d\widetilde z_p}=1\), so \(\phi=\widetilde z_p+c\).

3.

Twisted action of the Veech group. The fractional linear action \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\curvearrowright\mathbb H\) gives \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\cong\mathbb H\), by \(A\mapsto A\cdot i\). The linear action \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\curvearrowright\mathbb R^2\cong\mathbb C\) gives \[\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\backslash\SL_2(\mathbb R)\cong\mathbb H, \qquad A\longmapsto\frac{A(i)}{A(1)}.\] As \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\)-spaces, \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\) and \(\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\backslash\SL_2(\mathbb R)\) are isomorphic. With respect to the second action, \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is discrete. The map between the two quotient spaces is \(A\mapsto A^{-1}\); on \(\mathbb H\) it is \(t\mapsto-\overline t\).

One conjugates the linear action of \(\SL(X,\omega)\) on \(\mathbb H\) by \(t\mapsto-\overline t\) to make it fractional linear. Thus \(\mathbb H/\SL(X,\omega)\longrightarrow M_g\) is a Teichmüller curve.

4.

Define \[\begin{split} \operatorname{Aff}^+(X,\omega):=\{\phi\colon X\to X:\;& \phi\in\operatorname{Diff}^+(X),\ \phi(Z(\omega))=Z(\omega),\\ &\text{locally }\phi(x,y)=A\binom xy+b,\quad A\in\SL_2(\mathbb R)\}. \end{split}\]

Then \(D\phi=A\), so \(A\cdot(X,\omega)=(U_p,A\circ\widetilde z_p)=(X,\omega)\). We obtain \(\operatorname{Aff}^+(X,\omega)\xrightarrow{D}\SL(X,\omega)\to1\); the identity map gives surjectivity. We have \(A=\id\) if and only if \[\phi\in\Aut(X,\omega):= \{\phi\colon X\to X:\phi\in\Aut(X),\ \phi^*\omega=\omega\}.\]

By Hurwitz’s theorem, for \(g>1\), \(|\Aut(X,\omega)|<84(g-1)\). Thus \[1\longrightarrow\Aut(X,\omega)\hookrightarrow \operatorname{Aff}^+(X,\omega)\xrightarrow{D}\SL(X,\omega) \longrightarrow1.\] For \(g>1\), \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is virtually the affine symmetry group.

Definition 6 — Primitive Teichmüller curve

\((X,\omega)\) is said to be primitive if there is no \(f\colon X\to Y\) such that \(f^*\eta=\omega\) with \(\eta\in\Omega Y\). A Teichmüller curve generated by a primitive curve \((X,\omega)\in\Omega M_g\) is a primitive Teichmüller curve.

If \((X,\omega)\) is primitive, then \(\Aut(X,\omega)=\{\id\}\). Hence \(\SL(X,\omega)\cong\operatorname{Aff}^+(X,\omega)\).

5.

Proof of the proposition. \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is discrete because, for \(g\in\SL_2(\mathbb R)\) close to \(\id\), \(\operatorname{dilatation}(g)=1\) if and only if \(g\in\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\), but \(\operatorname{SO}_2(\mathbb R)\) does not preserve \(\SL(X,\omega)\). \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is not cocompact, because otherwise \[\SL_2(\mathbb R)/\SL(X,\omega)\cong \SL_2(\mathbb R)\cdot(X,\omega)=\operatorname{Orb}(X,\omega)\] would be compact, but \[\left(g_t=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-t}&0\\0&e^t\end{pmatrix}\right) \cdot(X,\omega)\xrightarrow{\pi}X_t\] is noncompact in \(M_g\).

Summary

1.

\(\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde\omega_{\mathrm{WP}})\) descends to \(M_g\).

2.

Every \((X,\omega)\in\Omega M_g\) gives a translation structure.

3.

\(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\curvearrowright\Omega M_g\) stretches the translation structure.

4.

Fix \((X,\omega)\in\Omega M_g\). We have the following diagram, where \(F(A)=A\cdot(X,\omega)\) and \(f\) is an isometric immersion.

5.

The Veech groups \(\operatorname{Stab}(X,\omega)=\SL(X,\omega)\) are discrete and not cocompact.

6.

If \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is a lattice in \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\), we obtain Teichmüller curves \(V\cong\mathbb H/\SL(X,\omega)\longrightarrow M_g\).

7.

There is a twisted action of \(\SL(X,\omega)\) on \(\mathbb H\).

8.

\(\SL(X,\omega)\cong \operatorname{Aff}^+(X,\omega)/\Aut(X,\omega)\) is virtually the affine symmetry group for \(g>1\).

9.

Define the trace field \(K:=\mathbb Q\{\operatorname{tr}(A):A\in\SL(X,\omega)\}\subset\mathbb R\). This is a totally real number field with \(\deg(K/\mathbb Q)\le g\). This is a connection to number theory.

10.

A Teichmüller curve generated by \((X,\omega)\) has the following invariants:

(i)

\(\SL(X,\omega)\) is unique to \(V\hookrightarrow M_g\) up to conjugacy, since \(\SL(X,\omega)\cong\Deck(\mathbb H/V)\);

(ii)

the trace field \(K\);

(iii)

the stratum to which \((X,\omega)\) belongs.

Broad Goals

1.

Understand the \(\SL_2(\mathbb R)\) action on the strata \(\Omega M_g(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\): ergodicity, equidistribution, and so on.

2.

Classify \(\SL(X,\omega)\) and \(\mathbb H/\SL(X,\omega)\) when \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is a lattice.

3.

Understand the geometry of the strata of \(\Omega M_g\).

Billiards and Teichmüller Curves

Let \(P\) be a polygon with angles in \(\mathbb Q\pi\), that is, rational multiples of \(\pi\), such that every edge has a pairing with another parallel edge of the same length.

This immediately gives a translation structure on \(P/{\sim}\) because the charts are given by translations away from singular points.

In general, \(dz\) descends to a flat metric with cone singularities at finitely many points. How many points? Say \(k\). Triangulate the surface, or the polygon. Then \[\chi(X)=\chi(P/{\sim})=-(2g-2)=f-e+v,\qquad e=\frac32f.\] Thus \(2-2g=f-\frac32f+v\), giving \(f=(4g-4)+2v\). The angle sum of each triangle is \(\pi\), so the total angle sum is \(\pi f=(4g-4)\pi+2\pi v\).

Proposition 10

The angle at a cone singularity is a multiple of \(2\pi\).

Proof. How do you compute cone angles from \(P/{\sim}\)?

The cone angle at \(e\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^n\theta_i\). For every \(v_i\) in the sequence above, there is a \(v_j\parallel v_i\). To come back to \(v_1\), one must have completed several rounds of the circle. Consequently \(2\pi\mid\sum_{i=1}^n\theta_i\).

Say the cone angles are \(2\pi(n_i+1)\) at \(p_i\) in \(P/{\sim}\). Then \[2\pi\sum_{i=1}^k n_i=\pi f-2\pi k=(4g-4)\pi, \qquad 2\pi n_i=2\pi(n_i+1)-2\pi.\] Hence \(\boxed{\sum_{i=1}^k n_i=2g-2}\).

From Translation Structure to Polygon

Proposition 11

Between any two singular points of a translation structure on \(X\), there is a geodesic in every homotopy class of arcs joining those points.

Proof. Let \([\gamma]\) be a homotopy class joining \(p,q\in\Sigma\). Break \(\gamma(t)\) into finitely many segments, each in some local chart. One can first construct a geodesic polygonal path joining \(p\) and \(q\), as shown in the picture; call it \(\widetilde\gamma\). By construction, \(\widetilde\gamma\in[\gamma]\), that is, \(\widetilde\gamma\sim\gamma\). Now inductively straighten the polygonal path to a geodesic.

This proves the proposition.

This shows that we can triangulate the surface \(X\) by joining singular points. Therefore one obtains a polygonal representation.

Billiards and Polygons

Reference: H. Masur, Rational Billiards and Flat Structures. Let \(G_Q\) be the group generated by reflections along the sides. Set \(N=|G_Q|<\infty\). For \(\theta\in S^1\), look at \(G_Q\cdot\theta=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{|G_Q|}\} =\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_N\}\). Consider \(2N\) copies of \(Q\). Pick a side \(s\) of \(Q_i\) and reflect \(\theta_i\) along \(s\); it is \(\theta_j\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\). Glue the identical sides \(s\) in \(Q_i\) and \(Q_j\).

The resulting object is a genus-\(g\) surface with a flat metric having cone singularities. We have \[\operatorname{genus}(P/{\sim}) =1+\frac N4\left(k-2-\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{n_i}\right),\] where the angles of the billiard \(k\)-gon are \(\pi m_i/n_i\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\).

Billiard Dynamics

Topologically optimal.

\(\gamma(t)\) is dense or periodic.

Ergodically optimal.

\(\gamma(t)\) is periodic or equidistributed: \[\underbrace{\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T f(\gamma(t))\,dt}_{\text{time average}} = \underbrace{\frac1{\Area(P)}\int_P f(z)|dz|^2}_{\text{space average}}.\] Reference: L. DeMarco, Conformal Geometry of Billiards.

Polygonal lattice.

If \((X,\omega)\) is obtained from \(P\) by unfolding and \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is a lattice, we call \(P\) a polygonal lattice. \[\text{polygonal lattice}\Longrightarrow\text{ergodically optimal} \Longrightarrow\text{topologically optimal}.\]

Theorem 12 — Veech

Every regular polygon is a primitive Teichmüller curve.

Thus billiard dynamics gives us curves in \(M_g\). For \(g=2\): the pentagon, octagon, and decagon.

Theorem 13 — McMullen

If \(\operatorname{genus}(X)=2\), then the following are equivalent: \((X,\omega)\) is ergodically optimal; \((X,\omega)\) is topologically optimal; and \(\SL(X,\omega)\) is a lattice.
excerptHtml: Let \(T_g\) denote the Teichmüller space of closed genus-\(g\) surfaces. We have the well-known identification \(M_g\approx T_g/\MCG(g)\). The action \(\MCG(g)\curvearrowright T_g\) is properly discontinuous. Consequently \(M_g\) is a complex orbifold of dimension \(3g-3\).

title: Locally Trivial Bundles
