title: Vector Bundles
excerptHtml: A vector bundle is a fibre bundle \(\eta = (E, B, V, p)\) with the following specifications:-
html:
A common feature in mathematics is linearizing studies of different objects: be it representation theory which looks at groups as objects sitting in \(GL(V)\) for some vector space \(V\), or differential geometry which turns to linear operators \(Df\) defined on mixed tensor spaces to say something qualitative about morphisms between manifolds, or Riemannian geometry that studies multilinear operators \(\nabla_XY\) to generalize Euclidean concepts like lengths, angles, and curvature, or rational homotopy theory which turns a blind eye to the torsion elements in higher homotopy groups (by looking at \(\_ \otimes\mathbb{Q}\)) and aims to classify spaces upto this error. Following this trend, let us try to linearize homotopy theory. (Atiyah 2018)

Definition 3.1 — Vector Bundles

A vector bundle is a fibre bundle \(\eta = (E, B, V, p)\) with the following specifications:-

  1. \(V\in \text{Ob(Vect)}\) (a vector space).

  2. \(G = \text{Aut}(V)\) (linear automorphism).

  3. The action of \(G\) on \(V\) is the standard linear action of \(\text{Aut}(V)\) on \(V\).

  4. Local trivializations \(\{\varphi_{\alpha}\}\) are linear isomorphism on the fibres.

If \(\text{dim}(V) = n\), then we say \((E, B, V, p)\) is a vector bundle of dimension \(n\) over \(B.\)

Remarks (on Definition 3.1):-

  • Vector bundle homomorphisms are linear maps on fibres. It is essentially a continuously parametrized family of linear maps.

  • Given locally trivializing maps \(\{\varphi_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) as follows:-

    Let \(\{v_{\beta}\}_{\beta}\) be a basis of \(V\) and let \(s_{\beta}^{\alpha}: U_{\alpha} \rightarrow p^{-1}(U_{\alpha})\) to be \(s_{\beta}^{\alpha}(x):= \varphi_{\alpha}(x, v_{\beta})\). The collection of sections \(\{s_{\beta}^{\alpha}\}_{\beta}\) is called a local frame on \(U_{\alpha}\).

  • Given a local frame, one can define a local trivialization by tracing back the argument above.

  • If \(V\) is a vector space over \(\mathbb{C}\), \(\mathbb{R}\), then \((E, B, V, p)\) is called a complex vector bundle, real vector bundle (respectively).

  • If \(\text{dim}(V) < \infty\), then \(\eta\) is called a finite dimensional vector bundle.

  • From this point on we shall only care about real/complex finite dimensional vector bundles. Denote by \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(B)\) the category of \(\mathbb{K}\)-vector bundles over \(B\) of dimension \(n\) upto isomorphisms, where \(\mathbb{K}\) stands for \(\mathbb{C}\) or \(\mathbb{R}\).

  • Denote by \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\) the category of continuously varying family of vector spaces over \(X\). In particular, we make no restriction on the dimension of fibres, apart from those imposed by continuity1.

Examples (of vector bundles):-

  1. Tangent and Cotangent bundles over a smooth manifold \(M\).

  2. \((M, S^1, \mathbb{R}, p)\) with the following data:-

    • \(M = \big([0,1]\times\mathbb{R}\big)/\sim\).

    • \((0, r) \sim (1, -r)\).

    • \(p\big([t, r]\big) := t\).

    is called the Möbius Bundle.

  3. Let \(\eta = (E, B, V, p)\) and \(V' \subseteq_{\text{subspace}} V\), define, \[E':= \big\{\varphi_{\alpha}(b,v) | \varphi_{\alpha} \in \{\varphi_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}, b\in U_{\alpha}, v\in V'\big\}\] then, \[\eta' := \big(E', B, V', p\big|_{E'}\big)\] is called the sub-bundle of \(\eta\).

  4. \(\eta = (B, B, \{0\}, \text{id}_B)\) is called the 0-bundle over \(B\).

  5. \(\eta = (E, B, \mathbb{K}, p)\) is called a line bundle over \(B\).

Now lets implement the general means to construct new bundles discussed in the previous section on the class of vector bundles.
Constructing New Vector Bundles:-

We shall begin by illustrating the pullback construction with two important examples, thereafter present the same procedure in its functorial ((i.e.) general) form.

  1. Direct Sum:- Let \(\eta = (E, B, V, p)\) and \(\widetilde{\eta} = \big(\widetilde{E}, B, \widetilde{V}, \widetilde{p}\big)\) be two vector bundles, then \(\big(E\times\widetilde{E}, B\times B, V\times\widetilde{V}, p\times \widetilde{p}\big)\) is a vector bundle. Define, \[\Delta: B \rightarrow B\times B\] \[\Delta(b):= (b,b)\] Consider the pullback square:-

    and define, \[(E, B, V, p)\oplus (\widetilde{E}, B, \widetilde{B}, \widetilde{p}):= \big((E\times\widetilde{E})\times_B(B\times B), B, V\oplus\widetilde{V}, \widehat{p}\big)\] Note, \[\widetilde{\widehat{\varphi}}_{\alpha\beta}(x) = \begin{pmatrix} \widetilde{\varphi}_{\alpha\beta}(x) & 0\\ 0 &\widetilde{\varphi}_{\alpha\beta}(x) \end{pmatrix}\]

    Let us denote the total space of the pullback bundle \(\Delta^*(\eta\times\widetilde{\eta})\) by \(E\oplus\widetilde{E}\). We shall call the bundle \((E\oplus\widetilde{E}, B, V\oplus\widetilde{V}, \widehat{p})\) the Whitney sum of bundles \(\eta\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\).

    Another way to look at it would be via the following gauge group homomorphisms:- \[\rho: \text{Aut}(V)\times\text{Aut}(\widetilde{V}) \rightarrow \text{Aut}(V\oplus\widetilde{V})\] \[\rho(T, S):= T\oplus S\] Let \(B':= \{(b, b) \in B\times B\}\), and \(B'\xhookrightarrow{i} B\) be the inclusion of the diagonal \(\Delta(B)\), then clearly, \[(E\oplus\widetilde{E}, B, V\oplus\widetilde{V}, \widehat{p}) \cong i^*\rho(\eta\times\widetilde{\eta})\]

    We are now in a position to prove an analogue of Whitney Embedding Theorem for vector bundles.

    Theorem 3.1 — Embedding Theorem

    Let \(\eta = (E, B, F, p)\) be a vector bundle, \(B\) a compact Hausdorff space. Then \(\eta\) can be realized as a sub-bundle of a trivial bundle over \(B\).

    Proof. \(B\) being compact admits a finite partition of unity subordinate to \(\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) (the local trivializing cover of \(\eta\)); denote it by \(\{\psi_i\}_{i=1}^{k}\). Let \(g_i \equiv (\psi_i)\times(\pi_i\circ\varphi_{\alpha_i}^{-1})\), where \(\pi_i:U_{\alpha_i}\times\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n\) is the canonical projection. Set \(\mathbb{R}^N = \mathbb{R}^n\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}^n\). Define, \[g: E \rightarrow B\times\mathbb{R}^N\] \[g(e):= (p(e), g_1(e),\ldots, g_k(e))\] \(g_i\) is a linear injection on fibres over \(\supp{(\psi_i)}\), which implies, \(g\) is a linear injection on fibres over \(B\). Therefore, \(g(E)\) is a sub-bundle of \(B\times\mathbb{R}^N\).

    Remarks:-

    1. One could have defined the map \(g\) to be the following:- \[g(e):= (\psi_1(e),\ldots, \psi_k(e), g_1(e),\ldots, g_k(e))\] in which case one would have had a local embedding, and if \(B\) were a compact manifold then one can redefine \(g\) to make it into an embedding into \(\mathbb{R}^M\).

    2. Let \(p(E)^{\perp}\) be the fibre-wise orthogonal complement to \(p(E)\), then \(\big(p(E)\oplus p(E)^{\perp}, B, p(F)\oplus p(F)^{\perp}, \pi\big)\) would be isomorphic to \((B\times\mathbb{R}^N, B, \mathbb{R}^N, \pi)\). In other words, for every bundle \(\eta\) over a compact Hausdorff base, there exists another bundle \(\eta^{\perp}\) that untwines the twists of \(\eta\).

    3. If one loosens the hypothesis on \(B\) to paracompact Hausdorff spaces, one would get an embedding into \(B\times \mathbb{R}^{\infty}\) via the same proof technique.

    4. Whatever is done above can be imitated for the field of complex numbers.

  2. Tensor Product:- Let \(\eta\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\) be bundles as above. Define, \[\rho: \text{Aut}(V)\times\text{Aut}(\widetilde{V}) \rightarrow \text{Aut}(V\otimes\widetilde{V})\] \[\rho(T, S):= T\otimes S\] Let \(B'\) and \(i\) be as above, define, \[\eta\otimes\widetilde{\eta}:= i^*\rho(\eta\times\widetilde{\eta})\] \(\eta\otimes\widetilde{\eta}\) is called the tensor product of the bundles \(\eta\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\). Note that by definition, the gauge group element associated to the transition function of the tensor bundle will be the tensor product of the gauge group elements associated to the transition functions of \(\eta\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\). Tensoring is a commutative operation: Let \(\eta\otimes\widetilde{\eta}\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\otimes\eta\) be two bundles, and let \(\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) be the common refinement of the local trivializing cover of \(B\). Define, \[h_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\times F\rightarrow U_{\alpha}\times F'\] \[h_{\alpha}\bigg(x, \sum_{i}{c_i(v_i\otimes w_i)}\bigg):= \bigg(x, \sum_{i}{c_i(w_i\otimes v_i)}\bigg)\] Let \(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\eta}\otimes\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\widetilde{\eta}}\) and \(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\widetilde{\eta}}\otimes\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\eta}\) be the transition functions of \(\eta\otimes\widetilde{\eta}\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\otimes\eta\), where \(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\eta}\), \(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\widetilde{\eta}}\) are transition functions of \(\eta\), \(\widetilde{\eta}\) respectively. Then, \[\big(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\widetilde{\eta}}\otimes\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\eta}\big)\circ h_{\alpha} = h_{\beta}\circ\big(\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\eta}\otimes\varphi_{\alpha\beta}^{\widetilde{\eta}}\big)\] So, the bundles, \(\eta\otimes\widetilde{\eta}\) and \(\widetilde{\eta}\otimes\eta\) are cohomologous, (i.e.) \(\eta\otimes\widetilde{\eta} \cong \widetilde{\eta}\otimes\eta\).

    The following properties concerning pullbacks, tensors and Whitney sums are easy to verify:-

    Constructing bundles this way gives us the following for free: Let \(\eta_1\), \(\eta_2\), \(\eta_3\) be bundles in \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(B)\), then:-

    • \((\eta_1\oplus\eta_2)\oplus\eta_3 \cong \eta_1 \oplus (\eta_2\oplus\eta_3)\)

    • \(\eta_1\oplus\eta_2\cong\eta_2\oplus\eta_1\)

    • \((\eta_1\otimes\eta_2)\otimes\eta_3 \cong \eta_1 \otimes (\eta_2\otimes\eta_3)\)

    • \(\eta_1\otimes(\eta_2\oplus\eta_3) \cong (\eta_1\otimes\eta_2)\oplus (\eta_1\otimes\eta_3)\)

    • \((\eta_1\oplus\eta_2)\otimes\eta_3 \cong (\eta_1\otimes\eta_3)\oplus (\eta_2\otimes\eta_3)\)

    • \(\eta_1\otimes\overline{1} \cong \overline{1}\otimes\eta_1 \cong \eta_1\) (where \(\overline{1}\) is the trivial line bundle over \(B\)).

    • \(\eta_1\oplus\overline{0} \cong \overline{0}\oplus\eta_1 \cong \eta_1\) (where \(\overline{0}\) is the \(0\)-bundle over \(B\)).

    • \(\eta_1\otimes\overline{0} \cong \overline{0}\otimes\eta_1 \cong \overline{0}\)

    These relations are consequences of the fact that the same is true for matrices representing the transition function captured by \(\rho\). For instance, associativity of Whitney sums is the trivial consequence of the following being a commutative square:-

  3. Generalization:- Let \(\{\eta_i\}_{i\in I}\) be vector bundles with fibres \(\{V_i\}_{i\in I}\) over \(B\), and let \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}\) be the category of \(\mathbb{K}\)-vector spaces. Let \(F\) be a functor, \[F: \bigg[\prod\limits_{i\in I}\text{Vect}\bigg]\rightarrow \text{Vect}\] Define, \[\rho: \bigg[\prod\limits_{i\in I}\text{Aut}(V_i)\bigg]\rightarrow \text{Aut}\bigg(F\big((V_i)_{i\in I}\big)\bigg)\] \[\rho\big((T_i)_{i\in I})\big):= F\big((T_i)_{i\in I})\big)\] The above is a group homomorphism as \(F\) is a functor. Let \(B' = \{(b)_i\in \prod_iB | b\in B\}\) and \(B'\xhookrightarrow{i} B\) be the inclusion, define, \[F\big((\eta_i)_{i\in I})\big):= i^*\rho\bigg(\prod_j\eta_j\bigg)\] Following the prescription above one can construct bundles corresponding to the following functors. Let \(V, W\) \(\in \text{Ob}(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}})\),

Reduction of Gauge Groups

As we just saw, gauge groups play a very crucial role in the construction of vector bundles as they govern how the fibres are glued together. One can introduce additional structure on the vector bundles if one imposes on it the following:-

\[\widetilde{\varphi}_{\alpha\beta}: U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta} \rightarrow H \subseteq_{\text{subgroup}} G\]

The phenomenon described above is called reduction of the gauge group \(G\). We shall now see an instance of such a reduction. To proceed we will need the following topological fact:-

FACT:- A paracompact Hasudorff space is normal and also admits a partition of unity.

Let \((E, B, V, p)\) be a \(\mathbb{K}\)-bundle on dimension \(n\), \(B\) a paracompact Hasudorff space, and \(V\) an inner product space, with \(\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) as the local trivializing cover. Define, \[x\in U_{\alpha} \xlongrightarrow{f_{\alpha}} \big(\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle: p^{-1}(x)\times p^{-1}(x) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\big)\] as follows, \[f_{\alpha}(x)(e, e'):= \big\langle\pi(\varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}(e)), \pi(\varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}(e'))\big\rangle\] Clearly, \(f_{\alpha}\) is continuous on \(U_{\alpha}\). Now let \(\{\psi_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) be the partition of unity subordinate to \(U_{\alpha}\). Define, \[\overline{f}_{\alpha}(x):= \begin{cases} \psi_{\alpha}(x)f_{\alpha}(x), & \text{ if } x \in U_{\alpha}\\ 0, & \text{ else } \end{cases}\] \(\overline{f}_{\alpha}\) is defined continuously on \(B\). Now set, \[f(x):= \sum_{\alpha}{\big(\psi_{\alpha}(x)\cdot\overline{f}_{\alpha}(x)\big)}\] Note that, \[f(x)(e, e') > \psi_{\alpha}(x)\overline{f}_{\alpha}(x)(e, e') >0\] where \(\psi_{\alpha}\) is such that \(\psi_{\alpha}(x) >0\). Thus the bundle can now be equipped with the additional structure of an inner-product; such bundles are called Euclidean bundles. This additional structure would reflect in its structure group: Let \(\{v_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) be an orthonormal basis of \(V\). Recall the local orthonormal frame \(\{s_{\alpha}^{\beta}\}_{\alpha}\) on \(U_{\beta}\), let \(\{s_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\}_{\alpha}\) be the same for \(U_{\gamma}\). Then, \[\widetilde{\varphi}_{\beta\gamma}: \text{span}_{\mathbb{K}}\big(\{s_{\alpha}^{\gamma}\}_{\alpha})\rightarrow \text{span}_{\mathbb{K}}\big(\{s_{\alpha}^{\beta}\}_{\alpha})\] \[\implies\widetilde{\varphi}_{\beta\gamma} \in O_{\mathbb{K}}(V)\]

where \(O_{\mathbb{K}}(V)\) is the orthogonal subgroup of \(GL(V)\). Thus the original structure group has now been reduced to the subgroup \(O_{\mathbb{K}}(V)\)

Notations/Conventions:-

  • We shall denote by \(\big(E\xrightarrow{p}B\big)\) or \(E\) the bundle \((E, B, F, p)\).

  • \(f^*E\) would mean \(f^*\eta\).

  • \(E\big|_{B'}\) would mean the bundle E restricted to \(B'\).

  • Denote by \(\text{HOM}(E, E')\) the bundle corresponding to the Hom functor.

  • \(\Gamma(E)\), \(\Gamma(\eta)\), or \(\Gamma(E\xrightarrow{p}B)\) shall be used to denote the set of all sections of the bundle \(E\).

  • \(\text{Hom}(E, E')\) will be the set of all vector bundle homomorphisms between \(E\) and \(E'\).

  • By default, \(B\) would be the base space, \(E\) the total space, \(V\) or \(F\) the fibre.

Having described fibre bundles, we ask if vector bundles are familiar objects in disguise.

What separates a vector bundle from a fibre bundle with structure group \(O(n)\) or \(U(n)\) is that we demand the homomorphisms to preserve the linear structure. There is a way to encode this extra information via the language of principal \(G\)-bundles.

Let \(\big(E\xrightarrow{p} B\big)\) be a principal \(G\)-bundle, let \(X\) be a left \(G\)-space, then define \(E\times_G X:= (E\times X)/\sim\), with \((e\cdot g, x) \sim (e, gx)\), called the balanded product. Now, set \(\overline{p}: E\times_G X \rightarrow B\) to be the map \([e, x] \rightarrow p(e)\). We shall begin by proving that \((E\times_G X, B, X, \overline{p})\) is a fibre bundle with gauge group \(G\):-

  1. \(\overline{p}\) is well-defined as \(\overline{p}[eg, x] = p(eg) = p(e) = \overline{p}[e,gx]\).

  2. Let \(\overline{p}^{1}(b):= \{[e,x] | e\in p^{-1}(x)\} \cong X\), as \(p^{-1}(b)\times X \rightarrow X\), the projection onto X factors through \(\overline{p}^{-1}(b)\) homeomorphicaly. By the universal property of quotients we have a map \(\psi\):-

    \(\psi\) is clearly a surjection, and \(\psi([e, x]) = \psi([e',x']) = x\), which implies \(x = x'\) and \(eg=e'\) for some \(g\in G\) giving us injectivity of \(\psi\). Let \(O\subseteq_{\text{open}} (\overline{p})^{-1}(b)\), then \(\pi_b^{-1}(O)\) is saturated in \(p^{-1}(b)\times X\), and as projections are open maps, \(\psi\) is open. In conjunction, \(\psi\) is a homeomorphism.

  3. Let \(\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) be a locally trivializing cover for \((E\xrightarrow{p} B)\), then define, \[\psi_{\alpha}: (U_{\alpha}\times G)\times_G X \rightarrow U_{\alpha}\times X\] \[\psi_{\alpha}([u_{\alpha}, g, x]):= (u_{\alpha}, x)\] By an argument similar to that in (ii), \(\psi_{\alpha}\) is a homeomorphism. Now let, \[\overline{\psi}_{\alpha}: (\overline{p})^{-1}(U_{\alpha}) \rightarrow (U_{\alpha}\times G)\times_G X\] \[\overline{\psi}_{\alpha}([e, x]):= [\varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}(e), x]\] We shall now prove that \(\widehat{\psi}_{\alpha}:= \psi_{\alpha}\circ \overline{\psi}_{\alpha}\) is a homeomorphism. Consider,

    By the universal property of quotients, \(\overline{\psi}_{\alpha}\) is continuous, \(\psi_{\alpha}\) is open as \((e, x) \rightarrow (\varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}(e), x)\) is open, for the same reason \(\overline{\psi}_{\alpha}\) is surjective. Injectivity of \(\widehat{\psi}_{\alpha}\) is evident. The maps \(\{\widehat{\psi}_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) triviaize \(E\times_G X\) over \(\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\). It is fruitful to see what the transition functions would look like:-

    Explicitly speaking, \[\widehat{\psi}_{\alpha\beta}(b, x) = (b, \varphi_{\alpha\beta}(x))\]

The bundle \((E\times_G X)\) is called the bundle associated to \(E\). Note that all associated principal \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\)- bundles are \(\mathbb{K}\)-vector bundles. In fact, the converse is also true.

Theorem 3.2

Let \(\mathcal{P}_{GL_n(\mathbb{K})}(B)\) denote the category of principal \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\)-bundles over \(B\). The following is a bijective correspondence:- \[\mathcal{P}_{GL_n(\mathbb{K})}(B) \longleftrightarrow \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(B)\]

Proof. We shall first define the map between the two categories, then prove that that map is bijective.

Map:- \(\Phi: \mathcal{P}_{GL_n(\mathbb{K})}(B) \rightarrow \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(B)\)
\(\Phi(E):= E\times_{GL_n{\mathbb{K}}}\mathbb{K}^n\)

Surjectivity:- Let \(p: X \rightarrow B\) be a vector bundle with fibres \(\{X_b | b\in B\}\). Set \(E_b = \text{Iso}(\mathbb{K}^n, X_b)\) and
\(E= \coprod\limits_{b \in B}E_b\). Let \(q:E\rightarrow B\) be given by the universal property of colimit for the functions \(E_b \rightarrow \{b\}\in B\). Let \(\{(U_{\alpha}, \varphi_{\alpha})\}_{\alpha}\) trivialize \(X\rightarrow B\), then, \[\overline{\varphi}_{\alpha}: q^{-1}(U) = \coprod\limits_{b\in U}E_b \rightarrow U\times \text{Iso}(\mathbb{K}^n, \mathbb{K}^n)\] given by, \[e_b \in E_b \rightarrow \bigg(b, \varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}\big|_{p^{-1}(b)}\circ e_b\bigg)\] with transition functions, \[(b, \gamma) \rightarrow \bigg(b, \varphi_{\beta}\big|_{p^{-1}(b)}\circ \varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}\big|_{p^{-1}(b)}\circ \gamma\bigg)\] which are clearly homeomorphisms as \(\varphi_{\beta}\big|_{p^{-1}(b)}\circ \varphi_{\alpha}^{-1}\big|_{p^{-1}(b)}\) are so too; "trivialize" \(E\). That is, there exists a unique topology on \(E\) that would make \(q^{-1}(U)\) open in \(E\) and \(\{\overline{\varphi}_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) homeomorphisms on \(\{q^{-1}(U_{\alpha})\}_{\alpha}\). The fibre-wise right \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\) action becomes continuous, turning \(\overline{\varphi}_{\alpha}\) equivariant. Clubbing the above observations: \(E\rightarrow B\) is a principle \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\)-bundle, called the frame bundle of \(X\rightarrow B\). Further, \[E\times_{GL_n(\mathbb{K})} \mathbb{K}^n \cong X \text{(as vector bunles)}\] Indeed, as they both have the same transition functions.
Injectivity:- Given two principal \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\)-bundles \(E\), \(E'\), say we have:- \[E\times_{GL_n(\mathbb{K})} \mathbb{K}^n \xlongrightarrow[\sigma]{\cong} E'\times_{GL_n(\mathbb{K})} \mathbb{K}^n\] \[\sigma([b, g, v])= [b',g',v']\] By definition, \(\sigma\) is a fibre-preserving map. Clearly, \(\widetilde{\sigma}\) is fibre-preserving. Let \(\widetilde{g}\in GL_n(\mathbb{K})\), then \(\widetilde{\sigma}(b, g\widetilde{g}) = (b', g'\widetilde{g})\) (as \([b, g\widetilde{g}, v] = [b, g, \widetilde{g}v]\)), which implies that \(\widetilde{\sigma}\) is an isomorphism.

With a little extra work, the correspondence above can be shown to induce an equivalence of categories. Therefore, vector bundles are associated principal \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\)-bundles. In other words, associated principal \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\)-bundles capture the required gauge group action on the fibres.

References

Atiyah, Michael. 2018. K-Theory. CRC press. https://www.routledge.com/K-theory/Atiyah/p/book/9780367091309.

  1. Dimension of fibres over a connected component should remain invariant↩︎

title: Classification of Vector Bundles
excerptHtml: Of abundant importance to any theory is a robust classification theorem. With that interest in mind let us prove the following theorem pointing in that direction for vector bundles.
html:
Homotopy Theorem

Of abundant importance to any theory is a robust classification theorem. With that interest in mind let us prove the following theorem pointing in that direction for vector bundles.

Theorem 3.3

Given a vector bundle \(\eta = (E, B, V, p)\), and \(f_0\), \(f_1\) \(: A \rightarrow B\) homotopic maps, where \(A\) is paracompact Hausdorff, we have:- \[f_0^*\eta \cong f_1^*\eta\]

Proof. We shall do it in three steps, each important in itself.

STEP 1:- \(\text{Hom}(E, E') \longleftrightarrow \Gamma(\text{HOM}(E, E'))\).

This is where specific description of the HOM bundle will play a role. Define, \[\rho: \text{Aut}(V)\times \text{Aut}(V')\rightarrow \text{Aut}(\text{Hom}(V, V'))\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{1} \rho(T, S)(A) := SAT^{-1} \end{equation}\]

Following the functorial construction would yield the \(\rho\) above, that is, \[\rho(E, E') = \text{HOM}(E, E')\] Now let \(f\in \text{Hom}(E, E')\) and let \(\{\varphi^1_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) and \(\{\varphi^2_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) be local trivializations of \(E\) and \(E'\) (after passing to a common refinement in \(B\)). We have, \[\big((\varphi^2_{\alpha})^{-1}\circ f \circ \varphi^1_{\alpha}\big)(x, h) = (x, f_{\alpha}(x)h)\] \[\widetilde{\varphi}^2_{\beta\alpha}\circ f_{\alpha} \equiv f_{\beta}\circ \widetilde{\varphi}^1_{\beta\alpha}\] Clearly, \(f_{\alpha}\) is a local section of HOM\((E, E')\) because if \(\{\varphi_{\beta\alpha}\}_{\alpha, \beta}\) are transition functions of it, then by \((1)\), \[f_{\beta} = \varphi_{\beta\alpha}\circ f_{\alpha}\] which implies that \(\{f_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) can be glued together on \(B\) to yield a global section.

STEP 2:- If \(B\) is paracompact Hausdorff and \(B\subseteq_{\text{closed}} B\) and let \(E\big|_{B'} \rightarrow E'\big|_{B'}\) be an isomorphism. Then there exists \(U\subseteq_{\text{open}} B\), \(B'\subseteq U\) such that the isomorphism can be extended to \(E\big|_{U} \rightarrow E'\big|_{U}\).

We shall now make use of the following:-

FACT:- If \(f: B\rightarrow X\) is continuous, \(B\subseteq_{\text{closed}} \widetilde{B}\), where \(\widetilde{B}\) is paracompact Hausdorff, then \(f\) can be extended to \(\widetilde{B}\)

By STEP 1, \(f\in \Gamma\big(\text{HOM}(E\big|_{B'}, E'\big|_{B'}\big)\), and by the fact above, \(f\) can be extended to \(\widetilde{f}\) such that \(\widetilde{f} \in \Gamma\big(\text{HOM}(E, E'\big)\). Also, the point \(x\in B\) for which \(\widetilde{f}(x)\) is an isomorphism is open in \(B\).

STEP 3:- Let \(F: A\times I\rightarrow B\) be the homotopy, let \(F_t:= F(\cdot, t)\), and let \(\pi:A\times I\rightarrow A\) be the projection. \[\implies F_t\circ \pi : A\times I \rightarrow B\] Consider the bundles \(F^*E\) and \((F_t\circ \pi)^*E\), note that, \(F_t\circ \pi = F\big|_{A\times \{t\}}\). Applying STEP 2 to \(F^*E\) and \((F_t\circ \pi)^*E\) restricted to \(A\times \{t\} \subseteq_{\text{closed}} A\times I\), we see that all bundles \(F^*E\big|_{A\times \{\widetilde{t\}}}\), for \(\widetilde{t} \in (t-\delta, t+\delta)\) are isomorphic for some \(\delta\). As \([0,1]\) is connected, we get that:- \[f_0^*\eta \cong f_1^*\eta\]

Corollary. If \(f:A\rightarrow B\) is a homotopy equivalence, then, \(f^*: \text{Vect}^n(B)\rightarrow \text{Vect}^n(A)\) is a bijection. ((i.e.) vector bundles are homotopy invariant). Proof. Let \(g:B\rightarrow A\) be such that \(f\circ g \sim \text{id}_B\) and \(g\circ f\sim \text{id}_A\), then \(g^*\) is the required inverse for \(f^*\), as \(f^*g^* \cong \text{id}^*_A\) and \(g^*f^* \cong \text{id}^*_B\)

Classification of Vector Bundles (over compact Hausdorff spaces)

Let \(\tau_c\) be the category of compact Hausdorff spaces upto homotopy. Note that \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n: \tau_c^{\text{op}} \rightarrow \text{Sets}\), is a presheaf on \(\tau_c\), and hence asking for a good classification theorem is akin to asking if \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n\) is representable. The answer:- Yes, by the infinite Grassmannian \(\text{Gr}(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\). More specifically, one can obtain all vector bundles over \(X\) by pulling back via maps \(X\rightarrow \text{Gr}(n , \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\) the bundle associated to the universal bundle over \(\text{Gr}(n , \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\). For reasons apparent, \(\text{Gr}(n , \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\) is called the classifying space of the gauge group \(GL_n(\mathbb{K})\).

Theorem 3.4

The map \(\phi: [X, \text{Gr}(n , \mathbb{K}^{\infty})] \rightarrow \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n\) is a bijective correspondence for compact Hausdorff spaces \(X\), where \([X, Y]\) denotes the set of maps \(X\rightarrow Y\) upto homotopy, and \(\phi([f]):= f^*\).

Remark. A more general result is true:- Given a group \(G\), let \(\mathcal{P}_G(B)\) denote the set of all principal \(G\)-bundles, where \(B\) is compact Hausdorff, then there exists a \(G\)-bundle \(EG\rightarrow BG\), with a contractible total space, such that the following is a bijective correspondence:- \[[X, BG] \longleftrightarrow \mathcal{P}_G(B)\] \(EG\) is called the universal bundle and \(BG\) the classifying space for the gauge group \(G\). This generalizes the theorem above for \(G= GL_n{(\mathbb{K})}\), because of the correspondence between \(GL_n{(\mathbb{K})}\)-bundles and vector bundles of dimension \(n\) established before, and the fact that \(BGL_n{(\mathbb{K})} \cong \text{Gr}(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\) with \(EG = V(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty}) \sim \{*\}\) as its universal bundle.

Primer:- Note that the homotopy theorem ensures that the pullback of bundes via maps in \([X, \text{Gr}(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})]\) is well-defined. The reason we impose \(X\) to be compact Hausdorff is largely because such spaces are compactly generated, in particular, they satisfy:- \[\text{Hom}(X\times Y, Z) \cong \text{Hom}(X, \text{Hom}(Y, Z))\]

As a result, even if the hypothesis on \(X\) can be loosened to admit paracompact Hasudorff spaces, one ignores. The hypothesis that \(X\) is compact Hausdorff is only exploited to establish surjectivity. Therefore, the following is always an injective correspondence:- \[[X, \text{Gr}(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})] \hookrightarrow \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n\] \[[f] \rightarrow f^*\big(V(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times_{O_{\mathbb{K}}(n)}\mathbb{K}^n\big)\]

Proof. To establish injectivity we need the following lemma:-

Lemma 3.1

Let \(j_{\text{ev}}\), \(j_{\text{odd}}\) \(: \mathbb{R}^{\infty} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\infty}\) be defined as follows:- \[j_{\text{ev}}(x_1, x_2, \ldots) := (0, x_1, 0, x_2, 0, \ldots)\] \[j_{\text{odd}}(x_1, x_2, \ldots) := (x_1, 0, x_2, 0, \ldots)\] Then \(j_{\text{ev}} \sim j_{\text{odd}} \sim \text{id}_{\mathbb{R}^{\infty}}\)

Proof. We prove it for \(j_{\text{ev}}\), and for \(j_{\text{odd}}\) the proof is analogous. Define, \[H: \mathbb{R}^{\infty} \times [0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\infty}\] \[H(x,t):= tj_{\text{ev}}(x) + (1-t)x\] Clearly, \(H\) is the required homotopy. Now suppose \(t\in (0,1)\) and \(H(x,t) = 0\), then, \[\big(((1-t)x_1, tx_1 + (1-t)x_2, (1-t)x_3\big) = (0,0,0,\ldots)\] which implies, \(x=(0,0,\ldots)\). So, the homotopy is via linear embeddings

Let \(f\), \(g\) \(: X\rightarrow \text{Gr}(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\) be maps, denote the associated bundle \(\big(V(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times_{GL_n{\mathbb{K}}} \mathbb{K}^n\big)\) by \(\gamma_n\), and suppose \(\alpha: f^*\gamma_n \xrightarrow{\cong} g^*\gamma_n\) is an isomorphism. Note that WLOG one can assume \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) to be distinct subspces in \(\mathbb{R}^{\infty}\) or work with \(j_{\text{ev}}\circ f\) and \(j_{\text{odd}}\circ g\). We shall need the following fact about the topology of the Grassmannian:-

FACT:- \(\text{Gr}(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty}) \cong V(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})/O(n) \cong \{P\in \text{Hom}(\mathbb{K}^N, \mathbb{K}^n) | P \text{ is orthogonal}\}\)

So, \(f\), \(g\) can be viewed as a family of orthogonal projections of \(\mathbb{K}^{\infty}\) onto \(\mathbb{K}^n\) varying continuously over \(X\). Consider,

\(\alpha\) being an isomorphism between \(f^*\gamma_n\) and \(g^*\gamma_n\) is an isomorphism on the fibre over \(f(x)\). Now define, \[\widetilde{H}: X\times [0,1] \rightarrow Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\] \[\widetilde{H}(x, t):= (tf(x) + (1-t)[p\circ \alpha\circ z](f(x)))\] Clearly, \(\widetilde{H}\) is continuous, \(\widetilde{H}(x, 1) \equiv f\), \(\widetilde{H}(x, 0) \equiv [p\circ \alpha\circ z](f(x)) = g(x)\) (as \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism).

Now let’s establish surjectivity. Let \(E\xrightarrow{p} X\) be a vector bundle of rank \(n\). \(E\) can be embedded in \(X\times \mathbb{K}^N \subset X\times \mathbb{K}^{\infty}\). Let that embedding be \(j\). Define, \[f:X \rightarrow Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\] \[f(x) := \text{Proj}(\mathbb{K}^{\infty} \rightarrow j(E_x)) = j(E_x) \sim \mathbb{K}^n\] where the last equality is written keeping the fact (above) in mind, and \(j(E_x) \xhookrightarrow{\sim} x\times \mathbb{K}^N \hookrightarrow x\times \mathbb{K}^{\infty} \cong \mathbb{K}^{\infty}\). Using the local trivialization on \(E\rightarrow X\), one can easily prove that \(f\) is locally continuous, (i.e.) continuous. To establish \(f^*\gamma_n \cong E\) we need to look at the associated bundle differently. Set, \[G_n:= \{(V, x) | v \in Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty}), x\in V\}\] Then, \[\big(V(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times_{GL_n{\mathbb{K}}}\mathbb{K}^n\big) \rightarrow G_n\] \[\big((v_1, \ldots, v_n), (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)\big) \rightarrow \bigg(\langle v_1,\ldots, v_n\rangle, \sum_i\lambda_i v_i\bigg)\] is an isomorphism on fibres, which implies one can transfer bundle strucutre of the former to the latter. Clearly, \(f^*G_n \cong E\) via the map:- \[(V, v, x)\in G_n\times_{Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})} X \rightarrow j(v)\in E\] with inverse, \[v\in E \rightarrow \big(j(E_{p(v)}), j(v), p(v)\big) \in G_n\times_{Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})} X\] which is continuous component-wise. \(G_n\) is often referred to as the tautological bundle.

Remark:- If \(p:E\rightarrow B\) is a vector bundle, then one has the fibre preserving sequence \(\mathbb{K}^n \rightarrow E\rightarrow B\). This gives rise to a long exact sequence of homotopy groups:- \[\cdot\rightarrow\pi_k(\mathbb{K}^n) \rightarrow \pi_k(E) \rightarrow \pi_k(B) \rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(\mathbb{K}^{n-1})\rightarrow \cdots\] As \(\mathbb{K}^n\) is contractible, we get the following:- \[\pi_k(E) \cong \pi_k(B)\] In other words, \(E\) is weakly homotopic equivalent to \(B\). The above is in fact true for any fibre bundle with contractible fibre, but for the case of vector bundles one can show that the weak equivalence is actually a homotopy equivalence, where the zero section is the prescribed inverse of \(p\). This along with the corollary to the homotopy theorem and the classification theorem tells us that:-

\(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(B)\) holds homotopic information about \(B\) in a linear fashion.

title: Stable Isomorphism Classes of Vector Bundles
excerptHtml: The functor \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n\) is representable. We now aim to give it more structure by lifting it to commutative rings, after some minor adjustments. This is a generic categorical trend: one yearns to understand elements of a category by studying presheaves on it, which is akin to studying groups by studying its action. Then one asks if the presheaves can be lifted to some nice category to obtain, for instance, algebraic invariants like the homotopy groups. The ideas developed here can be found in (Atiyah and Hirzebruch 1961)
html:
Generalized Cohomology

The functor \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n\) is representable. We now aim to give it more structure by lifting it to commutative rings, after some minor adjustments. This is a generic categorical trend: one yearns to understand elements of a category by studying presheaves on it, which is akin to studying groups by studying its action. Then one asks if the presheaves can be lifted to some nice category to obtain, for instance, algebraic invariants like the homotopy groups. The ideas developed here can be found in (Atiyah and Hirzebruch 1961)

Stable Isomorphism Classes of Vector Bundles

Given a compact Hausdorff space \(X\), theorems on \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(X)\) proved in the previous section can easily be extended to \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\) component by component. Note that, \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\) is a contravariant functor, \[\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}: \tau_c^{\text{op}} \rightarrow \text{Sets}\] Clearly, \(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}\) lifts to the category of commutative monoids (denoted by CMon), (i.e.) one has:-

Given any commutative monoid \(M\), one can create a group \(Gk(M)\) via what’s called a groupification, such that the following universal property holds:- Given \(f:M \rightarrow G\), \(G\) a group, \(f\) a monoid homomorphism, there exists a unique group homomorphism \(\widetilde{f}: Gk(M) \rightarrow G\) such that the following commutes:-

Let us now construct the functor \(Gk: \text{CMon} \rightarrow \text{CGrps} \text{ (the category of }\mathbb{Z}\text{-modules})\) explicitly. Define, \[Gk(M):= (M\times M)/\sim\] where \((m, m') \sim (n,n')\) if \(m+n'+a = m'+n+a\) for some \(a\in M\). Give \(Gk(M)\) the additive structure borrowed from \(M\) (imposed component-wise).

  1. Associativity and commutativity of addition is clear.

  2. \([(e, e)]\) is the identity.

  3. \([(m, n)]\) is the inverse of \([(n,m)]\) as \([(n+m, m+n)] = [(e, e)]\).

  4. \(\widetilde{f}([(m,n)]):= f(m)f(n)^{-1}\). \(\widetilde{f}\) clearly satisfies the universal property. Indeed, the inclusion, \(M\hookrightarrow Gk(M)\) is given by, \(m\rightarrow [(m, e)]\), then as:-

    we have, \(\widetilde{f}([(m, e)]) = f(m)\), which implies \(\widetilde{f}([(m, n)]) = \widetilde{f}([(m, e)]+[(e, n)]) = \widetilde{f}([(m, e)]) = \widetilde{f}([(n, e)]) = f(m)f(n)^{-1}\).

We define the functor, \[K: \tau_c^{\text{op}} \rightarrow \text{CGrps}\] \[K:= Gk\circ \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}\] In other words, we have the following diagram:-

Elements of \(K(X)\) are called stable isomorphism classes of vector bundles.

Let \((E, E') \in \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\times \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\), then \((E, E') \sim (F, F')\) iff \(E\oplus F'\oplus A \cong E'\oplus F\oplus A\). Now, \(\forall A \in \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\), there exists \(A' \in \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\) such that \(A\oplus A' \cong \epsilon^n\), where \(\epsilon^n\) is a trivial bundle of dimension \(n\) over \(X\). So, \[(E, E') \sim (F,F') \iff \exists \epsilon^n \text{ such that,}\] \[E\oplus F'\oplus \epsilon^n \cong E'\oplus F\oplus \epsilon^n\] Also, for \(E'\in \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X)\), let \(E''\) be such that \(E'\oplus E'' \cong \epsilon^m\), this gives us that:- \[(E, E') \sim (E\oplus E'', E' \oplus E'') = (E\oplus E'', \epsilon^m)\] Therefore, \[K(X) = \{[(E, \epsilon)] \in Gk(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}(X))\}\] In other words, embedding theorem gives us the above elegant description of the stable isomorphism classes of vector bundles. Define, \[\otimes: K(X)\times K(X) \rightarrow K(X)\] \[[(E, \epsilon^m)]\otimes [(E, \epsilon^n)] := [(E\otimes E' \oplus \epsilon^m\otimes \epsilon^n, E'\otimes \epsilon^m\oplus E\otimes \epsilon^n)]\] From our discussion on the tensor products of bundles and Whitney sums, it is clear that \(K\) lifts to CRings, (i.e.) we have:-

This lifted commutative ring object \(K(X)\) is called the Grothendieck ring of vector bundles over \(X\).

Question:- Is the functor \(K\in \text{PSh}(\tau_c)\) representable?

Representation of the \(K\)-functor

Let \(\{x_0\} \in X\), then \(\{x_0\} \xhookrightarrow{i} X\) induces the map:- \[i^*: K(X) \rightarrow K(x_0)\] Define, \[\widetilde{K}(X) := \text{Ker}(i^*)\] called the reduced ring over \(X\). Note that \(K(x_0) = \{[(\epsilon^n, \epsilon^m)]\}_{n, m} \cong \mathbb{Z}\), and that one has the following exact sequence:- \[0\rightarrow \widetilde{K}(X) \rightarrow K(X) \rightarrow K(X_0) \rightarrow 0\] As \(K(x_0)\) is free, the above sequence splits to give:- \[K(X)\cong \widetilde{K}(X)\oplus K(x_0)\] Suppose \([(E, \epsilon^n)] = [(E', \epsilon^m)]\) belong to \(\text{Ker}(i^*)\), then by definition there exists \(\epsilon^k\) such that \(E\oplus \epsilon^{n+k} \cong E'\oplus \epsilon^{m+k}\). Say \(E\sim_s E'\) whenever such an isomorphism holds. Let, \[i_{n, m}: \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(X) \rightarrow \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^{n+m}(X)\] \[i_{n, m}(E):= E\oplus \epsilon^m\] Then, \(\{i_{n, m}\}_{n, m}\) defines the following diagram of a directed system in Sets. \[D: \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^0(X) \xhookrightarrow{i_{0,1}} \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^1(X) \xhookrightarrow{i_{1,1}} \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^2(X) \xhookrightarrow{i_{2,1}} \text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(X) \xhookrightarrow{i_{3,1}} \cdots\] Observe that, \[\text{colim}(D) = \bigg(\coprod\limits_{n}\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(X)\bigg)\bigg/\sim_s = \widetilde{K}(X)\] We now look for maps \(\{j_{n,m}\}_{n,m}\) such that the following commutes:- \((†)\)

then, \[\text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}([X, Gr(n+m, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})]) \cong \text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}(\text{Vect}_{\mathbb{K}}^n(X))\] which would imply, \[\begin{equation*} \begin{split} \widetilde{K}(X) & \cong \text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}(\text{Hom}_{\tau_c}(X, Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})))\\ & \cong \text{Hom}_{\tau_c}(X, \text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})) \end{split} \end{equation*}\] Now, \(K(X) \cong \widetilde{K}(X) \oplus \mathbb{Z}\) gives, \[\begin{equation*} \begin{split} K(X) & \cong \text{Hom}_{\tau_c}(X, \text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})) \oplus \mathbb{Z}\\ & \cong \text{Hom}_{\tau_c}(X, \text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times \mathbb{Z}) \end{split} \end{equation*}\] Therefore the colimit of infinite Grassmannians \(\big[\text{colim}_{j_{n,m}}Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times \mathbb{Z}\big]\) represents the presheaf \(K\). Now note that the function, \[\xi_{n,m}: Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty}) \rightarrow Gr(n+m, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\] \[\xi_{n,m}(P):= \mathbb{K}^m\oplus P\] leading to; \[j_{n, m}: [X, Gr(n, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})] \rightarrow [X, Gr(n+m, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})]\] \[j_{n,m}(f):= \xi_{n,m}\circ f\] by the very construction of Whitney sums and pullbacks gives us a canditate family of morphisms \(\{j_{n,m}\}_{n,m}\) that make \((\dagger)\) commute. The discussion above is summarized as,

Theorem 4.1

Let \(X\) be a compact Hausdorff space, we have, \[K(X) \cong [X, Gr(\infty, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times \mathbb{Z}]\] (i.e.) the space \(Gr(\infty, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\times \mathbb{Z}\) represents the functor \(K\).

Remark (Notation):- Recall that for a group \(G\), we denote by \(BG\) its classifying space, and by \(EG\) the universal bundle. Turns out, for \(U:= \text{colim} U(n)\), the classifying space \(BU \cong Gr(\infty, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\), and \(BU(n) \cong Gr(\infty, \mathbb{K}^{n})\), so we shall use the symbol \(BU\) for \(Gr(\infty, \mathbb{K}^{\infty})\). Similarly, we use \(BU(n)\), \(EU(n)\), to denote analogous objects. From now on, by a bundle we shall mean a finite dimensional complex vector bundle over a compact Hausdorff space.

Remark Note that \((\dagger)\) does not talk about the ring structure of \(K(X)\). To say that \([X, BU]\) with the usual direct sum and tensor product of maps induced point-wise by \(BU\) is isomorphic to \(\widetilde{K}(X)\), we need to check the following two things:-

  1. \((f\oplus' g)^*EU(n+m) \cong f^*EU(n)\oplus g^*EU(m)\)

  2. \((f\otimes' g)^*EU(nm) \cong f^*EU(n)\otimes g^*EU(m)\)

where \(\oplus'\) and \(\otimes'\) denote the sum and product in the ring of maps. The isomorphisms (i), (ii), are nearly tautological if one appeals to the tautological bundle rather than looking at \(EU(n)\)1. Then, passing on to colimits would give us an isomorphism that preserves the algebraic structure.

References

Atiyah, Michael F, and Friedrich Hirzebruch. 1961. Vector Bundles and Homogeneous Spaces. https://bookstore.ams.org/PSPUM/3.

  1. This, in a way justifies the name.↩︎

title: Bott Periodicity and the Genesis of K-Theory
excerptHtml: As \(K\) is represented by the space \(BU\times \mathbb{Z}\), any theorem about the homotopy type of \(BU\times \mathbb{Z}\) could potentially be of extreme significance. Bott’s Periodicity is in that sense the grandest of theorems one could prove.
html:
Bott Periodicity and the Genesis of K-Theory

As \(K\) is represented by the space \(BU\times \mathbb{Z}\), any theorem about the homotopy type of \(BU\times \mathbb{Z}\) could potentially be of extreme significance. Bott’s Periodicity is in that sense the grandest of theorems one could prove.

Theorem 4.2 — Bott Periodicity

\(BU\times \mathbb{Z} \sim \Omega^2(BU\times \mathbb{Z})\)

For proof, refer (Milnor 2016). An immediate consequence of Bott’s theorem is the following theorem which shall subsequently also be referred to as Bott’s Periodicity Theorem.

Theorem 4.3

\(\widetilde{K}(\Sigma^2X) \cong \widetilde{K}(X)\)

Proof. Observe that, \[\widetilde{K}(X) \cong [(X, x_0), (BU\times \mathbb{Z}, (y_0, 0))]\] as it is the kernel of the map \([X, BU\times \mathbb{Z}] \rightarrow [x_0, BU\times \mathbb{Z}]\), which is precisely the set of homotopy classes of maps sending \(x_0\) into \(BU\times \{0\}\). Now, by Bott’s Theorem, \[\widetilde{K}(X) \cong [X, \Omega^2(BU\times \mathbb{Z})]_{\text{based}} \cong [\Sigma^2X, BU\times \mathbb{Z}]_{\text{based}}\] giving us, \[\widetilde{K}(X) \cong \widetilde{K}(\Sigma^2X)\]

An important consequence of the theorem above is that one can build a cohomology theory on \(\tau_c\). Generally speaking, a cohomology theory on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) of topological pairs is the following data:- \[F^k: \mathcal{C}^{\text{op}} \rightarrow \text{Ab (category of abelian groups)}\] \(\{F^k\}_{k}\) a sequence of presheaves on \(\mathcal{C}\) with natural transformations, \[\delta: F^k(A) := F^k(A, \emptyset) \rightarrow F^{k+1}(X, A)\] satisfying the following axioms (Eilenberg and Steenrod 1945) (due to Eilenberg and Steenrod):-

Axiom 1 (Homotopy Axiom):- If \(f\), \(g\) \(:(X, A) \rightarrow (Y,B)\) are homotopic as map of pairs, then \(f^*, g^*\) \(:F^k(Y, B) \rightarrow F^k(X, A)\) are equal, \(\forall k\in \mathbb{Z}\), where \(f^*:= F^k(f)\).

Axiom 2 (Sequence Axiom):- For a pair \((X, A)\), the above maps induce a long exact sequence:- \[\cdots \rightarrow F^k(X, A)\rightarrow F^k(X) \rightarrow F^k(A) \rightarrow F^{k+1}(X, A)\rightarrow \cdots\]

Axiom 3 (Excision Axiom):- If \(U\subseteq \overline{U} \subset \text{Int}(A)\), then \(F^k(X\backslash U, A\backslash U) \cong F^k(X, A)\), \(\forall k\), \(k\in \mathbb{Z}\).

To build K-Theory on the category of pairs of compact Hausdorff spaces we need the following two propositions; proofs are taken from (Hatcher 2003).

Proposition 4.1

Consider \(A\xrightarrow{i} X \xrightarrow{q} X/A\), where \(i\), \(q\) are the canonical inclusion and quotient maps. Then, \[\widetilde{K}(X/A) \xrightarrow{q^*} \widetilde{K}(X) \xhookrightarrow{i^*} \widetilde{K}(A)\] is an exact sequence of rings.

Proof. Note that \(i^*\circ q^* = (q\circ i)^*\), where \(q\circ i\) is the composition \(A\rightarrow A\subset X \rightarrow A/A\), and \(\widetilde{K}(A/A) = \{0\}\). So, \(\text{Im}(q^*) \subseteq \text{Ker}(i^*)\). Now we show \(\text{Ker}(i^*) \subseteq \text{Im}(q^*)\). If \([E] \in \text{Ker}(i^*)\), \(\big[E\big|_{A}\big] = 0\), in other words, \[E\big|_{A}\oplus \epsilon^n(A) \cong \epsilon^{n+m}(A)\] Therefore, we may WLOG assume that \(E\big|_{A}\) is trivial, with trivialisation, \[\psi: E\big|_{A} \rightarrow A\times \mathbb{C}^n\] Let \(E/\psi\) denote the quotient space, where \(\psi^{-1}(x, v) \sim \psi^{-1}(y, v)\), for all \(x, y\in A\). We claim that \(E/\psi\) is a bundle over \(X/A\), and that \(q^*(E/\psi) \cong E\). To show the former, note that for a locally trivializing cover \(\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}\) of \(E\), the modified locally trivializing collection of open1 sets \(\{U_{\alpha}\backslash A\}_{\alpha}\) erect a bundle over \(X\backslash A\). Note that that bundle is a subbundle of \(E\), and for that to extend to a bundle on \(X/A\), one would need a local trivialization at the point \(q\circ i(A)\). As \(E\big|_{A}\) is trivial, one has a frame \(\sigma_i\) over \(A\) which can (by a partition of unity argument) be extended to a frame over an open set containing \(A\); for the set of points \(p\) satisfying, \[\det(\sigma_1(p), \sigma_2(p),\ldots, \sigma_n(p)) \neq 0\] is open, thereby facilitating the required extension. Now note that by definition, the natural map \(E\rightarrow E/\psi\) lifts the quotient map, (i.e.) one has the following commutative diagram:-

which is also an isomorphism on the fibres. It is easy to see that \(E\) satisfies the universal property of pullbacks.

Remark:- Interpreting the proposition in terms of the classifying space perspective yields the following:- Given a classifying map \(f\) of some bundle over \(X\), such that \(f\big|_A\) is nullhomotopic, then there exists an open neighbourhood \(U\) of \(A\) such that \(f\big|_{U}\) is nullhomotopic. Loosely speaking, the space \(BU\) is such that around any compact set there are neighbourhoods with no holes. If you think about it, the above is not unexpected at all, for the spaces \(BU(n)\) are locally contractible.

Proposition 4.2

If \(A\) is contractible, then \(q^*: \widetilde{K}(X/A) \rightarrow \widetilde{K}(X)\) is an isomorphism.

Proof. We begin by identifying \(\widetilde{K}(X)\) by \(\pi_b(X, BU)\). Following the remark above, note that if \(A\) is contractible then for any classifying map \(f: X\rightarrow BU\), \(f\big|_A\) is nullhomotopic, and that there exists an open neighbourhood \(U\) of \(A\) such that \(f\big|_U\) is also nullhomotopic. Let, \[F:U\times [0,1] \rightarrow BU\] \[F_0\equiv f\big|_U, F_1 \equiv b_0\] be the nullhomotopy. As compact Hausdorff spaces are normal, by Urysohn’s lemma we have, \[\alpha :X \rightarrow [0,1]\] \[\alpha\big|_A = 1, \supp{\alpha} \subset U\] Define \(Q(f): X \rightarrow BU\) by,

\[\begin{equation*} Q(f) := \begin{cases} F(x,\alpha(x)),& \text{ if } x\in U\\ f(x), & \text{ else} \end{cases} \end{equation*}\] which is clearly continuous. As \(Q(f)\) is constant on \(A\), it factors through \(X/A \rightarrow BU\). It is easy to see that such factored maps give the inverse of \(q^*\), so we call them \((q^*)^{-1}(f)\), for \(f\in \pi_b(X, BU)\). It remains to check that the map \(Q\) is well-defined, which essentially boils down to proving that \(Q(f)\) depends only on the homotopy type of \(f\). Let \(f\), \(g\) \(:X \rightarrow BU\) be homotopic, with, \[H: X\times [0,1] \rightarrow BU\] \[H_0 \equiv f, H_1 \equiv g\] the homotopy between them. Now as \(A\) is contractible, so is \(A\times [0,1]\), implying that, \(H\big|_{A\times [0,1]}\) is nullhomotopic. Let the homotopy be given by the map \(N\). Now, again apply Urysohn’s lemma for the space \(X\times [0,1]\) to get, \[\beta: X\times [0,1] \rightarrow [0,1]\] \[\beta\big|_{A\times [0,1]} \equiv 1, \supp{\beta} \subset V\times [0,1]\] Repeat the construction above by defining, \[G(H_t):= \begin{cases} N((x, t), \beta(x)), & \text{ if } x\in V\\ H_t(x), & \text{ else} \end{cases}\] To finish the proof, let’s do away with one small yet essential detail: One can define a straightline homotopy between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta_t\), hence the function \(Q\) is independent of the open sets nullhomotoping \(f\) and \(g\).

Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\cup \{0\}\), define, \[\widetilde{K}^{-n}(X, A):= \widetilde{K}(\Sigma^nX/\Sigma^n A)\] \[\widetilde{K}^{2n}(X, A) := \widetilde{K}(X/A)\] \[\widetilde{K}^{2n+1}(X, A) := \widetilde{K}(\Sigma(X/A))\] For the sequence of functors defined above, homotopy axiom follows from the representation of the functor \(K\), and the excision axiom is just the trivial statement \((X\backslash U)/(A\backslash U) = X/A\). To investigate the sequence axiom, we need to define the requisite natural transformations; for this purpose, Proposition \(4.2\) will come in handy. Given a pair \((X, A)\) we have the following sequence of spaces called the Puppe sequence:-

Note that as cones are contractible, we have the isomorphism:- \[\widetilde{K}(X\cup CA) \cong \widetilde{K}((X\cup CA)/CA) \cong \widetilde{K}(X/A)\] which gives rise to a cofibration like complex:- \[\widetilde{K}(A) \xleftarrow{} \widetilde{K}(X) \xleftarrow{} \widetilde{K}(X/A) \xleftarrow{} \widetilde{K}(\Sigma A) \xleftarrow{} \widetilde{K}(\Sigma X) \xleftarrow{} \widetilde{K}(\Sigma X/\Sigma A) \xleftarrow{} \cdots\] Therefore by Bott’s Theorem, the above induces the following:-

which written in a more recognizable form, is, \[\cdots \rightarrow \widetilde{K}^n(X, A)\rightarrow \widetilde{K}^n(X) \rightarrow \widetilde{K}^n(A) \rightarrow \widetilde{K}^{n+1}(X, A)\rightarrow \cdots\]

The periodicity theorem essentially allows us to wrap the sequence on itself. Exactness at various places will be given by Proposition \(4.1\) applied to relevant sections of the Puppe sequence, along with the observation that \((X\cup CY)/CY \sim X/Y\). So, \(\{K^n\}_{n}\) satisfies the sequence axiom for pairs. In other words, we have been successful in building what we initially called K-Theory for the category of pairs of compact Hausdorff spaces, which we compile in the theorem below:-

Theorem 4.4

The sequence of functors \(\widetilde{K}^n\) define a generalized cohomology theory on the category of compact Hausdorff pairs.

Having accomplished our main goal in the three sections, we shall compute \(K\)-groups of spheres and tori to give some concreteness to the mathematics developed thus far; and wrap up by leaving the reader with things to think about. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be compact Hausdorff; one has the following exact sequence of pointed spaces:- \[\begin{equation} \tag{2} X\vee Y \hookrightarrow X\times Y \rightarrow X\wedge Y:= (X\times Y)/(X\vee Y) \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{3} X\hookrightarrow X\vee Y \rightarrow Y \cong (X\vee Y)/X \end{equation}\] Note that \((2)\) and \((3)\) yield the following split exact sequence:- \[0\rightarrow \widetilde{K}(X\wedge Y) \rightarrow \widetilde{K}(X\times Y) \rightarrow \widetilde{K}(X)\oplus \widetilde{K}(Y) \xrightarrow{} 0\] which gives the isomorphism, \[\begin{equation} \tag{4} \widetilde{K}(X\times Y) \cong \widetilde{K}(X)\oplus \widetilde{K}(Y)\oplus \widetilde{K}(X\wedge Y) \end{equation}\]

Computations:-

  1. (K-Groups of Spheres): Note that, \(\widetilde{K}(S^k) \cong \pi_k(BU) \cong \pi_{k+1}(U)\); here we exploit the fact implicit in Bott’s Theorem that \(U\sim \Omega BU\). Now, we need to compute two distinct homotopy groups of the stable unitary group \(U\). Note, \[\pi_1(U) = \pi_1(U(1)) = \pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}\] \[\pi_2(U) = \pi_2(U(2)) \cong \pi_2(S^1\times SU(2)) \cong \pi_2(SU(2)) \cong \pi_2(S^3) = 0\] By Bott periodicity, we have \(\pi_{2n}(U) \cong 0\), and \(\pi_{2n+1}(U) \cong \mathbb{Z}\), for \(n\in \mathbb{N}\). This gives us that:- \[\widetilde{K}(S^n) = \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}, &\text{ if }2|n\\ 0, & \text{ else} \end{cases}\]

  2. (K-Groups of \(n\)-Torus): Apply \((4)\) to the spaces \(T^{n-1}\) and \(S^1\), to get:- \[\widetilde{K}^i(T^n) \cong \widetilde{K}^i(T^{n-1})\oplus \widetilde{K}^i(S^1)\oplus \widetilde{K}^{i+1}(T^{n-1})\] By induction one gets the following:- \[\widetilde{K}^i(T^n)= \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}^{\oplus(2^{n-1} -1)}, & \text{ if } 2|i\\ \mathbb{Z}^{\oplus(2^{n-1})}, & \text{ else} \end{cases}\]

Questions for the Reader:-

  1. Is there a space whose K-group has torsion elements? If so, what feature of the space is responsible for it?

  2. Is there a way to connect K-groups to homotopy groups?

  3. Note that as \(\mathbb{D}^n\) is contractible, \(\widetilde{K}^m(\mathbb{D}^n) = \{0\}\), can we use this and the values of the K-groups of \(S^n\)’s to compute K-groups of CW-complexes?

  4. Is K-Theory related to other cohomology theories in any natural way?

  5. Can analogous theories be build for the field of reals and quaternions?

References

Eilenberg, Samuel, and Norman E Steenrod. 1945. “Axiomatic Approach to Homology Theory.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 31 (4): 117–20. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.31.4.117.
Hatcher, Allen. 2003. “Vector Bundles and k-Theory.” Im Internet Unter Http://Www. Math. Cornell. Edu/~ Hatcher. https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/VBKT/VB.pdf.
Milnor, John. 2016. “Morse Theory.(AM-51), Volume 51.” In Morse Theory.(AM-51), Volume 51. Princeton university press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400881802.

title: Rings, Ideals, and Prime Ideals
html:
Let’s begin with two fundamental objects: rings and modules.

Rings and ideals

Definition 1

A ring \(R\) satisfies the following conditions:

(i)

\((R,+)\) is an abelian group.

(ii)

For all \(x,y,z\in R\), \((xy)z=x(yz)\), \(x(y+z)=xy+xz\), and \((y+z)x=yx+zx\) (associativity and distributivity).

(iii)

\(xy=yx\) (commutativity).

(iv)

There exists \(1\in R\) such that \(1x=x1=x\) (identity).

If \(S\subseteq R\) satisfies (i)–(iv), then \(S\) is a subring of \(R\).

Example 1

(i)

\((\Z,+,\times)\), the ring of integers.

(ii)

\((\kk,+,\times)\), a field.

(iii)

\((\End_{\Ab}(G),+,\circ)\), the ring of endomorphisms of the abelian group \((G,+)\), where \(\circ\) denotes composition.

(iv)

\((\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n],+,\times)\), the ring of polynomials over \(\kk\).

(v)

\((\{0\},+,\times)\), the zero ring.

Definition 2

For rings \(A\) and \(B\), a ring homomorphism \(f:A\to B\) is a map satisfying \[f\in\Hom_{\Ab}(A,B),\qquad f(xy)=f(x)+f(y),\qquad f(1)=1.\]

Example 2

(i)

\(\Z\hookrightarrow\Q\), the field of rationals.

(ii)

For \(P\in\kk^n\), the evaluation map \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to\kk\), \(f\mapsto f(P)\), is a ring homomorphism.

(iii)

If \(f:A\to B\) and \(g:B\to C\) are ring homomorphisms, then \(g\circ f:A\to C\) is a ring homomorphism.

Remark

Denote by \(\CRing\) the category of commutative rings. Then:

(i)

\(\Z\) is an initial object of \(\CRing\): for \(A\in\Ob(\CRing)\) there exists a unique \(f:\Z\to A\).

(ii)

\(\{0\}\) is the final object: for a given \(A\) there exists a unique \(g:A\to\{0\}\).

(iii)

If \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^n\subseteq\Ob(\CRing)\), then there exists \(A\in\Ob(\CRing)\), called the product, \[A=\prod_{i=1}^n A_i,\] with pointwise addition and multiplication, and \((1,\ldots,1)\) as identity. It comes equipped with projections \(P_i:A\to A_i\). For any collection of morphisms \(g_i:B\to A_i\),

there exists a unique \(f:A\to B\) such that the diagram below commutes.

Of all rings \(B\) projecting onto \(A_i\), \(A\) is “universal”.

(iv)

Coproducts need not exist in \(\CRing\), that is, \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^n A_i\) may not exist. Said differently, among all rings \(B\) which include \(A_i\) (\(A_i\hookrightarrow B\)), there may not be any universal element.

Note that if \(A_i\in\Ob(\mathsf{AbGps})\), then \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^n A_i\) exists; it is universal among maps \((A_i\to B)\in\Hom_{\Ab}(A_i,B)\). If the \(A_i\) are decorated with ring structure \((A_i,\times,1)\), then \[(1\in A_i)\longmapsto\underbrace{(0,0,\ldots,1,\ldots,0)}_{a_i}\in\bigoplus A_i.\] So \(a_i=1\) for all \(i\), which is absurd.

Definition 3

For an ideal \(\aa\subseteq A\), one can check that \(A/\aa\) is a ring. As an abelian group, its multiplication is well defined because \(A\aa\subseteq\aa\).

Indeed, \[(x+\aa)(y+\aa)=xy+x\aa+y\aa+\aa^2 =xy+(x+y+\aa)\aa=xy+\aa.\]

Remark

One can view ideals \(\aa\) as subgroups of \(A\) with an action of \(A\), captured by \[\psi\in\Hom_{\CRing}(A,\End_{\Ab}(\aa)),\qquad \psi(x)(a):=xa\quad(x\in A,\ a\in\aa).\] We shall return to this soon.

Example 3

(i)

If \(f\in\Hom_{\CRing}(A,B)\), then \(\ker f\) is an ideal of \(A\).

(ii)

For \(a\in A\), \((a):=\{xa\mid x\in A\}\) is an ideal of \(A\) generated by \(a\). Similarly, for a subset \(S\subseteq A\), \[(S):=\left\{\sum_{i\in F}x_i y_i\ \middle|\ x_i\in A,\ y_i\in S,\ F\text{ finite}\right\}\] is the ideal generated by \(S\), that is, the smallest ideal in \(A\) containing \(S\).

(iii)

\((0)\) and \((1)\) are the only ideals of \(\kk\). Hence, by (i), every morphism \(f:\kk\to B\) with \(B\ne0\) is injective.

(iv)

If \(\{\aa_i\}_{i\in I}\) are ideals of \(A\), then so are \[\sum_{i\in I}\aa_i:=\left\{\sum_{i\in F}a_i\ \middle|\ a_i\in\aa_i,\ F\subseteq I\text{ finite}\right\}, \qquad \bigcap_{i\in I}\aa_i,\] and \(\prod_{i\in F}\aa_i\), the ideal generated by \(\{\prod_{i\in F}a_i\mid a_i\in\aa_i\}\),

where \(F\subseteq I\) is finite.

(v)

In \(\Z\), all ideals are of the form \((n)\).

(vi)

If \(\aa,\bb\) are ideals of \(A\), then so is the ideal quotient \[(\aa:\bb):=\{x\in A\mid x\bb\subseteq\aa\}.\] If \(\aa=(0)\), then \((0:\bb)=:\Ann(\bb)\) is called the annihilator of \(\bb\).

(vii)

For an ideal \(\aa\) of \(A\), \(\rad(\aa):=\{x\in A\mid x^n\in\aa\}\) is also an ideal of \(A\), called the radical of \(\aa\), since nilpotent elements of \(A/\aa\) form an ideal by the binomial theorem.

(viii)

Let \(\aa\) be an ideal of \(A\) and \(\bb\) an ideal of \(B\). For \(f\in\Hom_{\CRing}(A,B)\), the ideal \((f(\aa))\) generated by \(f(\aa)\) in \(B\) is called the extension of \(\aa\) to \(B\), denoted \(\aa^e\). The ideal \(f^{-1}(\bb)\) of \(A\) is the contraction of \(\bb\) in \(A\), denoted \(\bb^c\).

Distribution of ideals of \(A\)

(i)

Let \(\Sigma\) be the set of all ideals in \(A\), excluding \(A\). This is a poset under inclusion. Since \(0\in\Sigma\), \(\Sigma\ne\varnothing\). If \(\{\aa_i\}_{i\in I}\) is a chain of ideals, then \(\bigcup_{i\in I}\aa_i\in\Sigma\) (as \(1\notin\bigcup_i\aa_i\)); furthermore, this union is an upper bound

for the chain. By Zorn’s lemma, \(\Sigma\) has a maximal element. Therefore every ideal \(\aa\) is contained in a maximal ideal, as illustrated below: the same argument can be made in \(A/\aa\).

(ii)

If \(\mm\) is a maximal ideal of \(A\), then \[\mm^c=\{x\mid x^{-1}\in A,\text{ or }(x)+\mm=A\}.\] If \(\mm^c=\{x\mid x^{-1}\in A\}\), then \(\mm\) is the unique maximal ideal. Such a ring is called local. Since \(\mm\) is maximal, \(A/\mm\) has no proper ideals except \((0)\); hence \(A/\mm\) is a field.

(iii)

Let \[\begin{aligned} 0\in D_0&:=\{x\in A\mid xy=0,\ y\in A\} &&\text{(zero-divisors)},\\ 1\in D_1&:=\{x\in A\mid xy=1,\ y\in A\} &&\text{(one-divisors, or units)}. \end{aligned}\]

Clearly, \(D_0\cap D_1=\varnothing\). In any ring an element belongs to either \(D_0\), \(D_1\), or \(D_0^c\cap D_1^c\).

If \(A\setminus\{0\}=D_1\), then \(A\) is a field. If \(A\setminus\{0\}=D_0^c\), then \(A\) is an integral domain.

(iv)

If, for an ideal \(\pp\) of \(A\), \(A/\pp\) is an integral domain, then \(\pp\) is a prime ideal; equivalently, \(xy\in\pp\Rightarrow x\in\pp\) or \(y\in\pp\).

Lemma 1 — Prime avoidance

If \(\{\pp_i\}_{i=1}^n\) are prime ideals and \(\aa\) is an ideal with \(\aa\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^n\pp_i\), then \(\aa\subseteq\pp_i\) for some \(i\).

Proof. The case \(n=1\) is clear. Assume the result for \(n-1\). For \(1\le i\le n\), if \(x\in\aa\Rightarrow x\in\pp_j\) for \(j\ne i\), then \(\aa\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ne i}\pp_j\). By the induction hypothesis, \(\aa\subseteq\pp_j\) for some \(j\). Therefore, for every \(1\le i\le n\), there exists \(x_i\in\aa\) such that \(x_i\notin\pp_j\) for \(j\ne i\), so \(x_i\in\pp_i\). Now let \[y=\sum_{i=1}^n x_1\cdots x_{i-1}x_{i+1}\cdots x_n.\] Then \(y\in\aa\), but \(y\notin\bigcup_i\pp_i\), a contradiction.

Consequently, no ideal is covered by a bunch of prime ideals as depicted here.

Lemma 2 — Factoring

If \(\{\aa_i\}_{i=1}^n\) are ideals and \(\pp\) is a prime ideal such that \(\pp\supseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^n\aa_i\), then \(\pp\supseteq\aa_i\) for some \(i\).

Proof. If \(\aa_i\nsubseteq\pp\) for every \(i\), choose \(x_i\in\aa_i\) with \(x_i\notin\pp\). But \(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\in\bigcap_i\aa_i\subseteq\pp\), a contradiction.

Remark

In particular, if \(\pp=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\aa_i\), then \(\pp=\aa_i\) for some \(i\). This is relevant because, if the \(\aa_i\) are coprime, then \(\prod\aa_i=\bigcap\aa_i\), and the lemma above yields uniqueness of factorization of \(\pp\).

Proposition 3

\[\rad((0))=\bigcap_{\pp\text{ prime}}\pp.\]

Proof. If \(f\in\rad((0))\), then \(f^n=0\in\pp\), so \(f\in\pp\) and hence \(f\in\bigcap_{\pp\text{ prime}}\pp\). If \(f\notin\rad((0))\), let \(\Sigma\) be the poset of all ideals \(\aa\) such that \(f^n\notin\aa\) for every \(n\). As \(0\in\Sigma\), this poset is nonempty. If \(\{\aa_i\}_{i\in I}\) is a chain, then \(\bigcup_i\aa_i\in\Sigma\) and bounds the chain. By Zorn’s lemma, \(\Sigma\) has a maximal element \(\mm\). Claim: \(\mm\) is prime.

Let \(x,y\notin\mm\). Then \(\mm+(x),\mm+(y)\notin\Sigma\) by maximality. Therefore, \(f^a\in\mm+(x)\) and \(f^b\in\mm+(y)\), so \(f^{a+b}\in\mm+(xy)\) and thus \(xy\notin\mm\). Therefore \(f\notin\mm\), implying \(f\notin\bigcap_{\pp\text{ prime}}\pp\).

The following picture summarizes what we have seen thus far.

title: Modules, Tensor Products, and the Determinant Trick
html:
Modules

Definition 4

\(M\) is an \(A\)-module if \(M\in\Ob(\mathsf{AbGps})\) and \(\Hom_{\CRing}(A,\End_{\Ab}(M))\ne\varnothing\). If \(M'<M\) satisfies the second condition, then \(M'\) is an \(A\)-submodule of \(M\).

Remark

Unwrapping the second condition, say \(f\in\Hom_{\CRing}(A,\End(M))\), gives \[f(a)\in\End_{\Ab}(M),\quad f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b),\quad f(ab)=f(a)f(b),\quad f(1)=1.\] Writing \(f(a)(x)\) as \(ax\), these become \[a(x+y)=ax+ay,\quad(a+b)x=ax+bx,\quad(ab)x=a(bx),\quad1x=x.\]

Example 4

(i)

Ideals of \(A\) are \(A\)-modules.

(ii)

\(G\in\Ob(\mathsf{AbGps})\) is a \(\Z\)-module.

(iii)

A \(\kk\)-vector space is a \(\kk\)-module.

(iv)

If \(M'\subseteq M\) are \(A\)-modules, then so is \(M/M'\).

(v)

If \(\{M_i\}_{i\in I}\) are \(A\)-submodules of \(M\), then so is \(\sum_{i\in I}M_i\), defined analogously to the sum of ideals.

(vi)

Products and coproducts exist in the category of \(A\)-modules. Thus, if the \(M_i\) are \(A\)-modules, so are \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\) (direct sum) and \(\prod_{i\in I}M_i\) (direct product).

Definition 5

A map \(f:M\to M'\) between \(A\)-modules is a module homomorphism if

\(f\in\Hom_{\Ab}(M,M')\) and \(f(ax)=af(x)\). Thus \(f\) is equivariant with the ring action of \(A\) on \(M,M'\).

Remark

Let \(\AMod\) denote the category of \(A\)-modules. There are functors \[\Hom_{\AMod}(-,N):\AMod\to\AMod,\qquad \Hom_{\AMod}(N,-):\AMod\to\AMod.\] Fact: These functors are left exact, that is, the sequence \(0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0\) is exact if and only if \(0\to F(M'')\to F(M)\to F(M')\) is exact. One similarly defines right exactness.

Tensor products

If \(M,N\) are \(A\)-modules, there is a universal object among all \(A\)-bilinear maps from \(M\times N\) to \(P\), denoted \(M\otimes N\). Thus \(f:M\times N\to P\) factors through an \(A\)-linear map \(\widetilde f\), as shown.

Construction.

Consider the direct sum \(\bigoplus_{i\in M\times N}A\). Let \(C\) be the submodule generated by \[\begin{gathered} (x+x',y)-(x,y)-(x',y),\qquad (x,y+y')-(x,y)-(x,y'),\\ (ax,y)-a(x,y),\qquad(x,ay)-a(x,y). \end{gathered}\] Then \(M\otimes N:=\bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in M\times N}A\bigr)/C\).

It is easy to check that \(-\otimes N:\AMod\to\AMod\) and \(N\otimes-:\AMod\to\AMod\) are functors. The source records the map \(\Psi(f):(x,y)\mapsto f(x)(y)\).

Claim

\[\Hom(M\otimes N,P)\cong\Hom(M,\Hom(N,P)).\]

Proof.

Given \(\widetilde\varphi\in\Hom(M\otimes N,P)\), there is a unique \(A\)-bilinear map \(\varphi:M\times N\to P\). Define \[\Phi:\Hom(M\otimes N,P)\longrightarrow\Hom(M,\Hom(N,P)), \qquad \Phi(\widetilde\varphi):=\varphi(x,-).\] Similarly, for \(f\in\Hom(M,\Hom(N,P))\), the map \(\widetilde{\Psi(f)}\) is the inverse of \(\Phi\).

Claim

The tensor-product functors above are right exact.

The source records the exact-sequence calculation \[\Hom(E,\Hom(N,P))\text{ is exact} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \Hom(E\otimes N,P)\text{ is exact} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ E\otimes N\text{ is exact}.\]

Finitely generated modules

Definition 6

An \(A\)-module \(M\) is finitely generated if there exist \(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n\) in \(M\) such that [unfinished in the source].

The module \(M\) is free if \(M=\bigoplus_i A\). Further, if \(M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n A\), then \(\dim(M)=n\). (If \(A^m\cong A^n\), then [unfinished in the source].)

The source also records \(A\otimes_A A\cong A\), \(A/\aa\otimes_A A\cong A/\aa\), and \(A/\aa\otimes_A A/\bb\) without a completed right-hand side.

Definition 7

\(N\) is flat if \(-\otimes N\) is an exact functor. It is already right exact; equivalently, \(N\) is flat if \[(0\to M'\to M)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (0\to M'\otimes N\to M\otimes N).\]

Theorem 4 — Cayley–Hamilton

Let \(M\) be a finitely generated \(A\)-module, \(\varphi\in\End_{\AMod}(M)\), and \(\varphi(M)\subseteq\aa M\), where \(\aa\) is an ideal of \(A\). Then \[\varphi^n+a_1\varphi^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\]

for some \(a_i\in\aa\), \(n>0\).

Proof. Let \(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n\) generate \(M\). Since \(\varphi(x_i)\in\aa M\), write \(\varphi(x_i)=\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\). Equivalently, \[\sum_{j=1}^n(\delta_{ij}\varphi-a_{ij})(x_j)=0, \qquad B\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\\vdots\\x_n\end{pmatrix}=0.\] Let \(\widetilde B\) be the cofactor matrix of \(B\). Then \[\widetilde B B\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\\vdots\\x_n\end{pmatrix}=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \det(B)I\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\\vdots\\x_n\end{pmatrix}=0.\] Thus \(\det(\delta_{ij}\varphi-a_{ij})\in\End(M)\) is the zero endomorphism.

Lemma 5 — Nakayama

Let \(M,\aa\) be as before. If \(\aa\subseteq\bigcap_{\mm\text{ maximal}}\mm\) (the Jacobson radical) and \(M=\aa M\), then \(M=0\).

Proof. Cayley–Hamilton for \(\varphi=\id\) yields, for \(x=1+a_1+\cdots+a_n\equiv1\pmod\aa\), that \(xM=0\). Since \(x\equiv1\pmod\aa\), \[1-x\in\bigcap_{\mm\text{ maximal}}\mm \ \Longrightarrow\ (1-x)\in\mm\ \text{for every maximal }\mm \ \Longrightarrow\ x\in\mm^c\ \text{for every maximal }\mm.\] Hence \(x\) is a unit. Therefore \(M=x^{-1}(xM)=0\).

title: Localization: Rings, Modules, and Prime Ideals
html:
Motivations for localization

Recall the construction of \(\Q\) from \(\Z\): \[\Q:=\{(x,y)\in\Z\times\Z\}/{\sim},\qquad (x_1,y_1)\sim(x_2,y_2)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ x_1y_2-y_1x_2=0.\]

We want to generalize this to arbitrary commutative rings. If \(X\) is a variety and \(x\in X\), then a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x\) corresponds to a localization of the coordinate ring \(A(X)\). Thus localization is the geometric equivalent of seeing a point locally.

Definition 8

Let \(S\subseteq A\) be a multiplicatively closed set in a commutative ring. Consider the equivalence relation on \(A\times S\) given by \[(a,s)\sim(b,t)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (at-bs)u=0\quad\text{for some }u\in S.\] Set \(S^{-1}A:=(A\times S)/{\sim}\), the localization of \(A\) by \(S\).

Remark

(i)

\(S^{-1}A\) has a ring structure: \[\frac as+\frac bt=\frac{at+bs}{st},\qquad \left(\frac as\right)\left(\frac bt\right)=\frac{ab}{st}.\]

(ii)

If \(A\) is an integral domain and \(S=A\setminus\{0\}\), then \(S^{-1}A\) is a field, called the field of fractions.

(iii)

Universal property. \(S^{-1}A\) is the initial object in the category \[\{g:A\to B\mid g\in\Hom_{\CRing}(A,B),\ g(s)\text{ is a unit for all }s\in S\}.\] For every \(g\), there is a unique \(h\) as drawn below; pointwise, \(h(a/s):=g(a)g(s)^{-1}\).

(iv)

For the map \(f:A\to S^{-1}A\), one has:

  • If \(s\in S\), then \(f(s)\) is a unit in \(S^{-1}A\).

  • \(f(a)=0\) implies \(as=0\) for some \(s\in S\).

  • Every element of \(S^{-1}A\) is of the form \(f(a)+f(s)^{-1}\).

These properties determine the initial object in (iii) uniquely up to isomorphism.

Example 5

If \(\pp<A\) is prime, then \(S=A\setminus\pp\) is multiplicatively closed. We write \(S^{-1}A\) as \(A_{\pp}\). The set \(\mm:=\{a/s\mid a\in\pp,\ s\in S\}\) is an ideal. If \(\aa\nsubseteq\mm\), there exists \(b/t\in\aa\) with \(b/t\notin\mm\). Hence \(b\notin\pp\), so \(b\) is a unit. Thus \(A_{\pp}\) is a local ring.

Localization can be attempted on \(A\)-modules in exactly the same way. For an \(A\)-module \(M\), let \[S^{-1}M:=\{(m,s)\mid m\in M,\ s\in S\}/{\sim}.\]

For \(f:M\to N\), one has \(S^{-1}f:S^{-1}M\to S^{-1}N\), \(m/s\mapsto f(m)/s\).

Proposition 6

(i)

\(S^{-1}\) is an exact functor.

(ii)

\(S^{-1}(N+P)=S^{-1}N+S^{-1}P\).

(iii)

\(S^{-1}(N\cap P)=S^{-1}N\cap S^{-1}P\).

(iv)

\(S^{-1}(M/N)\cong S^{-1}M/S^{-1}N\).

Here \(N,P\) are \(A\)-submodules of \(M\).

A property \(P\) of an \(A\)-module \(M\) is a local property if \[(M\text{ satisfies }P)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (M_{\pp}\text{ satisfies }P\text{ for every prime }\pp).\]

Example 6 — Local properties

(i)

\(M=0\Longleftrightarrow M_{\pp}=0\Longleftrightarrow M_{\mm}=0\) for every maximal \(\mm\). To see this, let \(x\in M\), \(x\ne0\), and \(\aa=\Ann(x)\), say \(\aa\subseteq\mm\). Then \(x/1\in M_{\mm}\) and \(x/1=0\), so \(x\) is killed by some element in \(A\setminus\mm\).

(ii)

A map \(\varphi:M\to N\) is injective if and only if \(\varphi_{\pp}:M_{\pp}\to N_{\pp}\) is injective, if and only if \(\varphi_{\mm}:M_{\mm}\to N_{\mm}\) is injective. Indeed, \(\ker\varphi=0\Longleftrightarrow\ker\varphi_{\pp}=0\Longleftrightarrow\ker\varphi_{\mm}=0\).

(iii)

Surjectivity of \(\varphi:M\to N\) is also a local property.

Extended and contracted ideals

Proposition 7

(i)

Every ideal in \(S^{-1}A\) is extended.

(ii)

For an ideal \(\aa<A\),

\[\aa^{ec}=\bigcup_{s\in S}(\aa:s).\] Consequently, \(\aa^e=(1)\) if \(\aa\) meets \(S\).

(iii)

\(\aa\in\mathcal C\), the set of contracted ideals, if and only if no element of \(S\) is a zero-divisor in \(A/\aa\).

(iv)

Prime ideals of \(S^{-1}A\) correspond to prime ideals of \(A\) not meeting \(S\).

(v)

\(S^{-1}\) commutes with finite sums, products, intersections, and radicals.

Proof. (i) If \(\bb\) is an ideal in \(S^{-1}A\) and \(x/s\in\bb\), then \(x/1\in\bb\), so \(x\in\bb^c\). Hence \(x/s\in\bb^{ce}\). Since \(\bb\supseteq\bb^{ce}\), we obtain \(\bb=\bb^{ce}\).

(ii) One has \[\begin{aligned} x\in\aa^{ec}=(S^{-1}\aa)^c &\Longleftrightarrow x/1=b/t\quad\text{for some }b\in\aa,\ t\in S\\ &\Longleftrightarrow(xt-b)u=0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow xtu\in\aa\qquad(tu\in S)\\ &\Longleftrightarrow x\in\bigcup_{s\in S}(\aa:s). \end{aligned}\] (iii) \(\aa\in\mathcal C\Longleftrightarrow\aa^{ec}\subseteq\aa\Longleftrightarrow(sx\in\aa\text{ for some }s\in S\Rightarrow x\in\aa)\). In other words, we can extend \(\aa\), cancel \(s\), and contract. This is equivalent to no \(s\in S\) being a zero-divisor in \(A/\aa\).

(iv) If \(\qq\) is prime in \(S^{-1}A\), then \(\qq^c\) is clearly prime. If \(\pp\) is prime in \(A\), then \(A/\pp\) is an integral domain. Let \(\overline S\) be the image of \(S\) in \(A/\pp\). Then \[S^{-1}A/S^{-1}\pp\cong\overline S^{-1}(A/\pp),\] which is either zero or contained in the field of fractions of \(A/\pp\), hence an integral domain.

Thus \(S^{-1}\pp\) is prime or \((1)\), and \(S^{-1}\pp=(1)\) if and only if \(S\cap\pp\ne\varnothing\).

(v) Exercise.

Corollary 8

(i)

If \(R\) is the nilradical of \(A\), then \(S^{-1}R\) is the nilradical of \(S^{-1}A\).

(ii)

If \(\pp\) is prime in \(A\), then primes in \(A_{\pp}\) correspond to primes in \(A\) contained in \(\pp\).

(iii)

If \(M\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module, then \(S^{-1}(\Ann M)=\Ann(S^{-1}M)\). Note that \[S^{-1}(\Ann(M+N))=S^{-1}(\Ann M\cap\Ann N) =\Ann(S^{-1}(M+N)).\] Thus it is enough to check the result for \(M\) generated by a single element.

(iv)

For \(f:A\to B\), a prime \(\pp\) is contracted if and only if \(\pp^{ec}=\pp\).
excerptHtml: Recall the construction of \(\Q\) from \(\Z\): \[\Q:=\{(x,y)\in\Z\times\Z\}/{\sim},\qquad (x_1,y_1)\sim(x_2,y_2)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ x_1y_2-y_1x_2=0.\]

title: Primary Decomposition and Uniqueness
html:
Primary decomposition

Definition 9

An ideal \(\qq<A\) is primary if \[xy\in\qq\ \Longleftrightarrow\ x\in\qq\text{ or }y\in\qq\text{ or }x,y\in\rad(\qq).\] Equivalently, every zero-divisor in \(A/\qq\) is nilpotent. If \(\rad(\qq)=\pp\), then \(\qq\) is \(\pp\)-primary.

Claim

\(\rad(\qq)\) is the smallest prime ideal containing \(\qq\).

Proof.

If \(xy\in\rad(\qq)\), then \(x^ny^n\in\qq\) for \(n>0\). Hence \(x^n\in\qq\), \(y^n\in\qq\), or \(x^n,y^n\in\rad(\qq)\); thus \(x\) or \(y\) belongs to \(\rad(\qq)\).

Example 7

(i)

In \(A=\Z\), \((0)\) and \((p^n)\) are primary ideals.

(ii)

In \(A=\kk[x,y]\), let \(\qq=(x,y^2)\). Then \(A/\qq\cong\kk[y]/(y^2)\), whose zero-divisors are multiples of \(y\). Hence \(\qq\) is primary. Moreover, \(\rad(\qq)=(x,y)=\pp\) is prime, and \(\pp^2\subset\qq\subset\pp\). Thus not all primary ideals are powers of prime ideals.

(iii)

If \(\rad(\aa)\) is maximal, then \(\aa\) is primary. In particular, \(\mm^n\) is \(\mm\)-primary. Here \(A/\aa\) has only one prime ideal: \(\rad(\aa)=\mm\) implies that \(A/\aa\setminus\mm\) consists of units.

Remark

In \(\Z\), unique factorization gives \(n=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_n^{a_n}\), where \(n\in\Z\) and the \(p_i\) are primes. Equivalently, \[(n)=\prod_{i=1}^n(p_i)^{a_i}=\bigcap_{i=1}^n(p_i)^{a_i}.\] An appropriate generalization of this phenomenon to arbitrary rings requires replacing powers of primes by primary ideals. For certain rings, every ideal has an “almost” unique primary decomposition, \(\aa=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\qq_i\), where \(\qq_i\) is \(\pp_i\)-primary.

Definition 10

For an ideal \(\aa<A\), an expression \[\aa=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\qq_i,\qquad\qq_i\text{ is }\pp_i\text{-primary},\tag{*}\] is a primary decomposition of \(\aa\). The set \(\{\pp_i\}_{i=1}^n\) is the set of primes associated to \(\aa\).

Remark

If \(\qq_j\supseteq\bigcap_{k=1}^{\ell}\qq_{i_k}\), then \(\qq_j\) is redundant in (*). Henceforth we assume our primary decomposition is irredundant, or minimal.

Lemma 9

If the \(\qq_i\) are \(\pp\)-primary, then so is \(\bigcap_i\qq_i\).

Proof. We have \(\rad(\qq)=\rad(\bigcap_i\qq_i)=\bigcap_i\rad(\qq_i)\).

If \(xy\in\qq\) and \(y\notin\qq\), then there exists \(i\) with \(xy\in\qq_i\) and \(y\notin\qq_i\), so \(x\in\pp\).

Consequence.

If \(\aa=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\qq_i\) is a primary decomposition, we can assume that the primes \(\pp_i\) for which \(\qq_i\) is \(\pp_i\)-primary are all distinct.

Lemma 10

Let \(\qq\) be \(\pp\)-primary and \(x\in A\).

(i)

If \(x\in\qq\), then \((\qq:x)=A\).

(ii)

If \(x\notin\qq\), then \((\qq:x)\) is \(\pp\)-primary, and consequently \(\rad((\qq:x))=\pp\).

Proof. (i) is clear. For (ii), \(y\in(\qq:x)\Rightarrow xy\in\qq\). As \(x\notin\qq\), we get \(y\in\pp\). Thus \[\qq\subseteq(\qq:x)\subseteq\pp \ \Longrightarrow\ \rad(\qq)\subseteq\rad((\qq:x))\subseteq\rad(\pp) \ \Longrightarrow\ \rad((\qq:x))=\pp.\] If \(yz\in(\qq:x)\) and \(y\notin\pp\), then \(xyz\in\qq\), so \(xz\in\qq\) and hence \(z\in(\qq:x)\).

Theorem 11 — First uniqueness theorem

The associated primes in an irredundant primary decomposition depend only on \(\aa\).

Proof. Note that \[\rad((\aa:x))=\bigcap_i\rad((\qq_i:x))=\bigcap_{x\notin\qq_i}\pp_i.\] If \(\rad((\aa:x))\) is prime, then it equals \(\pp_j\) for some \(j\). Since the decomposition is irredundant, for every \(1\le i\le n\) there exists \(x_i\notin\qq_i\) with \(x_i\in\bigcap_{j\ne i}\qq_j\). This yields \(\rad((\aa:x_i))=\pp_i\). Therefore the \(\pp_i\) are precisely the primes of the form \(\rad((\aa:x))\), and hence depend on \(\aa\).

Lemma 12

Let \(S\) be a multiplicatively closed subset of \(A\) and \(\qq\) a \(\pp\)-primary ideal.

(i)

If \(S\cap\pp\ne\varnothing\), then \(S^{-1}\qq=S^{-1}A\).

(ii)

If \(S\cap\pp=\varnothing\), then \(S^{-1}\pp\)-primary ideals of \(S^{-1}A\) correspond to \(\pp\)-primary ideals of \(A\).

Proof. (i) If \(s\in S\cap\pp\), then \(s^n\in S\cap\qq\) for some \(n>0\), so \(S^{-1}\qq\) contains a unit.

(ii) If \(\qq\) is \(\pp\)-primary, then \(S^{-1}\qq\) is \(S^{-1}\pp\)-primary: \[\frac xs\frac yt\in S^{-1}\qq\ \Longrightarrow\ xy\in\qq \ \Longrightarrow\ x\in\qq\text{ or }y^n\in\qq \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac xs\in S^{-1}\qq\text{ or }\left(\frac yt\right)^n\in S^{-1}\qq.\] Also, \(\rad(S^{-1}\qq)=S^{-1}\rad(\qq)=S^{-1}\pp\). Similarly, one can show that if \(S^{-1}\qq\) is \(S^{-1}\pp\)-primary, then \(\qq\) is \(\pp\)-primary.

Isolated and embedded primes

Second uniqueness theorem.

Let \(\Sigma\) be a set of prime ideals associated to \(\aa\). Say \(\Sigma\) is isolated if \(\pp'\subseteq\pp\in\Sigma\Rightarrow\pp'\in\Sigma\). Set \[S=A\setminus\bigcup_{\pp\in\Sigma}\pp.\] Clearly \(S\) is multiplicatively closed. Further, \(\pp'\in\Sigma\Rightarrow\pp'\cap S=\varnothing\), while \(\pp'\notin\Sigma\Rightarrow\pp'\nsubseteq\bigcup_{\pp\in\Sigma}\pp\) by prime avoidance, since \(\pp'\nsubseteq\pp\) for every \(\pp\in\Sigma\). Thus \(\pp'\cap S\ne\varnothing\).

Let \(\{\pp_i\}_{i=1}^n\) be the primes associated to \(\aa\), and let \(\{\pp_{i_1},\ldots,\pp_{i_k}\}\) be its minimal elements under inclusion. Then \(\Sigma:=\{\pp_{i_j}\}_{j=1}^k\) is isolated. Hence \[(S^{-1}\aa)^c =\bigcap_{i=1}^n(S^{-1}\qq_i)^c =\bigcap_{j=1}^k(S^{-1}\qq_{i_j})^c =\bigcap_{j=1}^k\qq_{i_j}.\]

Therefore \(\bigcap_{j=1}^k\qq_{i_j}\) is determined only by \(\aa\). The primes minimal among \(\{\pp_i\}_{i=1}^n\) are called isolated primes; the rest are embedded primes.

Remark

One can generalize this to modules and prove analogous results. Briefly, for an \(A\)-module \(M\), set \[\Ass(M):=\{\pp<A\text{ prime}\mid\pp=\Ann(m),\ m\in M\}.\] The primes associated to \(\aa<A\) are elements of \(\Ass(A/\aa)\). We say \(N\) is a \(\pp\)-primary submodule of \(M\) if \(\Ass(M/N)=\{\pp\}\).

Lasker proved, using methods from elimination theory, that affine rings admit primary decomposition for all ideals. Noether later developed the notion of chain conditions and extended Lasker’s result to a wide range of rings satisfying these conditions. In her honour, these rings are named Noetherian rings.

title: Noetherian and Artinian Rings
html:
Noetherian modules

Definition 11

A module \(M\) is Noetherian (respectively, Artinian) if every ascending (respectively, descending) chain of submodules is eventually constant. A ring \(A\), viewed as a module over itself, is Noetherian (Artinian) if every ascending (descending) chain of ideals is eventually constant.

Definition 12

For a ring \(R\), let \[d:=\max\{n\mid\pp_0\subset\pp_1\subset\cdots\subset\pp_n,\ \pp_i\text{ prime in }R\}.\] Then \(d\) is the dimension of \(R\), written \(\dim(R)=d\).

Comment.

We shall focus on Noetherian rings, for Artinian rings will turn out to be Noetherian of dimension zero.

Example 8

(i)

\(\Z/n\Z\), as a \(\Z\)-module, is Artinian and Noetherian.

(ii)

\(\kk[x]\), being a PID, is Noetherian, but \((x)\supset(x^2)\supset(x^3)\supset\cdots\) forces it not to be Artinian.

(iii)

\(\kk[x_1,x_2,\ldots]\) is neither Noetherian nor Artinian.

(iv)
