If \(R\hookrightarrow K\), where \(K\) is the field of fractions of \(R\), then \(K\) is both Artinian and Noetherian, but \(R\) can be neither, as in (iii), which is merely a domain.

Proposition 13

\(M\) is Noetherian if and only if every submodule of \(M\) is finitely generated.

Proof. Suppose \(M\) is Noetherian and \(N\) is a submodule of \(M\). Set \[\Sigma=\{N_0\subseteq N\mid N_0\text{ is a finitely generated submodule}\}.\] Since \(0\in\Sigma\), this set is nonempty. Every chain in \(\Sigma\) is eventually constant, so

Zorn’s lemma gives a maximal \(N_0\in\Sigma\). If \(N_0\ne N\), choose \(x\in N\setminus N_0\); then \(N_0\subset N_0+(x)\), absurd.

Conversely, let \(M_1\subseteq M_2\subseteq\cdots\) be a chain of submodules. Then \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}M_i\) is a submodule of \(M\), hence is finitely generated, say by \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). If \(x_i\in M_{n_i}\), then for \(n=\max_i\{n_i\}\) one has \(M_n=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}M_i\).

Proposition 14

If \(0\to M'\to M\xrightarrow{\beta}M''\to0\) is exact, then \(M\) is Noetherian if and only if \(M'\) and \(M''\) are Noetherian.

Proof. If \(M\) is Noetherian, every chain in \(M'\) is a chain in \(M\), and a chain in \(M''\) corresponds to a chain in \(M\) containing \(M'\).

Conversely, let \(L\) be a submodule of \(M\). Let \(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n\) generate \(\beta(L)\) and \(\{y_j\}_{j=1}^m\) generate \(L\cap M'\). For \(x\in L\), write \[\beta(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n r_i x_i\qquad(r_i\in A,\ x_i\in M'').\] Since \(M/M'\cong M''\), write \(x_i=[\widetilde x_i]\), with \(\widetilde x_i\in L\), and \(\beta(x)=[x]\). Then \[x\equiv\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\widetilde x_i\pmod{M'},\qquad x-\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\widetilde x_i\in L\cap M'.\] Thus \(x-\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\widetilde x_i=\sum_{j=1}^m s_jy_j\), so \[x=\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\widetilde x_i+\sum_{j=1}^m s_jy_j\qquad(x\in L).\] Therefore \(\{\widetilde x_i\}_{i=1}^n\cup\{y_j\}_{j=1}^m\) generates \(L\), and \(M\) is Noetherian.

Corollary 15

(i)

If \(M_1,\ldots,M_n\) are Noetherian, then \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^n M_i\) is Noetherian.

(ii)

If \(M\) is finitely generated over Noetherian \(A\), then \(M\cong A^n/P\) is Noetherian.

(iii)

If \(\aa<A\) is an ideal of a Noetherian ring, then \(A/\aa\) is Noetherian.

(iv)

If \(\varphi:A\twoheadrightarrow B\) and \(A\) is Noetherian, then \(B\cong A/\ker\varphi\) is Noetherian.

(v)

If \(A\) is Noetherian, then \(S^{-1}A\) is Noetherian. In particular, for prime \(\pp\), \(A_{\pp}\) is Noetherian.

Theorem 16 — Hilbert’s basis theorem

If \(A\) is Noetherian, then \(A[x]\) is Noetherian.

Proof. Let \(\aa<A[x]\) be an ideal. Construct \(I=(\text{leading coefficients of elements in }\aa)\). Since \(I<A\), it is finitely generated, say by \(\{a_i\}_{i=1}^n\). For every \(1\le i\le n\), there exists \(f_i\in\aa\) with \(f_i=a_ix^{r_i}+\text{lower terms}\). Set \(r=\max_{1\le i\le n}\{r_i\}\), and let \(\aa':=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\subset\aa\).

Let \(f=ax^m+\text{lower terms}\in\aa\). Then \(a\in I\), so \(a=\sum_{i=1}^n u_ia_i\). If \(m\ge r\), then \(f-\sum_{i=1}^n u_if_ix^{m-r_i}\in\aa\) has degree less than \(m\). Proceeding in this way gives \(f=g+h\), with \(\deg g<r\) and \(h\in\aa'\).

Let \(M\) be the \(A\)-submodule of \(A[x]\) generated by \(1,x,\ldots,x^{r-1}\). Then \(\aa=(\aa\cap M)+\aa'\). The module \(M\) is finitely generated, hence so is \(\aa\cap M\). If \(\{g_i\}_{i=1}^k\) generates \(\aa\cap M\), then \(\{f_i\}_{i=1}^n\cup\{g_i\}_{i=1}^k\) generates \(\aa\).

Corollary 17

(i)

If \(A\) is Noetherian, then \(A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is Noetherian.

(ii)

A finitely generated algebra over Noetherian \(A\) is Noetherian.

Noether’s work on primary decomposition

Definition 13

An ideal \(\aa<A\) is irreducible if \(\aa=\bb\cap\mathfrak c\Rightarrow\aa=\bb\) or \(\aa=\mathfrak c\).

Proposition 18

Every irreducible ideal in a Noetherian ring is primary.

Proof. Let \(\aa<A\) be irreducible. Then \(\aa\) is primary if and only if \((0)\) is primary in the Noetherian ring \(A/\aa\). Let \(xy=0\), \(y\ne0\). Consider \(\Ann(x)\subseteq\Ann(x^2)\subseteq\cdots\). There exists \(n\) such that \(\Ann(x^n)=\Ann(x^{n+1})=\cdots\).

Claim: \((x^n)\cap(y)=(0)\). If \(a\in(y)\), then \(ax=0\); and if \(a\in(x^n)\), then \(a=bx^n\), so \(bx^{n+1}=0\). Hence \(b\in\Ann(x^{n+1})=\Ann(x^n)\), giving \(a=0\).

Since \(\aa\) is irreducible, so is \((0)\) in \(A/\aa\). As \(y\ne0\), we get \(x^n=0\). Thus \((0)\) is primary in \(A/\aa\).

Theorem 19

Every ideal in a Noetherian ring admits primary decomposition.

Proof. Set \(\Sigma=\{\aa<A\mid\aa\text{ is not a finite intersection of irreducible ideals}\}\). If \(\Sigma\ne\varnothing\), then, as every chain in \(A\) stabilizes, \(\Sigma\) qualifies for Zorn’s

lemma, which yields a maximal element \(\aa\). This ideal is reducible, so \(\aa=\bb\cap\mathfrak c\) with \(\aa\subset\bb\) and \(\aa\subset\mathfrak c\). By maximality, \(\bb,\mathfrak c\notin\Sigma\); they are finite intersections of irreducible ideals, and hence so is \(\aa\). This is absurd. Therefore \(\Sigma=\varnothing\).

Artinian rings

In the following chain of propositions we sketch why Artinian rings are a special kind of Noetherian ring, thereby justifying our focus on Noetherian modules.

(i)

In an Artinian ring every prime is maximal. If \(\pp\) is prime, then \(A/\pp\) is an Artinian integral domain. For \(0\ne x\in A/\pp\), there is some \(n\) with \((x^n)=(x^{n+1})\). Thus \(x^n=x^{n+1}y\). Since \(A/\pp\) is a domain, \(x^n\ne0\) and \(xy=1\). Hence \(A/\pp\) is a field and \(\pp\) is maximal.

(ii)

An Artinian ring has only finitely many maximal ideals. Define \[\Sigma=\left\{\bigcap_{i=1}^n\mm_i\ \middle|\ n\in\N,\ \mm_i\text{ maximal}\right\}.\] Since \(A\) is Artinian, every chain in \(\Sigma\) has a lower bound. By Zorn’s lemma, there exists a minimal \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n_0}\mm_i\in\Sigma\). For any maximal ideal \(\mm\), minimality yields \(\mm\cap(\bigcap_i\mm_i)=\bigcap_i\mm_i\).

Thus \(\bigcap_i\mm_i\subseteq\mm\), so \(\mm_i=\mm\) for some \(i\).

(iii)

The nilradical of an Artinian ring is nilpotent.

Theorem 20

If \(A\) is Artinian, then \(A\) is Noetherian and \(\dim(A)=0\).

Sketch. If \(A\) is Artinian, then \(\dim(A)=0\). Let \(\{\mm_i\}_{i=1}^n\) be the maximal ideals of \(A\). For some \(k\), \[\prod_{i=1}^n\mm_i^k\subseteq\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n\mm_i\right)^k =\bigl(\rad((0))\bigr)^k=0.\] Fact: If \(\prod_{i=1}^n\mm_i=0\), with the \(\mm_i\) maximal and not necessarily distinct, then \(A\) is Noetherian.

Indeed, \(A\) is Noetherian if and only if \(\mm_1\) and \(A/\mm_1\) are Noetherian. The latter is a field, hence Noetherian, so \(A\) is Noetherian if and only if \(\mm_1\) is Noetherian. Further, \(\mm_1\) is Noetherian if and only if \(\mm_1\mm_2\) and \(\mm_1/\mm_1\mm_2\) are Noetherian. Since \(\mm_2(\mm_1/\mm_1\mm_2)=0\), the quotient is an \(A/\mm_2\)-vector space. The module \(\mm_1\) is Artinian because \(A\) is Artinian; hence \(\mm_1/\mm_1\mm_2\) is an Artinian \(A/\mm_2\)-module, thus a finite-dimensional vector space. It is therefore a Noetherian \(A/\mm_2\)-module, and consequently a Noetherian \(A\)-module. Thus \(\mm_1\) is Noetherian if and only if \(\mm_1\mm_2\) is Noetherian.

Proceeding inductively to \(\mm_1\mm_2\cdots\mm_n=0\) yields the fact.

Remark

The converse is also true.
excerptHtml: A module \(M\) is Noetherian (respectively, Artinian) if every ascending (respectively, descending) chain of submodules is eventually constant. A ring \(A\), viewed as a module over itself, is Noetherian (Artinian) if every ascending (descending) chain of ideals is eventually constant.

title: Integral Dependence
html:
We introduced rings and modules and various operations on them: sums, products, intersections, quotients, radicals, and localizations. We then introduced certain functors on \(\AMod\) and outlined their features. Two essential theorems to keep in mind are Cayley–Hamilton for finitely generated modules and Nakayama’s lemma.

If \(\varphi\in\End_{\AMod}(M)\) and \(\varphi(M)\subseteq\aa M\) for an ideal \(\aa<A\), then there exist \(a_i\in\aa\) such that \(\varphi^n+a_1\varphi^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\). For \(\varphi=\id\), there exists \(x\in A\) with \(x\equiv1\pmod\aa\) and \(xM=0\). Further, if \(\varphi=\id\), \(\varphi(M)=\aa M\), and \(\aa\) is contained in the Jacobson radical, then \(x\) divides \(1\); thus \(x^{-1}(xM)=M=0\).

We also introduced primary ideals and saw how ideals in Noetherian rings can be factorized, or decomposed, into primary ideals. Let’s introduce a little geometry.

Generalization of integers

Consider \(\Z\hookrightarrow\Q\), and let \(r/s\in\Q\). Then \[r/s\in\Z\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists f\in\Z[x]\text{ such that }f(r/s)=0\text{ in }\Q.\]

Indeed, if \(r/s\in\Z\), then \(s=\pm1\), and \(f(x):=x-sr\) works. Conversely, if \((r/s)^n+a_1(r/s)^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\), then \(r^n+a_1r^{n-1}s+\cdots+a_ns^n=0\).

Thus \(s\mid r^n\), a contradiction, since we can require \(\gcd(r,s)=1\). Hence \(y\in\Q\) is integral if and only if some \(f\in\Z[x]\) satisfies \(f(y)=0\). We generalize this concept to arbitrary rings.

Definition 14

Let \(A\) be a subring of \(B\). An element \(y\in B\) is integral over \(A\) if there exists \(f\in A[x]\) such that \(f(y)=0\) in \(B\). If every \(y\in B\) is integral over \(A\), we say \(B\) is integral over \(A\), or that \(A\) is integrally closed in \(B\). If \(A\) is a domain, we say \(A\) is integrally closed if it is integrally closed in its field of fractions \(K\).

Proposition 21

For rings \(A,B\) as above, the following are equivalent:

(i)

\(x\in B\) is integral over \(A\).

(ii)

\(A[x]\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module.

(iii)

\(A[x]\) is contained in a subring \(C\) of \(B\) that is a finitely generated \(A\)-module.

This is essentially a consequence of Cayley–Hamilton.

Proof. (i)\(\Rightarrow\)(ii): There exist \(a_i\in A\) with \(x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\). Thus \(1,x,\ldots,x^{n-1}\) generate \(A[x]\), since \(x^{n+r}=-(a_1x^{n+r-1}+\cdots+a_nx^r)\).

(ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iii): Set \(C=A[x]\).

(iii)\(\Rightarrow\)(i): Let \(\varphi\in\End_{\AMod}(C)\) be \(\varphi(y):=xy\) for \(y\in C\). Then \(\varphi(C)\subseteq C\), so Cayley–Hamilton gives \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) such that \(\varphi^n+a_1\varphi^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n\equiv0\). Evaluating at \(1\in C\) yields

\(x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\).

Corollary 22

(i)

If \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in B\) are integral over \(A\), then \(A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module, by induction on \(n\).

(ii)

Let \(\overline A:=\{x\in B\mid x\text{ is integral over }A\}\). Then \(\overline A\) is a subring of \(B\), called the integral closure of \(A\) in \(B\). Indeed, for \(x,y\in\overline A\), \(A[x,y]\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module by (i), and \(A[x\pm y]\) and \(A[xy]\) are contained in it.

(iii)

If \(A\subseteq B\subseteq C\) are rings, \(B\) is integral over \(A\), and \(C\) is integral over \(B\), then \(C\) is integral over \(A\).

(iv)

For rings \(A\subseteq B\), one has \(\overline{\overline A}=\overline A\).

Proof. For (iii), let \(x\in C\). There exist \(b_i\in B\) such that \(x^n+b_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+b_n=0\). Now \(A[b_1,\ldots,b_n]\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module, and \(A[b_1,\ldots,b_n,x]\) is a finitely generated \(A[b_1,\ldots,b_n]\)-module. Thus it is a finitely generated \(A\)-module, and it contains \(A[x]\).

For (iv), if \(x\in B\) is integral over \(\overline A\), apply (iii) to \(A\subseteq\overline A\subseteq B\) to conclude that \(x\) is integral over \(A\).

These observations culminate in the fact that the integral closure of \(A\) in \(B\) is integrally closed in \(B\), as expected!

Now we see how integrality behaves under a few operations on rings.

Proposition 23

Let \(A\subseteq B\) be rings, with \(B\) integral over \(A\).

(i)

If \(\bb<B\) is an ideal and \(\aa=\bb^c=A\cap\bb\), then \(B/\bb\) is integral over \(A/\aa\).

(ii)

If \(S\) is multiplicatively closed, then \(S^{-1}B\) is integral over \(S^{-1}A\). In fact, \(S^{-1}\overline A=\overline{S^{-1}A}\).

(iii)

For an integral domain \(A\), being integrally closed is a local property.

Proof. (i) For \(x\in B\), reduce the relation \(x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\), with \(a_i\in A\), modulo \(\bb\).

(ii) For \(x/s\in S^{-1}B\), the same relation gives \[(x/s)^n+(a_1/s)(x/s)^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n/s^n=0.\] Thus \(x/s\) is integral over \(S^{-1}A\). This proves \(S^{-1}\overline A\subseteq\overline{S^{-1}A}\). Conversely, if \(x/s\) is integral over \(S^{-1}A\), write \[(x/s)^n+(a_1/s_1)(x/s)^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n/s_n=0, \quad a_i\in A,\ s_i\in S.\] Set \(t=s_1\cdots s_n\). Then \[(ts)^n\sum_{i=0}^n(x/s)^i(a_{n-i}/s_{n-i}) =(xt)^n+b_1(xt)^{n-1}+\cdots+b_n=0,\qquad b_i\in A.\]

Hence \(xt\in\overline A\), so \(x/s=xt/st\in S^{-1}\overline A\), proving the reverse inclusion.

(iii) Let \(K\) be the field of fractions of \(A\), and use the usual inclusion \(A\hookrightarrow\overline A\). The ring \(A\) is integrally closed if and only if \(\overline A/A=0\), equivalently \[(\overline A/A)_{\pp}=0 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ (\overline A)_{\pp}/A_{\pp}=0 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \overline{A_{\pp}}/A_{\pp}=0,\] where the last equivalence follows from (ii).
excerptHtml: We introduced rings and modules and various operations on them: sums, products, intersections, quotients, radicals, and localizations. We then introduced certain functors on \(\AMod\) and outlined their features. Two essential theorems to keep in mind are Cayley–Hamilton for finitely generated modules and Nakayama’s lemma.

title: The Nullstellensatz and Affine Geometry
html:
Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz

Definition 15

A ring \(R\) is Jacobson if, for every prime \(\pp\), \[\pp=\bigcap_{\substack{\mm\supseteq\pp\\\mm\text{ maximal}}}\mm.\]

Example 9

(i)

A field \(\kk\) is a Jacobson ring.

(ii)

\(\Z\) is Jacobson: every nonzero prime ideal is maximal, and \((0)=\operatorname{nilradical}(\Z)=\bigcap_{\mm\text{ maximal}}\mm=\bigcap_{\pp\text{ prime}}\pp\).

(iii)

\(\kk[x]\) is Jacobson. It is a PID by the division algorithm. Every prime is generated by an irreducible polynomial and is therefore maximal. Since \(\kk[x]\) is a domain, as in (ii), \((0)=\bigcap_{\mm\text{ maximal}}\mm=\bigcap_{\pp\text{ prime}}\pp\).

The following lemma characterizes Jacobson rings.

Lemma 24

\(R\) is Jacobson if and only if, for prime \(\pp\) and \(0\ne b\in R/\pp\), whenever \((R/\pp)_{(b)}\) is a field, \(R/\pp\) is a field.

Proof. Suppose \(R\) is Jacobson. Then \(S:=R/\widetilde\pp\) is Jacobson for prime \(\widetilde\pp\). In \(S\), \[(0)=\bigcap_{\pp\text{ prime}}\pp=\bigcap_{\mm\text{ maximal}}\mm.\tag{*}\] Suppose \(S_{(b)}\) is a field. If \(\pp\) is a nonzero ideal and \(\pp\cap(b)=\varnothing\), then \((b)^{-1}\pp\) is a nonzero proper ideal of \(S_{(b)}\), absurd. Therefore every nonzero \(\pp\) meets \((b)\); but (*) gives \(b=0\), again absurd. Thus \((0)\) is maximal and \(S\) is a field.

Conversely, let \(\qq<R\) be prime and set \(I=\bigcap_{\pp\supseteq\qq,\ \pp\text{ prime}}\pp\). We must show \(I=\qq\). Suppose not, and choose \(f\in I\setminus\qq\). Set \[\Sigma=\{\pp\text{ prime in }R\mid\pp\supseteq\qq,\ f\notin\pp\},\] ordered by inclusion. By Zorn’s lemma there is a maximal \(\widetilde\pp\in\Sigma\). Clearly \(\widetilde\pp\) is not a maximal ideal, as \(f\) is in every maximal ideal containing \(\qq\). Hence \(S:=R/\widetilde\pp\) is not a field, but \(S_{(f)}\) is a field, since \(\widetilde\pp\) is maximal in \(R_{(f)}\). This is a contradiction.

Theorem 25 — Nullstellensatz, strong version

Let \(R\) be a Jacobson ring and \(S\) a finitely generated \(R\)-algebra. Then:

(i)

\(S\) is a Jacobson ring.

(ii)

If \(\nn<S\) is maximal, then \(\mm:=\nn\cap R\) is maximal in \(R\), and \(S/\nn\) is a finite field extension of \(R/\mm\).

Lemma 26

Let \(A\subseteq B\) be domains, with \(B\) integral over \(A\). Then \(B\) is a field if and only if \(A\) is a field.

Proof. Let \(A\) be a field and \(y\in B\). Write \(y^n+a_1y^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0\), \(a_i\in A\). As \(B\) is an integral domain, \(a_n\ne0\), so \(a_n\) is a unit. Hence \[-a_n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^n y^i a_{n-i} =y\bigl(-a_n^{-1}(y^{n-1}+a_1y^{n-2}+\cdots+a_{n-1})\bigr)-1=0.\] Thus \(y^{-1}=-a_n^{-1}(y^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1})\),

and \(B\) is a field. Conversely, if \(B\) is a field and \(x\in A\), then \(x^{-1}\in B\) is integral over \(A\). Thus \(x^{-m}+a_1x^{-m+1}+\cdots+a_m=0\), with \(a_i\in A\). Therefore \[x^{-1}=-(a_1x^{-m+1}+\cdots+a_m)x^{m-1} =-(a_1+a_2x+\cdots+a_mx^{m-1})\in A.\] Hence \(A\) is a field.

Corollary 27

\(\qq<B\) is maximal if and only if \(\qq^c=\qq\cap A<A\) is maximal.

Proof. \(B/\qq\) is integral over \(A/\qq^c\). Since \(\qq,\qq^c\) are prime, the two quotients are domains.

Proof of the strong Nullstellensatz. Strategy. To show \(S\) is Jacobson, we must show that, for prime \(\pp<S\) and \(0\ne b\in S/\pp\), if \((S/\pp)_{(b)}\) is a field, then \(S/\pp\) is a field. The ring map \(R\to S\) induces \(R/\pp^c\hookrightarrow S/\pp\). Both quotients are domains. It therefore suffices to show that, for domains \(R\hookrightarrow S\), if \(b\in S\) and \(S_{(b)}\) is a field, then \(S\) is a field. We will also show that \(R\) is a field and \(S\) is a finite extension of \(R\), thereby proving both assertions at once. Proceed by induction on the number of generators of the algebra \(S\).

Base case. Suppose \(S\) is generated by one element \(t\). There is a map \(R[x]\to S\), sending \(x\) to \(t\), so \(S=R[x]/\mathfrak g\). If \(\mathfrak g=0\), then some \(b\in R[x]\) makes \(R[x]_{(b)}\) a field. Hence \(K[x]_{(b)}\) is a field, where \(K\) is the field of fractions of \(R\). But \(K[x]\) is a Jacobson domain, so the lemma, applied to \((0)\), would make \(K[x]\) a field, absurd.

Thus \(\mathfrak g\ne0\). Choose \(p(x)\in\mathfrak g\), \(p(x)=p_nx^n+\cdots+p_0\). In \(S\) one has \(p_nt^n+\cdots+p_0=0\). Consequently, \(S_{(p_n)}\) is integral over \(R_{(p_n)}\), so \(b/p_n\) is integral over \(R_{(p_n)}\). Clearing denominators gives \(q_mb^m+\cdots+q_0=0\). Since \(S\) is a domain, divide by enough powers of \(b\) to assume \(q_0\ne0\). Then \(S_{(b)}\) is integral over \(R_{(p_nq_0)}\), since \[0=\frac{q_mb^m+\cdots+q_0}{q_0b^m} =\left(\frac1b\right)^m+\frac{q_1}{q_0}\left(\frac1b\right)^{m-1}+\cdots+\frac{q_m}{q_0}.\] Because \(S_{(b)}\) is a field, \(R_{(p_nq_0)}\) is a field. Since \(R\) is a Jacobson domain, \(R\) is a field. As \(S=R[x]/\mathfrak g\), \(S\) is a finite extension of \(R\).

Inductive step. If \(S\) is an \(R\)-algebra generated by \(r\) elements, let \(S'\) be the \(R\)-subalgebra generated by \(r-1\) of them. By induction \(S'\) is Jacobson, and so is \(S\) by the base case. If \(\nn\) is maximal in \(S\), then \[R/(R\cap\nn)\xhookrightarrow{\ 1\ }S'/(S'\cap\nn) \xhookrightarrow{\ 2\ }S/\nn,\] where both 1 and 2 are finite field extensions.

Corollary 28

Let \(\kk\) be algebraically closed. Every maximal ideal of \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) has the form \(\mm_P=(x_1-a_1,\ldots,x_n-a_n)\) for \(P=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\kk^n\).

Proof. Since \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mm_P\cong\kk\), \(\mm_P\) is maximal. If \(\nn\) is maximal in \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), then \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\nn\) is algebraic over \(\kk/(\nn\cap\kk)=\kk\). Since \(\kk\) is algebraically closed, \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\nn=\kk\). Let \(a_i=[x_i]\) in this quotient and \(P=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). Then \(\mm_P\subseteq\nn\). Since \(\mm_P\) is maximal, \(\nn=\mm_P\).

A little geometry

Consider the two objects \(\kk^n\) and \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). To \(I\subseteq\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) associate \[Z(I):=\{P\in\kk^n\mid f(P)=0\text{ for every }f\in I\}.\]

Clearly \(Z(I)=Z((I))\). Sets of this form are algebraic sets of \(\kk^n\). For ideals \(\{J_i\}_i\) of \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \[\bigcap_i Z(J_i)=Z\left(\bigcup_i J_i\right),\qquad \bigcup_{i=1}^n Z(J_i)=Z\left(\prod_{i=1}^n J_i\right).\] On an algebraic set \(X\), declaring algebraic subsets of \(X\) to be closed defines the Zariski topology.

For a subset \(X\subseteq\kk^n\), set \(I(X):=\{f\in\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\mid f(P)=0\text{ for every }P\in X\}\). Clearly \(I(X)\) is an ideal. For algebraic \(X\), define its coordinate ring, also called an affine ring, by \(A(X):=\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I(X)\).

If \(f\in A(X)\) and \(f^n\equiv0\), then \(f^n(P)=0\) for all \(P\in X\). Since \(\kk\) is a domain, \(f\equiv0\). Thus \(\{0\}\) is the only nilpotent element in \(A(X)\), and \(I(X)=\rad(I(X))\). Such ideals are called radical ideals.

Theorem 29 — Nullstellensatz, weak version

Let \(\kk\) be algebraically closed and \(I\) an ideal in \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Then \[I(Z(\aa))=\rad(\aa).\]

Proof. Since all maximal ideals of \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) are of the form \(\mm_P\), and these are maximal, points of \(\kk^n\) correspond to maximal ideals of \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Hence \[I(Z(\aa))=\bigcap_{P\in Z(\aa)}\mm_P =\bigcap_{\substack{\mm\supseteq\aa\\\mm\text{ maximal}}}\mm =\bigcap_{\substack{\pp\supseteq\aa\\\pp\text{ prime}}}\pp =\rad(\aa),\] since \(\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is Jacobson.

Remark

Clearly \(Z(I(X))=X\). Thus we have the correspondences \[\begin{aligned} \text{algebraic sets}&\longleftrightarrow\text{radical ideals}\\ &\longleftrightarrow\text{quotients of }\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\text{ by radical ideals}\\ &\longleftrightarrow\text{coordinate rings}. \end{aligned}\]

Definition 16

Let \(X\subseteq\kk^m\) and \(Y\subseteq\kk^n\) be algebraic sets. A map \[F:\kk^m\to\kk^n,\qquad (a_1,\ldots,a_m)\mapsto(f_1(a_1,\ldots,a_m),\ldots,f_n(a_1,\ldots,a_m)),\] where \(f_i\in\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_m]\), is a morphism of \(X\) to \(Y\) if \(F|_X:X\to Y\).

Given \(F:X\to Y\), we have \[F^{\#}:\kk[y_1,\ldots,y_n]\longrightarrow\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_m], \qquad y_i\longmapsto f_i(x_1,\ldots,x_m).\] This induces \(F^{\#}:A(X)\to A(Y)\). With \(X\mapsto A(X)\) and \(F\mapsto F^{\#}\), we obtain an equivalence of categories:

\[\boxed{\text{algebraic sets}\ \longleftrightarrow\ \text{reduced }\kk\text{-algebras}}\] thereby giving us a bridge between algebra and geometry!
excerptHtml: A ring \(R\) is Jacobson if, for every prime \(\pp\), \[\pp=\bigcap_{\substack{\mm\supseteq\pp\\\mm\text{ maximal}}}\mm.\]

title: The Spectrum of a Ring
html:
Spectrum of a ring

Throughout, \(A\) is a commutative ring.

Definition 17

(i)

\(\Spec(A):=\{\pp\mid\pp\text{ is prime in }A\}\). In particular, \(\Spec(0)=\varnothing\).

(ii)

For an ideal \(I<A\), set \[V(I):=\{\pp\in\Spec(A)\mid I\subseteq\pp\},\qquad D(f):=A\setminus V((f))\quad(f\in A).\]

Proposition 30

For ideals \(I,J<A\):

(i)

\(V(I)\cup V(J)=V(I\cap J)\).

(ii)

\(\bigcap_{\lambda}V(I_{\lambda})=V(\sum_{\lambda}I_{\lambda})\).

(iii)

\(V(A)=\varnothing\) and \(V(0)=\Spec(A)\).

Proof. (i) If \(I\cap J\subseteq\pp\), then either \(I\subseteq\pp\) or \(J\subseteq\pp\). Clearly \(V(I)\cup V(J)\subseteq V(I\cap J)\).

(ii) If \(\pp\in\bigcap_{\lambda}V(I_{\lambda})\), then \(I_{\lambda}\subseteq\pp\) for every \(\lambda\), so \(\sum_{\lambda}I_{\lambda}\subseteq\pp\). Conversely, \(\pp\in V(\sum_{\lambda}I_{\lambda})\) implies \(\sum_{\lambda}I_{\lambda}\subseteq\pp\), and therefore \(I_{\lambda}\subseteq\pp\) for every \(\lambda\).

The proposition gives a topology on \(\Spec(A)\) whose closed subsets are the \(V(I)\), for ideals \(I<A\). In particular, \(D(f)\) is open for every \(f\in A\). These are the distinguished open sets,

and \(\{D(f)\}_{f\in A}\) forms a basis for this topology, called the Zariski topology.

Lemma 31

\(\{\pp\}\subseteq\Spec(A)\) is closed if and only if \(\pp\) is maximal.

Proof. \(\{\pp\}\) is closed if and only if \(\{\pp\}=V(I)\) for an ideal \(I<A\). This is equivalent to \(I\subseteq\pp\) and \(I\nsubseteq\qq\) for prime \(\qq\ne\pp\), and hence to \(\pp\) being maximal.

Remark

Not all points of \(\Spec(A)\) are closed, so \(\Spec(A)\) cannot be Hausdorff. Closed points of \(\Spec(A)\) correspond to maximal ideals of \(A\).

For \(A=\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\), with \(\kk\) algebraically closed, Nullstellensatz gives the correspondences \[\begin{aligned} \text{maximal ideals of }A &\longleftrightarrow(x-\alpha_1,\ldots,x-\alpha_n),\quad\alpha\in\kk^n\\ &\longleftrightarrow\text{closed points of }A\\ &\longleftrightarrow\text{maximal ideals of }\kk[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\text{ containing }I\\ &\longleftrightarrow\{\alpha\in\kk^n\mid p(\alpha)=0,\ p\in I\}. \end{aligned}\]

Example 10

(i)

\(\Spec(\C[x])=:\mathbb A^1_{\C}\) has primes \((0)\) and \((x-a)\), \(a\in\C\). Closed points correspond to \(a\in\C\), \(a\ne0\). The point \(0\) is not closed; in fact, \(\overline{\{0\}}=\mathbb A^1_{\C}\). Such points are called generic.

(ii)

\(\Spec(\Z)=\{(0),p\Z\mid p\text{ prime}\}\).

(iii)

\(\Spec(\kk[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))=\{(\epsilon)\}\).

Table of analogies

Algebra Geometry
Ring \(A\) \(\Spec A\)
Prime ideals Points of \(\Spec(A)\)
Maximal ideals Closed points of \(\Spec(A)\)
\(a\in A\) Regular function on \(\Spec(A)\): \(a([\pp]):=a\pmod\pp\)
\(a\in\pp\) Functions that vanish at \([\pp]\)
\(V(I)\) Vanishing set of \(I\)
\(D(f)\) Nonvanishing domain of \(f\)

Example 11 — More examples

(i)

In \(\Spec(\kk[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))\), \(\epsilon([(\epsilon)])=0\), but \(\epsilon\ne0\). Thus \(f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in\Spec A\) does not imply \(f\equiv0\).

(ii)

\(\Spec(\R[x])=\{(0),(x-a),(x^2+ax+b)\}\). Pictorially it looks like a folding of the complex plane.

Let \(\varphi:A\to B\) be a ring homomorphism. It induces \(f=\Spec(\varphi):\Spec(B)\to\Spec(A)\).

Claim

\(f\) is continuous, so \(\Spec\) is a functor.

Proof. For \(V(I)\) in \(\Spec(A)\), \[\begin{aligned} f^{-1}(V(I)) &=\{\qq\in\Spec(B)\mid\varphi^{-1}(\qq)\in V(I)\}\\ &=\{\qq\in\Spec(B)\mid\qq\in\varphi(V(I))\}\\ &=\{\qq\in\Spec(B)\mid\qq\in V(I^e)\} =V(I^e). \end{aligned}\]
excerptHtml: \(\Spec(A):=\{\pp\mid\pp\text{ is prime in }A\}\). In particular, \(\Spec(0)=\varnothing\).

title: Sheaves, Stalks, and Ringed Spaces
html:
Sheaves

Definition 18

Let \(X\) be a topological space. A presheaf \(\mathcal F\) consists of:

(i)

An abelian group \(\mathcal F(U)\) for every open \(U\subseteq X\).

(ii)

For open \(V\subseteq U\), a group morphism \(\rho_{UV}:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F(V)\) such that, for open \(W\subseteq V\subseteq U\), \(\rho_{VW}\circ\rho_{UV}=\rho_{UW}\).

Definition 19

A presheaf \(\mathcal F\) is a sheaf if, for \(U=\bigcup_i U_i\), the sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathcal F(U)\xrightarrow{d_0}\prod_i\mathcal F(U_i) \xrightarrow{d_1}\prod_{i,j}\mathcal F(U_i\cap U_j)\] is exact, where \(d_0:s\mapsto s|_{U_i}\) and

\(d_1:\prod_i s_i\mapsto s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}-s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\). Here \(\ker d_0=0\) is uniqueness, and \(\operatorname{im}d_0=\ker d_1\) is gluing.

Definition 20

The stalk of \(\mathcal F\) at \(p\), denoted \(\mathcal F_p\), is \[\{(f,U)\mid p\in U,\ f\in\mathcal F(U)\}/{\sim},\] where \((f,U)\sim(g,V)\) if there exists \(W\subset U,V\), \(p\in W\), with \(\rho_{UW}f=\rho_{VW}g\). These are germs at \(p\).

Remark

One can also set \(\mathcal F_p:=\operatorname{colim}_{p\in U}\mathcal F(U)\).

Definition 21

A poset \((S,\ge)\) is filtered if, for every \(x,y\in S\), there exists \(z\) such that \(x,y\ge z\). More generally, a category \(C\) is filtered if:

(i)

For \(x,y\in C\), there exists \(z\) with arrows \(x\to z\) and \(y\to z\).

(ii)

For every \(u,v:x\to y\), there exists \(w:y\to z\) such that \(w\circ u=w\circ v\).

Suppose \(\mathcal I\) is a filtered indexing category. Any diagram indexed by \(\mathcal I\) has the following colimit:

\[\varinjlim_{i\in\mathcal I}A_i =\left\{(a_i,i)\in\coprod_{i\in\mathcal I}A_i\right\}/{\sim},\] where \((a_i,i)\sim(a_j,j)\) if there exist \(f:A_i\to A_k\) and \(g:A_j\to A_k\) with \(f(a_i)=g(a_j)\). Thus \(\mathcal F_p=\varinjlim_{p\in U}\mathcal F(U)\).

For a sheaf \(\mathcal F\), one has \(\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F_p\), \(s\mapsto s_p\), for \(p\in U\).

Lemma 32

If \(s,t\in\mathcal F(X)\) and \(s_x=t_x\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(s=t\).

Proof. Without loss of generality, assume \(t=0\). For every \(x\in X\), there exists \(U_x\) such that \(s|_{U_x}=0\). Hence \(s\equiv0\) by the uniqueness axiom of \(\mathcal F\).

Morphisms of (pre)sheaves.

A morphism \(\alpha:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\) is a collection of group morphisms \(\alpha(U):\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\) for every open \(U\subseteq X\).

Sheafification.

Given a presheaf \(\mathcal F\), there exists a unique sheaf \(\mathcal F^+\) with \(\theta:\mathcal F\to\mathcal F^+\) such that, for every \(\alpha:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\) of presheaves, there is a unique \(\widetilde\alpha\) making the diagram commute.

\[\mathcal F^+(U):=\left\{ f:U\to\coprod_{x\in U}\mathcal F_x\ \middle|\ \begin{array}{l} \text{for every }x\in U\text{ there exist }x\in V,\ s\in\mathcal F(V)\\ \text{such that }f(x)=s_x\text{ for every }x\in V \end{array}\right\}.\]

Ringed topological spaces

Definition 22

(i)

\((X,\mathcal O_X)\) is a ringed topological space if \(X\in\mathsf{Top}\) and \(\mathcal O_X\) is a sheaf of rings such that \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\) is a local ring for every \(x\in X\). Here \(\mathcal O_X\) is the structure sheaf, and \(\mathcal O_{X,x}/\mm_x\) is the residue field.

(ii)

A morphism \((f,f^{\#}):(X,\mathcal O_X)\to(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\) of ringed topological spaces consists of a continuous \(f:X\to Y\) and a sheaf map \(f^{\#}:\mathcal O_Y\to f_*\mathcal O_X\), where \(f_*\mathcal F(V):=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V))\), such that \[f_x^{\#}:\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}\longrightarrow f_*\mathcal O_{X,x}\] is a local homomorphism, that is, \(f_x^{\#}(\mm_{f(x)})\subseteq\mm_x\).

(iii)

\((f,f^{\#})\) is an open (closed) immersion if \(f\) is an open (closed) embedding and \(f_x^{\#}\) is an isomorphism for every \(x\in X\).

For \(X=\Spec(A)\), define \(\mathcal O_X(D(f)):=A_f\). On the left these are functions where \(f\) does not vanish; on the right is the ring in which \(f\) is invertible.

Lemma 33

\(V(I)\subseteq V(J)\) if and only if \(J\subseteq\sqrt I\).

Also, \(D(g)\subseteq D(f)\) implies \(g\in\sqrt{(f)}\), so there exist \(m\ge1\) and \(b\in A\) with \(g^m=fb\).

Thus \(f\) is invertible in \(A_g\), giving a map \(A_f\to A_g\). Hence \(\mathcal O_X\) is a presheaf. Note that \(\mathcal O_X(X)=A\), and for every \(\pp\in X\), \(\mathcal O_{X,\pp}:=A_{\pp}\) is local. Therefore \((X,\mathcal O_X)\) is a ringed topological space.

Definition 23

(i)

An affine scheme is something isomorphic to a ringed topological space \((X,\mathcal O_X)\) as above.

(ii)

A scheme is a ringed topological space with an open cover [unfinished in the source].
excerptHtml: For open \(V\subseteq U\), a group morphism \(\rho_{UV}:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F(V)\) such that, for open \(W\subseteq V\subseteq U\), \(\rho_{VW}\circ\rho_{UV}=\rho_{UW}\).

title: Hyperbolic Geometry
html:
Four questions lead us into hyperbolic geometry and its role in complex dynamics:

1.

What are hyperbolic surfaces?

2.

Why care about them?

3.

What is so special about them?

4.

What does this have to do with complex dynamics?

Let us address these one by one. Riemann’s brilliant insight is that geometry on a manifold requires a smoothly varying symmetric positive-definite bilinear form \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_p\) on \(T_pM\). This inner product leads to geodesics (lines), distances, angles, area, volume, curvature, and so on. In parallelisable spaces, defining length looks natural: glide along a curve and sum infinitesimal distances \(|\gamma'(t)|\), using \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\gamma(t)}\).

Constructing smooth sections of \(T^*M\otimes T^*M\) is also easy, since \(TM\cong M\times\mathbb R^n\).

Hyperbolic spaces are not like that. Moreover, we ask for more than just some metric: that can always be obtained by locally pushing the Euclidean metric to \(M\) and patching with a partition of unity, however abstract this may be. First, some context.

Theorem 26 — Uniformisation

Every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally isomorphic to one of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) (spherical), \(\mathbb C\) (Euclidean), or \(\mathbb H\cong\mathbb D\) (hyperbolic).

Thus a hyperbolic surface is a Riemann surface whose universal cover is \(\mathbb D\). We want to make it a Riemannian manifold in a way that preserves its Riemann-surface automorphisms. Start with \(\mathbb D\) or \(\mathbb H\), which differ by a Cayley transform.

Theorem 27 — Poincaré metric on \(\mathbb H\)

Up to multiplication by a constant, there is a unique Riemannian metric on \(\mathbb H\) invariant under every element of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb H)\).

In other words, every \(g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb H)\) is an isometry. This construction is a special case of a general correspondence.

A symmetric Riemannian metric has the form \(g_{11}\,dx\otimes dx+2g_{12}\,dx\otimes dy+g_{22}\,dy\otimes dy\). For a conformal map \(f=u+iv\), taking the \((dx,dy)\) tangent plane to the \((du,dv)\) tangent plane, \[du=u_x\,dx+u_y\,dy,\qquad dv=v_x\,dx+v_y\,dy, \qquad \begin{pmatrix}du\\dv\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}u_x&u_y\\v_x&v_y\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}dx\\dy\end{pmatrix}.\] This is the differential \(df\) in these coordinates. Hence \[\begin{align*} du\otimes du+dv\otimes dv ={}&(u_x^2+v_x^2)\,dx\otimes dx +2(u_xu_y+v_xv_y)\,dx\otimes dy\\ &+(u_y^2+v_y^2)\,dy\otimes dy. \end{align*}\] Conformality gives \(u_xu_y+v_xv_y=0\) and \(u_x^2+v_x^2=u_y^2+v_y^2\), motivating the following definition.

Definition 18 — Conformal metric

A metric \(ds^2=g_{11}dx^2+2g_{12}dx\,dy+g_{22}dy^2\), where \(ds^2\) denotes \(ds\otimes ds\), is conformal if \(g_{11}=g_{22}\) and \(g_{12}=0\).

Proof of Theorem 27. We know \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb H)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\). Given \(w_0\in\mathbb H\), choose \((az+b)/(cz+d)\) such that \[cw_0^2+(d-a)w_0-b=0,\qquad \left.\left(\frac{az+b}{cz+d}\right)'\right|_{w_0}=i.\] For such an automorphism, the derivative at \(w_0\) as a real-linear map is \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Thus \[df_{w_0}\left(c\frac\partial{\partial x}+d\frac\partial{\partial y}\right) =-d\frac\partial{\partial x}+c\frac\partial{\partial y}.\] Let \(g_0=g_{11}du^2+2g_{12}du\,dv+g_{22}dv^2\) be an invariant metric. Then \[\begin{align*} g_{w_0}\left(c\partial_x+d\partial_y,a\partial_x+b\partial_y\right) &=acg_{11}+bdg_{22}+2bcg_{12}\\ &=\widehat g_{w_0}\left(-d\partial_x+c\partial_y,-b\partial_x+a\partial_y\right), \end{align*}\] where \(\widehat g\) is the pushforward. Thus \(\widehat g_{w_0}=g_{22}dv^2-2g_{12}dv\,du+g_{11}du^2\), forcing \(g_{12}=0\) and \(g_{11}=g_{22}\). An invariant metric is therefore conformal, and unique up to constant multiplication.

A conformal metric is \(ds^2=\gamma(x+iy)^2(dx^2+dy^2)\), positive definite, so its norm is \(ds=\gamma(z)|dz|\). Invariance under \(f\) reads \(\gamma(f(z))|df(z)|=\gamma(z)|dz|\). Evaluate this on \(\partial_x\), which maps to \(v=u_x\partial_x+v_x\partial_y\): \[\gamma(z)\sqrt{dx^2(\partial_x,\partial_x)+dy^2(\partial_x,\partial_x)} =\gamma(f(z))\sqrt{dx^2(v,v)+dy^2(v,v)}.\] We obtain \(\gamma(f(z))=|f'(z)|^{-1}\gamma(z)\). It is a simple computational exercise to verify that \(\gamma(x+iy)=1/y\) satisfies this for all \(f\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\).

Using the Cayley transform \((z+i)/(z-i)\) transfers this to the invariant metric \(ds=2|dz|/(1-|z|^2)\) on \(\mathbb D\). Let us use it to construct a metric on \(\mathbb D/\Gamma\), with \(\Gamma<\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\) discrete.

Let \(S\) be hyperbolic, with universal cover \(P\colon\mathbb D\to S\). For \(y\in S\), let \(U_y\) be evenly covered. Choose \(V_a\subset\mathbb D\) so that \(P|_{V_a}\colon V_a\to U_y\) is biholomorphic, and set \[\gamma_a(P|_{V_a}(z))=\frac{\rho(z)}{|P'(z)|},\] where \(\rho(z)|dz|\) is the Poincaré metric on \(\mathbb D\). Let \(\{\psi_y\}_y\) be a partition of unity subordinate to

\(\{U_y\}_{y\in S}\). Patch by setting \[g=ds^2=\sum_y\psi_y\bigl(\gamma_a(P|_{V_a}(z))\bigr)^2(dx^2+dy^2).\] It remains to check that the pushforward is well-defined. Given \(x,a\in P^{-1}(y)\), normality of the covering gives a deck transformation \(\phi\colon\mathbb D\to\mathbb D\) with \(P=\phi\circ P\) and \(\phi(x)=a\). Thus \(P'(a)=P'(x)\phi'(a)\). As \(\phi\) is a Möbius transformation in \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)\), \[|\phi'(a)|=\frac{1-|x|^2}{1-|a|^2}=\frac{\rho(a)}{\rho(x)},\qquad \frac{\rho(a)}{|P'(a)|}=\frac{\rho(x)}{|P'(x)|}.\] Therefore \(\gamma_a(P|_{V_a}(z))=\gamma_x(P|_{V_x}(z))\), as required.

This metric defines distances. For a smooth or piecewise smooth path \(p\colon[0,1]\to S\), \[\operatorname{length}(p)=\int_pds=\int_0^1|p'(t)|\,dt, \qquad |p'(t)|=\sqrt{ds\otimes ds(p'(t),p'(t))}.\] The formula for smooth paths extends in the same way to piecewise smooth paths.

Definition 19 — Poincaré distance

For \(z_0,z_1\in S\), let \(\mathcal Z\) be the smooth or piecewise smooth paths joining them. Define \(\dist_S(z_0,z_1)=\inf_{p\in\mathcal Z}\operatorname{length}(p)\).

Let us prove an important fact about hyperbolic spaces with this newly endowed distance.

Lemma 28 — Completeness

The space \((S,\dist_S)\) is complete. Given any \(z_0,z_1\in S\), there is a path \(p\) with \(\operatorname{length}(p)=\dist_S(z_0,z_1)\); in other words, there is at least one geodesic.

Proof. First take \(S=\mathbb D\). We may assume \(z_0=0\) and \(z_1=r\in\mathbb R\), with \(0<r<1\), by applying an automorphism of \(\mathbb D\). Let \(p\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb D\) join \(0\) to \(r\), and write \(p(t)=(x(t),y(t))\). Then \[\sqrt{\frac4{(1-|p(t)|^2)^2}\bigl(dx^2(p',p')+dy^2(p',p')\bigr)} \ge\sqrt{\frac4{(1-x(t)^2)^2}\,dx^2(p',p')}.\] Thus \[\int_pds=\int_p\frac{2|dz|}{1-|z|^2} \ge\int_p\frac{2|dx|}{1-x^2} \ge\int_0^r\frac{2\,dx}{1-x^2} =\log\frac{1+r}{1-r}.\] Equality holds if and only if \(y(t)=0\). If \(\psi\) takes \(z_0,z_1\) to \(0,r\), then \[\dist_{\mathbb D}(z_0,z_1) =\dist_{\mathbb D}(\psi(z_0),\psi(z_1)) =\log\frac{1+|\psi(z_1)|}{1-|\psi(z_0)|}.\]

Hyperbolic balls in \(\mathbb D\) are Euclidean balls, generally with different centres. Thus on \(\widetilde S=\overline{B_r(0)}\), \(r<1\), the hyperbolic and Euclidean metrics give the same topology. Therefore \(\mathbb D\) is complete, and geodesics exist and are uniquely determined by two distinct points.

Now let \(S\) be any hyperbolic surface. For small enough \(\varepsilon\), the set \(\{z\in S:\dist_S(z,z_0)\le\varepsilon\}\) is compact. In fact, if \(P\colon\mathbb D\to S\) is the covering map with \(P(0)=z_0\), then the restriction of \(P\) over a sufficiently small ball is an isometry. Also \[\dist_S(P(z_0),P(z_1))\le\dist_{\mathbb D}(z_0,z_1),\] since a path in \(\mathbb D\) of length \(\ell\) projects to a path of the same length. A closed metric ball of radius \(r\) is compact, being a closed subset in \(\overline{B_{2r}(0)}\). For a Cauchy sequence \(\{x_n\}\), there is \(N\) such that its tail lies in \(\{z:\dist_S(x_N,z)\le\varepsilon\}\). It therefore converges.

Remark

Heine–Borel holds for hyperbolic spaces: \(N_r(z_0)=\{z\in S:\dist_S(z,z_0)\le r\}\) is compact for every \(r>0\).

An explicit geodesic construction is sketched below. Let \(B\) be a ball of local isometry about \(z_0\), and choose a path \(p\) to \(z_1\) with \(\operatorname{length}(p)=\dist(z_0,z_1)+\varepsilon\), possible by the definition of infimum.

Consider paths \(p_j'\) with lengths \(\dist(z_0,z_1)+\varepsilon_j'\), where \(\varepsilon_j'\le\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon_j'\to0\). If they cross \(\partial B\) at \(x_j\), choose an accumulation point \(x\). Join \(z_0\) to \(x\) by a geodesic, then repeat.

We care about hyperbolic surfaces because the other surfaces are well known: \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), \(\mathbb C\), \(S^1\times S^1\), and \(S^1\times\mathbb R\). This follows by checking fixed-point-free automorphisms of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) and discrete subgroups of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb C)\); their quotients give all spherical and Euclidean surfaces. They all have abelian fundamental group. Thus a surface with nonabelian fundamental group is immediately hyperbolic: hyperbolic surfaces abound.

Lemma 29

The surface \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{p,q,r\}\) is hyperbolic.

Proof. It is a Riemann surface with nonabelian fundamental group: \(\pi_1(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{p,q,r\})\cong\pi_1(\mathbb C\setminus\{p,q\})\cong\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z\).

Corollary 30 — Picard’s theorem

If a holomorphic map \(f\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) omits two distinct values, it is constant.

Proof. If \(f\) omits \(a,b\), it maps \(\mathbb C\) to the hyperbolic surface \(\mathbb C\setminus\{a,b\}\). It lifts to \(\widetilde f\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb D\).

Liouville’s theorem makes \(\widetilde f\) constant. Here we regard \(\mathbb D\subset\mathbb C\) without giving it its Poincaré metric.

In fact, hyperbolic surfaces are embedded as submanifolds in every Riemann surface. If \(\mathbb C\) or \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) covers \(S\), it only remains to consider the cylinder and torus. Removing one point there removes infinitely many points in \(\mathbb C\); the resulting cover sits in \(\mathbb C\setminus\{p,q\}\), or in \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{p,q,r\}\).

The following theorem makes hyperbolic surfaces special.

Theorem 31 — Pick’s theorem

Let \(f\colon S\to S'\) be holomorphic between hyperbolic surfaces. Then:

1.

\(f\) is a conformal isomorphism;

2.

\(f\) is a covering map;

3.

on every compact subset \(K\), \(f|_K\) is a contraction mapping.

Proof. For \(p\in S\), the differential is \(df_p\colon T_pS\to T_{f(p)}S'\). Distances depend on \(\|v\|\) and \(\|df_p(v)\|\), so it is natural to study the operator norm \(\|df_p\|\). Lift \(f\) to \(F\) as follows, with \(F(0)=0\), \(\pi_1(0)=p\), and \(\pi_2(0)=f(\pi_1(0))=f(p)=p'\).

Schwarz’s lemma gives \(|F'(0)|\le1\), hence \(\|DF_0\|\le1\). Indeed, \[\|DF_0\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|DF_0(v)\| =\sup_{\|a+ib\|=1}\|F'(z)(a+ib)\|=|F'(z)|.\] Here \(F'(z)\) is a real-linear map \(\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\), identified with a complex-linear map \(\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\). Therefore \(\|Df_p\|\le1\). If \(F\) is a conformal isomorphism, \(\pi_2\circ F\) is a covering map, so \(f\) is a covering map and \(\|Df_p\|=1\). Thus \(f\) is a local isometry; if \(\pi_1,\pi_2\) are biholomorphisms, it is a global isometry.

If \(f\) is not a covering map, then \(\|df_p\|<1\). The ratio \(\|df_p(v)\|/\|v\|\) is continuous in \(p,v\), being locally smooth in \(p\) and bounded linear in \(v\). Thus \[\sup_{p\in K,\ \|v\|=1}\|df_p(v)\|\le c_K<1.\] Enlarge \(K\) if necessary, for example to \(\overline{B_{2\diam(K)}(z_0)}\). For a path \(p\), \[\operatorname{length}(p)=\int_0^1\|p'(t)\|\,dt,\qquad \operatorname{length}(f\circ p)=\int_0^1\|Df_{p(t)}(p'(t))\|\,dt \le c_K\operatorname{length}(p).\] Hence \(\dist_{S'}(f(p),f(q))\le c_K\dist_S(p,q)\).

Hyperbolic surfaces matter in complex dynamics because they help identify spaces on which a family of functions is stable. More precisely:

Lemma 32

A family \(\mathcal F\) of holomorphic functions from \(S\) to \(T\) is normal.

We defer the proof of this lemma and other Montel-like lemmas. We will soon see how hyperbolic surfaces are integral to complex dynamics.
excerptHtml: Let us address these one by one. Riemann’s brilliant insight is that geometry on a manifold requires a smoothly varying symmetric positive-definite bilinear form \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_p\) on \(T_pM\). This inner product leads to geodesics (lines), distances, angles, area, volume, curvature, and so on. In parallelisable spaces, defining length looks natural: glide along a curve and sum infinitesimal distances \(|\gamma'(t)|\), using \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\gamma(t)}\).

title: Rational Dynamics on the Riemann Sphere
html:
Given a holomorphic map \(f\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\), one studies the iterates of \(f\). It is true that the poles and zeros of a holomorphic map determine the nature of \(f\) to a large extent, in the following sense.

Let dots denote zeros and crosses denote poles. Then \(f\) has a power-series expansion in a disc with radius as large as the distance to the pole nearest the centre. But if one wants to study iterates of \(f\), one must look at properties preserved by a change of coordinates: \[\varphi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}\sim f\quad\text{(dynamically)},\qquad \varphi\circ f^{\circ n}\circ\varphi^{-1} =(\varphi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1})^{\circ n}\sim f^{\circ n}.\] Zeros and poles are, after all, two points on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\): change coordinates via a Möbius transformation, and \(0,\infty\) go to other points.

Thus one must look for an invariant of \(f\) that is preserved even after a suitable change of coordinates.

Here \(\varphi\) changes coordinates, i.e. it biholomorphically changes the base space. One naturally expects the dynamics to be preserved. Investigation along these lines leads us to two natural invariants: fixed points and critical points (check!).

We shall base our study entirely on these invariants. Dynamics is essentially the study of taming the iterates of \(f\) on sets where minor changes in points lead to major changes in their iterated images. More precisely:

Definition 1 — Fatou set

Let \(f\colon S\to S\) be a holomorphic function on a Riemann surface \(S\). A point \(z\) belongs to the Fatou set \(F\) of \(f\) if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(z\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) is normal.

Definition 2 — Julia set

The set \(J=S\setminus F\) is defined to be the Julia set.

Motivations aside, when we say that we want to study the dynamics of \(f\) on \(S\), we essentially want to study the structure of the Fatou and Julia sets of \(f\). We propose to do this by studying the invariants mentioned above.

Definition 3 — Classification of fixed points

A fixed point \(f(\widehat p)=\widehat p\) is

  • attracting if \(|f'(\widehat p)|<1\);

  • repelling if \(|f'(\widehat p)|>1\);

  • indifferent if \(|f'(\widehat p)|=1\).

Here \(f'(\widehat p)\) means the derivative of the coordinate function of \(f\).

There is a natural dilemma at this juncture. The dynamics of \(f\) and \(f^{\circ n}\) must be the same, for if \(\{f^{\circ m}|_U\}_m\) is normal, so is \(\{f^{\circ mn}|_U\}_m\). Should we merely focus our study on the fixed points and critical points of \(f\), or should we pick a suitable iterate \(f^{\circ10000}\) and study its critical and fixed points? The following lemmas will help clear this dilemma.

Lemma 1 — Invariance lemma

\(z\in J\) if and only if \(f(z)\in J\).

Proof. It is enough to show \(z\in F\Longleftrightarrow f(z)\in F\). If \(z\in F\), then \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) is normal, so it is contained in a compact set \(K\subset\Hol(U,S)\).

Notice that \(f\circ K\) is compact in \(\Hol(U,S)\). For if \(C\subseteq S\) is compact and \(\{g_k\}_k\subset K\) converges uniformly on \(C\), then, since \(f\) is uniformly continuous on compact sets, an estimate \(|g_{k_0}(x)-g(x)|<\varepsilon\) for every \(k_0\ge N\) and \(x\in C\) ensures, after increasing \(N\) if necessary, that \[|f\circ g_{k_0'}(x)-f\circ g(x)|<\varepsilon \quad(k_0'\ge N',\ x\in C).\] Indeed, \(f\) is uniformly continuous on the compact set \(\overline{B_\varepsilon(g(C))}\). Thus \(\{f^{\circ(n+1)}|_U\}_n\) is normal, and hence \(f(z)\in F\).

Conversely, if \(f(z)\in F\), there is a neighbourhood \(V\) of \(f(z)\) on which \(\{f^{\circ n}|_V\}_n\) is normal. Since \(f\) is open, there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(z\) with \(f(U)\subseteq V\). Hence \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) is also normal, and \(z\in F\).

The Fatou and Julia sets are invariant under orbits. The next lemma makes this more explicit.

Lemma 2

\(J(f^{\circ n})=J(f)\).

Proof. By the previous lemma, it suffices to show \(F(f^{\circ n})=F(f)\). Certainly \(z\in F(f)\) implies \(z\in F(f^{\circ n})\). If \(z\in F(f^{\circ n})\), there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(z\) such that \(\{f^{\circ nm}|_U\}_m\subset K\subseteq\Hol(U,S)\), with \(K\) compact. Then \[\{f^{\circ m}|_U\}_m\subseteq\bigcup_{i=0}^{n-1}(f^{\circ i}\circ K) \subseteq\Hol(U,S),\] and this finite union is again compact.

It therefore does not matter which iterate of \(f\) one chooses to work with: the dynamics loses no information, so there is no compromise. What does it mean to work with fixed points of \(f^{\circ m}\)?

Definition 4 — Periodic orbits

Let \(f\colon S\to S\) be holomorphic. An orbit \(f\colon z_0\mapsto z_1\mapsto\cdots\mapsto z_m=z_0\), with all \(z_i\) distinct before returning to \(z_0\), is called a periodic orbit of period \(m\). Classifying fixed points of \(f^{\circ m}\) amounts to dealing with \[\lambda=(f^{\circ m})'(z_i)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}f'(z_i),\] often called the multiplier of the orbit.

We shall not deal separately with periodic orbits of different periods. We shall prove theorems for fixed points and expect the reader to extend the argument to their favourite iterate of \(f\). As far as we are concerned, our study, as proposed, will be complete by looking at period-\(1\) orbits (fixed points) and critical points. Before proceeding further, we explain the classification topologically.

Attraction, repulsion, and indifference

Attraction: multiplier \(|\lambda|<1\).

This is usually called topological attraction. Let us first state explicitly the intuitive idea of attraction to a point \(\widehat p\). A point \(\widehat p\in S\) is said to be attracting if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\widehat p\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) converges uniformly on \(U\) to the constant map \(z\mapsto\widehat p\).

Lemma 3

Let \(f(\widehat p)=\widehat p\), where \(f\in\Hol(S,S)\). Then \(|f'(\widehat p)|<1\) if and only if \(\widehat p\) is attracting.

Proof. Let \(\widehat f\) be the coordinate expression of \(f\) locally at \(\widehat p\), centred at \(\widehat p\). For simplicity assume \(\widehat f=f\). If \(f(0)=0\) and \(|\lambda|=|f'(0)|<1\), analyticity gives \(f(z)=\lambda z+O(z^2)\). Thus there is \(r_0>0\) such that \(|f(z)-\lambda z|=O(|z|^2)\) for \(z\in\mathbb D_{r_0}\), and \[|f(z)|\le |\lambda z|+C|z|^2\le (|\lambda|+C|z|)|z|.\] If \(z\in\mathbb D_{r_0}\) is small enough that \(|\lambda|+C|z|<1\), then \(f\) becomes a contraction mapping, proving what we want.

One can choose \(|\lambda|<c<1\) and \(0<r\le r_0\) with \(|\lambda|+Cr<c\). In particular, \(|\lambda|+C|z|<c<1\) for all \(z\in\mathbb D_r\). Hence \(|f(z)|<c|z|\), \(f(z)\in\mathbb D_r\), and \(|f^{\circ n}(z)|<c^n|z|\), so \(f^{\circ n}\to(z\mapsto0)\).

Conversely, if \(\widehat p\) is attracting, there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(f^{\circ n}(\mathbb D_\varepsilon)\subset\mathbb D_\varepsilon\). By Schwarz’s lemma, \(|(f^{\circ n})'(0)|<1\), so \(|f'(0)|<1\).

Notice that we need holomorphicity of \(f\) to conclude that \(|\lambda|<1\) is geometrically attracting.

Repulsion: multiplier \(|\lambda|>1\).

This is usually called topological repulsion. Let \(f(\widehat p)=\widehat p\). The point \(\widehat p\) is repelling if there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\widehat p\) such that, for every \(p\in U\setminus\{\widehat p\}\), there is \(N_p\) with \(f^{\circ n}(p)\notin U\) for every \(n\ge N_p\). In other words, all orbits except that of \(\widehat p\) eventually escape \(U\).

Lemma 4

\(|f'(\widehat p)|>1\) if and only if \(\widehat p\) is repelling.

Proof. If \(|\lambda|=|f'(\widehat p)|>1\), the Taylor expansion \(f(z)=\lambda z+O(z^2)\) gives \(f^{\circ k}(z)=\lambda^kz+O(z^2)\). Thus, for the corresponding open set in \(S\), the orbits of its elements eventually escape.

Conversely, if \(\widehat p\) is topologically repelling, the previous lemma implies \(|f'(\widehat p)|\not<1\), and hence \(|f'(\widehat p)|\ge1\). Thus \(f\) is locally univalent. There is a compact neighbourhood \(N\) of \(\widehat p\) such that all orbits of that neighbourhood escape \(N\), and \(f\colon N\to f(N)\) is a homeomorphism. Set \[N_k=\bigcap_{i=0}^{k}f^{-i}(N).\] This is the set of all points whose iterates up to \(k\) do not escape \(N\). By our choice of \(N\), \(\diam(N_k)\to0\) as \(k\to\infty\), and \(f(N_k)=N_{k-1}\cap f(N)\). For large \(k\), \(N_{k-1}\subset f(N)\), so \(f(N_k)=N_{k-1}\). Since \(f|_N\) is univalent, \(f\colon N_k\to N_{k-1}\) is a biholomorphism.

Let \(U_k\) be the component of \(N_k\) containing \(\widehat p\). Then \(f^{-1}\colon U_{k-1}\to U_k\) is a biholomorphism. Clearly \(U_k,U_{k-1}\) are hyperbolic, so by Pick’s theorem \(f^{-1}\) is a contraction mapping. Thus \(\widehat p\) is attracting for \(f^{-1}\), giving \(|\lambda^{-1}|<1\), and hence \(|\lambda|>1\).

Indifference: \(|\lambda|=1\).

This does not have an easy-to-visualise topological picture. We will deal with this case in detail in the post on parabolic points.

Having seen this, let us collect all points \(z\in S\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_n\) converges to an attracting point \(\widehat p\). This set is called the basin of attraction of \(\widehat p\). Such basins belong to the Fatou set; repelling points belong to the Julia set, as do indifferent points of certain kinds. Checking that basins of attraction belong to the Fatou set is a rather generic analysis.

If \(z\in\mathcal A(\widehat p)\), the basin of attraction, then \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_n\to z_0\). There is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(z_0\) with \(U\subset F(f)\), and some \(N\) such that \(f^{\circ N}(z)\in U\). Hence \(f^{\circ N}(z)\in F(f)\), and the invariance lemma gives \(z\in F(f)\).

Repelling points are to be placed in the Julia set. Let us introduce a subclass of fixed points, to be taken up in detail later.

Definition 5 — Parabolic fixed point

A fixed point \(f(\widehat p)=\widehat p\) is parabolic if \(|f'(\widehat p)|\) is a root of unity and \(f^{\circ n}\ne\id\) for every \(n\).

Lemma 5

Parabolic points belong to the Julia set.

Proof. Locally, \(f(w)=w+a_qw^q+a_{q+1}w^{q+1}+\cdots\), so \(f^{\circ k}(w)=w+ka_qw^q+\cdots\). Consequently, \[\left.\frac{d^q(f^{\circ k})}{dz^q}\right|_0=q!\,ka_q\longrightarrow\infty \qquad(k\to\infty).\] Thus \(\{f^{\circ n}\}_n\) cannot converge locally uniformly, for then the sequence of \(q\)th derivatives at \(0\) would also converge.

Therefore attracting basins lie in the Fatou set, while repelling and parabolic points belong to the Julia set.

In the next few posts we shall see our initial proposal—studying dynamics through fixed and critical points—in action. For now, let us briefly illustrate it when \(f\colon\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) is rational with \(\deg(f)\ge2\).

Dynamics of rational maps on the Riemann sphere

We shall see how the Julia set spreads across the sphere, its topological structure, and more.

First things first: is \(J\) nonempty?

Proposition 6 — Nonemptiness

\(J(f)\ne\varnothing\).

Proof. If \(J(f)=\varnothing\), there is a sequence \(\{n_j\}_j\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n_j}\}_j\) converges uniformly on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) to a rational map \(g\), since \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) is compact. For sufficiently large \(j\), \[\dist(f^{\circ n_j}(z),g(z))<\dist(\text{north pole},\text{south pole})=\pi \quad(z\in\widehat{\mathbb C}).\] Define \(H\colon I\times\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) by \(H(t,z)=\gamma_{g(z)\to f^{\circ n_j}(z)}(t)\), where \(\gamma\) is the unique geodesic path between those two points. Since \(\gamma_{a\to b}\) is continuous in both \(a\) and \(b\), \(H\) is continuous. Thus \(f^{\circ n_j}\) and \(g\) are homotopic. By Rouché’s theorem, their numbers of zeros and poles must be the same, giving \(\deg(f^{\circ n_j})=\deg(g)\). But \(\deg(f^{\circ n_j})\to\infty\) as \(j\to\infty\), a contradiction.

Before revealing the expansive nature of the Julia set, let us distinguish periodic orbits from eventually periodic orbits.

Definition 6 — Grand-orbit-finite points

For \(z\in S\), define \[\operatorname{GO}(z,f)=\{z'\in S:\operatorname{orbit}(z)\cap\operatorname{orbit}(z')\ne\varnothing\}.\] A point whose grand orbit is finite is called exceptional.

The set of all such points is denoted by \(\mathcal E(f)\) and called the grand-orbit-finite set. The set \(\operatorname{GO}(z,f)\) is the grand orbit of \(z\).

The reason for calling \(\mathcal E(f)\) grand-orbit-finite is evident. We now state the following lemma.

Lemma 7

\(|\mathcal E(f)|\le2\). All exceptional points are superattracting.

This sounds good! No?! Proof. For \(z\in\mathcal E(f)\), \(\operatorname{GO}(z,f)\) is a single periodic orbit; otherwise one can keep tracing back. For any \(\widehat z\in\widehat{\mathbb C}\), \(f^{-1}(\widehat z)\) has \(d\) preimages counted with multiplicity, since \[f(z)=\frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}=\widehat z \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P(z)-\widehat zQ(z)=0\] has \(d\) zeros counted with multiplicity. If the multiplicity of \(z_j\in f^{-1}(\widehat z)\) is greater than one, then \(z_j\) is critical: the order of the zero of \(f(z_j)-\widehat z\) is greater than one, so \(f'(z_j)=0=(f(z_j)-\widehat z)'\).

Write \(\operatorname{GO}(z,f)=\{a_0\mapsto a_1\mapsto\cdots\mapsto a_m=a_0\}\). Clearly all \(a_i\) are superattracting, so \(a_i\in F(f)\) and \(\mathcal E(f)\subset F(f)\). If \(|\mathcal E(f)|\ge3\), let \(U=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal E(f)\). Then \(U\) is hyperbolic and \(f(U)=U\), so \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) is normal. This gives \(U\subset F(f)\) and \(J(f)=\varnothing\), a contradiction.

Proposition 8 — Expansion

Let \(z\in J\). If \(N\) is a neighbourhood of \(z\), then \[\bigcup_{n\ge0}f^{\circ n}(N)\supseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal E(f).\] Equality holds for sufficiently small \(N\).

Proof. If \(U=\bigcup_{n\ge0}f^{\circ n}(N)\) omits three points, note that \(f(U)\subseteq U\). Since \(U\) is hyperbolic, \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) is normal, so \(z\in F(f)\), a contradiction. Thus \(|\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus U|\le2\). As \(f(U)\subseteq U\), the points in \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus U\) must belong to the grand-orbit-finite set. Finally, equality holds if \(N\subset\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal E(f)\).

Proposition 9 — Empty interior

If \(\operatorname{Int}(J)\ne\varnothing\), then \(J=\widehat{\mathbb C}\).

Proof. If \(\operatorname{Int}(J)\ne\varnothing\), there is a point \(z\) with a neighbourhood \(N\subseteq J\). By the invariance lemma, \(\bigcup_n f^{\circ n}(N)\subseteq J\). Since \(J\) is closed, \(J\supseteq\overline{\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal E(f)}=\widehat{\mathbb C}\), giving the assertion.

Recall that basins belong to the Fatou set: there open sets shrink, whereas for the Julia set, open sets expand to fill almost all of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\). Let us put these two concepts together.

Proposition 10 — Basin boundary equals Julia set

If \(\mathcal A\) is an attracting basin, then \(\partial\mathcal A=J\).

Proof. The Julia set expands open sets around it. If \(z\in J\) and \(N\) is a neighbourhood of \(z\), there is \(k_0\) with \(f^{\circ k_0}(N)\cap\mathcal A\ne\varnothing\). By invariance, \(N\cap\mathcal A\ne\varnothing\), so \(J\subseteq\overline{\mathcal A}\). Since \(J\cap\mathcal A=\varnothing\), \(J\subseteq\partial\mathcal A\).

Now let \(z\in\partial\mathcal A\). Every neighbourhood \(N\) of \(z\) meets both \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal A^c\). For \(z'\in N\cap\mathcal A\), \(f^{\circ n}(z')\) converges to a point, whereas this is not so for \(z''\in N\cap\mathcal A^c\). Thus there is a discontinuity (jump) across the boundary, and \(\partial\mathcal A\subseteq J\). Therefore \(J=\partial\mathcal A\).

Remark

This property essentially spells out the nature of the dynamics of \(f\). An attracting basin has connected components, or islands, separated by a thin set \(J\) (it has no interior). Along with these are the Fatou components of \(f\).

Let us analyse the topological structure of \(J\) further, for the nature of a boundary also reveals what it bounds.

Dense subsets of the Julia set

  • For \(z_0\in J\), \[J=\overline{\bigcup_{n\ge0}f^{-n}(z_0)}.\] Let \(N\) be a neighbourhood of a point \(z\in J\). Expand \(N\) until it hits a point \(w\in\widehat{\mathbb C}\). We may take \(w=z_0\), since \(z_0\notin\mathcal E(f)\). Thus \(f^{-n}(w)\cap N\ne\varnothing\), giving \(\overline{\bigcup_n f^{-n}(w)}\supseteq J(f)\). The reverse inclusion follows from invariance.

  • \(J\) has no isolated points. If \(J\) were finite, then \(J\subseteq\mathcal E(f)\), which is impossible since exceptional points are superattracting. If it is infinite, take a limit point \(z_0\). The set \(\bigcup_{n\ge0}f^{-n}(z_0)\) is dense in \(J\), hence \(J\) has no isolated points. If \(w\in J\) is isolated, take \(z_0\in J\) to be a limit point of \(\{f^n(w)\}_n\). This set cannot be perfect, since \(S\) is a locally compact, compact metric space. Choose \(z_0\notin\{f^n(w)\}_n\).

Remark

Since \(\bigcup_n f^{-n}(z_0)\) is dense in \(J\), for a neighbourhood \(N\) of \(z_0\) the set \(V=\bigcup_n f^{-n}(N)\) is dense and open. As the closed set \(J\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}\) is compact, choose a finite open cover \(\{N_{ij}\}_{i=1}^{M}\). Set \(V_{ij}=\bigcup_n f^{-n}(N_{ij})\); these sets are dense and open. Then \(\bigl(\bigcap_{i=1}^{M}V_{ij}\bigr)\cap J\) is a dense open subset of \(J\). Choose the sets \(N_{ij}\) with diameter less than \(1/j\). If \[z\in\left(\bigcap_j\bigcap_{i=1}^{M}V_{ij}\right)\cap J,\] again a dense set, then \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_n\) meets every possible \(N_{ij}\). Finally, the Lebesgue number lemma shows that \(\{z,f(z),f^2(z),\ldots\}\) is dense in \(J\) for every \(z\) belonging to a dense subset of \(J\).

Remark — Self-similarity

Another striking feature of the Julia set is that it repeats shapes and patterns infinitely often. Mathematically, \((J,z)\) is locally conformally isomorphic to \((J,z')\) if there are neighbourhoods \(N,N'\) of \(z,z'\), respectively, and a biholomorphism \(\varphi\colon N\to N'\) such that \(\varphi(z)=z'\) and \(\varphi(N\cap J)=N'\cap J\).

By density of the preimages of any \(z_0\in J\), the set of \(z\) such that \((J,z)\cong(J,z_0)\) is dense in \(J\), unless every backwards orbit \(z_0\leftarrow z_1\leftarrow z_2\leftarrow\cdots\) contains a critical point \(z_k\) of \(f\). Otherwise \(f\) is locally univalent and one can keep backtracking \(z_0\).
excerptHtml: Given a holomorphic map \(f\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\), one studies the iterates of \(f\). It is true that the poles and zeros of a holomorphic map determine the nature of \(f\) to a large extent, in the following sense.

title: Attracting and Repelling Fixed Points
html:
Let’s look at the local behaviour of a holomorphic map \(f\colon S\to S\), where \(S\) is a Riemann surface. For this, it would “suffice” to study the local behaviour at fixed points of \(f\). Recall that \(S\) decomposes into components of basins with fractal-like boundaries (elements of the Julia set). Our goal is to describe the dynamics of \(f\) locally in certain such basins. The underlying phenomenon governing these dynamics is the distribution of the critical points of \(f\), especially for rational maps on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\). We shall explain this phenomenon.

Understanding the dynamics near fixed points amounts to finding a change of coordinates in which the orbits of \(f\) are easy to describe, as expected. A general technique is to construct a local biholomorphism \(\phi\) such that the following diagram commutes.

That is, \(\phi\circ f\circ\phi^{-1}=g\) locally around \(0\), where \(g\) is preferably a polynomial. One begins by finding maps \(\{\phi_k\}_k\) such that \(\phi_k\circ f=g\circ\phi_{k+1}\), then proves that \(\phi_k\to\phi\) uniformly. Consequently, \[\lim_{k\to\infty}(\phi_k\circ f)=\lim_{k\to\infty}(g\circ\phi_{k+1}), \quad\phi\circ f=g\circ\phi, \quad\phi\circ f\circ\phi^{-1}=g.\]

Definition 7

A fixed point is superattracting if its multiplier \(\lambda\) is \(0\), geometrically attracting if \(0<|\lambda|<1\), and repelling if \(1<|\lambda|\).

We deal with all fixed points except those for which \(\lambda\in S^1\). First let us understand the dynamics locally, and then describe the phenomenon governing it.

Geometrically attracting and repelling points

For \(f\in\Hol(S,S)\), let \(\varphi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}=\widehat f\) be its coordinate representation locally around, and centred at, a fixed point. Here \(\widehat f'(0)\notin\{0,1\}\). On sufficiently small domains, \(\widehat f\) behaves like \(\widehat f'(0)z=\lambda z\). If \(\lambda<1\), \(f\) pulls; if \(\lambda>1\), \(f\) pushes. More precisely:

Theorem 11 — Koenigs linearisation

If the multiplier satisfies \(|\lambda|\notin\{0,1\}\), there is a map \(\phi\), unique up to multiplication by a nonzero constant, such that the following diagram commutes.

Proof. Case 1: \(|\lambda|<1\). Identify \(f\) with its local coordinate expression \(\widehat f\). Let \(0\) be the fixed point. We have \(f(z)=\lambda z+O(z^2)\) in \(\mathbb D_{r_0}\) for some \(r_0<1\), and \[|f(z)|\le|\lambda z|+C|z|^2\le(|\lambda|+C|z|)|z|\qquad(|z|<r_0).\] Since \(|\lambda|<1\), choosing \(|z|\) small enough keeps \(|\lambda|+C|z|\) within \(\mathbb D\). More precisely, choose \(0<r\le r_0\) such that \(|\lambda|+Cr<1\), and put \(c=|\lambda|+Cr\). Then \(|f(z)|\le c|z|\) for every \(z\in\mathbb D_r\), so \(f(z)\in\mathbb D_r\) and \(|f^{\circ n}(z)|\le c^n|z|<c^nr\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\).

This is precisely the push/pull we were discussing. There is \(r<1\) such that \(|f(z)|<c|z|\) on \(\mathbb D_r\), with \(c<1\). Let \(\{z_n\}_n\) be the orbit of \(z_0\in\mathbb D_r\). All these orbits converge to the origin, since \(|z_n|\le rc^n\), and \(|z_{n+1}-\lambda z_n|\le C|z_n|^2\le Cr^2c^{2n}\). Set \(w_n=z_n/\lambda^n\). Then \[\begin{align*} |w_{n+1}-w_n| &=\left|\frac{z_{n+1}}{\lambda^{n+1}}-\frac{z_n}{\lambda^n}\right| =\frac{|z_{n+1}-\lambda z_n|}{|\lambda|^{n+1}}\\ &\le\frac{Cr^2c^{2n}}{|\lambda|^{n+1}} =\frac{Cr^2}{|\lambda|}\left(\frac{c^2}{|\lambda|}\right)^n. \end{align*}\] Choose \(c\) with \(c^2<|\lambda|<c\). The sequence \(\{w_n\}_n\) is Cauchy, and its geometric bound is independent of \(z_0\). The map \(\phi_n(z_0)=f^{\circ n}(z_0)/\lambda^n\) is holomorphic on \(\mathbb D_r\), with \(\phi_n(f(z_0))=\lambda\phi_{n+1}(z_0)\). Taking \(\phi=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi_n\) gives \(\phi\circ f=\lambda\phi\). Also, \(\phi_n'(0)=1\), so \(\phi'(0)=1\), and \(\phi\) is a local conformal isomorphism around \(0\).

Case 2: \(|\lambda|>1\). Since \(f'(0)\ne0\), \(f\) is locally invertible. Its local inverse has multiplier \(0<|1/\lambda|<1\) at \(0\).

For uniqueness, if \(\phi,\psi\) are two such Koenigs maps, then \(\psi\circ\phi^{-1}\) commutes with \(z\mapsto\lambda z\). If \(\psi\circ\phi^{-1}(w)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_nw^n\), then \(\lambda b_n=b_n\lambda^n\). Thus \(b_k=0\) for every \(k\ge2\), and \(\psi=b_1\phi\).

Superattracting fixed points

If \(f'(0)=0\), then locally \(f(z)=a_nz^n+a_{n+1}z^{n+1}+\cdots\). Thus \(f\) has a zero of order \(n\) at \(0\), and in a suitable domain \(f(z)=h(z)^nz^n\). Close to the origin in this domain, \(f\) acts almost like the polynomial \(a_nz^n\). The following theorem makes a much sharper claim.

Theorem 12 — Böttcher

If \(0\) is a superattracting fixed point of \(f\), with a zero of order \(n\) at \(0\), there is a map \(\phi\), unique up to multiplication by an \((n-1)\)st root of unity, such that the following diagram commutes.

Proof. Locally around \(0\), write \(f(z)=b_0z^n+b_1z^{n+1}+b_2z^{n+2}+\cdots\). Since \(cf(z/c)=b_0z^n/c^{n-1}+\cdots\), choosing \(c^{n-1}=b_0\) allows us to assume that the leading coefficient is \(1\).

Choose \(r\) small enough that \(f\) maps \(\mathbb D_r\) into itself. The orbit of \(z\) has the form \[f^{\circ k}(z)=\left(z^n\left(1+\sum_{j\ge1}b_jz^j\right)\right)^{\circ k} =z^{n^k}(1+n^{k-1}b_1z+\cdots).\] Set \(\phi_k(z)=z(1+(b_1/n)z+\cdots)\), taking the local root so that \((\phi_k(z))^{n^k}=z^{n^k}(1+n^{k-1}b_1z+\cdots)=f^{\circ k}(z)\). Direct substitution gives \(\phi_k(f(z))=(\phi_{k+1}(z))^n\).

It remains to prove that \(\phi_k\) converges uniformly. Conjugate \(f\) and \(\phi_k\) by \((z\mapsto e^z)|_{\mathbb H_r}\). Let \(\eta(z)=\sum_{j\ge1}b_jz^j\). Then \[F(z)=\log f(e^z)=\log\bigl(e^{nz}(1+\eta(z))\bigr) =nz+\log(1+\eta(z)),\] so \(|F(z)-nz|=|\log(1+\eta(z))|<\log2<1\) whenever \(|\eta(z)|<1/2\).

Set \(\Phi_k(z)=\log\phi_k(e^z)=F^{\circ k}(z)/n^k\). Then \[|\Phi_{k+1}(z)-\Phi_k(z)| =\frac{|F^{\circ(k+1)}(z)-nF^{\circ k}(z)|}{n^{k+1}} <\frac1{n^{k+1}}.\] This is again a uniform bound. Since \(e^z\colon\mathbb H_r\to\mathbb D_r\) is distance-reducing, \[|\phi_{k+1}(z)-\phi_k(z)| <|\log\phi_{k+1}(e^z)-\log\phi_k(e^z)|<\frac1{n^{k+1}}.\] Thus \(\{\phi_k\}_k\) has a uniform limit \(\phi\). Uniqueness again follows because \(\phi\circ\psi^{-1}\) commutes with \(z\mapsto z^n\).

Remark

A crucial fact is that \(f(z)\ne0\) for \(z\in\mathbb D_r\setminus\{0\}\), so \(\log f(e^z)\) makes sense. This is a useful technique for bounding quantities: shift one’s domain to another hyperbolic surface and demand the luxuries of Pick’s theorem.

Now that we understand the local dynamics near geometrically attracting, repelling, and superattracting points, to what extent can we extend this knowledge? In other words, on how large a domain is the nature of \(f\) near these fixed points as we asserted? Let us globalise this local behaviour as far as nature allows, primarily for rational maps on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\).

Global linearisation

Koenigs’ function \(\phi\) extends holomorphically to the basin of attraction \(\mathcal A\) of the fixed point \(\widehat p\).

Proof. The formula \(\lim_{n\to\infty}f^{\circ n}(z)/\lambda^n\) is valid on \(\mathcal A\), since it converges uniformly on compact sets. For every \(z\in\mathcal A\), there is a neighbourhood \(\overline U\subseteq\mathcal A\) on which \(f^{\circ n}\) converges uniformly to \(\widehat p\). Thus there is \(N\) such that \(f^{\circ n}(z)\in U\), the domain of \(\phi\), for every \(n\ge N\) and \(z\in\overline U\). Then

\[\frac{\phi(f^{\circ N}(z))}{\lambda^N} =\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f^{\circ n}(z)}{\lambda^n}.\] Indeed, \(\phi\) extends to \(\mathcal A\).

The local inverse \(\psi=\phi^{-1}\) of Koenigs’ function extends to an entire function when \(\widehat p\) is a repelling fixed point.

The proof follows the same lines: drag values in \(\mathbb C\) into \(\mathbb D_\varepsilon\) for small \(\varepsilon\), invert via \(\phi^{-1}\), and compose with a suitable iterate of \(f\) to make the diagram commute. Locally, \[\psi(w)=f^{\circ N}\left(\phi^{-1}\left(\frac w{\lambda^N}\right)\right),\qquad f\circ\psi(w)=f^{\circ(N+1)}\left(\phi^{-1}\left(\frac w{\lambda^N}\right)\right),\] while \(\psi\circ\lambda(w)=f^{\circ N}\bigl(\phi^{-1}(w/\lambda^{N-1})\bigr)\).

Remark

Such an extension is not possible for Böttcher coordinates: to make the diagram commute one must deal with \(p\mapsto\sqrt[n^k]{\phi(f^{\circ k}(p))}\), but the root is not well-defined. One can, however, extend \(|\phi|\), since roots in \(\mathbb R_+\) are well-defined.

The phenomenon of critical points: analytic aspects

Critical points govern rational dynamics in three significant ways:

1.

Critical points form the boundary beyond which Koenigs and Böttcher coordinates cannot be extended biholomorphically (analytic).

2.

Critical points determine the number of attracting periodic points or orbits (analytic).

3.

They determine the topological shape of the Julia set (topological; we shall see this in another post).

The analysis of a rational map is essentially determined by its roots and poles, whereas in dynamics its critical points become essential. We address these phenomena one by one. Unless otherwise stated, \(f\) is a rational map with \(\deg(f)\ge2\), and the surface is \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\).

Biholomorphic extension

Definition 8

Given an attracting fixed point \(\widehat p\) of a map \(f\colon S\to S\), let \(\mathcal A_0\) denote the connected component of its basin of attraction that contains \(\widehat p\).

Theorem 13

There is a maximal \(r\) such that \(\psi\colon\mathbb D_r\to\mathcal A_0\) is a holomorphic inverse of the Koenigs coordinate \(\phi\). The closed disc \(\overline{\mathbb D_r}\) and \(\psi(\overline{\mathbb D_r})\) are homeomorphic, and \(\psi(\partial\mathbb D_r)\) contains a critical point of \(f\).

Proof. Suppose \(\phi^{-1}\) extends biholomorphically to an entire function. We would then have the following commutative diagram, implying that \(f|_{\psi(\mathbb C)}\) is injective.

Since \(\deg(f)\ge2\), \(J(f)\ne\varnothing\). By Picard’s theorem, \(|\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\psi(\mathbb C)|\le2\), because \(\psi\) is entire. But \(J(f)\) is either connected or has uncountably many components, so \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\psi(\mathbb C)\) is a single point. By invariance, \(f\) is injective on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), which is impossible when \(\deg(f)\ge2\). There is consequently a maximal \(r\) such that the following diagram commutes.

The set \(\lambda\overline{\mathbb D_r}\) is a compact subset of \(\mathbb D_r\), and the image of \(\mathbb D_r\) under multiplication by \(\lambda\) lies in \(\lambda\overline{\mathbb D_r}\). Thus there is a compact \(K\subset U\) with \(f(U)\subset K\), and \(f(\overline U)\subseteq\overline{f(U)}\subseteq K\subset U\subset\mathcal A\).

By invariance, \(\overline U\subset\mathcal A\), so \(\phi\) is holomorphic on \(\overline U\), since it extends to the whole basin. Let \(w_0\in\partial\mathbb D_r\) and suppose \(\partial U\) contains no critical point of \(f\). Then \(f\) is locally invertible at each \(z_0\in\partial U\). But \(\psi(w_0)\) may not yet be well-defined: the curve \(t\mapsto\psi(tw_0)\) as \(t\to1\) might accumulate at several points.

Let \(z_0\in\partial U\) be an accumulation point of \(\psi(tw_0)\) as \(t\to1\). Since \(f\) has a local inverse there, define, on a neighbourhood \(V\) of \(w_0\), \[\psi(w)=f^{-1}(\psi(\lambda w))\qquad(w\in V).\] Do this at every point. The identity theorem patches the local pieces over the compact set \(\partial\mathbb D_r\), extending \(\psi\) biholomorphically to a larger disc. That the extension is biholomorphic is again a consequence of the identity theorem.

Thus critical points form the obstruction that stops, or contains, biholomorphic extension within a domain in \(\mathcal A\).

Theorem 14

There is a maximal \(0<r\le1\) such that the Böttcher coordinate \(\phi\) has a biholomorphic inverse on \(\mathbb D_r\). If \(r=1\), then \(\mathbb D\cong\mathcal A_0\), and the superattracting point \(\widehat p\) is the only critical point in \(\mathcal A\). Otherwise there is another critical point in \(\mathcal A_0\), on \(\partial\psi(\mathbb D_r)\).

Proof. As before, a maximal \(r\le1\) exists. For the following diagram to commute, the image of \(\mathbb D_r\) under \(z\mapsto z^n\), and all its subsequent iterates, must lie in \(\mathbb D_r\), since \(f^{\circ n}(\mathcal A_0)\subseteq\mathcal A_0\).

Before, we had the luxury of the extended map \(\phi\) on \(\mathcal A\), so continuation of the holomorphic inverse by the identity theorem was a biholomorphic extension. We do not have that now, and must make do with the extension of \(|\phi|\).

The map \(\psi\) has no critical points in \(\mathbb D_r\), since \(\psi'(w)=0\) implies \(\psi'(w^n)=(f\circ\psi)'(w)=f'(\psi(w))\psi'(w)=0\). Thus \(w^n\), and all \(w^{n^k}\), would be critical points, which is impossible by the identity theorem. Hence \(\psi\) is locally injective (biholomorphic).

The set \(\{(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb D_r\times\mathbb D_r:\psi(w_1)=\psi(w_2)\}\) is closed. Thus choose \(|w_1|=|w_2|\) minimal

with \(\psi(w_1)=\psi(w_2)\). Since \(|\phi|\) extends to \(\mathcal A\), we have \(|\phi(\psi(w))|=|w|\) for all \(w\in\mathbb D_\varepsilon\), the domain of biholomorphy. By the identity theorem, \(|\phi(\psi(w))|=|w|\) for every \(w\in\mathbb D_r\). Consequently \(\psi(w_1)=\psi(w_2)\) implies \(|w_1|=|w_2|\).

Let \(w_1'\in B_\varepsilon(w_1)\). The set \(\psi^{-1}(\psi(B_\varepsilon(w_1)))\) contains \(w_2\), so \(\psi(B_\varepsilon(w_1))\cap\psi(B_\varepsilon(w_2))\ne\varnothing\). There are therefore \(w_1',w_2'\) with \(|w_1'|<|w_1|\) and \(\psi(w_1')=\psi(w_2')\), a contradiction. Thus \(\psi\) is injective, hence biholomorphic onto \(\psi(\mathbb D_r)\).

If \(r=1\) and \(\psi(\mathbb D)\subsetneq\mathcal A_0\), take \(z_0\in\partial U\cap\mathcal A_0\). Approximate \(z_0\) by \(\psi(w_j)\). Then \(|\phi(\psi(w_j))|=|w_j|\to1\), so \(|\phi(z_0)|=1\), and \(z_0\) does not tend to \(0\), contradicting \(z_0\in\mathcal A_0\).

If \(r<1\), just as before, a critical point on the boundary prevents extension of \(\psi\) beyond its maximal disc \(\mathbb D_r\).

Remark

We defer the homeomorphism part to the next post, where we explore topological properties, including continuous extension to \(\partial\mathbb D_r\) of the inverses of Böttcher and Koenigs coordinates, and much more.

The number of attracting periodic points

Theorem 15

There are finitely many attracting periodic orbits.

Proof. For fixed points this follows because all immediate basins contain critical points, and a rational map has finitely many critical points. Given an attracting orbit \(z_0\mapsto z_1\mapsto\cdots\mapsto z_0\) in \(n\) steps, consider \(f^{\circ n}\).

Alternate proof. Let \(\widehat p\in O\) be an attracting fixed point, where \(O\) is its immediate basin. If \(O\) has no critical value of \(f\), then there is a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\widehat p\) and, for every \(k\ge1\), a map \(g_k\colon U\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) inverse to \(f^{\circ k}\). The family \(\{g_k\}_k\) is normal, but \(g_k'(\widehat p)\) is unbounded, since it is \(\lambda^k\) with \(\lambda>1\).

Critical points therefore keep count of the number of attracting periodic orbits. Let us try to extend this theorem to noncompact Riemann surfaces and nonrational maps.

Definition 9

For \(f\colon S\to S'\), a critical value is the image under \(f\) of a critical point.

Definition 10

If there is a curve \(\gamma\colon[0,1)\to S\) that eventually leaves compact sets, but \(\lim_{t\to1}f(\gamma(t))=v\), then \(v\) is an asymptotic value.

Theorem 16

Every proper holomorphic self-map \(f\colon S\to S\) has a critical value in every immediate basin of an attracting orbit.
excerptHtml: Let’s look at the local behaviour of a holomorphic map \(f\colon S\to S\), where \(S\) is a Riemann surface. For this, it would “suffice” to study the local behaviour at fixed points of \(f\). Recall that \(S\) decomposes into components of basins with fractal-like boundaries (elements of the Julia set). Our goal is to describe the dynamics of \(f\) locally in certain such basins. The underlying phenomenon governing these dynamics is the distribution of the critical points of \(f\), especially for rational maps on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\). We shall explain this phenomenon.

title: Parabolic Fixed Points and the Flower Theorem
html:
Consider a fixed point \(f(\widehat p)=\widehat p\) whose multiplier satisfies \(\lambda^q=1\). Such points are called parabolic fixed points. It is immediately clear that the expected dynamics should be different. For instance, consider the orbits of \(\pm1\) and \(\pm i\) under \(f(z)=z+z^3\).

The map \(f\) throws \(1,-1\) violently away, while pulling \(i,-i\) violently towards \(\widehat p=0\). Notice that it pushes and pulls from two directions. The following theorem tells us that such patterns reappear. For now, no neighbourhood of \(\widehat p=0\) can be expected to be a “basin”, since \(\widehat p\) is a sink only in certain directions.

Definition 11

Let \(f(z)=z+az^{n+1}+O(z^{n+2})\). A vector \(v\in\mathbb C\) is attracting if \(nav^n=+1\), and repelling if \(nav^n=-1\).

Remark

The equation \(nav^n=\pm1\) has \(2n\) equally spaced solutions. Also \(f\) is locally invertible, with \(f^{(n+1)}(0)\ne0\), \(f'(0)=1\), and \(f^{(k)}(0)=0\) for \(1<k\le n\).
