Thus \[(f^{-1})''(0)=-\frac{f''(0)}{(f'(0))^3}=-a\quad(n=1),\] and \[(f^{-1})'''(0)=\frac{3(f''(0))^2-f'(0)f'''(0)}{(f'(0))^5} =-f'''(0)=-a\quad(n=2).\] Inductively, \(-f^{(n+1)}(0)=(f^{-1})^{(n+1)}(0)\). Thus attracting and repelling vectors exchange roles for \(f^{-1}\).

The next theorem explains why these vectors have their names, and shows that all maps with a parabolic point behave somewhat like \(z+z^3\).

Theorem 17

If an orbit \(\{z_k\}_k\) of \(z_0\) tends to \(0\) and \(z_k\ne0\) for every \(k\), then \(z_k\sim v_j/k^{1/n}\) as \(k\to\infty\) for some attracting vector \(v_j\). The analogous assertion holds for orbits converging to \(0\) under \(f^{-1}\).

Proof. We employ the same technique mentioned earlier. First let us state explicitly what we expect. Set \(v_j=e^{\pi ij/n}v_0\): \(v_j\) is attracting if \(2\nmid j\), and repelling if \(2\mid j\).

As illustrated, we expect the rays \(\{v_j\}_j\) to fall on each other as the arrows indicate. Some domain in \[\Delta_j=\{re^{i\theta}v_j:r>0,\ |\theta|<\pi/n\}\] must contain the orbit eventually; it must also approach \(0\) asymptotically in direction \(v_j\) (\(2\nmid j\)). We hope to obtain the necessary bounds by conjugating the iterates to another hyperbolic surface, leaving the rest to Pick’s theorem. Define the biholomorphism \[\varphi\colon\Delta_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R_{(-1)^j}, \qquad\varphi(z)=\frac c{z^n},\quad c=-\frac1{na}.\]

On \(\Delta_j\), \(f(z)=z(1+az^n+o(z^n))\). Shift this to the slit plane \(\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R_{(-1)^j}\), and let \(\psi_j=\varphi^{-1}\). Then \[f\circ\psi_j(w)=\sqrt[n]{\frac c w}\left(1+\frac{ac}{w}+o(1/w)\right), \qquad w\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R_{(-1)^j},\] where the \(n\)th root makes sense. Consequently, \[\begin{align*} F_j(w)=\varphi\circ f\circ\psi_j(w) &=w\left(1+\frac{ac}{w}+o(1/w)\right)^{-n}\\ &=w\left(1-\frac{nac}{w}+o(1/w)\right) =w\left(1+\frac1w+o(1/w)\right)\\ &=w+1+o(1). \end{align*}\] Writing the same calculation with big-\(O\) notation yields \[F_j(w)=w+1+O\!\left(\frac1{\sqrt[n]{|w|}}\right). \tag{*}\] This follows by writing \(f(z)=z(1+az^n+O(z^n))\) and following the same steps. We shall use this later.

For \(|w|>R\), with \(R\) large, \(|F_j(w)-w-1|<1/2\). Thus \(\Re F_j(w)>\Re w+1/2\).

When \(|w|\) is large, \(|\psi_j(w)|\) is small. Thus for small \(|z|\), \(\Re\varphi(f(z))>\Re\varphi(z)+1/2\). For the orbit \(\{z_k\}_k\), this gives \(\Re\varphi(z_{k+1})>\Re\varphi(z_k)+1/2\). Eventually \(\varphi(z_k)\in\mathbb H_R\) for large \(R\), and \(F_j(\mathbb H_R)\subseteq\mathbb H_R\). Hence \(f(\psi_j(\mathbb H_R))\subseteq\psi_j(\mathbb H_R)\). Call \(\psi_j(\mathbb H_R)=P_j(R)\). Thus eventually all \(z_k\) belong to \(\Delta_j\) for some \(j\).

Since \(F_j(w)-w=1+o(1)\), putting \(w_k=\varphi(z_k)\) gives \(w_{k+1}-w_k\to1\), and \[\frac{w_k-w_0}{k}=\frac1k\sum_{h=0}^{k-1}(w_{h+1}-w_h)\longrightarrow1.\]

Thus \(w_k/k\to1\), so \(w_k\sim k\). Since \(1/w_k=-naz_k^n\), we get \(naz_k^n\sim-1/k\). As \(nav_j^n=-1\), this gives \(z_k^n\sim v_j^n/k\).

Write \(z_k=r_ke^{i\alpha_k}\) and \(v_j=re^{i\alpha}\). Then \(z_k^n=r_k^ne^{ni\alpha_k}\) and \(v_j^n/k=(r^n/k)e^{ni\alpha}\). The modulus of their ratio tends to one, so \(r_k\sim r/k^{1/n}\). Also \(e^{n(\alpha_k-\alpha)i}\to1\), so eventually \(\alpha_k-\alpha\in(2\pi/n)\mathbb Z\). But eventually \(z_k\in P_j(R)\subset\Delta_j\), and \(|\alpha_k-\alpha|<\pi/n\), forcing \(\alpha_k-\alpha\to0\). Therefore \(z_k\sim v_j/k^{1/n}\).

Having seen this, let us identify the basin of attraction for \(\widehat p\).

Definition 12

The set \(\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\) consists of all \(p_0\) whose orbit \(p_0\mapsto p_1\mapsto p_2\mapsto\cdots\) under \(f\) tends to \(\widehat p\) along \(v_j\). Since \(P_j(R)\subset\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\), there is a unique connected component \(\mathcal A_j^0\) with \(f(\mathcal A_j^0)\subseteq\mathcal A_j^0\). This is called the immediate basin.

We now know vaguely that there are domains in \(\Delta_j\) around \(\widehat p\) where \(f\) pushes or pulls. We do not yet know whether those domains surround \(\widehat p\); nothing so far prevents gaps. The domain \(P_j(R)\subset\Delta_j\) satisfies \(f(P_j(R))\subseteq P_j(R)\), and an orbit tending to \(\widehat p\) along \(v_j\) eventually enters it. Let us generalise this phenomenon.

Definition 13 — Attracting and repelling petals

Let \(N\) be a neighbourhood of \(\widehat p\) on which \(f\) is univalent. A set \(P\subset N\) is an attracting petal for \(f\) at \(\widehat p\), associated with an attracting vector \(v_j\), if

  • \(f(P)\subseteq P\);

  • an orbit \(\{z_k\}_k\) enters \(P\) eventually if and only if \(z_k\to\widehat p\) along \(v_j\).

Repelling petals are defined similarly by considering \(f^{-1}\) on \(f(N)\).

Clearly \(P\) contains exactly one \(v_j\); these sets therefore look like petals around the “base branch” \(v_j\). The next theorem says that the attracting and repelling petals surround \(\widehat p\): they fit together into a round flower.

Theorem 18 — Flower theorem

There are petals \(\{P_j\}_{j=0}^{2n-1}\), each attracting or repelling, such that \(\{\widehat p\}\cup P_0\cup\cdots\cup P_{2n-1}\) is an open neighbourhood of \(\widehat p\). The sets \(P_j\) and \(P_j\cap P_{j\pm1}\) are simply connected regions, except when \(n=1\).

Proof. We cannot simply take \(P_j(R)\). Although \(\{\widehat p\}\cup\bigcup_{j=0}^{2n-1}P_j(R)\) forms a neighbourhood of \(\widehat p\), it does not quite form a flower, so we modify \(\mathbb H_R\) slightly. Let \[W_R=\{u+iv:u+|v|>2R\},\qquad\mathbb H_{2R}\subset W_R.\] Then \(P_j=\psi_j(W_R)\subset\Delta_j\) is an attracting petal for odd \(j\) and large \(R\). Similarly, \(P_j=\psi_j(-W_R)\) is a repelling petal.

Now note the following correspondence, since \(\varphi\) preserves orientation by being locally conformal around \(\widehat p\).

Thus \[\varphi(\Delta_j\cap\Delta_{j+1})= \begin{cases}\text{upper half-plane},&2\mid j,\\ \text{lower half-plane},&2\nmid j. \end{cases}\] Also \(\psi_j(P_j\cap P_{j+1})=V_R^+\) or \(V_R^-\), where \(V_R^\pm\) are components of \(W_R\). Hence \(P_j\) and \(P_j\cap P_{j\pm1}\) are simply connected. Clearly \(\{\widehat p\}\cup\bigcup_{j=0}^{2n-1}P_j\) contains a ball around \(\widehat p\), since each \(P_j\) contains \(|z|<\varepsilon_j\) for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon_j\). This is the flower theorem, due to Leau and Fatou.

We now ask the question suggested by the case \(0<|\lambda|<1\): can we understand the dynamics separately in at least each of the \(2n\) petals? The next theorem addresses this completely.

Theorem 19 — Parabolic linearisation

For any petal \(P\), there is a conformal embedding \(\alpha\colon P\to\mathbb C\), unique up to translation, making the following diagram commute. In the literature, \(\alpha\) is called a Fatou coordinate.

Before proving the theorem, let us make a few observations. Recall that \(\Re F_j(w)>\Re w+1/2\) and \(|F_j(w+1)-w-1|=O(1/\sqrt[n]{|w|})\).

Observation — 1

For \(\widehat w\in\mathbb H_R\), the maps \(\beta_k(w)=F_j^{\circ k}(w)-F_j^{\circ k}(\widehat w)\) converge locally uniformly to a biholomorphic map.

By Cauchy’s estimate, \(|F'(w)-1|<C/S^{1+\varepsilon}\) when \(|w|\ge2S\ge2R\). Given \(w',w''\in\mathbb H_{2S}\), \[\frac1{w''-w'}\int_{\gamma_{w'\to w''}}(F'(w)-1)\,dw =\frac{F(w'')-F(w')}{w''-w'}-1,\] so the modulus of the right-hand side is at most \(C/S^{1+\varepsilon}\). Since \(\Re F^{\circ k}(w)>k/2\), eventually \[\left|\frac{\beta_k(w)}{\beta_{k-1}(w)}-1\right| \le\frac{C'}{k^{1+\varepsilon}}\qquad(k\ge R). \tag{1}\] Consequently \[1-\frac{C'}{k^{1+\varepsilon}} \le\left|\frac{\beta_k(w)}{\beta_{k-1}(w)}\right| \le1+\frac{C'}{k^{1+\varepsilon}}.\] The series \(\sum_k C'/k^{1+\varepsilon}\) converges, so the product \(\prod_k(1+C'/k^{1+\varepsilon})\) converges, say to \(P\). Therefore \[\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left|\frac{\beta_i(w)}{\beta_{i-1}(w)}\right|\le P, \qquad |\beta_k(w)|\le|\beta_0(w)|P=|w-\widehat w|P. \tag{2}\]

Multiplying (1) and (2), with \(k-1\) in the latter, gives \[|\beta_k(w)-\beta_{k-1}(w)|\le\frac{PC'|w-\widehat w|}{k^{1+\varepsilon}}.\] Thus \(\beta_0(w)+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\beta_k(w)-\beta_{k-1}(w))\) is absolutely convergent, since the corresponding series of bounds is. We obtain \(\beta_k(w)\to\beta(w)\) and \(\beta_k(w)/\beta_0(w)\to\beta(w)/\beta_0(w)\), so \(\beta\) is holomorphic.

To see univalence, choose \(k_0\) such that \(1-C'/k_0^{1+\varepsilon}>0\). Then \(|\beta_k(w)/\beta_{k-1}(w)|>0\), so \(F_j^{\circ k}\) is eventually univalent: the positive lower bound is independent of \(w,\widehat w\) for every \(k\ge k_0\). Hence \(\beta\) is univalent.

Observation — 2

\(\beta(F_j(w))=\beta(w)+1\).

Fix \(k\). We have \(\beta_k(w)\sim F_j^{\circ k}(w)\) and \(|F_j(w+1)-(w+1)|=O(1/\sqrt[n]{|w|})\).

Thus \(F_j^{\circ k}(w)\sim w+k\sim w\), and \[\begin{align*} \lim_{k\to\infty}\beta_k(F_j(w)) &=\lim_{k\to\infty}\beta_{k+1}(w) +\lim_{k\to\infty}\bigl(F_j^{\circ(k+1)}(w)-F_j^{\circ k}(w)\bigr),\\ \beta(F_j(w))&=\beta(w)+o(w+k+1-w+k)=\beta(w)+1. \end{align*}\]

The map \(\beta|_{\mathbb H_{2R}}\) is univalent and satisfies this equation. Also, for sufficiently large \(k\), \(F^{\circ k}(\mathbb H_R)\subseteq\mathbb H_{2R}\). Extending in this way makes \(\beta\) univalent on \(\mathbb H_R\).

Observation — 3

If \(\beta(\mathbb H_R)=U\), then \(\{U+n\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\) covers \(\mathbb C\): \(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}(U+n)=\mathbb C\).

Since \(\beta(w)\sim w\), for sufficiently large \(S\) we have \(|\beta(w)-w|<|w|/3\) for all \(w\in\mathbb H_R\) with \(|w|>S\). Given \(\overline w_0\in\mathbb C/\mathbb Z\), choose a representative \(w_0\) with \(|w_0|>2S\) and \(\overline{B_{|w_0|/2}(w_0)}\subseteq\mathbb H_R\). For every \(w\) in this disc, \(S<|w|<3|w_0|/2\), and therefore \(|\beta(w)-w|<|w_0|/2\).

On its boundary, \(|\beta(w)-w|<|w-w_0|\). Thus \(w-w_0\) and \((\beta(w)-w)+(w-w_0)\) have the same number of roots. It follows that \(w_0\in\beta(B_{|w_0|/2}(w_0))\), proving \(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}(U+n)=\mathbb C\).

Having observed these three crucial facts, let us prove existence and uniqueness of the Fatou coordinate. Proof of Theorem 19. Existence. For any petal \(P\) and \(z\in P\), some iterate enters \(P_j(R)\). We have the following commutative diagram.

For \(P=P_j(R)\), define \(\alpha(z)=\beta(\varphi(z))\). For any \(z\in P\), choose \(k_0\) so that \(f^{\circ k}(z)\in P_j(R)\) for all \(k\ge k_0\), and define \(\alpha(z)=\alpha(f^{\circ k}(z))-k\).

This ensures that the following diagram also commutes.

Uniqueness. Let \(\alpha,\alpha'\) be two Fatou coordinates. Then \(g=\alpha'\circ\alpha^{-1}\) commutes with \(z\mapsto z+1\), so \(g(w+1)=g(w)+1\). If \(\alpha\colon P\to U\) and \(\alpha'\colon P\to U'\) are biholomorphisms, then \(g\colon U\to U'\) is a biholomorphism. Since the translates \(U+n\) sweep out \(\mathbb C\), extend \(g\) to an entire function by integer translations, obtaining \(\widehat g\colon\mathbb C\to U'+\mathbb Z\).

Its image misses at most one point. If \(U'+\mathbb Z=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\), without loss of generality, then \(1\in U'+\mathbb Z\), so some integer \(n\) belongs to \(U'\). Hence \(0\in U'-n\subseteq U'+\mathbb Z\), a contradiction. Thus \(\widehat g(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C\) and \(\widehat g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb C)\). By the identity theorem, \(\widehat g(w+1)=\widehat g(w)+1\).

Therefore \(\alpha\) is unique up to translation.

Remark

Critical points again play a crucial role; we will not elaborate on this. If \(\alpha\) is the Fatou coordinate for the petal wrapping \(v_j\), it extends to \(\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\), and \(\alpha^{-1}\) extends to some \(\mathbb H_R\) with \(R\) optimal. This is analogous to the Koenigs-coordinate situation. For every \(\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\) there is a maximal petal \(P_{\max}\subseteq\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\) to which \(\alpha\) extends biholomorphically, and \(f\) has a critical point on \(\partial P_{\max}\) that prevents further univalent extension.

Remark

We have \(\alpha(z)\to\infty\) as \(z\to0\), and \(0\) is a parabolic fixed point. The preimages \(\{f^{-n}(0)\}\) form a dense subset of the basin boundary, obstructing expansion of \(\alpha\).

Remark

In conclusion, the \(\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\) are disjoint basins with \(\partial\mathcal A_j(\widehat p)\subseteq J\). Each basin has a Fatou coordinate describing its local behaviour on a maximal petal \(P_{\max}\).
excerptHtml: Consider a fixed point \(f(\widehat p)=\widehat p\) whose multiplier satisfies \(\lambda^q=1\). Such points are called parabolic fixed points. It is immediately clear that the expected dynamics should be different. For instance, consider the orbits of \(\pm1\) and \(\pm i\) under \(f(z)=z+z^3\).

title: Dense Subsets of Julia Sets
html:
How many periodic points are there for a rational map \(f=P/Q\colon\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) with \(\deg(f)=d\ge2\)? It turns out that

1.

the number of attracting periodic orbits is at most \(2d-2\);

2.

the number of indifferent periodic orbits is at most \(4d-4\) (\(\lambda\ne1\));

3.

there are infinitely many repelling periodic orbits.

The first assertion is elementary: every attracting basin has a critical point, and \[\begin{align*} \#\{\text{critical points of }P/Q\} &=\#\{\text{zeros of }(P/Q)'\}\\ &=\#\left\{\text{zeros of }\frac{P'}Q-\frac{Q'P}{Q^2}\right\} =\#\{\text{zeros of }QP'-Q'P\}\\ &\le\deg(QP'-Q'P)\le2d-2. \end{align*}\] Compare the leading coefficients in the worst case, \(\deg P=\deg Q=d\). Now let us prove the second assertion.

Proposition 20

The number of indifferent, nonparabolic cycles is at most \(4d-4\).

Proof. We separate the proof into two stages. Perturbation. We will holomorphically deform \(f(z)=P(z)/Q(z)\) into the polynomial \(z^d\), the simplest rational map of degree \(d\).

We do this for two important reasons (revisit them):

1.

If \(\{z_j\}_j\) is an indifferent cycle, deform the \(z_j\) holomorphically, along with their multipliers \(\lambda_j\). We plan to convert them into attracting cycles and use the bound on attracting cycles.

2.

Deforming to \(z^d\) helps ensure that this conversion happens for a “large proportion” of indifferent cycles.

Define \[f_t(z)=\frac{P(z)-tz^d}{Q(z)-t},\qquad f_0(z)=f(z),\qquad f_\infty(z)=z^d.\] This remains a degree-\(d\) map unless, for some \(t\in\widehat{\mathbb C}\), zeros and poles collide as the parameter approaches \(t\). For that to happen, \(Q(z)=t\) and \(P(z)=tz^d\), so \(z^d=P(z)/Q(z)=f(z)\). Thus the number of solutions of \(f(z)=z^d\) determines the number of exceptional parameters at which the degree drops.

Let \(\{f_0^{\circ k}(z_j)\}_{k=1}^n\) be an \(n\)-cycle of \(f_0\) with \(|\lambda_j(0)|=0\). Set \(\widetilde f(t,z)=f_t^{\circ n}(z)-z\). Since \(\widetilde f(0,z_j)=0\), the implicit function theorem gives neighbourhoods \(U\) of \(0\) and \(V\) of \(z_j\) and a holomorphic map \(z_j(t)\colon U\to V\) with \(\widetilde f(t,z_j(t))=0\).

The multiplier \(\lambda_j(t)=(f_t^{\circ n})'(z_j(t))\) is also locally holomorphic. If it were locally constant, the identity theorem would shatter all hope of turning these indifferent points into attracting ones.

Lemma 21

The map \(t\mapsto\lambda_j(t)\) is not locally constant.

Proof. Suppose it is, and let us see how far this paralysis extends. Choose a ray \(\{re^{i\theta}:0\le r\le+\infty\}\) avoiding every parameter where \(\deg(f_t)<d\). Extend \(\lambda_j(t)\) to a neighbourhood of this ray so that \(f_t\) has an indifferent periodic point \(z_j(t)\) with multiplier \(\lambda_j(t)\).

If \(z_j(t)\to z_j(\widehat t)\) along the ray as \(t\to\widehat t\), continuity gives \(\widetilde f(t,z_j(t))\to\widetilde f(\widehat t,z_j(\widehat t))=0\). The implicit function theorem makes \(z_j\), and hence \(\lambda_j\), analytic near \(\widehat t\). Thus the domain of analytic continuation is both open and closed. It follows that \(z^d\) has an indifferent cycle \(\{f_\infty^{\circ k}(z_j(\infty))\}_k\) with \(|\lambda_j(\infty)|=1\). This is impossible: the periodic points of \(z^d\) are \(0,\infty\),

and roots of unity, none of whose multipliers lie on \(S^1\).

There is therefore hope: the functions \(\lambda_j(t)\) are not paralysed; they are indeed “dynamic”.

Converting cycles. Near \(t=0\), write \[\frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_0(t)}=1+a_jt^{n_j}+o(t^{n_j}),\qquad |\lambda_j(t)|=1+\Re(a_jt^{n_j})+o(t^{n_j}).\]

Set \(\sigma_j(\theta)=\operatorname{sign}\Re(a_je^{i\theta n_j})\). For small \(r\), \(\sigma_j(\theta)=+1\) implies \(|\lambda_j(re^{i\theta})|>1\), while \(\sigma_j(\theta)=-1\) implies \(|\lambda_j(re^{i\theta})|<1\). This is the desired conversion.

Clearly \((2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}\sigma_j(\theta)\,d\theta=0\). Let \(\ell\) be odd and no greater than the number of indifferent cycles of \(f_0\). Then \[\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\sigma_k(\theta)\,d\theta=0.\] For some \(\theta\), at least \((\ell+1)/2\) multipliers have modulus less than one. Hence, for \(t=re^{i\theta}\), the map \(f_t\) has at least \((\ell+1)/2\) attracting cycles. Since \((\ell+1)/2\le2d-2\), the number of indifferent cycles is finite and at most \(4d-4\).

Remark

Parabolic points may be included with attracting cycles, because their basins also contain critical points, or accommodated in the list of indifferent cycles.

We now prove that there are infinitely many repelling periodic points. The assertion we use to deduce this quantitative result is qualitative.

Proposition 22

The closure of the set of repelling periodic points is the Julia set.

Proof due to Fatou. Let \(z_0\in J(f)\) be neither a fixed point nor a critical value of \(f\). Then \(f^{-1}(z_0)=\{z_i\}_{i=1}^d\), with all \(z_i\) distinct. Choose a neighbourhood \(N\) of \(z_0\) on which \(f^{-1}\) has \(d\) branches \(\varphi_j\), with \(\varphi_j(z_0)=z_j\).

For some \(n\) and some \(z\in N\), \(f^{\circ n}(z)\in\{z,\varphi_1(z),\varphi_2(z)\}\). Otherwise take \(N\) small enough to be hyperbolic and

set \[g_n(z)=\left(\frac{f^{\circ n}(z)-\varphi_1(z)}{f^{\circ n}(z)-\varphi_2(z)}\right) \left(\frac{z-\varphi_2(z)}{z-\varphi_1(z)}\right).\] Then \(g_n\colon N\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\) is a normal family. A subsequence \(g_{n_j}\) converges to \(g\) on compact subsets \(K\subset N\). Rearranging, \[\frac{f^{\circ n}(z)-\varphi_1(z)}{f^{\circ n}(z)-\varphi_2(z)} =g_n(z)\frac{z-\varphi_1(z)}{z-\varphi_2(z)},\] and hence \[f^{\circ n_j}(z)\longrightarrow \frac{\varphi_2(z)-\varphi_1(z)}{g(z)\dfrac{z-\varphi_1(z)}{z-\varphi_2(z)}-1}+\varphi_2(z).\] Thus \(\{f^{\circ n}|_N\}\) is normal, contradicting \(z_0\in J(f)\). Therefore some \(z\in N\) satisfies either \(f^{\circ n}(z)=z\) or \(f^{\circ n}(z)=\varphi_j(z)\); in the latter case, \(f^{\circ(n+1)}(z)=f(\varphi_j(z))=z\). Thus \(z\) is periodic, of period \(n\) or \(n+1\).

The closure of periodic points is the Julia set: since \(J(f)\) has no isolated points, density away from the fixed points and critical values gives density in all of \(J(f)\).

By the previous proposition, only finitely many of these periodic points are nonrepelling, and repelling points lie in the Julia set. Hence \[\overline{\{\text{repelling periodic points}\}}=J(f).\]

There are therefore infinitely many repelling periodic points. A small topological argument is needed.

title: Critical Points and Julia-Set Connectivity
html:
Let’s see how the critical points of polynomials on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) determine the shape and structure of the Julia set. The following is a well-known fact.

Theorem 23

If \(\mathcal A_0\) is an immediate basin of attraction, then \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal A_0\) is either connected or has uncountably many components.

Proof. Choose \(N_0\) small enough that \(f(\overline{N_0})\subset N_0\) and \(\partial N_0\) contains no forward image of a critical point. Such images are at most countable, because \(\{z:f'(z)=0\}\) is finite. Let \(\widehat z\) be the fixed point, and let \(N_k\) be the component of \(f^{-k}(N_0)\) containing \(\widehat z\).

By invariance, \(N_0\subset N_1\subset N_2\subset\cdots\). The iterates converge locally uniformly on compact sets. Given a path \(P\) from \(\widehat z\) to any \(z\in\mathcal A_0\), we have \(f^{\circ k}(P)\subseteq N_0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Thus \(z\in f^{-k}(N_0)\), and \(\bigcup_kN_k=\mathcal A_0\).

Therefore \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal A_0=\bigcap_k(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus N_k)\). If each \(\partial N_k\) is connected, being a Jordan curve, and has no components, then \(\{\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus N_k\}_k\) is a nested sequence of compact connected sets. Hence \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal A_0\) is connected.

Otherwise, \(\overline{N_k}\) is a \(d\)-fold branched covering of \(\overline{N_{k-1}}\), and the same holds for their components: if \(C\) and \(D\) are such components, \(f|_C\colon C\to D\) is a \(d\)-fold branched covering. Thus \[f\colon\overline{N_k}\setminus f^{-1}(N_{k-1})\longrightarrow \overline{N_{k-1}}\setminus N_{k-1}\] is also a \(d\)-fold branched covering. The following figure completes the proof. Since \(f\) is conformal on \(\partial N_k\), it sends the interior of \(\partial N_k\) to the interior of \(f(\partial N_k)\), preserving angles and therefore direction.

The union of intersections of these Jordan-curve interiors forms \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal A_0\), which is evidently uncountable.

We now ask when \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\mathcal A_0\) is connected. This reveals the topological shape of polynomial Julia sets. Let us see the role of critical points, working in the ambient plane \(\mathbb C\subset\widehat{\mathbb C}\).

Definition 14 — Filled Julia set

The filled Julia set is \(K=\{z\in\mathbb C:\text{the orbit of }z\text{ is bounded}\}\).

Description of the filled Julia set

For \(f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}a_kz^k\) of degree \(d\ge2\), first normalise by \(cf(z/c)\) to make \(f\) monic. There is \(r\) with \(B_r(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal A(\infty)\), so the filled Julia set is \(\mathcal A(\infty)^c\). Recall that if \(J\) has interior, then \(J=\widehat{\mathbb C}\), which is not the case here. Thus \(J=\partial K\), and all bounded Fatou components belong to \(\operatorname{Int}(K)\).

By the maximum modulus principle, \(|f(z)|\le r\) for every \(z\in\operatorname{Int}(K)\). All bounded Fatou components are simply connected: pick any Jordan curve in a Fatou component; by the Jordan curve theorem, its bounded complementary component is simply connected. Now let us see how critical points enter the picture.

Theorem 24

The sets \(K\) and \(\partial K\) are connected if and only if every critical point has a bounded orbit.

Proof. The polynomial has an attracting basin at infinity, denoted \(\mathcal A(\infty)\). Critical points govern how far the Böttcher map can extend as a conformal isomorphism.

  • If \(\mathcal A\cong\mathbb D\), inversion of the sphere gives \(\psi\colon\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\to\mathbb C\setminus K\) conformally. Moreover, \[J=\partial K=\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\overline{\psi(A_{1+\varepsilon})}.\] Thus \(J\) is connected, and hence \(K\) is connected.

  • If \(\mathcal A\cong\mathbb D_r\) with \(r<1\), inversion gives \(\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D_r}\cong U\subset\mathbb C\setminus K\), now with \(r>1\). The set \(\mathcal A=\mathbb C\setminus K\) contains a critical point \(c\) of \(f\).

Set \(v=f(c)\), and let \(\phi\) denote the inverted Böttcher coordinate. Then \(\phi(c)\in\partial\mathbb D_r\) and \(\phi\circ f=z^d\circ\phi\), giving \[|\phi(v)|=|\phi(f(c))|=|\phi(c)^d|=r^d>r>1.\]

Consider the ray \(R=\{t\phi(v):t\ge1\}\) in \(\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb D_r\), and let \(R'=\psi(R)\), where \(\psi=\phi^{-1}\).

The critical point \(c\) helps break the domain into two components. At \(c\), the equation \(f(z)=v\) has two solutions, at least locally, yielding two noncompact external rays \(R_1',R_2'\).

The union \(R_1'\cup R_2'\) cuts the plane into \(V_0,V_1\). Since \(f\) is open, \(f(V_k)\supseteq\mathbb C\setminus R'\supset K\), giving \(f(J\cap V_0)\supset J\). Thus \(f(J_0)=J=f(J_1)\), where \(J_0=J\cap V_0\) and \(J_1=J\cap V_1\) are disjoint compact sets.

Repeat inductively: \[J_{10}=J_1\cap f^{-1}(J_0),\quad J_{00}=J_0\cap f^{-1}(J_0),\quad J_{01}=J_0\cap f^{-1}(J_1),\quad J_{11}=J_1\cap f^{-1}(J_1).\] These are all nonempty disjoint compact sets. Continuing produces \(J_{10100110\ldots}\) for every word \(10100110\ldots\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\). Each such set is a component, so \(J\) has uncountably many components. One can similarly prove the same for \(K\).
excerptHtml: Let’s see how the critical points of polynomials on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) determine the shape and structure of the Julia set. The following is a well-known fact.

title: The Quadratic Family
html:
Normalization and the Mandelbrot set

Start with \(f(z)=az^2+bz+c\). Conjugating by a dilation gives \[\lambda^{-1}f(\lambda z)=z^2+\alpha z+\beta, \qquad \lambda=\frac1a.\] We then conjugate by a translation: \[\begin{aligned} (z-d)\circ(z^2+\alpha z+\beta)\circ(z+d) &=(z+d)^2+\alpha(z+d)+\beta-d\\ &=z^2+(2d+\alpha)z+d^2-d+\beta. \end{aligned}\] Taking \(d=-\alpha/2\), the critical point, gives the normal form \(z^2+c\), denoted by \(P_c\).

Now suppose that \(\varphi\) is a Möbius map, \(c\ne c'\), and \[\varphi^{-1}\circ(z^2+c)\circ\varphi=z^2+c'.\] On \(\Chat\), the points \(\{\infty,0\}\) are critical points of both \(z^2+c\) and \(z^2+c'\). Hence \(\varphi\equiv\lambda z+d\), and there are unique \(\lambda,d\) conjugating any quadratic polynomial to \(z^2+c\). Thus \[\Moduli(\text{quadratic polynomials})\cong\C.\]

Definition 1 — Mandelbrot set

The Mandelbrot set is \[\M:=\{c\in\C\mid (P_c^{\circ n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ is bounded}\}.\]

Critical points and connectedness

Theorem 1 — Connected and Cantor filled Julia sets

Let \(P\) be any polynomial, and let \(K_P\) be its filled Julia set. Then:

(i)

\(\Crit(P)\subset K_P\) if and only if \(K_P\) is connected.

(ii)

If \(\Crit(P)\cap K_P=\varnothing\), then \(K_P\) is a Cantor set.

Proof. Write \(P(z)=a_dz^d+a_{d-1}z^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0\), and set \[A=\max_{0\le i\le d}\{|a_i|\}, \qquad R=\max\left\{1,\frac{2+A}{|a_d|}\right\}.\] Then \[\begin{aligned} |P(z)|&\ge |a_d||z|^d-\bigl(|a_{d-1}||z|^{d-1}+\cdots+|a_0|\bigr)\\ &\ge |a_d||z|^d-A|z|^{d-1}\\ &\ge |z|^{d-1}(|a_d||z|-A)\ge2|z| \qquad (|z|\gg R). \end{aligned}\] Thus there is an \(R_0\) such that, if \(z\in(\overline{D_R(0)})^c\), then \(P^{\circ n}(z)\to\infty\). Consequently, \[\begin{equation} K_P=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}P^{-n}(\overline{D_R(0)}). \tag{$*$} \end{equation}\] Set \(U_0=\Chat\setminus\overline{D_R(0)}\) and \(U_n=P^{-1}(U_{n-1})\). We have \(U_0\subset U_1\subset U_2\subset\cdots\) and, by (*), \(\bigcup_{n\ge0}U_n=\C\setminus K_P\).

(i) If \(\Crit(P)\subset K_P\), then \(P\colon U_n\to U_{n-1}\) is a branched cover ramified at \(\{\infty\}\), with degree \(d\). Hence \(U_n\) is connected. Since \(\chi(U_0)=1\), the Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives \[\chi(U_n)=d\chi(U_{n-1})-(d-1)=1\] by induction. Therefore \(U_n\) is a hyperbolic Riemann surface with \(U_n\cong\D\).

If \(\Crit(P)\not\subset K_P\), then \(P\colon U_n\to U_{n-1}\) has other points where it is ramified. Thus \(\chi(U_n)<1\), so \(U_n\) is not simply connected. Its complement \(U_n^c\) has more than two components, and \(K_P\) is not connected.

(ii) If \(\Crit(P)\cap K_P=\varnothing\), then (*) again gives an \(m\) large enough that \[\Crit(P)\cap P^{-m}(D_R(0))=\varnothing.\] Put \(V=P^{-m}(D_R)\) and \(W=P^{-(m-1)}(D_R)\). Then \(\overline V\subset W\) and \(P\colon V\to W\) is a covering map. Let \((z,\xi)\) be a tangent vector at \(z\). By Pick’s theorem applied to \(V\hookrightarrow W\), \[|(z,\xi)|_V\ge C|(z,\xi)|_W\qquad(C>1),\] and \[|(P(z),P'(z)\xi)|_W=|(z,\xi)|_V\ge C|(z,\xi)|_W.\] Let \(M=\max\{\diam(\text{components of }V)\}\). The maximum diameter of a component of \(P^{-n}(V)\) is \(MC^{-n}\), which tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\). Hence \(K_P=\bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty}P^{-n}(V)\) is a Cantor set.

Corollary 2 — Connected Julia sets

\[\M=\{c\mid K(P_c)\text{ is connected}\} =\{c\mid J(P_c)\text{ is connected}\}.\]

Escape bounds and the real slice

Theorem 3 — Basic properties of the Mandelbrot set

(i)

\(\M\subseteq\{c\mid |c|\le2\}\), and \(\M\) is closed and simply connected.

(ii)

\(\M\cap\mathbb R=[-2,1/4]\).

(iii)

\(|P_c^{\circ n}(0)|\le2\) for all \(n\ge1\) if and only if \(c\in\M\).

Proof. (i) If \(|c|>2\), induction gives \[|P_c^{\circ n}(0)|\ge |c|(|c|-1)^{2^{n-1}},\qquad n\ge1.\] Thus \(|P_c^{\circ n}(0)|\to\infty\) and \(c\notin\M\), giving (i).

(iii) Suppose \(|P_c^{\circ m}(0)|=2+\delta>2\) for some \(m\ge1\). If \(|c|=|P_c(0)|>2\), then \(c\notin\M\). If \(|c|\le2\), then \[|P_c^{\circ(m+1)}(0)|\ge(2+\delta)^2-2\ge2+4\delta.\] By induction, \(|P_c^{\circ(m+k)}(0)|\ge2+4^k\delta\to\infty\), so again \(c\notin\M\). If \(c_m\to c\) with \(c_m\in\M\), then \(|P_c^{\circ n}(0)|\le2\) for every \(n\); hence \(\M\) is closed.

Aside. If \(\C\setminus\M\) has bounded components, then \(|P_c^{\circ n}(0)|>2\) for some \(n\), and the maximum modulus principle disallows this.

(ii) For \(c\in\mathbb R\), the polynomial \(P_c(x)-x\) has no real roots if \(c>1/4\), one real root if \(c=1/4\), and two real roots if \(c<1/4\). If \(c>1/4\), then \(P_c^{\circ n}(0)\to\infty\); otherwise the orbit would accumulate at an \(x\in\mathbb R\) with \(P_c(x)=x\).

If \(c\le1/4\), let \(a=(1+\sqrt{1-4c})/2\) be the larger of the two roots of \(P_c(x)-x\). If also \(c\ge-2\), then \(a\ge|c|=|P_c(0)|\).

Therefore \[|P_c^{\circ n}(0)|\le a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad |P_c^{\circ(n+1)}(0)| =|(P_c^{\circ n}(0))^2+c|\le a^2+c=a.\] The sequence \(\{P_c^{\circ n}(0)\}_n\) is bounded, and \(\M\cap\mathbb R=[-2,1/4]\).

Attracting cycles and stability

Theorem 4 — Continuation of attracting cycles

Let \(a\in\Int(\M)\), and suppose \(P_a\) has an attracting cycle of length \(m\). Let \(W\) be the component of \(\Int(\M)\) containing \(a\). Then, for every \(c\in W\), \(P_c\) has an attracting cycle \(\{z_1(c),\ldots,z_m(c)\}\) of length \(m\), and \(c\mapsto z_i(c)\) is holomorphic for every \(1\le i\le m\).

Proof. Consider \(P_c^{\circ m}(z)-z\). By the implicit function theorem, we obtain an attracting periodic point of period \(m\), say \(z_1(c)\), in a small neighbourhood of \(a\). The sequence \(\{P_c^{\circ jm}(0)\}\) is bounded. Hence all subsequences of this sequence converge to an analytic continuation of \(z_1(c)\) over \(W\).

The point \(z_1(c)\) could be repelling, but convergence \(P_c^{\circ jm}(0)\to z_1(c)\) would then imply \(P_c^{\circ jm}(0)=z_1(c)\), by the local Koenigs dynamics. This happens for countably many points (false by the implicit function theorem).

Thus \(|(P_c^{\circ m})'(z_1(c))|\le1\). By the maximum modulus principle, \(z_1(c)\) is an attracting fixed point on all of \(W\). The other functions are \(\{P_c^{\circ i}(z_1(c))\}_{0\le i<m}\).

Theorem 5 — Density of the interior

\(\Int(\M)\) is dense in \(\M\).

Proof. Let \(U\) be a disk that meets \(\partial\M\), with \(0\notin U\).

Suppose \(U\) has no \(c\) for which \(0\) is periodic under \(P_c\). Consider a branch of \(\sqrt{-c}\) on \(U\). Then \(P_c^{\circ n}(0)\ne\sqrt c\), because \(P_c^{\circ(n+1)}(0)=0\). Consequently, the family \[\left\{\frac{P_c^{\circ n}(0)}{\sqrt{-c}}\right\}_n\] omits \(\{0,1,\infty\}\) and is normal in \(c\). But \(U\) meets \(\partial\M\), so for some \(c\in U\) the sequence explodes, whereas for some \(c\) it remains bounded, violating normality.

Corollary 6 — \(J\)-stability

\[\{c\mid P_c\text{ is }J\text{-stable}\}=\C\setminus\partial\M.\]

Proof. By definition, if \(c\in\Int(\M)\), the sequence \(\{P_c^{\circ n}(0)\}_n\) is bounded and hence forms a normal family, so \(c\) is \(J\)-stable. If \(c\in\Ext(\M)\), then \(P_c^{\circ n}(0)\to\infty\), again giving normality and \(J\)-stability. As in the preceding theorem, normality fails exactly on the boundary.

Components, invariant line fields, and corrections

Summary

1.

\(\M\) is closed and simply connected, and is contained in \(\{c\mid |c|\le2\}\).

2.

\(\Int(\M)\) is dense in \(\M\).

3.

\(\{c\mid P_c\text{ is }J\text{-stable}\}=\C\setminus\partial\M\).

4.

Connected components of \(\M\) are characterized by the length of the attracting cycle they admit, if they do admit one.

5.

\(\M=\{c\mid J(P_c)\text{ is connected}\}\).

Non-hyperbolic components

Theorem 7 — Invariant line fields

If \(c\in\M\), then \(c\) belongs to a non-hyperbolic component of \(\M\) if and only if \(J(P_c)\) has positive measure and carries an invariant line field.

Proof. If \(c\) belongs to a non-hyperbolic component, then \(P_c\) has neither an attracting cycle nor an indifferent cycle, because indifferent points are persistently indifferent. A polynomial has no Herman ring, so by the Sullivan–Fatou classification, \(J(P_c)\) is full.

The critical points of \(P_\lambda\) are in \(K(P_\lambda)\), so the Böttcher coordinate extends conformally. Hence \(\phi_\lambda(z)\) is a holomorphic motion of \(\C\setminus K(P_c)\).

By the \(\lambda\)-lemma, \(\phi_\lambda\) extends quasiconformally to \(\overline\phi_\lambda\colon\Chat\to\Chat\).

If \(J(P_c)\) has measure zero, then \(P_c\) and \(P_\lambda\) are conjugate by a Möbius map. For \(c\ne\lambda\), this is not possible.

Now suppose \(J(P_c)\) has positive measure and supports an invariant line field \(\mu\). Positive measure implies that \(c\notin\Ext(\M)\), so \(c\in\M\), as \(P_c\) is not hyperbolic. Solve \[\frac{\partial_{\overline z}\phi_t}{\partial_z\phi_t}=t\mu\] to obtain a holomorphic family of quasiconformal maps \(\phi_t\colon\C\to\C\), with \(t\in\D\). Set \(g_t=\phi_t\circ P_c\circ\phi_t^{-1}\), and normalize suitably to obtain \(g_t(z)=z^2+c(t)\).

We prove that \(c(t)\) is injective. If \(c(t_1)=c(t_2)\) and \(\phi_{t_1},\phi_{t_2}\) are conformal outside \(\C\setminus J(P_c)\), then, by continuity, \(\phi_{t_1}=\phi_{t_2}\) on \(J(P_c)\). Hence \(t_1\mu=t_2\mu\). By the open mapping theorem, \(\{c(t)\mid t\in\D\}\) is an open set in \(\M\) containing \(c\).

MLC and a few corrections

MLC.

\(\partial\M\) is locally connected.

(i) Correction to Theorem 4. The point \(z_1(c)\) could be repelling at uncountably many \(c\). Then there is a \(j\) such that \(P_c^{\circ jm}(0)=z_1(c)\) for uncountably many \(c\). By the identity theorem, \(z_1(c)\) is a polynomial in \(c\), and \(P_c^{\circ m}(z_1(c))=z_1(c)\) can have only finitely many solutions. Hence \(z_1(c)\) is repelling only at countably many points.

(ii) Indifferent points lie on \(\partial\M\). Here the parameters in question are \(\{c\mid P_c\text{ has an indifferent point}\}\). Consider the variety \(P_c^{\circ m}(z)-z=0\) in \(\C^2\), of dimension one. It has finitely many singular points. Away from these finitely many points, we have a Riemann surface \(V\), and \(V\to\C\), \((z,c)\mapsto c\), is a \(2^m\)-sheeted branched cover.

Consider an indifferent point in \(\Int(\M)\), say \(a\). Let \(V_0\) be an irreducible component of \(V\) containing \(a\). The map \[V_0\longrightarrow\C, \qquad (z,c)\longmapsto(P_c^{\circ m})'(z)\] would be locally constant around \(a\), hence constant on \(V_0\) (but \(V_0\) projects onto \(\C\)).

Quasicircles and uniformisation

The principal hyperbolic component

Theorem 8 — Quasicircle Julia sets

If \(c\) is in the principal hyperbolic component, then \(J(P_c)\) is a quasicircle.

Proof. This is true for a much more general class of functions: if \(R\) is a hyperbolic rational map with two Fatou components, then \(J(R)\) is a quasicircle.

Let \(D_1,D_2\) be the two Fatou components. Choose \(\gamma_1\) so that \(U_1\) has no critical points, and let \(\gamma_2=R^{-1}(\gamma_1)\). One can choose \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\) to be analytic, since \(D_1\) is a holomorphic image of the disk (the extension of the Koenigs coordinate is simply connected). The restriction \(R|_{\gamma_2}\colon\gamma_2\to\gamma_1\) is a \(d\)-fold covering map, where \(d=\deg(R)\).

Pick a Riemann map \(\widetilde R\colon U_1^c\to\Chat\setminus\overline{\D}_{\rho^d}\). This extends analytically (conformally, and quasisymmetrically) to \(\psi_1\colon\partial U_1\to S^1_{\rho^d}\).

We have \(\psi_1(R(z))=\psi_2(z)^d\). Fill \(U_1\setminus U_2\) with a quasiconformal map, via the Ahlfors–Beurling extension: \[\psi\colon\overline{U_1\setminus U_2}\longrightarrow\overline{A}_{\rho,\rho^d}.\] Define \[g_1(z)= \begin{cases} R(z),&z\in U_2,\\ \widetilde R^{-1}(\psi(z)),&z\in U_1\setminus U_2,\\ \widetilde R^{-1}(\widetilde R(z)^d),&z\in D_1\setminus U_1. \end{cases}\]

Using \(g_1\), we can produce a \(g_1\)-invariant Beltrami form on \(D_1\): \[\mu_1= \begin{cases} 0,&U_1^c,\\ \psi^*(0),&U_1\setminus U_2,\\ (f^{\circ n})^*\mu,&\text{elsewhere } \left(\displaystyle\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}g_1^{-n}(U_1\setminus U_2)\right). \end{cases}\] Similarly, produce \(\mu_2\) for \(D_2\), and set \[\mu=\begin{cases}\mu_i&\text{on }D_i,\\0&\text{elsewhere},\end{cases} \qquad g=\begin{cases}g_i&\text{on }D_i,\\0&\text{elsewhere}.\end{cases}\] By the measurable Riemann mapping theorem, there is a straightening map \(\varphi\) such that \(R_0:=\varphi\circ g\circ\varphi^{-1}\) is analytic. The map \(R_0\) has critical fixed points of degree \(d-1\) each at \(0\) and \(\infty\), since \(g_1,g_2\) have the same. Thus \(R_0\equiv z^d\), so \(J(R)=\varphi(S^1)\), which is a quasicircle.

Uniformisation of the complement of the Mandelbrot set

Theorem 9 — Uniformisation of \(\C\setminus\M\)

Recall that, if \(c\in\M^c\), then \(A_c(\infty)\) is the only Fatou component, and the Julia set is totally disconnected.

For the map \(P_c\), we have \(A_c(\infty)\subseteq\widetilde A_c(\infty)\), the basin of the superattracting point.

The Böttcher map satisfies \[\varphi_c(P_c(z))=\varphi_c(z)^2, \qquad \varphi_c(z)=\lim_{n\to\infty}[P_c^n(z)]^{2^{-n}}.\] Moreover, \[\begin{aligned} \varphi_c(z) &=z\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{P_c^n(z)}{P_c^{n-1}(z)^2}\right)^{2^{-n}}\\ &=z\prod_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(1+\frac{c}{P_c^n(z)^2}\right)^{2^{-(n+1)}}. \end{aligned}\] Hence, if defined, \[\varphi_c(c)=c\prod_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(1+\frac{c}{P_c^n(z)^2}\right)^{2^{-(n+1)}},\] which has a simple pole at \(\infty\).

Using \(\varphi_c(P_c(z))=\varphi_c(z)^2\), we can extend \(\varphi_c\) conformally until we hit a critical point of \(P_c\), namely \(0\). Set \(G_c(z)=\log|\varphi_c(z)|\). Then \[\begin{equation} G_c(P_c(z))=2G_c(z). \tag{$\star$} \end{equation}\] This can be extended to all of \(\widetilde A_c(\infty)\).

For \(G_c(z)>G_c(0)\), the map \(\varphi_c(z)\) is analytic and maps that set conformally to \(\{\zeta\mid |\zeta|>e^{G_c(0)}\}\). Also, \[K(P_c(z))=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} P_c^{-n}\bigl(\{z\mid G_c(z)\le G_c(0)\}\bigr).\] By \((\star)\), as \(z\to\partial\widetilde A_c(\infty)\), that is, \(J(P_c)\), we have \(G_c(z)\to0\). Extend \(G_c\) to the whole plane by defining it to be zero elsewhere.

One can show that \(G_c(z)\) is jointly continuous in \(c\) and \(z\), via some basic calculus. Notice that \[P_c(0)=c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_c(c)=2G_c(0)>G_c(0).\] Thus \(\varphi_c(c)\) is well-defined and analytic in \(c\). As \(c\to\M\), say \(c_n\to c_0\in\M\), we have \(G_{c_n}(z)\to G_{c_0}(z)\) uniformly in \(\C\), so \[G_{c_n}(c_n)\longrightarrow G_{c_0}(c_0)=0 \qquad\bigl(\text{as }c_0\in\partial\widetilde A_{c_0}(\infty)\bigr).\] Consequently, \(|\varphi_c(c)|\to1\) as \(c\to\M\). We therefore have an analytic map, with a simple pole at \(\infty\), \[\Chat\setminus\M\longrightarrow\Chat\setminus\D, \qquad c\longmapsto\varphi_c(c).\] If \(\varphi_c(c)\) were not surjective, there would be a sequence \(\{c_n\}_n\) with \(c_n\to\M\) but \(|\varphi_{c_n}(c_n)|\not\to1\). Let \(z_0\in\C\setminus\D\). We know that \[\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma \frac{\varphi_c'(c)}{\varphi_c(c)-z_0}\,dc\] is continuous in \(z_0\). By the argument principle, it must be \(-1\), because \(\Chat\setminus\M\) is connected.\(\square\)
excerptHtml: Start with \(f(z)=az^2+bz+c\). Conjugating by a dilation gives \[\lambda^{-1}f(\lambda z)=z^2+\alpha z+\beta, \qquad \lambda=\frac1a.\] We then conjugate by a translation: \[\begin{aligned} (z-d)\circ(z^2+\alpha z+\beta)\circ(z+d) &=(z+d)^2+\alpha(z+d)+\beta-d\\ &=z^2+(2d+\alpha)z+d^2-d+\beta. \end{aligned}\] Taking \(d=-\alpha/2\), the critical point, gives the normal form \(z^2+c\), denoted by \(P_c\).

title: Prime Ends and Landing of External Rays
html:
Recall the Riemann mapping theorem.

Theorem 33 — Riemann mapping theorem

For a simply connected domain \(U\subset\mathbb C\), there is a biholomorphism \(\varphi\colon U\to\mathbb D\), unique after prescribing suitable initial values, namely \(\varphi^{-1}(0)\) and \((\varphi^{-1})'(0)\).

Nothing in this theorem says that the map extends homeomorphically to \(\overline U\). We first sketch Carathéodory’s work on extension, then interpret it for a monic polynomial \(f\colon\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) of degree at least two, with \(J=\partial K\) connected. Equivalently, \(\mathcal A(\infty)\) contains no finite critical point of \(f\).

A sketch of Carathéodory’s work

Let \(\varphi\colon U\to\mathbb D\) be a conformal isomorphism. For now we avoid hyperbolic geometry: the spherical metric \(\rho(z)|dz|\) on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) captures Carathéodory’s strategy. Impose it on both \(\mathbb D\) and \(U\).

For a square \(I^2\subset\widehat{\mathbb C}\), its area is \(\iint_{I^2}\rho(x+iy)^2\,dx\,dy\), and the length of a horizontal segment \(y=C\) is \(\int_I\rho(x+iC)\,dx\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[\left(\int_I\rho(x+iy)\,dx\right)^2 \le\left(\int_I1^2\,dx\right)\left(\int_I\rho(x+iy)^2\,dx\right).\] Hence \(\int_I L(y)^2\,dy=O(\operatorname{Area}(I^2))\). Thinking of \(I^2\cong\mathbb D\), we conclude that for almost every radial line \(r\mapsto re^{i\theta}\), the limit \(\lim_{r\to1}\varphi^{-1}(re^{i\theta})\in\partial U\) exists.

For almost every \(\theta\in(0,2\pi]\), this gives a candidate for \(\varphi^{-1}(e^{i\theta})\). To ensure continuous extension to the boundary, every sequence \(z_j\to e^{i\theta}\) must satisfy \(\varphi^{-1}(z_j)\to\varphi^{-1}(e^{i\theta})\).

The idea is to divide \(U\) by crosscuts \(A\subset U\), with \(A\cong(0,1)\), \(\overline A\cong[0,1]\), and \(|\partial A\cap\overline U|=2\).

For example, a crosscut \(A\) joins boundary points \(x,y\). Since \(U\cong\mathbb D\), every sequence \(x_i\to\partial U\) has its image accumulating on \(\partial\mathbb D\). Thus there is a homeomorphism \(\widetilde\varphi\colon\overline U/\partial U\to\overline{\mathbb D}/\partial\mathbb D\cong S^2\).

Viewed in \(S^2\), \(A\) is a Jordan curve, so it divides \(U\) into \(U^+,U^-\), the signs depending on the orientation of \(A\). These are called crosscut neighbourhoods.

To prevent failure of boundary continuity of \(\varphi\) or \(\varphi^{-1}\), build a lasso around boundary points: a fundamental chain \(\mathcal N=\{N_j\}_j\) of crosscut neighbourhoods with \(N_1\supset N_2\supset\cdots\). If \(A_j\) are the corresponding crosscuts, require \(\overline A_j\cap\overline A_i=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(\diam(\overline A_j)\to0\).

Combining measure-theoretic and topological arguments, using \(\mathbb H^+\) as the universal cover of \(\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}\), Carathéodory shows that fundamental chains are a topological invariant. This makes the following natural.

Definition 20 — Carathéodory compactification

For two fundamental chains \(\mathcal N,\mathcal N'\) of \(U\), put \(\mathcal N\sim\mathcal N'\) if some \(N_j\subset N_k'\) or some \(N_k'\subset N_j\). Let \(\mathcal E\) denote this equivalence class, called the prime end for \((\overline U,\partial U)\). The compactification is \[\widehat U=U\sqcup\left(\bigsqcup_{\mathcal N\in\mathcal E}\mathcal N\right).\]

Clearly \(\overline{\mathbb D}\cong\widehat{\mathbb D}\cong\widehat U\). To extend \(\varphi\) continuously, it remains to compare the topologies of \(\widehat U\) and \(\overline U\). Thus Carathéodory shows that extension is independent of the particular map and depends entirely on the topology of the domain.

Theorem 34 — Carathéodory

A conformal isomorphism \(\psi\colon\mathbb D\to U\) extends continuously onto \(\widetilde\psi\colon\overline{\mathbb D}\to\overline U\) if and only if \(\partial U\) is locally connected.

In our setting the conformal isomorphism is the Böttcher map \(\phi\colon\mathbb C\setminus K\to\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\). The sets \(\{z:\arg\phi(z)=\theta\}\) are external rays, incident at angle \(\theta\). For \(\theta\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), let \(R_\theta=\{re^{2\pi i\theta}:r>1\}\) in the exterior disc. Set \[\gamma(t)=\lim_{r\to1}\phi^{-1}(re^{2\pi it}).\] If this exists, we say that \(R_t\) lands at \(\gamma(t)\in\partial K=J\). Let us translate Carathéodory’s work into this setting.

Theorem 35 — Landing criterion

The following are equivalent:

  • every ray \(R_t\), \(t\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), lands, and \(\gamma(t)\) is continuous;

  • \(J=\partial K\) is locally connected;

  • \(K\) is locally connected;

  • \(\phi^{-1}\colon\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\to\mathbb C\setminus K\) extends continuously to the boundary.

Proof. Immediate from Carathéodory’s theorem.

We offer a slightly deeper insight than the landing criterion.

Theorem 36 — Rational rays land

Every periodic rational ray \(R_t\) lands at a repelling or parabolic periodic point, or an eventually periodic point.

Before proving this, we need a preparatory lemma that is significant in its own right.

Lemma 37 — Snail lemma

Suppose \(p\colon[0,\infty)\to V\setminus\{0\}\) and \(f(0)=0\), with \(f(z)=\lambda z+a_2z^2+\cdots\) on \(V\). Then

  • \(f(p(t))=p(t+1)\) for every \(t\ge0\) implies \(|\lambda|<1\) or \(\lambda=1\);

  • \(f(p(t))=p(t-1)\) for every \(t\ge1\) implies \(|\lambda|>1\) or \(\lambda=1\).

Lemma 38 — Preparatory lemma

If \(R_t=f(R_t)\) lands at \(z_0\), then \(z_0\) is a repelling or parabolic fixed point.

Proof. Parametrise the ray by \(p\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C\setminus K\), where \(p(s)=z\) is determined by \(\log\log|\phi(z)|=s\). This \(z\) is unique: the argument is fixed by \(R_t\), and the modulus is fixed by \(|\phi(z)|=e^{e^s}\). Also \(z_0=\gamma(t)=\lim_{s\to-\infty}p(s)\).

Since \(\phi(f(z))=\phi(z)^n\), we have \(\log|\phi(f(z))|=n\log|\phi(z)|\), and \(\log\log|\phi(f(z))|=\log n+\log\log|\phi(z)|\). Therefore \(f(p(s))=p(s+\log n)\). The landing point is fixed, and the snail lemma gives \(|\lambda|>1\) or \(\lambda=1\).

Proof of Theorem 36. We must return to hyperbolic geometry to go beyond the spherical landing criterion. Give \(\mathbb C\setminus K\) its Poincaré metric using \(\mathbb C\setminus K\cong\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\). The map \(\psi\colon\mathbb H^+\to\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\), \(\psi(w)=e^w\), is a covering.

Recall the parametrisation \(f(p(s))=p(s+\log n)\). Then \[R_t=p(\mathbb R)=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}I_k =\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}p([k\log n,(k+1)\log n]),\] with \(f(I_k)=I_{k+1}\). Also \(G(p(s))=e^s\to0\) as \(s\to-\infty\). Thus any limit point \(\widehat z\) of \(p(s)\) has \(\log|\phi(\widehat z)|=0\), so \(\phi(\widehat z)\in\partial\mathbb D\) and \(\widehat z\in\partial K=J\). Such a limit point exists because \(\overline{\mathbb C\setminus K}\) is compact in \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\). We are in the right setting for the lemma, illustrated again below.

For a neighbourhood \(N\) of \(\widehat z\), there is a smaller neighbourhood \(N'\subset N\) containing an entire \(I_k\), since \(\operatorname{length}(I_k)=\log n\). Hence \(N\cap f(N)\ne\varnothing\), as \(f\) maps one endpoint of \(I_k\) to the other. This holds for every neighbourhood of \(\widehat z\), so \(\widehat z\) is fixed.

The limit set \(\bigcap_t\overline{p(( -\infty,t])}\) is connected, while the fixed-point set is finite. Therefore \(R_t\) lands at \(\widehat z\), which is repelling or parabolic by the preparatory lemma.

Remark

We have \(f(I_k)=I_{k+1}\). A holomorphic map on a hyperbolic surface is distance-reducing unless it is a covering map. Here \(z\mapsto z^n\) on \(\mathbb C\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\) is a covering, so \(f\) is a local isometry. Since \(f|_{I_k}\) is injective, it maps \(I_k\) isometrically to \(I_{k+1}\).

Remark

One can also prove the converse of Theorem 36.

Remark

The classification of hyperbolic self-maps, together with Sullivan’s no-wandering theorem and the snail lemma, gives Sullivan’s classification of Fatou components for rational maps.
excerptHtml: For a simply connected domain \(U\subset\mathbb C\), there is a biholomorphism \(\varphi\colon U\to\mathbb D\), unique after prescribing suitable initial values, namely \(\varphi^{-1}(0)\) and \((\varphi^{-1})'(0)\).

title: The Chain Rule and a Family of Complex Planes
html:
Given a manifold \(M\), local coordinates \((U,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) tell us the whereabouts of points in \(U\). Directions, however, cannot be represented in terms of the \(x_i\). That luxury is available only in Euclidean spaces such as \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(x_i\) is projection onto the \(i\)-th coordinate. There, moving in the \(i\)-th coordinate means moving in the direction \(x_i\). To say something similar on a manifold, we introduce tangent spaces.

If a path allows us to associate a direction coherently at every point, for instance a smooth curve \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\), then \(\gamma'(t)\) is a point of \(T_{\gamma(t)}M\cong\mathbb R^n\).

By identifying \(\gamma'(t)\) with a vector in \(\mathbb R^n\), one can associate an infinitesimal direction. Changing direction amounts to changing one’s path at a given point \(P\), as below. Thus tangent spaces allow us to navigate a manifold.

As in \(\mathbb R^n\), moving in the \(i\)-th coordinate on \(M\), or moving along \(x_i\), means moving only along \(x_i\): the rate of change along \(x_j\), for \(j\ne i\), is zero. Thus \(\{\left.\partial/\partial x_i\right|_p\}_{i=1}^n\) is an appropriate basis for \(T_pM\). After a first course in differential geometry, this is made precise: one says that one is going in the direction \(x_i\) if \[L_{\chi_j}(\widetilde\gamma)=0\quad(j\ne i),\qquad \chi_j(p)=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right|_p.\] Here \(\chi_j\) is the global field on \(U\), \(\widetilde\gamma\) is the vector field generated by \(\gamma'(t)\), \(t\in[0,1]\), on \(\gamma([0,1])\), and \(L_{\chi_j}(\widetilde\gamma)\) denotes the Lie derivative.

If the coordinates change from \((U,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) to \((U,y_1,\ldots,y_n)\), then \(T_pM\), \(p\in U\), has two bases. Write \[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j}.\] The simplest way to find this change of basis is to evaluate both sides on \(y_k\). This gives \(a_k=\partial y_k/\partial x_i\); the matrix is \(\bigl(\partial y_k/\partial x_i\bigr)_{1\le i,k\le n}\). Changing coordinates is therefore no trouble: this matrix acts like a dictionary!

The same can be done for complex manifolds. On a real or complex manifold, the directions along \(\gamma(t)\) are \[\gamma'(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i'(t) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_{\gamma(t)}\in TM,\] where \(TM\) is the tangent bundle.

There is a dual notion to navigation on a manifold: obstruction. Suppose the curve moves in the direction \[\gamma_1'(t)\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}\right|_{\gamma(t)} +\gamma_2'(t)\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}\right|_{\gamma(t)}.\] To know what obstructs \(\gamma\) from moving purely in the \(x_1\)-direction, we must retrieve the extra luggage \(\gamma_2'(t)\left.\partial/\partial x_2\right|_{\gamma(t)}\), which is misdirecting its flow. To study flow, or navigation, we looked naturally at functions \(\gamma:\mathbb R\to M\). To study its dual, obstruction, focus instead on \(f:M\to\mathbb R\), \(f\in C^\infty(M)\).

Define the differential of \(f\) at \(p\) by \(df_p(v)=v_p(f)\), where \(v\in T_pM\). Thus \(df_p\) is a covector: it is a linear functional on \(T_pM\), given by evaluation. The family \(\{dx_i\}_{i=1}^n\) is a smooth coframe on \(U\), so \[df_p=a_i(p)(dx_i)|_p,\qquad a_i(p)=df_p\left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_p\right) =\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right|_p.\] Consequently \(df_p=\left.(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\,dx_i)\right|_p\).

Since \(\partial f(p)/\partial x_i\) is smooth, \(df\) is a smooth covector field. Set \(f=x_2\). Then \[df_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t)\bigr) =\gamma_1'(t)\left.\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial x_1}\right|_{\gamma(t)} +\gamma_2'(t)\left.\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial x_2}\right|_{\gamma(t)} =\gamma_2'(t).\] The obstruction to the flow \(\gamma(t)\) along \(x_2\) is therefore given by \((dx_2)_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))\), and \(df_p\in T_p^*M\), the dual tangent space. Flows and obstructions can be discussed using the two bundles \(TM\) and \(T^*M\) hovering over the manifold.

Let us now combine flow and obstruction. For a smooth curve \(\gamma:J\to M\) and \(f:M\to\mathbb R\), \(f\in C^\infty(M)\), one has \[(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=df_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t)\bigr).\] In plain English, the obstruction to \(\gamma(t)\) along \(f\) is the same as the flow of \(f\circ\gamma\). In modest terms, the chain rule chains together flows and obstructions in a very intricate manner! Let us see what more it can offer.

For \(f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\), viewed as a map \(\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\), we know \(df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy\). Alternatively, \[df=f_z\,dz+f_{\bar z}\,d\bar z,\qquad dz=dx+i\,dy,\quad d\bar z=dx-i\,dy,\] where \[\partial_z:=\frac{\partial}{\partial z} =\frac12\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}-i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right), \qquad \partial_{\bar z}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar z} =\frac12\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+i\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right).\] As \(df\) acts linearly pointwise, focus on one point rather than on the smooth covector field. For \(df_z:T_z\mathbb C\to T_{f(z)}\mathbb C\), set \[\mu_f=\frac{\partial_{\bar z}f}{\partial_zf},\qquad \alpha=\arg(\partial_zf),\qquad \theta=\arg\mu_f,\] assuming that \(\mu_f\) is defined and \(|\mu_f|<1\). Then \[df_z(\omega)=e^{i\alpha}|\partial_zf| \bigl(\omega+|\mu_f|e^{i\theta}\bar\omega\bigr).\] The vectors \(e^{i\theta/2}\) and \(e^{i(\pi+\theta)/2}\) are eigenvectors of \(df_z/e^{i\alpha}\). Linear maps pull ellipses back to ellipses, giving the following picture.

Before proceeding, observe that \[d(f\circ g)_z=df_{g(z)}\circ dg_z =(f_z\circ g)\,dg_z+(f_{\bar z}\circ g)\,d\bar g_z.\] Expanding gives \[\begin{aligned} d(f\circ g)_z={}& \bigl[(f_z\circ g)g_z+(f_{\bar z}\circ g)\overline{g_{\bar z}}\bigr]\,dz\\ &+\bigl[(f_z\circ g)g_{\bar z} +(f_{\bar z}\circ g)\overline{g_z}\bigr]\,d\bar z. \end{aligned}\] From this simple composition of linear maps one obtains the chain rule for the Wirtinger derivatives: \[\begin{aligned} \partial_z(f\circ g)&=(f_z\circ g)g_z+(f_{\bar z}\circ g)\overline{g_{\bar z}},\\ \partial_{\bar z}(f\circ g)&=(f_z\circ g)g_{\bar z}+(f_{\bar z}\circ g)\overline{g_z}. \end{aligned}\] Hence, in the notation of the notes, \[\mu_{f\circ g}= \frac{\mu_2+\mu_1e^{-2i\arg(\partial_zg)}} {1+\mu_1\mu_2e^{-2i\arg(\partial_zg)}}.\] This is a consequence of the complex chain rule!

The coefficient \(\mu_f(z)\) captures the shape of the ellipse pulled back from \(T_{f(z)}\mathbb C\). Its ratio of major to minor axes is \[K_f=\frac{1+|\mu_f|}{1-|\mu_f|}.\]

Now let \(\mu:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) be a function with \(|\mu|\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\). A very deep theorem tells us that there exists an almost differentiable \(\varphi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) such that \[(d\varphi_z)^{-1}(S^1)=\text{the ellipse given by }\mu(z) \quad\text{almost everywhere}.\] Thus, given \(|\mu|\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\), one can find a \(\varphi\) for which the ellipses generated by \(\mu\) on \(T_z\mathbb C\) are precisely those pulled back from circles in \(T_{\varphi(z)}\mathbb C\). Denote this additional structure by \((\mathbb C,\mu_\varphi)\).

This generates a family of complex planes. Our familiar complex plane is \((\mathbb C,\mu_z)\), where \(\mu_z\) gives circles everywhere. Define \[[\mu_h,\mu_f]:=\log\bigl(K_{h\circ f^{-1}}(f(z))\bigr), \qquad d\bigl((\mathbb C,\mu_h),(\mathbb C,\mu_f)\bigr) =\sup[\mu_h,\mu_f].\]

This \(d\) is called the Teichmüller distance between the complex planes. The chain rule therefore also tells us when a family of complex planes is close to our complex plane. In these two ways, the chain rule quite literally chains together concepts and structures!

title: Quasiconformal Mappings
html:
The dynamics of a map \(f:S\to S\) is a topological invariant. Fixed points, critical points, and the nature of periodic orbits—attracting, repelling, superattracting, parabolic, or non-linearizable—remain as they were when coordinates on \(S\) are changed by a biholomorphism. But conformal maps are too rigid. If the rate of attraction near a fixed point is \(\lambda\), then a biholomorphic change of coordinates preserves \(\lambda\), the multiplier; it similarly preserves the essence of other invariants.

For flexibility, we shall first introduce a way to measure how conformal a map is. Then we shall see what happens to a biholomorphism \(\varphi:S\to S'\) when we reduce the extent to which it is conformal. Certainly \(\varphi\) must be a homeomorphism, since we want the dynamics preserved. We want quantities describing the dynamics, such as multipliers, to have some flexibility. The proposed almost-conformal maps should connect flexibility in conformality with flexibility in the analytic aspects of the dynamics. Let’s put a meter on a function’s conformality and look at ways of studying it; the next post turns to its use in dynamics.

A meter on conformality

For \(f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\), conformality is equivalent to saying that the real-linear map \(df_z:T_z\mathbb C\to T_{f(z)}\mathbb C\) is complex-linear, under the appropriate identifications. Let \(f\) be continuously differentiable. In \(dz,d\bar z\) coordinates, \[df_{z_0}=\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\right|_{z_0}dz +\underbrace{\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\bar z}\right|_{z_0}d\bar z}_{\text{extra luggage}}.\] Denote this linear map by \(T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\), and write \(T\binom{x}{y}=\binom XY\). For \(x^2+y^2=r^2\), \(r>0\) fixed, if \(T\) is invertible then \[(x,y)\binom xy=r^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (X,Y)(T^{-1})^{\mathsf T}T^{-1}\binom XY=r^2.\] As \(T\) is real symmetric, it has two eigenvalues \(a,b\) and can be diagonalized, giving \(aX^2+bY^2=r^2\). Thus \(df_{z_0}\) pulls an ellipse back from a circle in its codomain. Removing the extra luggage makes it pull back a perfectly round circle.

The differential is not invertible everywhere, but Sard’s theorem tells us that circles can be pulled back from \(T_{f(z)}\mathbb C\) almost everywhere in \(f(\mathbb C)\). Set \[a=f_z(z_0),\qquad b=f_{\bar z}(z_0),\qquad \theta=\arg(b/a),\qquad \mu_{z_0}=b/a.\] Writing \(a=|a|e^{i\alpha}\), we get \[df_{z_0}(z)=|a|e^{i\alpha} \bigl(z+|\mu|e^{i\theta}\bar z\bigr).\] Then \(e^{i\theta/2}\) and \(e^{i(\theta+\pi)/2}\) are eigenvectors of \(df_{z_0}\), corresponding to \(|a|(1+|\mu_{z_0}|)\) and \(|a|(1-|\mu_{z_0}|)\).

The dilatation at \(z_0\) is \[K_{z_0}(f):=\frac{\text{major axis}}{\text{minor axis}} =\frac{1+|\mu_{z_0}|}{1-|\mu_{z_0}|}.\] Conformal maps merely dilate and rotate, preserving circles. We propose to study maps that also change their shapes. If \(\esssup_{z_0\in\mathbb C}K_{z_0}(f)=K<\infty\), then \(K\) measures the failure of \(f\) to be conformal. This could be formalized by introducing Teichmüller distance, but we shall not do so here.

The \(C^1\) assumption was rather unmotivated: it was imposed so that Sard’s theorem could be used. There are other ways to ensure that pullback can be done almost everywhere.

Definition 21 — First analytic definition of quasiconformal maps

A map \(\varphi:U\to V\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal if it is a homeomorphism, is ACL, and satisfies the ellipse criterion \[|\partial_{\bar z}\varphi|\le k|\partial_z\varphi| \quad\text{almost everywhere},\qquad k=\frac{K-1}{K+1}.\]

Why is this the right definition? First, how does one differentiate continuous functions, and what does ACL mean?

Definition 22 — Absolutely continuous on lines

A function \(f:U\to\mathbb C\) is ACL if, for every family of parallel lines in every disc \(D\Subset U\), it is absolutely continuous on almost all of them.

Remark

Standard Lebesgue differentiation theory tells us that an ACL function has derivatives almost everywhere. It therefore suffices to require absolute continuity on lines parallel to the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes.

Almost-everywhere differentiability along these axes gives directional derivatives almost everywhere, hence absolute continuity almost everywhere in all directions. Thus \(\partial_zf\) and \(\partial_{\bar z}f\) make sense.

The definition therefore makes sense. Why it is the right one is the content of what follows.

Lemma 39 — Gehring–Lehto

If \(\varphi\) has partial derivatives almost everywhere and is an open map, then it is differentiable almost everywhere.

Proof. Consider a bounded measurable region \(\Omega\), of finite measure, and the sequence \[\varphi_n(z):=\sup_{0<|h|<1/n} \left|\frac{\varphi(z+h)-\varphi(z)}h-\varphi_x(z)\right|.\] By Egoroff’s theorem, \(\varphi_n\) converges uniformly to zero on \(E\), where \(E=\Omega\) almost everywhere. Thus \(\varphi_x,\varphi_y\) are continuous on \(E\), since the difference quotients converge uniformly. Almost every line contains almost every point in \(E\).

For almost every \((x_0,y_0)\in E\), Lebesgue’s differentiation theorem gives \[\lim_{\substack{m(R)\to0\\(x_0,y_0)\in R}} \frac1{m(R)}\int_R\mathbf1_E\,dm=1,\] where \(R\) is a square of side \(2h\).

By Fubini’s theorem, this becomes \[\lim_{\substack{m(R)\to0\\(x_0,y_0)\in R}} \frac1{m(R)}\int_{y_0-h}^{y_0+h} \int_{x_0-h}^{x_0+h}\mathbf1_{E_y}(x)\,dx\,dy=1.\] Choose \(x_0,y_0\) such that the horizontal and vertical lines through \((x_0,0)\) and \((0,y_0)\) contain almost every point of \(E\) in \(\Omega\). Such points satisfying the limit occur almost everywhere in \(E\). Then \[\lim_{h\to0}\frac1{2h}\int_{x_0-h}^{x_0+h} \mathbf1_{E_{y_0}}(x)\,dx=1.\] Thus \(x_0\) is a density point of \(E_{y_0}\), and vice versa. Translate so that \((x_0,y_0)=(0,0)\). Uniform convergence gives, for \(\varepsilon>0\), a \(\delta>0\) such that \[\begin{gathered} |\varphi_x(z)-\varphi_x(0)|<\varepsilon,\qquad |\varphi_y(z)-\varphi_y(0)|<\varepsilon,\\ \left|\frac{\varphi(z+h)-\varphi(z)}h-\varphi_x(z)\right|<\varepsilon,\qquad \left|\frac{\varphi(z+ik)-\varphi(z)}k-\varphi_y(z)\right|<\varepsilon \end{gathered}\] whenever \(|x|,|y|,|h|,|k|<\delta\) and \(z\in E\). The triangle inequality gives \[\begin{aligned} |\varphi(x+iy)-\varphi(0)-x\varphi_x(0)-y\varphi_y(0)| &\le|\varphi(x+iy)-\varphi(x)-y\varphi_y(x)|\\ &\quad+|\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)-x\varphi_x(0)|\\ &\quad+|y(\varphi_y(x)-\varphi_y(0))| \le3\varepsilon|z|. \end{aligned}\tag{*}\]

The final inequality holds if \(|y(\varphi_y(x)-\varphi_y(0))|<\varepsilon|z|\), which holds if \(x\in E\). We want differentiability at zero, but have shown only \[\left|\varphi(z)-\varphi(0) -(\varphi_x(0),\varphi_y(0))\binom xy\right|\longrightarrow0\] as \(x,y\to0\) with \(x\in E\); similarly with \(y\in E\). Exploit the fact that zero is a coordinatewise density point of \(E\): \[\frac{m(E\cap(-x,x))}{2|x|}\longrightarrow0\quad(x\to0).\] There is a \(\delta\) such that, for \(|x|<\delta\), \[m(E\cap(-x,x))>\frac{2+\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}|x|.\]

Consequently \((x/(1+\varepsilon),x)\cap E\ne\varnothing\); otherwise \[m(E\cap(-x,x))<m((-x,x/(1+\varepsilon))) =|x|+\frac{|x|}{1+\varepsilon} =\frac{2+\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}|x|.\] For \(|z|<\delta/(1+\varepsilon)\), repeat the argument for \((x,(1+\varepsilon)x)\). We may arrange \(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2\in E\) with \[\frac{x}{1+\varepsilon}<x_1<x<x_2<(1+\varepsilon)x,\qquad \frac{y}{1+\varepsilon}<y_1<y<y_2<(1+\varepsilon)y.\] The estimate \((*)\) holds on \(\partial R\), where \(R=(x_1,x_2)\times(y_1,y_2)\).

Since \(\varphi\) is open, it satisfies the maximum modulus principle. For \((x,y)\in R\), choose \(z^*=x^*+iy^*\in\partial R\) such that \[\begin{aligned} |\varphi(x+iy)-\varphi(0)-x\varphi_x(0)-y\varphi_y(0)| &\le|\varphi(z^*)-\varphi(0)-x\varphi_x(0)-y\varphi_y(0)|\\ &\le3\varepsilon|z^*|+|x-x^*|\,|\varphi_x(0)| +|y-y^*|\,|\varphi_y(0)|\\ &\le3\varepsilon(1+\varepsilon)|z| +\varepsilon|\varphi_x(0)||z| +\varepsilon|\varphi_y(0)||z|\\ &=\varepsilon|z|M. \end{aligned}\] This bound is independent of \(z^*\). Therefore \(\varphi\) is differentiable at \((x_0,y_0)\), hence almost everywhere.

This lemma tells us that quasiconformal maps can pull back circles because they are differentiable almost everywhere. Let \(m=m_1\times m_1\), where \(m_1\) is Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R\); naturally \(m\) is Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^2\). An absolutely continuous function takes a measure-zero subset of an interval to a measure-zero set in its image, directly from the definition. Locally, let \(\{x\}\times B_x\) have \(m_1\)-measure zero.

Here \(B_x\) is the projection of the relevant vertical slice of the local region where the measure is zero. Set \(A_x=\{x\}\times B_x\). Then \(f(\bigcup_{x\in\pi_1(U)}A_x)\) again has measure zero by Fubini, where \(U\) is the local region and \(\pi_1\) is projection onto the first coordinate. Locally, \(\varphi\) is \(C^1\) almost everywhere by Egoroff and takes measure-zero sets to measure-zero sets. The image of the critical set has measure zero by Sard’s theorem for absolutely continuous functions. Cover \(\mathbb C\) by countably many such local regions. The points where these properties fail still form a measure-zero set, since \(\mathbb C\) is Lindelöf.

Thus \(K\)-quasiconformal maps pull circles back to ellipses of dilatation at most \(K\). Modulo technical details, this is the right definition: dropping any condition loses something we want. Without a homeomorphism we cannot preserve dynamics. Replacing ACL by existence of partial derivatives almost everywhere does not ensure that critical values form a measure-zero set. Dropping \(|\partial_{\bar z}\varphi|\le k|\partial_z\varphi|\) loses the meter itself.

By the Lebesgue decomposition theorem, \(A(E):=m(\varphi(E))\) is sigma-finite and \[A(E)=\int_EJ_f(z)\,dm+\int_Ed\widetilde\mu,\qquad dA=J_f\,dm+d\widetilde\mu,\quad\widetilde\mu\perp m.\] Therefore \(\int_EJ_f(z)\,dx\,dy\le A(E)\), where \(J=|\varphi_z|^2-|\varphi_{\bar z}|^2\), and \[|\varphi_{\bar z}|^2\le|\varphi_z|^2\le\frac{J}{1-k^2}.\] Thus \(\varphi_{\bar z},\varphi_z\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\), leading to another definition.

Definition 23 — Second analytic definition of quasiconformal maps

A \(K\)-quasiconformal map \(\varphi:U\to V\) is a homeomorphism with locally integrable distributional derivatives satisfying \(|\varphi_{\bar z}|\le k|\varphi_z|\), the ellipse criterion.

The analytic definitions are useful only to an extent. A promising alternative, with its own limitations, is the geometric definition.

Definition 24 — Geometric definition of quasiconformal maps

An orientation-preserving homeomorphism \(\varphi:U\to V\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal if \[\frac1K\operatorname{mod}Q \le\operatorname{mod}\varphi(Q) \le K\operatorname{mod}Q\] for every topological quadrilateral \(Q\Subset U\).

The modulus changes from shape to shape; for a quadrilateral, it is the ratio of length to breadth, assuming it to be a rectangle.

The analytic definition makes it obvious that quasiconformality is local, whereas this is extremely nontrivial to derive geometrically. Conversely, the geometric definition makes it obvious that \(\varphi^{-1}\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal, which is not immediate analytically. The three definitions can be proved equivalent; we skip the proof to preserve the flow.

To ensure that our meter measures conformality and is not an artificial monster, we must recover conformality by reversing what we adjusted. The following powerful lemma ensures this.

Lemma 40 — Weyl’s lemma

A \(1\)-quasiconformal map is conformal.

Proof sketch. By the equivalence of definitions, it suffices to prove that a map \(\varphi\) with \(\partial\varphi/\partial\bar z=0\) in the sense of distributions is conformal. Construct \(f_n=\varphi_n*(\eta f)\), where \(\varphi_n\) is a scaled mollifier on \(\mathbb D\) and \(\eta\) is a test function. Then \(f_n\) is smooth and \(f_n\to f\) uniformly on compact sets. Since \[(f_n)_{\bar z}=(\eta f)_{\bar z}=0,\] the smooth functions \(f_n\) are holomorphic, and hence so is \(f\).

This ensures that the meter for conformality is dilatation! Next we shall see why we need to loosen the conformality condition.
excerptHtml: The dynamics of a map \(f:S\to S\) is a topological invariant. Fixed points, critical points, and the nature of periodic orbits—attracting, repelling, superattracting, parabolic, or non-linearizable—remain as they were when coordinates on \(S\) are changed by a biholomorphism. But conformal maps are too rigid. If the rate of attraction near a fixed point is \(\lambda\), then a biholomorphic change of coordinates preserves \(\lambda\), the multiplier; it similarly preserves the essence of other invariants.

title: The Mapping Theorem and Invariant Complex Structures
html:
An ellipse field on a Riemann surface is essentially an ellipse, modulo scaling, chosen in the tangent plane \(T_zS\) for almost every \(z\in S\). It is the pullback of a circle field via the expression \(\mu(z)\,d\overline z/dz\).

The mapping theorem says that if \(S\) is simply connected, hence by uniformisation one of \(\mathbb C\), \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), or \(\mathbb D\), then there is a quasiconformal map \(\phi\colon S\to\mathbb D\). This does not say much by itself. But once an ellipse field on \(S\) is fixed by a measurable complex dilatation \(\mu\) (the Beltrami coefficient), with \(\esssup_{z\in S}|\mu(z)|<\infty\), the map \(\phi\) is the unique such map pulling back the circle field on \(\mathbb C\), \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), or \(\mathbb D\) to the ellipse field given by \(\mu\).

This is also called the integrability theorem or measurable Riemann mapping theorem. We shall see an elementary example in which the mapping theorem joins forces with Weyl’s lemma to change the quantitative features of dynamics while keeping its topology

the same. Start with \(M_0\colon\mathbb D\to\mathbb D\), \(z\mapsto\lambda_0z\). View this as a map \(\mathbb D^*\to\mathbb D^*\) and lift it to the universal cover \(\mathbb H_\ell\).

Here \(v_0=\log\lambda_0\). Let \(L_v\) be the real-linear map on \(\mathbb H_\ell\) given by \(a\zeta+b\overline\zeta\), where \[a=\frac{v+\overline v_0}{v_0+\overline v_0},\qquad b=\frac{v-v_0}{v_0+\overline v_0}.\] The map \(L_v\) conjugates \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta+v_0\) to \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta+v\).

Finally descend \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta+v\) to \(\mathbb D^*\), obtaining the following diagram.

This is an instance in which a holomorphic map is quasiconformally conjugate to another holomorphic map. Here we constructed the conjugacy explicitly. Alternatively, pull back the circle field \(\mu_0\) on the bottom copy of \(\mathbb D^*\) to obtain \(\mu_v=\phi_v^*\mu_0\), then appeal to the mapping theorem. It gives a \(K\)-quasiconformal map \(\phi_v\colon\mathbb D\to\mathbb D\) pulling back the circle field. But how can we ensure that \(\phi_v\circ(z\mapsto\lambda_0z)\circ\phi_v^{-1}\) is conformal?

Usually quasiconformal conjugation does not yield a holomorphic map. It does yield a dynamical conjugate: a map with essentially the same dynamics, but with quantities of our choosing. In the preceding example we changed the multiplier from \(\lambda_0\) to \(e^v\)! In some lucky cases the following is prescribed.

Definition 15 — \(K\)-quasiregular map

A map \(g\colon U\to\mathbb C\), \(U\subseteq\mathbb C\), is \(K\)-quasiregular if \(g=f\circ\phi\), where \(\phi\colon U\to\phi(U)\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal and \(f\colon\phi(U)\to g(U)\) is holomorphic.

Lemma 25 — Surgery lemma

Let \(g\colon S\to S\), where \(S\cong\mathbb C\) or \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), be quasiregular. If \(\mu\) is a \(g\)-invariant Beltrami form with \(\|\mu\|_\infty=k<1\), then there is \(f\in\Hol(X)\), with \(X=\mathbb C\) or \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\), quasiconformally conjugate to \(g\).

Proof. The mapping theorem supplies \(\phi\colon S\to X\) in the following diagram; \(\mu_0\) denotes the circle field.

Then \(f^*\mu_0=\mu_0\), so \(f\) is \(1\)-quasiconformal and therefore conformal by Weyl’s lemma.

Taking our cue from this lemma, after surgically altering the dynamics quantitatively we want to retain a holomorphic map so that complex analysis remains available. For that, the conjugate \(\phi\circ g\circ\phi^{-1}\) must be a Beltrami-form-preserving quasiregular map.

In our original example, \(\phi_v\circ(z\mapsto\lambda_0z)\circ\phi_v^{-1}\) was conformal, hence circle-field-preserving and \(1\)-quasiregular. To stitch the incision after changing the quantitative dynamics, we must hope for an ellipse-field-preserving quasiregular map. Otherwise it is surgery gone wrong! More perspective on quasiregular maps may shed light on this.

Definition 16 — Second definition of \(K\)-quasiregularity

A map \(g\colon U\to\mathbb C\) is \(K\)-quasiregular if it is locally \(K\)-quasiconformal except on a discrete set.

Definition 17 — Third definition of \(K\)-quasiregularity

For every \(z\in U\), there are neighbourhoods \(N_z,N_{g(z)}\) of \(z,g(z)\), a \(K\)-quasiconformal map \(\psi\colon N_z\to\mathbb D\), and a conformal map \(\varphi\colon N_{g(z)}\to\mathbb D\) such that \[\varphi\circ g\circ\psi^{-1}(z)=z^d\qquad\text{for some }d\ge1.\]

We show that the three definitions are equivalent; this reveals enough content to perform a good surgery. The implication \((1)\Rightarrow(2)\) is clear.

For \((2)\Rightarrow(1)\), the Lindelöf property gives a countable family \(\{U_i\}_{i\in\mathbb N}\) on each of which \(g\) is \(K\)-quasiconformal except at a discrete set. Then \(\partial_zg,\partial_{\overline z}g\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\). Define \(\widehat\mu(z)=0\) outside \(U_i\), and \(\mu(z)=\partial_{\overline z}g(z)/\partial_zg(z)\) inside. There is a map \(\widehat\phi\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) pulling back the circle field to this ellipse field. Put \(\phi=\widehat\phi|_{U_i}\) and \(f=g\circ\phi^{-1}\).

By Weyl’s lemma, \(f\) is conformal except on a discrete set; continuity makes the singularities there removable.

For \((3)\Rightarrow(1)\), if \(\varphi\circ g\circ\psi^{-1}=z^d\) and \(d=1\), we are done. If \(d>1\), the map is a local homeomorphism except at discrete points, because \(0\) is the only point where this fails.

Those points are isolated, so \((3)\Rightarrow(2)\Rightarrow(1)\).

For \((1)\Rightarrow(3)\), suppose \(g=f\circ\phi\). If \(\phi(z)\notin\operatorname{Crit}(f)\), there are neighbourhoods \(N_{\phi(z)},N_{g(z)}\) such that \(f\colon N_{\phi(z)}\to N_{g(z)}\) is conformally invertible, and \(f^{-1}\circ g\circ\phi^{-1}=z^1\).

If \(\phi(z)\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\), choose these neighbourhoods so that \(f\) is a branched covering of degree \(d\), branched only at \(\phi(z)\).

Now consider the following self-explanatory diagram. Shrink \(N_{g(z)}\) to be simply connected, take its Riemann map \(R\), and lift \(R\) to \(\widetilde R\) (basically a deck transformation).

Then \(R\circ g\circ(\widetilde R\circ\phi)^{-1}\) is the required map.

Among the many things one must look out for in a good surgery, knowing one’s way around quasiregularity is important. There are deeper principles and schemes, due to Shishikura, governing how and when surgery can be performed. We will see them later. This gives a peek into the role of quasiconformality in loosening dynamics. As promised, the flexibility in conformality is deeply connected with flexibility in the resulting dynamics.

Addendum: two properties of quasiconformal maps

1.

Hölder’s inequality: \(|\varphi(z_1)-\varphi(z_2)|\le C|z_1-z_2|^{1/K}\).

2.

A \(K\)-quasiconformal family \(\{\varphi_n\}_{n\in\Lambda}\) is closed in the \(C^0\) topology, and in fact compact. For a sequence \(\{\varphi_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}\), equicontinuity and boundedness on a compact set give sequential compactness by Arzelà–Ascoli. Applying the same argument to \(\varphi_n^{-1}\) shows that the limit \(\varphi\) is a homeomorphism. Its \(K\)-quasiconformality follows from the analytic definition.

Addendum: full proof of Weyl’s lemma

Consider a domain \(D\) and a compact set \(K\subset D\). Since \(\mathbb C\) is normal, choose a neighbourhood \(U_K\) with \(K\subset U_K\subset\overline{U_K}\subset D\). Let \(\eta\in C_0^\infty(D)\) be identically one on \(U_K\) and supported in \(D\). Then \((\eta f)_{\overline z}\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

Set \[\varphi(z)=\begin{cases} C\exp\!\left(-\dfrac1{1-|z|^2}\right),&z\in\mathbb D,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \qquad\iint_{\mathbb D}\varphi(z)\,dx\,dy=1,\] choosing \(C\) accordingly. Define \(\varphi_n(z)=n^2\varphi(nz)\) and \[f_n(w)=\varphi_n*(\eta f)(w) =\iint_{\mathbb C}\varphi_n(w-z)\eta(z)f(z)\,dx\,dy.\] Then \((f_n)_{\overline z}=(\varphi_n*(\eta f))_{\overline z}=\varphi_n*(\eta f)_{\overline z}=0\), and for large \(n\), \(f_n\) is holomorphic in \(D\), being smooth with \(\partial f_n/\partial\overline z=0\).

For large \(n\), \(\supp(\varphi_n)=\mathbb D_{1/n}=\{z:|z|<1/n\}\). Compactness of \(K\) gives \(n\) such that \(B(w,1/n)\subset U_K\) for every \(w\in K\).

Since \(\eta=1\) on \(U_K\), \[\begin{align*} f_n(w)&=\iint_{|w-z|<1/n}\varphi_n(w-z)f(z)\,dx\,dy\\ &=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{1/n} \frac{n^2f(w+re^{i\theta})r}{\exp(1/(1-n^2r^2))}\,dr\,d\theta, \end{align*}\] while \(f(w)=\iint_{\mathbb D}f(w)\varphi(z)\,dx\,dy\). Thus \(|f_n-f|\to0\) uniformly on \(K\), independently of the input by continuity of \(f\). Hence \(f_n\to f\) uniformly on compact sets and \(f\) is holomorphic.

Remark

This immediately implies the Looman–Menchoff theorem.
