For any component \(I(U)\) of \(I(C)\), there exists quasisymmetrical mappings \(\hat{\phi}_1\) and \(\hat{\phi}_2\) mapping \(I(U)\) and \(\hat{f}(I(U))\) respectively to \(\mathbb{S}^1\) providing an equivalence between \(\hat{f}\) and \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d\geq 1\). If \(I(U)\) is fixed, \(\hat{f}\) and \(z\rightarrow z^d\) may not be quasisymmetrically conjugate.

(Note: The equivalence between \(\hat{f}\) and \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d\geq 1\) can be changed to an equivalence between \(\hat{f}\) and any Blaschke product of degree \(d\) on \(\mathbb{S}^1\). There is also a lot of freedom in the choices of the quasisymmetric maps \(\hat{\phi}_1\) and \(\hat{\phi}_2\) providing the equivalence, in that, for an arbitrary choice of one, one can obtain the other).

Proposition 6.17

(Dynamics of \(\hat{f}\) on Periodic Components of \(I(C)\)):- On each periodic component of \(I(C)\), the first return map is quasisymmetrically conjugate to one of the three rigid models.

Let us apply Propositions \(6.16\) and \(6.17\) in a sequence of surgeries to establish the main theorem.

Proof of Main Theorem. Suppose \(I(U)\) is periodic of period \(p\geq 1\). Following Proposition \(6.17\), let \(\hat{\phi}:I(U)\rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1\) be a quasisymmetric map so that \(\hat{\phi}\circ \hat{f}^p\circ \hat{\phi}^{-1}\) equals exactly one of the rigid models, say \(B_U\). Extend \(\hat{\phi}\) to a quasiconformal homeomorphism of \(\overline{\mathbb{D}}\). Denote the extension also by \(\hat{\phi}\). Choose a Riemann mapping \(R_U:U \rightarrow \mathbb{D}\) and set \(\phi:= \hat{\phi}\circ R_U:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}\). It follows that \(f^{\circ p}\) and \(B_U\) are compatible on the ideal boundary via \(\phi\). If \(p=1\) we are done: replacing \(f\) on \(U\) by the map \(\phi^{-1}\circ B_U\circ \phi\) and keeping \(f\) outside \(U\), it follows from the Gluing Lemma that we obtain a new quasirational map. If \(p>1\) then we have to replace \(f\) on the disc components \(U_j\) where \(I(U_j):= \hat{f}^j(I(U))\) for \(0\leq j\leq p-1\) with maps that are compatible with \(\hat{f}\) along the ideal boundaries and whose composition agrees with \(\phi^{-1}\circ B_U\circ \phi\) on \(U\). Let \(d_j\geq 1\) denote the degree of \(\hat{f}:I(U_j)\rightarrow I(U_{j+1})\) for \(0\leq j\leq p-1\). Then the sum \(\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}{d_j} = d\) where \(d=1\) in the elliptic case. From Proposition \(6.16\) \((3)\) we know that there exist a pair of quasisymmetric maps mapping \(I(U_j)\) and \(I(U_{j+1})\) respectively to \(\mathbb{S}^1\) and providing an equivalence between \(\hat{f}\) and \(B_j(z):= z^{d_j}\) for \(0\leq j\leq p-2\). From what we noted in Proposition \(6.16\) we know that we may choose one of the quasisymmetric maps arbitrarily. Let \(\hat{\phi}_0 = \hat{\phi}:I(U_0)\rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1\) from above. For \(j = 1,\ldots, p-1\) establish recursively \(\hat{\phi}_j:I(U_j)\rightarrow \mathbb{S}^1\) such that \(\hat{\phi}_j\circ \hat{f} = B_{j-1}\circ \phi_{j-1}\). Depending on the case we choose \(B_{p-1}\) to be the Blaschke product defined as

\[B_{p-1}(z):= \begin{cases} e^{2\pi i \theta}z, &\quad\text{in the elliptic case,}\\ z^{d_{p-1}} &\quad\text{in the hyperbolic case,}\\ \frac{z^{d_{p-1}}+a}{1 + az^{d_{p-1}}} &\quad\text{in the parabolic case, for} a = \frac{d-1}{d+1}\\ \end{cases}\]

The conditions in Corollary \(6.13\) are therefore satisfied. Hence, by replacing \(f\) on \(U_j\) by the map \(\phi_{j+1}^{-1}\circ B_j\circ \phi_j\) for \(j = 0, 1, \ldots, p-1\) and keeping \(f\) outside \(\cup_{j=0}^{p-1}{U_j}\) we obtain a new quasirational map.
After having dealt with all the periodic components of \(I(C)\) we work backwards along the preimages of each of them. If \(I(V)\) is one of them, and \(\hat{f}(I(V)) = I(W)\), then \(\hat{f}\) is quasisymmetrically equivalent to \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d\geq 1\). If \(d=1\) we keep the quasiconformal homeomorphism \(f\big|_V:V\rightarrow W\). Only if \(d>1\) we shall replace the map. Suppose this has been done up to \(V\). We construct as before gluing maps \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) using Riemann mappings \(R_V\) and \(R_W\) and define \(g:V\rightarrow W\) as \(g:= \phi_2^{-1}\circ z^d\circ \phi\). The new critical point \(c\) equals \(\phi_1^{-1}(0) \in V\) with critical value \(g(c)\) equals to \(\phi_2^{-1}(0)\). The orbit of \(c\) satisfies one of the conditions in the main theorem if the orbit of \(g(c)\) does. We choose the Riemann mapping \(R_W\) so that \(\phi_2^{-1}(0)\) has the correct orbital behaviour. Keep repeating this, after a finite number of steps we would have constructed a quasirational map, satisfying the conditions of the main theorem. After integration we get our desired rational map \(g\).
Now, to prove \(C = J(g)\), we first note that on all components of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C\), \(U_i\) such that \(U_i\cap f^{-1}(C)\neq \phi\), we replaced \(f\) with something else \(\implies\) after altering \(f\) to a quasirational map \(q\), we note that \(q^{-1}(C)=C\) \(\implies\) \((C, f) \sim (J(g), g)\) where \(g\) is the rational map quasiconformally conjugate to \(q\). \(C\) is connected nowhere dense totally invariant set for \(g\). It will hence suffice to show that \(C\subseteq J(g)\). Note that \(\forall\) \(x\in C\), there does not exist a neighbourhood \(U_x\) of \(x\) such that \(\{f^{\circ n}\big|_{U_x}\}_n\) is a normal family of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\) \(\implies\) \(\forall\) \(y\in C\) the same must be true, for we know that \(\{f^{\circ n}\big|_{U_x}\}_n\) expands to the whole of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\) barring at most two points \(\implies\) \(\{g^{\circ n}\big|_{\tilde{U}_y}\}_n\) must also expand for they are homeomorphic conjugates.

Therefore, we have established the following isomorphism \(\text{Mod}(C, f) \cong \text{Mod}(J(g), g)\). If we further show that \(\text{Mod}(J(g),g) \cong \text{Aut}(g)\), then we can show that the group \(\text{Mod}(C, f)\) is a finite group. Now to complete the proof of the main theorem let us prove the two aforementioned propositions.

Proof of Proposition \(6.16\). There are only finitely many components \(V_1, V_2,\ldots, V_k\) of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C\), which intersect \(f^{-1}(C)\) or contain a critical point. Set \(V = \{V_j\}_{1\leq j\leq k}\).
Proof of (1). If \(U\) is a component of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C\) not in \(V\), then \(f\) maps \(U\) onto another component of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C\) as a covering. Since \(U\) is a disk, \(f\big|_U\) is a quasiconformal homeomorphism onto its image.
Proof of (2). Let \(U\) be a component of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C\) not in \(V\). Suppose \(f^{\circ n}(U)\) is not in \(V\) for any \(n\geq 0\). Then, \(f^{\circ n}\) is normal on \(U\) and therefore \(f^{\circ n}(U)\) must eventually cycle, otherwise \(U\) would be a wandering domain which (as we saw before) is not possible for a rational map. Hence, \(U\) is eventually mapped onto a Fatou component whose first return map is a quasiconformal homeomorphism, and therefore a Siegel disk. It follows that \(I(U)\) is preperiodic. If, on the other hand, \(f^{\circ n}(U)\) is eventually mapped onto one of the components in \(V\) then \(I(U)\) must also be preperiodic. Indeed, if some iterate is mapped onto \(I(W)\) for \(W \notin V\), we can repeat the argument from before, the component \(W\) is eventually mapped onto the Siegel disk or onto one of the components in \(V\). Since there are only finitely many components in \(V\), the ideal boundary \(I(U)\) will eventually cycle. There is a finite number of periodic components in \(I(C)\), since there are at most finitely many cycles of Siegel disks and finitely many components in \(V\) (as the number of cycles of indifferent points is finite).
Proof of (3). If \(U\) is not in \(V\) then \(f\big|_U\) is a quasiconformal homeomorphism and \(\hat{f}:I(U)\rightarrow f(I(U))\) is quasisymmetrically equivalent to the identity. If \(U\) is one of the components in \(V\), then we can find an annulus \(U' \subset U\) such that \(\partial U \subset \partial U'\) and \(f\) is a covering on its image. Indeed, uniformize \(U\) and \(f(U)\) separately \(\implies\) \(\phi_1: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow U\) and \(\phi_2: \mathbb{D} \rightarrow f(U)\). Let \(K:= \text{crit}(f)\cup f^{-1}(C)\), then \(K\cap \partial U\), and \(f(K)\cap \partial f(U)\) are empty. This facilitates \(r_1, r_2\) such that \(\{z\) \(|\) \(|z|\geq r_1 \cap \phi_1^{-1}(K) = \phi\}\), and \(\{z\) \(|\) \(|z|\geq r_1 \cap \phi_2^{-1}(K) = \phi\}\). Let \(R = \max(r_1, r_2)\), so now let \(\tilde{\phi}_1 = \phi_1\big|_{\mathbb{A}_{R, 1}}\) and \(\tilde{\phi}_2 = \phi_2\big|_{\mathbb{A}_{R, 1}}\). This way we can simultaneously uniformize \(U'\) and \(f(U')\) for a suitable annulus \(U'\) as \(U'\cap \text{crit}(f) = \phi\). Note that, \(f\big|_{U'}: U' \rightarrow f(U')\) is a covering of degree \(d\), therefore, the induced covering map \(\tilde{f}: \mathbb{A}_{R, 1}\rightarrow \mathbb{A}_{R, 1}\) is conjugate to the map \(z\rightarrow z^d\) with the same extension to \(\mathbb{S}^1\) via the map \(\phi\) (say). The way to see that would be to use Schwarz Reflection principle to extend this to a covering self map on the unit circle and use classification theorem for connected covers of \(\mathbb{S}^1\). Choose Riemann maps \(R_U\), \(R_V\) for disks \(U\), \(V\) (respectively). Then \(\psi_1 = \phi\circ \tilde{\phi_1}\circ R_U^{-1}\) and \(\psi_2 = \phi\circ \tilde{\phi_2}\circ R_V^{-1}\) extend to \(\mathbb{S}^1\) providing and equivalence between \(\hat{f}:I(U) \rightarrow I(V)\) and \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d\geq 1\).
(Note: The choice of \(\phi_1\) determines \(\phi_2\), thereby also carrying that degree of freedom to \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\)).

Now let us devote some time to prove Proposition \(6.17\) through a sequence of lemmas which shall study each type of periodic component of \(I(C)\) separately. Let \(U\) be a component of \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash C\) for which \(I(U)\) is periodic under \(\hat{f}\). Replacing \(f\) by a suitable iterate, we may assume that \(I(U)\) is fixed. Recall from the discussion above that there is an annulus \(U' \subset U\) with \(\partial U \subset \partial U'\) and such that \(f\) is a covering onto its image.

Lemma 6.18

:- Suppose \(\hat{f}(I(U)) = I(U)\). If \(U'\) can be chosen to be a proper subset of \(f(U')\) then \(\hat{f}\) is quasisymmetrically conjugate to \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d>1\).

Proof.:- In the proof of the above lemma we shall use the following theorem. A complete treatment of the theorem and expanding maps can be found in (Shub and Sullivan 1985), (Hubbard and Douady 1982) and (De Melo and Van Strien 2012).

Theorem 6.19

:- Any expanding1 \(C^{1+\alpha}\) orientation preserving endomorphism of \(\mathbb{S}^1\) is quasisymmetrically conjugate to \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d>1\).

Let \(R_U:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}\) be the Riemann map, then \(R_U(U')\) is an annular region in \(\mathbb{D}\) as \(U' \subset f(U')\). We also have \(R_U\circ f\circ R_U^{-1}(R_U(U')=R_U(f(U'))\). Let \(\tilde{f} = R_U\circ f\circ R_U^{-1}\) \(\implies\) \(\tilde{f}\big|_{R_U(U')}: R_U(U') \rightarrow R_U(f(U'))\). Uniformize \(R_U(f(U'))\) to a standard annulus \(\mathbb{A}_{R,1}\), and via Schwarz Reflection principle extend the new conjugated map \(\tilde{\tilde{f}}\) past \(\mathbb{S}^1\). Therefore, \[\tilde{\tilde{f}}: A' \rightarrow \mathbb{A}_{R, 1/R}\]

is a holomorphic covering such that \(\mathbb{S}^1\) is totally invariant with respect to \(\tilde{\tilde{f}}\). Now, the Poincaré metric 2 on \(\mathbb{A}_{R, 1/R}\) is given by \(\lambda(z)|\text{dz}|\), where

\[\lambda(z) = \frac{-\pi}{2\log(R)}\left(\frac{1}{|z|\cos\left(\frac{\pi \log|z|}{2\log R}\right)}\right)\]

Now as \(\tilde{\tilde{f}}\) is a covering map, by Pick’s Theorem it is a local isometry \(\implies\) \(\lambda(\tilde{\tilde{f}})|d(f(z))| = \lambda(\tilde{\tilde{f}}(z))\). As for \(z\in \mathbb{S}^1\), \(\tilde{\tilde{f}} \in \mathbb{S}^1\), we have \(\lambda(\tilde{\tilde{f}}(z)) = \frac{-\pi}{2\log(R)}\), one can choose \(R\) such that \(\frac{\pi}{2}>\log(\frac{1}{R})\). By Theorem \(6.19\) the result follows as \(\tilde{\tilde{f}}\big|_{\mathbb{S}^1}\) is expanding.

Lemma 6.20

:- Suppose \(\hat{f}: I(U) \rightarrow I(U)\). Either \(\partial U \subset \partial V\) for some Fatou component \(V \subset U\) or \(\hat{f}:I(U)\rightarrow I(U)\) is quasisymmetrically conjugate to \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d>1\).

Proof.:- To prove this lemma we shall need the following theorem due to Zoretti which can be found in (Whyburn 1948).

Theorem 6.21

(Zoretti’s Theorem):- Let \(C\) be a component of a compact set \(J \subset \mathbb{R}^2\). For all \(\epsilon >0\) there exists a simple closed curve \(\gamma_{\epsilon}\) which encloses \(C\) and is such that \(\gamma_{\epsilon}\cap J = \emptyset\) and \(\text{dist}(C, x) < \epsilon\) for all \(x\in \gamma_{\epsilon}\).

In \(\overline{U}\), \(\partial U\) is a component of \(\overline{U}\cap\overline{J(f)}\) \(\implies\) one can apply Zoretti’s Theorem to get \(\gamma_n\) (simple closed curves) such that \(\gamma_n\) is in the Fatou set lying in an \(\epsilon_n\)-neighbourhood of \(\partial U\). As \(\partial U\) is disjoint from the boundaries of the Fatou components in \(U\), and as periodic Fatou components are finite - If \(\{U_i\}_{1\leq i\leq n}\) were the periodic components and \(K = \cup_{i=1}^{n}{U_i}\), then \(\partial U \cap \partial K = \emptyset\) \(\implies\) by compactness \(\exists\) \(\delta\) such that \(\text{dist}(\partial K, \partial U) > \delta\). Let \(\epsilon_n < \delta\) \(\implies\) \(\gamma_n\) does not go through any periodic Fatou component. Now choose \(n\) large enough such that the open annuli bounded by \(\gamma_n\) and \(\partial U\) also doesn’t have any critical values, further that if \(V'\) were such an annulus, then \(\text{mod}(V')\) be such that if \(V' \cong \mathbb{A}_{R, 1/R}\), then \(\frac{\pi}{2}> \log(1/R)\).
As \(\hat{f}(I(U)) = I(U)\), the thing implicit in this assumption is that \(f(U) = U\) \(\implies\) \(\exists\) \(U'\), a unique component of \(f^{-1}(V')\) bounded by \(\partial U\) and preimage of \(\gamma_n\). Since, \(\gamma_n\) isn’t in any periodic Fatou component, it must be disjoint from its preimages \(\implies\) \(U' \subset V'\) or \(V'\subset U'\), but as \(f:U'\rightarrow V'\) is a proper covering, \(\text{mod}(V')>\text{mod}(U')\). This gives us that \(U' \subset V'\) and the lemma follows from the previous lemma.

Now we are left to handle the cases \(\partial U \subset \partial V\), where \(V \subset U\) is a Fatou component. By the classification theorem of periodic Fatou components for rational maps, \(V\) can only be a Siegel disk, a Herman ring, a basin of (super)attraction, or a parabolic basin. We deal with these cases separately in a bunch of lemmas to follow.

Lemma 6.22

:- If \(V\) is fixed Siegel disk or a fixed Herman ring of rotation number \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Q}\), then \(\hat{f}\) is real analytically conjugate to the rigid rotation \(R_{\theta} = e^{2\pi i \theta}z\)

Proof.:- If \(V\) is a Siegel disk then \(U=V\) and a Riemann mapping \(R_U\), which maps the indifferent fixed point to \(0\), conjugates \(f\) to the rigid rotation on \(\mathbb{D}\). Hence \(\hat{f}\) on \(\mathbb{S}^1\) is actually equal to \(R_{\theta}\). If \(V\) is a Herman ring, then there is a conformal map \(\phi:V \rightarrow \mathbb{A}_r\) conjugating \(f\) to \(R_{\theta}\). In this case, arguing as we did in Proposition \(6.16\), we obtain that \(\hat{f}\) on \(I(U)\) is real analytically conjugate to \(R_{\theta}\).

Lemma 6.23

:- If \(V\) is an immediate basin of (super)attraction, or a parabolic basin whose parabolic fixed point is not on \(\partial U\), then \(\hat{f}\) is quasisymmetrically conjugate to \(z\rightarrow z^d\) for some \(d>1\).

Proof.:- Let \(W \subset V\) be a Jordan domain, for which \(f(W)\) is a proper subset of \(W\) and \(\overline{W}\) does not intersect \(\partial U\). In the (super)attraction case \(W\) may be chosen as disk surrounding the (super)attracting fixed point and mapping inside itself. In the parabolic case \(W\) may be chosen as an attracting petal in the parabolic basin so that \(\overline{W}\) intersects \(\partial V\) at the parabolic fixed point.
Let \(W_n\) be the component of \(f^{\circ (-n)}(W)\) containing \(W\), then \[\overline{W} \subset \overline{W_1} \subset \overline{W_2} \subset \ldots\]

and \(\cup_{n}{W_n} = V\). In the parabolic case, \(\partial U\) cannot contain any point in the grand orbit of the parabolic point since \(f(\partial U) = \partial U\), so \(W_n \cap \partial U = \emptyset\) for all \(n>0\). Observe that, if \(V\) is not simply connected, \(W_n\) will become multiply connected after a certain \(n_0\), since the union of all the \(W_n\)’s must account for all of \(V\).
For every \(n\), there is a component of \(\partial W_n\) which together with \(\partial U\) bounds an annulus \(A_n\) disjoint from \(W_n\). In general, \(A_n\) may contain infinitely many different components of the Julia set. Each annulus lies in an \(\epsilon_n\)-neighbourhood of \(\partial U\), where \(\epsilon_n \rightarrow 0\) as \(n\rightarrow \infty\). Otherwise there is a continuum in \(\partial V\) which lies in \(U\) and meets \(\partial U\), contradicting the fact that \(C\) is a component of the Julia set.
Choose \(n\) sufficiently large so that \(A_n\) contains no critical point. The component of \(\partial W_n\) such that the annulus bounded by that component and \(\partial U\) (denoted by \(A_n\)), and that \(A_n \cap W_n = \emptyset\), is essentially the component of \(\partial W_n\) that hits rays from \(\partial U\) to \(W_n\) first. This fact along with \(f(W_{n+1}) = W_n\) ensures that \(f(A_{n+1}) = A_n\). Again choose the modulus of \(A_n\) such that one can apply Lemma \(6.18\).

Lemma 6.24

:- If \(V\) belongs to a parabolic basin, with a parabolic fixed point on \(\partial U\), then \(\hat{f}\) on \(I(U)\) is quasisymmetrically conjugate to \(P_d(z)\) for some \(d>1\).

Proof.:- Let \(R_U:U\rightarrow \mathbb{D}\) be a Riemann map sending the parabolic fixed point to \(z=1\) (Note that any petal \(P\) contains an attracting vector, that vector yields the path \(\gamma: [0,1) \rightarrow U\) such that \(\lim_{t \rightarrow 1}{\gamma(t)} = \text{p}\). Therefore, \(\text{p}\) is accessible \(\implies\) so are all its preimages by Riesz’s Theorem radial limit exists). Then \(f\) and \(V\) carry over to \(\mathbb{D}\) where we also denote them by \(f\) and \(V\). Observe that \(f\) is not defined on the whole disk, and that its domain contains \(V\) and a one-sided neighbourhood of \(\mathbb{S}^1\). By Schwarz-Reflection Principle, \(f\) can be extended to a holomorphic map on the neighbourhood of \(\mathbb{S}^1\) having a parabolic fixed point at \(z=1\). The restriction to the unit circle is precisely \(\hat{f}\). We construct by hand a quasisymmetric conjugacy between \(\hat{f}\) and \(P_d\) where \(d\) is the degree of \(\hat{f}\) on \(\mathbb{S}^1\).
Consider an attracting petal \(W\), containing \(z=1\) on its boundary. For simplicity choose \(W\) so that \(\partial W\) is a \(C^{\infty}\) curve avoiding the critical orbits. As before, let \(W_n\) denote the component of \(f^{\circ (-n)}(W)\) containing \(W\). For \(n\) sufficiently large, \(W_n\) contains all critical points of \(V\), and hence there is a unique component of \(\gamma_n\) of \(\partial W_n\), lying between \(\partial U\) and \(W_n\), and touching \(\mathbb{S}^1\) at the \(n\)-th preimages of \(z=1\). This curve \(\gamma_n\) is contained in the annulus where \(f\) is covering.
The curves \(\gamma_n\) and \(\gamma_{n+1}\) bound a pinched annulus \(A_n\) with several components. This pinched annulus is, in a sense, a fundamental domain, since all forward orbits of points in between \(\mathbb{S}^1\) and \(\gamma_{n+1}\) must pass once and only once through \(A_n \cup \gamma_n\).
We may carry out the same discussion on another copy of the unit disk for the map \(P_d\), obtaining analogous sets \(W'_n\), \(\gamma_n'\), \(A'_n\), etc.
To construct the conjugacy, we start by fixing \(n\) sufficiently large and by choosing a \(C^1\)-diffeomorphism \(\phi\) from the curve \(\gamma_n\) onto \(\gamma_n'\), fixing \(z=1\), and sending preimages of \(z=1\) to their analogues in an appropriate fashion (To do this one basically has to construct a smooth graph joining points \((x_i, x_i')\)). Using the map \(f\), we define \(\phi\) on \(\gamma_{n+1}\) so that \(P_d\circ \phi = \phi \circ f\). We then extend \(\phi\) quasiconformally to the different components of \(A_n\) sending them to their analogues \(A_n'\). Using the dynamics of \(f\) and \(P_d\) we extend recursively to the whole pinched annulus in between \(\mathbb{S}^1\) and \(\gamma_n\), so that it conjugates \(f\) and \(P_d\). Such a map extends quasiconformally to the whole unit disk, and quasisymmetrically to \(\mathbb{S}^1\), conjugating \(\hat{f}\) and \(P_d\) as required.

This concludes the proof of Proposition \(6.17\) and Theorem \(6.3\) (1). Now the following proposition shall handle Theorem \(6.3\) (2), thereby finishing the proof of the central theorem behind this surgery.

Proposition 6.25

:- \(\text{Mod}(J(g), g) \cong \text{Aut}(g)\). \(\text{Mod}(C, f)\) is a finite group, given that \(C\) carries no invariant line field.

Proof.:- Let \(\phi\) be an element of \(\text{Mod}(J(g), g)\). We claim the ideal boundary values of \(\phi\) on any component of \(I(J(g))\) coincide with those of a conformal map commuting with \(g\). If so, by Corollary \(6.9\) there is a homotopy connecting \(\phi\) to a unique quasiconformal map \(\hat{\phi}\) which is conformal on \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\backslash J(g)\) and commutes with \(g\) everywhere. But if \(J(g)\) carries no invariant line field, such a map is conformal, for \(\hat{\phi}^*\mu_0\) being an invariant line field of \(J(g)\) must have \(0\) dilatation. Hence \([\phi]\) is represented by an element of \(\text{Aut}(g)\), completing the proof.
To establish the claim we note that as there are finitely many periodic components with say periods \(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_N\), then set \(M = \text{lcm}(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_N)\). So, the \(M\)-th iterate of \(g\) shall fix all the periodic components, which by our classification theorem happen to be - Siegel disks, parabolic basins, or (super)attracting basins, which conjugate to rigid models after uniformization.
As remarked earlier, the two models must be identical, and up to composition with uniformizing maps, \(\phi\) is a rotation commuting with the dynamics throughout the disk. Thus the ideal boundary values of \(\phi\) coincide with those of a conformal map commuting with \(g\).
Now let \(U\) be a preperiodic component, and let \(V = \phi(U)\), then there is a least integer \(k\) such that \(g^{\circ k}(U)\) (and consequently \(g^{\circ k}(V)\)) are components fixed by \(g\). If \(g^{\circ k}\) maps \(U\) by degree \(1\), as \(g^{\circ k}(U)\) and \(g^{\circ k}(V)\) are fixed, one can replace \(\phi\) with a conformal map \(\tilde{\phi}\) and the ideal boundary values won’t change. So, just use \(g^{\circ (-k)}\circ \tilde{\phi}\circ g^{\circ k}\) for \(U\).
On the other hand, if \(\text{deg}(g^{\circ k}) >1\), by Proposition \(6.16\), the critical values in \(g^{\circ k}(U)\) and \(g^{\circ k}(V)\) are unique (which either coincides with the center of a Siegel disk, or the critical point in the parabolic basin or the superattracting basin), and \(\tilde{\phi}\) will carry those to critical values via chain rule \(\implies\) \(\tilde{\phi}\) can be lifted, therefore even in this case suitable replacements can be arranged.

Before talking about Conjecture \(6.4\), let us briefly talk about buried sets.

Definition 6.26

(Buried Sets):- A collection of points in a closed set \(J \subset X\) will be called buried if it does not belong to the boundary of the components of \(X\backslash J\).

A classic example of such buried sets arise from Cantor-like sets. The boundaries of the components of the complement of the Cantor set are rational, and Cantor set being uncountable must have uncountably many buried points. A standard example of buried Julia components is given in the following proposition (proved in (McMullen 1988)), more information on buried Julia components can be found in (Godillon 2015) and (Wang et al. 2022).

Proposition 6.27

:- Let \(f(z) = z^2 + \frac{\lambda}{z^3}\). For all non-zero \(\lambda\) sufficiently small,

  1. \(J(f)\) has uncountably many buried components.

  2. \(J(f)\) has a unique forward invariant buried component.

  3. \(J(f)\) is homeomorphic to (a Cantor set) \(\times\) \(\mathbb{S}^1\)

Definition 6.28

(Exposed Critical Points):- We say \(f(z)\) has exposed critical points if every critical point lies in \(F(f)\) or on the boundary of a component of \(F(f)\).

In proving the special case of Conjecture \(6.4\) the following special case of a result of Strebel found in (Strebel 1978) was used. We shall state the special case here.

Theorem 6.29

(Strebel’s Theorem):- Let \(U\) be finitely connected domain in \(\hat{\mathbb{C}}\), and let \(\phi:\overline{U} \rightarrow \overline{U}\) be a quasiconformal homeomorphism which is identity on \(\partial U\). Then there is a unique quasiconformal map \(\psi\) of minimal dilatation among those homotopic to \(\phi\) (relative to \(\partial U\)). The absolute value of the Beltrami differential \(|\psi_{\bar{z}}/\psi_z|\) is constant on \(U\) (in fact, \(\psi\) is a Teichmüller mapping of finite norm).

Now we shall state a final theorem related to the difficult question of the existence of invariant line fields (very well explained in (McMullen 1994) and (McMullen 2016).

Theorem 6.30

:- If \(J(f)\) is connected and \(f\) has exposed critical points, then \(\text{Mod}(J(f), f)\) is a finite group.

References

Beardon, AF, and D Minda. 2011. “The Hyperbolic Metric and Geometric Function Theory, Quasiconformal Mappings and Their Applications, Narosa, New Delhi, 2007.” MR 2492498: 9–56. https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~bishop/classes/math401.F09/Beardon-Minda.pdf.
De Melo, Welington, and Sebastian Van Strien. 2012. One-Dimensional Dynamics. Vol. 25. Springer Science & Business Media. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-78043-1.
Garcia, Stephan Ramon, Javad Mashreghi, and William T Ross. 2018. Finite Blaschke Products and Their Connections. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-78247-8.
Godillon, Sébastien. 2015. “A Family of Rational Maps with Buried Julia Components.” Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems 35 (6): 1846–79. https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.3881.
Hubbard, JH, and A Douady. 1982. “Iteration Des Polynomes Quadratiques Complexes.” CR Acad. Sci. Paris 294: 123–26. https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hubbard/CR.pdf.
Imayoshi, Yoichi, and Masahiko Taniguchi. 2012. An Introduction to Teichmüller Spaces. Springer Science & Business Media. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-4-431-68174-8.
McMullen, Curt. 1988. “Automorphisms of Rational Maps.” In Holomorphic Functions and Moduli i. Springer. https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/papers/home/text/papers/aut/aut.pdf.
McMullen, Curtis T. 1994. “Frontiers in Complex Dynamics.” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 31 (2): 155–72. https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9410221.
McMullen, Curtis T. 2016. “Complex Dynamics and Renormalization (AM-135), Volume 135.” In Complex Dynamics and Renormalization (AM-135), Volume 135. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882557.
McMullen, Curtis T, and Dennis P Sullivan. 1998. “Quasiconformal Homeomorphisms and Dynamics III. The Teichmüller Space of a Holomorphic Dynamical System.” Advances in Mathematics-New York-. https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/papers/home/text/papers/qciii/qciii.pdf.
Shub, Michael, and Dennis Sullivan. 1985. “Expanding Endomorphisms of the Circle Revisited.” Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems 5 (2): 285–89. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ergodic-theory-and-dynamical-systems/article/expanding-endomorphisms-of-the-circle-revisited/E404C8549E3C4F441C7E66B5227EB82C.
Strebel, Kurt. 1978. “On Quasiconformal Mappings of Open Riemann Surfaces.” Comment. Math. Helv. 53 (3): 301–21. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02566081.

title: McMullen’s Surgery
html:
Ideal boundaries and induced maps

To glue different dynamical systems together, we need good boundary-extension theorems or suitable straightening theorems.

Ideal boundaries

Consider a Riemann map \(R_U\colon\mathbb D\to U\). How do you get to \(\overline{\mathbb D}\)?

Prime ends.

Consider \(\langle N_j\rangle_j\), with \(N_1\supset N_2\supset\cdots\); roughly, \(\bigcap_i\overline{N_i}\subset\partial U\).

Lemma 1

\(\mathcal N\sim\mathcal M\) or \(\mathcal N\wedge\mathcal M\) eventually.

Carathéodory.

The map \(R_U\colon\mathbb D\to U\) gives a homeomorphism \(\widehat R_U\colon\widehat{\mathbb D}\to\widehat U\) of the Carathéodory compactifications, where \(\widehat{\mathbb D}\cong\overline{\mathbb D}\) and \(\widehat U=U\cup\mathcal I(U)\).

We have \(\mathcal I(U)\cong S^1\), so ideal boundaries are \(1\)-manifolds. The restriction \(\widehat R|_{S^1}\colon S^1\to\mathcal I(U)\) gives impressions on \(\partial U\). If \(\partial U\) is locally connected, then \(\widehat R|_{S^1}\colon S^1\to\partial U\): the impressions turn out to be points. If \(U\) is a Jordan domain, this restriction is a homeomorphism \(S^1\cong\partial U\). Situations like the following violate injectivity.

Induced maps on ideal boundaries

By Schwarz reflection, \(\widehat f\) extends real-analytically to \(S^1\). We shall think of this as a coordinate function of a real-analytic map \(\widehat f\colon\mathcal I(U)\to\mathcal I(V)\), with both ideal boundaries homeomorphic to \(S^1\).

More generally, take \(C\subseteq J(f)\) with \(f(C)\subseteq C\), and consider \(f\colon\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus f^{-1}(C) \to\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus C\).

We obtain a real-analytic map \(\widehat f\colon\mathcal I(U)\to\mathcal I(V)\). Here \[\mathcal I(C):=\bigcup_{\substack{V\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus C\\ V\text{ a component}}}\mathcal I(V).\]

Regularity of the map

We loosen the regularity of \(f\) for convenience. Sullivan’s straightening theorem says that \(f\) is quasirational if and only if \(\langle f^{\circ n}\rangle_n\) is uniformly \(K\)-quasiregular. Here quasirational means \(f\equiv\varphi\circ R\circ\varphi^{-1}\), with \(R\) rational.

We have \(\widehat f=\widehat\phi^{-1}\circ\widehat R\circ\widehat\phi\); the map \(\widehat f\) is quasisymmetric.

McMullen’s gluing lemma

Hypotheses.
(i)

\(\mathcal I(U)\) is either a fixed component of \(\mathcal I(C)\), or strictly preperiodic, with \(f^{\circ n}(V)\cap U=\varnothing\).

(ii)

There are quasiconformal maps \(\phi_{U,V}\colon U,V\to\mathbb D\) such that \(B\) and \(f\) are compatible in the following diagram.

Claim

The map \[g(z):=\begin{cases} f(z),&z\notin U,\\ \phi_V^{-1}\circ B\circ\phi_U(z),&z\in U \end{cases}\] is quasirational.

Proof. Pick \(z\in\partial U\) such that \(f^{-1}\) is locally defined. This can be done for every \(z\in\partial U\), barring a few branch points. We have \[f^{-1}\circ g=\begin{cases} \text{identity},&z\notin U,\\ \psi\quad\text{(quasiconformal)},&z\in U. \end{cases}\]

The induced boundary map satisfies \(\widehat\psi|_{\mathcal I(U)} \equiv\operatorname{Id}\). We claim that this forces \(\sup_z|\psi(z)-z|_\rho<K'\). If so, then for any \(x_k\to x\), we know that \(B_K(x_k)\to x\) and \(\psi(x_k)\in B_K(x_k)\).

Hence \(f^{-1}\circ g\) is a homeomorphism. By Rickman’s lemma, \(f^{-1}\circ g\) is quasiconformal. On the larger ball there are two quasiconformal maps, \(\psi\equiv f^{-1}\circ g\) and \(\operatorname{id}\); these two agree on \(K\).

We just have to show that \(\psi\in H^1(\text{ball})\), the appropriate Sobolev space. Let \(u=\operatorname{Re}(\psi-\operatorname{Id})\). We need to show that \(u\in H^1\), and similarly for \(\operatorname{Im}(\psi-\operatorname{Id})\), since \(\operatorname{Id}\in H^1(\text{ball})\).

We have \(\eta_n\circ u\to u\), so \(u\in H^1\), and \(u_n=0\) on a neighbourhood of \(K\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Hence the dilatation of \(u\) is \(1\) almost everywhere on \(K\). This means that \(g\) is quasiregular in a neighbourhood of \(\partial U\), so \(g\) is quasiregular.

If \(\mathcal I(U)\) is fixed, then \(K(g^n)\leq K(f^n)\,K(\phi)^2\).

If \(\mathcal I(U)\) is strictly preperiodic, then \(K(g^n)\leq K(f^n)\,K(\phi_V)\,K(\phi_U)\). Thus \(K(g^n)\) is uniformly bounded, and by Sullivan’s straightening theorem, \(g\) is quasirational.

It remains to justify \(\sup_z|\psi(z)-z|_\rho<K\).

Let’s say there is a sequence \(\langle x_k\rangle_k\), with \(x_k\to x\), such that \(|\psi(x_k)-x_k|_\rho\to\infty\).

Then one would get \(\langle N_k\rangle_k\not\sim\langle\psi(N_k)\rangle_k\), violating the fact that \(\widehat\psi|_{\mathcal I(U)}\equiv\operatorname{id}\). Maybe conjugate it with a Riemann map and work in \(\mathbb D\).

The same story holds when \(\mathcal I(U)\) is periodic.

Rigid models

(i)

Elliptic: \(z\mapsto e^{2\pi i\theta}z\), where \(\theta\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\).

(ii)

Hyperbolic: \(z\mapsto z^d\), where \(d>1\).

(iii)

Parabolic: \(z\mapsto\dfrac{z^d+a}{1+az^d}\), where \(a=\dfrac{d-1}{d+1}\).

Any quasisymmetry that conjugates these rigid models must be a rotation.

The elliptic model.

Let \(B(z)=e^{2\pi i\theta}z\) and \(B\circ\phi\equiv\phi\circ B\). Lift this to \(\mathbb R\) to get \[f(z+\theta)=f(z)+\theta,\qquad f(z+m\theta)=f(z)+m\theta,\qquad f(n+m\theta)=f(0)+m\theta.\] Hence \(f(z)=z+\alpha\), since \(m\theta+n\) is dense in \(\mathbb R\).

The hyperbolic model.

Let \(B(z)=z^n\). For \(f(z^n)=f(z)^n\), set \(\widetilde f=f/f(1)\). Then \(\widetilde f(z^n)=\widetilde f(z)^n\), since \(f(1)=f(1)^n\). The map \(\widetilde f\) preserves all \(n\)th roots of unity and \(\widetilde f(1)=1\). As \(\widetilde f\) is orientation-preserving, its restriction to the \(n\)th roots of unity is the identity. The same is true for \(A=\{z\in S^1:z^{n^k}=1\}\). But \(A\) is dense in \(S^1\), so \(f(z)=f(1)z\).

The parabolic model.

Let \(B(z)=\dfrac{z^d+a}{1+az^d}\). If \(\phi\) is a quasisymmetric conjugacy between them, then one can conformally weld two copies of the dynamical system \((\mathbb D,B(z))\) to obtain a degree-\(d\) rational map with critical points at \(\{0,\infty\}\) of degree \(d-1\).

The initial argument in the notes is: that rational map must be \(z^d\), but \(z^d\) is hyperbolic, whereas \(B(z)\) has parabolic behaviour on its Julia set, at \(1\). This argument is marked for correction in the source.

Correction 1.

The rational map would have a quasicircle Julia set, so it can’t map a hyperbolic point to a parabolic point.

Goal.

Simplify rational maps by gluing these rigid models along \(\mathcal I(C)\) for \(C\subseteq J(R)\).

Correction 2.

If it maps a hyperbolic point to a parabolic point, the intersection of the single repelling and attracting petals would have an angle of \(\pi+\pi\). Thus \(J(R)\) will have a cusp. Quasicircles can’t have cusps (Ahlfors).

The gluing construction revisited

Recap.

We consider \(f\colon\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus f^{-1}(C) \to\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus C\) component-wise.

We have \(f^{-1}(C)\supseteq C\), but this means \(\partial C\subset\partial f^{-1}(C)\). We are only looking at those \(U\) such that \(\mathcal I(U)\subseteq\mathcal I(C)\).

Gluing lemma.

If \(U=V\), take \(\phi_V=\phi_U\). The component \(\mathcal I(U)\) is strictly preperiodic or fixed, with \(f^{\circ n}(V)\cap U=\varnothing\) in the strictly preperiodic case.

We require \(f\sim B\), compatibly on ideal boundaries.

For periodic \(\mathcal I(U)\), require \(B_i\sim f|_{U_i}\) compatibly around the cycle.

The parabolic rigid model

Recall the rigid models:

(i)

Elliptic: \(z\mapsto e^{2\pi i\theta}z\), where \(\theta\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\).

(ii)

Hyperbolic: \(z\mapsto z^d\), where \(d\geq2\).

(iii)

Parabolic: \(P_d(z)=\dfrac{z^d+a}{1+az^d}\), where \(a=\dfrac{d-1}{d+1}\).

Let us explain (iii). Note that if \(|z|=1\), then \(\left|\frac{z^d+a}{1+az^d}\right|=1\). Well, \[\frac{z^d+a}{1+az^d} =z^d\circ\left(\frac{z+a}{1+az}\right),\] so it is enough to show \(|z+a|=|1+az|\). Writing \(z=x+iy\), this is \(|x+a+iy|^2=|1+ax+iay|^2\), or \[\begin{aligned} (x+a)^2+y^2&=(1+ax)^2+a^2y^2,\\ x^2+2ax+a^2+y^2&=1+a^2x^2+2ax+a^2y^2. \end{aligned}\] After cancellation this becomes \(x^2(1-a^2)+y^2(1-a^2)+a^2=1\), that is, \((x^2+y^2)(1-a^2)+a^2=1\), or \(1-a^2+a^2=1\).

Thus \(P_d(S^1)=S^1\), and \(P_d\) is orientation-preserving. Hence \(P_d(\mathbb D)=\mathbb D\) and \(P_d(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}) =\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\). By Montel’s theorem, \(P_d\) is normal on \(\mathbb D\) and \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\overline{\mathbb D}\), so \(J(P_d)=1\).

Check.

\(P_d\) has only two critical points, \(\{0,\infty\}\), of equal degree, and a parabolic fixed point of multiplicity \(3\) at \(1\).

If there is a quasisymmetry \(\phi\) such that \(\phi\circ P_d=P_d\circ\phi\), then \(\phi(1)=1\); otherwise, \(\phi(1)\) must be a repelling fixed point on \(S^1=J(P_d)\).

Then we can weld two copies of \(P_d\) via \(\phi\) to get a rational map with a parabolic fixed point of multiplicity \(2\), by the parabolic Fatou flower theorem.

The intersection between the two petals has angles \(\frac{2\pi}{2}+\frac{2\pi}{2}\). Thus \(J(P_d)\) has a cusp at \(\phi(1)\). Quasicircles cannot have cusps (Ahlfors). Therefore \(\phi(1)=1\). By the orientation-preserving property, \(\phi\) must preserve all repelling points, so \(\phi\equiv\operatorname{Id}\).

Remark

This also proves that none of these maps are compatible with each other, except with themselves via rigid motions—in this case, rotations.

Application of McMullen’s surgery

Theorem 2

Let \(C\subseteq J(f)\) be a forward-invariant, closed component. Then \(f|_C\sim g|_{J(g)}\), where \(g\) is built out of rigid models.

Dynamics on the ideal boundary

Only finitely many components \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus C\) intersect \(f^{-1}(C)\) or contain a critical point. Denote this collection by \(\mathcal V\).

(i)

If \(U\notin\mathcal V\) is a component of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus C\), then \(f|_U\colon U\to f(U)\) is a covering. Since \(U\) is a disc, \(\deg(f)=1\). Thus \(\deg(f)>1\) on only finitely many components of \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus C\).

(ii)

If \(f^{\circ n}(U)\notin\mathcal V\) for all \(n\geq0\), then, by Montel, \(\langle f^{\circ n}|_U\rangle_n\) is normal. Hence \(U\) is a wandering Fatou component, so \(U\) is preperiodic, and the first return map has degree \(1\).

Thus \(U\) eventually hits a Siegel disc or a component in \(\mathcal V\). Since \(\mathcal V\) has finitely many elements, \(U\) is always preperiodic. Also, the number of periodic components is finite, bounded by the number of Siegel discs plus \(\#\mathcal V\).

Summary.

\(\mathcal I(U)\) is preperiodic, with finitely many periodic components, and \(\deg(f|_U)=1\).

(iii)

Suppose \(U\notin\mathcal V\). Here \(\phi_U\) and \(\phi_{f(U)}\) are Riemann maps. The following diagram gives \(\widehat f\sim\operatorname{id}|_{S^1}\) compatibly.

(iv)

If \(U\in\mathcal V\), consider \(f|_U\colon U\to V\) with \(V\neq U\), and \(f|_{U'}\colon U'\to V\). The sets \(U'\) and \(f(U')\) are annuli.

Write \(A_r=\{r<|z|<1\}\). We have a degree-\(d\) quasirational covering in annular coordinates. Choose anything on one side and its lift on the other.

It follows that \(\widehat f\sim z^d|_{S^1}\) compatibly.

But if \(U=V\), then \(z^d\not\sim\widehat f\), as the maps \[(\text{anything})\circ\phi_1\circ R_U \neq(\text{lift})\circ\phi_2\circ R_V.\]

Periodic components and the surgery

We have therefore handled compatibility for all but periodic components of \(\mathcal I(C)\).

Lemma 3

On periodic components of \(\mathcal I(C)\), the first return map is compatible with one of the rigid models.

Proof of Theorem 2: periodic case. Consider the periodic cycle and model maps below.

We set \[B_{p-1}(z):= \begin{cases} e^{2\pi i\theta}z,&\text{elliptic},\\ z^{d_{p-1}},&\text{hyperbolic},\\ P_{d_{p-1}},&\text{parabolic}, \end{cases} \qquad d=\sum_i d_i=\deg(f^{\circ p}).\] Then \[\begin{aligned} \phi_0^{-1}\circ B_p\circ\phi_0 &=\bigl(\phi_0^{-1}\circ B_{p-1}\circ\phi_{p-2}\bigr) \circ\cdots\circ\bigl(\phi_2^{-1}\circ z^{d_2}\circ\phi_1\bigr) \circ\bigl(\phi_1^{-1}\circ z^{d_1}\circ\phi_0\bigr),\\ f^{\circ p}&=\underbrace{f\circ\cdots\circ f}_{p\text{ times}}. \end{aligned}\] This holds because of the following comparison.

\[\phi_0^{-1}\circ B_p\circ\phi_0 =\phi_0^{-1}\circ B_{p-1}\circ z^{d_{p-2}} \circ z^{d_{p-3}}\circ\cdots\circ z^{d_1}\circ\phi.\] The model factors are displayed together: \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc} B_p&B_{p-1}&z^{d_{p-2}}&z^{d_{p-3}}&\cdots&z^{d_1}\\\hline e^{2\pi i\theta}&e^{2\pi i\theta}&z&z&\cdots&z\\ z^d&z^{d_{p-1}}&z^{d_{p-2}}&z^{d_{p-3}}&\cdots&z^{d_1}\\ P_d&P_{d_{p-1}}&z^{d_{p-2}}&z^{d_{p-3}}&\cdots&z^{d_1} \end{array}\] Here \(P_d=\left(z^d\circ\frac{z+a}{1+az}\right)\).

The strictly preperiodic, one-to-one case.

If \(d=1\), don’t perform surgery.

By our gluing lemma, after finitely many such surgical procedures, we end up with a quasirational map \(g\). Straighten it to get the required rational map \(R\), such that \(R|_{J(R)}\sim f|_C\) compatibly. The set \(J(R)=\phi(C)\) is connected, where \(\phi\) is a straightening map.

Features of the resulting map

(i)

\(J(R)\) is connected.

(ii)

Periodic Fatou components are Siegel discs, superattracting basins, and parabolic basins.

Compatibility on periodic components

Recap.

We have McMullen’s gluing lemma and the rigid models. The application is \(f|_C\sim g|_{J(g)}\): simplify \(f\).

Lemma 4

On each periodic component, the first return map is compatible with one of the rigid models.

Proof. This will be a case study.

Case 1: buried components

Consider a buried component \(\mathcal I(U)\): \(\partial U\) is not part of the boundary of any Fatou component. We will show that \(\widehat f\sim(z\mapsto z^d)\) compatibly.

The set \(V'\) is not part of any periodic Fatou component and contains no critical points. By Zoretti’s theorem, take the curves and annuli below.

We have \(f^{-1}(\gamma_n)\cap\gamma_n=\varnothing\) and \(f\colon U'\to V'\) of degree \(d\). Therefore \(\operatorname{mod}(V')\geq\operatorname{mod}(U')\), so \(U'\subseteq V'\).

By Schwarz reflection, \(R_U\circ f\circ R_U^{-1}\) is expanding on \(S^1\), by Pick’s theorem.

Thus there is a quasisymmetric conjugacy to \(z\mapsto z^d\).

Case 2: unburied, Siegel disc

Here \(\partial U\) is part of a Fatou boundary, so there is a Fatou component \(V\subseteq U\), which has to be periodic. Only one component can be accommodated; otherwise their shared boundary would hit \(\partial U\), hence become part of \(C\). This would force \(U\) not to be a disc.

We have \(V=U=\) a Siegel disc, since otherwise \(C\) would be disconnected. Via the linearizing map, \(\widehat f\sim(z\mapsto e^{2\pi i\theta}z)\), where \(\theta\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\). The same goes for \(V\) a Herman ring.

Case 3: unburied, (super)attraction

Let \(V\subseteq U\), where \(V\) is either an immediate basin of (super)attraction or a parabolic basin whose parabolic point is not on \(\partial U\). Choose \(W\subset V\) to be, respectively, a small disc around the (super)attracting point or an attracting petal. Then \(f(W)\subset\overline W\) and \(\overline W\cap\partial U=\varnothing\).

Let \(W_n=f^{-n}(W)\) denote the component containing \(W\). Clearly \(W_1\subset W_2\subset W_3\subset\cdots\) and \(\bigcup_n W_n=V\). Since \(f(\partial U)=\partial U\), we have \(W_n\cap\partial U=\varnothing\).

The boundaries \(\partial W_n\) slowly approximate \(\partial U\) and the Julia chunks in \(U\). Choose \(n\) large enough that \(A_n\) has no critical point.

Then \(f\colon A_{n+1}\to A_n\) is a covering, and, as before, \(\widehat f\sim(z\mapsto z^d)\) compatibly.

Case 4: unburied, parabolic

Let \(V\subseteq U\) be parabolic, with its parabolic point \(z_0\) on \(\partial U\). Choose a petal \(W\) with analytic boundary \(\partial W\) avoiding critical points, and uniformize \(U\), sending \(z_0\) to \(1\).

Define the \(W_n\) as before. We obtain the pinched annuli below.

Choose an orientation-preserving \(C^1\) diffeomorphism \(\phi\colon\gamma_n\to\gamma_n'\) taking \(1\) to \(1\) and the preimages of \(1\) to the preimages of \(1\).

The boundary compatibility gives a quasisymmetric map \(\phi_{n+1}\).

Fill \(A_n\) using \(\phi_n\) and \(\phi_{n+1}\) to get \(\Psi_n\colon A_n\to A_n'\), and lift to the next annulus.

Set \(\phi_{n+2}:=\widehat\Psi_{n+1}\colon\gamma_{n+2}\to\gamma_{n+2}'\). Continue the recursion.

Fill the whole pinched annulus between \(\gamma_n\) and \(S^1\) to get a quasisymmetric conjugacy between \(P_d\) and \(f\) on \(S^1\), by continuity.

Rigour.

First extend \(\Psi_n\) smoothly to the rest of the annulus bounded by \(S^1\) and \(\gamma_n\) to get \(\widehat\Psi_n\). Then say \(\widehat\Psi_n\to\Psi\), using the fact that \(H^1(\widetilde U)\) is Cauchy complete, where \(\widetilde U\) is the annulus bounded by \(S^1\) and \(\gamma_n\).

Take the trip back via \(R_U\) to get \(\widehat f|_{\mathcal I(U)}\sim P_d|_{S^1}\) compatibly.
excerptHtml: To glue different dynamical systems together, we need good boundary-extension theorems or suitable straightening theorems.

title: From Complex Dynamics to Measure-Preserving Systems
html:
Motivation from Complex Dynamics

Let me present to you one of my reasons for learning ergodic theory. Consider \[f\colon S\longrightarrow S, \qquad f\in\operatorname{Hol}(S),\quad S\text{ a Riemann surface}.\] If one feels uncomfortable with that level of generality, then simply consider \(p\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) (a polynomial), or \(S=\widehat{\mathbb C}\) (the Riemann sphere), forcing \(f\) to be a rational polynomial, \(f(z)=p(z)/q(z)\).

One is interested in studying how \(f\), and the iterates of \(f\), deform the space \(S\), which amounts to studying \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_{n\geq0}\) for a given \(z\in S\). In light of this, one asks:

  • What is the topological structure of sets \(U\) that deform via \(f\) in a stable manner?

  • What is the topological structure of sets \(J\) that deform via \(f\) in a chaotic manner?

More precisely:

Definition 1 — Fatou set

\[F(f):=\left\{x\in S:\text{there is a neighbourhood }U_x\text{ of }x \text{ such that }\{f^{\circ n}|_{U_x}\}_n\text{ is a normal family}\right\}.\] \(F(f)\) is called the Fatou set of \(S\), which is open by definition. It corresponds to stability.

Definition 2 — Julia set

\(J(f):=S\setminus F(f)\) is called the Julia set. It corresponds to chaos.

When one says one wants to study the dynamics of \(f\), among other things one usually means studying stable and chaotic sets (or Fatou and Julia sets). The following is the general philosophy for undertaking such a study.

Philosophy of complex dynamics.

Orbits of critical points, i.e. \(\{f^{\circ n}(z)\}_{n\geq1}\) with \(f'(z)=0\), and fixed points determine stable sets entirely, and chaotic sets to a large extent.

Here is why this should surprise you. If \(f\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) is holomorphic and, say, you know the zeros and poles of \(f\), then basic one-variable complex analysis will tell you that you can determine the function \(f\) to a large extent.

Let \((\bullet)\) denote zeros and \((\times)\) poles. If you know \(f^{(n)}(\bullet)\), then you know \[f(z)=\sum_{n\geq0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(\bullet)}{n!}(z-\bullet)^n\] on a disc that extends up to the nearest pole to \((\bullet)\). Furthermore, if \(f(z)=p(z)/q(z)\), then \((\bullet)\) and \((\times)\) completely determine \(f\). Yet the philosophy says that telling you precisely what \(f\) is is not enough to study its dynamics.

Now, here is why this should not surprise you. Let \(\varphi\colon S\to S'\) be a biholomorphism.

Notice that, since we have merely changed our coordinates (of the surface) via \(f\), the dynamics should remain the same. Indeed, we have:

  • \(\widetilde f^{\circ n}=(\varphi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1})^{\circ n} =\varphi\circ f^{\circ n}\circ\varphi^{-1}=\widetilde{f^{\circ n}}\).

  • If \(\{f^{\circ n}|_U\}_n\) is normal, then \(\{\widetilde f^{\circ n}|_{\varphi(U)}\}_n\) shall be normal.

Thus, to study dynamics one must naturally look for things that are invariant under coordinate transformations. Zeros and poles are not among such invariants, as can easily be seen. If \(f(z_0)=0\), then \(\widetilde f(\varphi(z_0))=\varphi(0)\), which need not be \(0\). But if \(\widehat z\) is a fixed or critical point, then:

  • \(\widetilde f(\varphi(z_k))=\varphi(z_k)\), so \(\varphi(z_k)\) is a fixed point of \(\widetilde f\);

  • \(\widetilde f'(\varphi(z_k))=0\), by the chain rule.

This is the reason for focusing one’s study on critical points and fixed points. Zeros and poles of \(f\colon\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}\) are merely points that map to the two poles. If you change your coordinates on \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\) via a Möbius transformation \[z\longmapsto\frac{az+b}{cz+d}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb C),\] then the zeros and poles shall be thrown out to points \(a/c\), \(b/d\) on the Riemann sphere.

Therefore, saying that one wants to study zeros

and poles of \(f\) is equivalent to saying that one has a preferred set of coordinates. This, mind you, is extremely useful while doing analysis, but irrelevant for dynamics. One of the many ways we propose to study dynamics is by reducing the function to a simpler one, in the right set of coordinates. In particular, if \(U\subset S\) and there is \(\varphi\colon U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb C\), then among all such \(\varphi\)’s we shall hunt for one that makes \(\varphi\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}\) simplest to study. For instance:

Then we know that, under this changed set of coordinates, \(f\) is an irrational rotation by the angle \(\theta\) on \(\mathbb D\).

Such results are called linearization theorems: one turns the function into as linear a function as possible, and the orbits of critical points bound the largest possible domain \(U\) in which \(f\) behaves like a polynomial. Usually these domains are considered to be neighbourhoods of fixed points of \(f\). In addition, orbits of critical points reveal a lot of the topological structure of Julia sets (or chaotic sets). Therefore, the following question is fundamental to complex dynamics.

Question.

How is \(\{f^{\circ n}(\widehat z)\}_n\) distributed on \(S\), where \(\widehat z\) is a critical point of \(f\)?

Ergodic theory comes along with many qualitative answers to such questions. In this course we shall focus only on those that shall lead us to the proof of Szemerédi’s theorem. Having motivated the need for ergodic theory for me, I encourage you to find a need of your own that would help you cling on to the kind of mathematics we shall be doing.

Introduction to Measure-Preserving Systems

Let \(X\) be a set and \(T\colon X\to X\) a map. We shall refer to \(X\) as the state space and \(T\) as the transformation (or deformation).

If, in addition, you impose some structure on \(X\), then we end up with the following.

Group structure.

If \(\Gamma\triangleleft G\), or \(\Gamma<G\), then there is a transitive \(G\)-action on \(G/\Gamma\), a homogeneous space of \(G\). If \(X\cong G/\Gamma\), then one has the transformation \(T_g\colon X\to X\), \(T_g(x):=g\cdot x\). One can study the dynamics of \(T_g\): a classical dynamical system.

Topological structure.

We study the dynamics of \(T\colon X\to X\), with \(T\) a continuous map. If, in addition, \(X\) is compact and metrizable and \(T\) is a homeomorphism, one is in the realm of topological dynamical systems.

Measure structure.

If it is a probability measure, one ends up with ergodic theory.

Of the three basic structures one can impose on a set, we shall impose the structure of a probability space. I will end by introducing the setup of ergodic theory.

Definition 3 — Measure-preserving system

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu)\) and \((Y,\mathcal C,\nu)\) be probability spaces. A measurable map \(\varphi\colon X\to Y\) is measure-preserving if \[\mu\bigl(\varphi^{-1}(B)\bigr)=\nu(B) \qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal C,\] and \(\mu\) is said to be \(\varphi\)-invariant. Finally, \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is a measure-preserving system if \(\mu\) is \(T\)-invariant.

Remark

  • To obtain qualitative results, we need some means to compare, so we introduce a measure-theoretic structure on our state space \(X\). We shall address the need for it to be a probability measure later.

  • Probabilistically, \(\varphi\colon X\to Y\) being measurable means that events of \(Y\) relate to events of \(X\).

  • \(\mu\) being \(\varphi\)-invariant means that the link \(\varphi^{-1}\) is deterministic. In other words, the likelihood of the occurrence of \(B\) forces the likelihood of the occurrence of \(\varphi^{-1}(B)\) to the same extent.

  • \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is a space of events with a deterministic link function \(T\).

  • The reason we define \(\mu(T^{-1}(B))=\nu(B)\), and not \(\mu(B)=\nu(T(B))\), is that the following properties do not hold for \(T\) in place of \(T^{-1}\): \[\begin{align*} \chi_A(T(x))&=\chi_{T^{-1}(A)}(x), &&\text{the link},\\ T^{-1}(A\cap B)&=T^{-1}(A)\cap T^{-1}(B),\\ T^{-1}(A\cup B)&=T^{-1}(A)\cup T^{-1}(B),\\ T^{-1}(A\mathbin\triangle B)&=T^{-1}(A)\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}(B). \end{align*}\] If \(A\) and \(B\) occur, then \(T^{-1}\) forces \(T^{-1}(A)\) and \(T^{-1}(B)\) to occur. \(T\) does not respect set-theoretic operations, so working with \(T\) would imply that the measure-preserving map is too special!

Having seen this, let us see what it means to preserve the structure of a measure-preserving system on \(X\).

Definition 4 — Measurable isomorphism

We write \[(X,\mathcal B_X,\mu_X,T)\cong(Y,\mathcal B_Y,\mu_Y,S)\] if there exists a measure-preserving map \(\varphi\colon X\to Y\) with \(\varphi^{-1}\colon Y\to X\), where \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi^{-1}\) are defined almost everywhere, such that the following diagram commutes.

At this point one must ask: how does one check for the measure-preserving property? Is there a litmus test?

Lemma 1 — Litmus test

Given \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\), with \(T\colon X\to X\) measurable, \(T\) will be \(\mu\)-invariant if \(T\) preserves measures of the semi-algebra that generates \(X\).

Proof. Let \[\mathcal J'=\{B\in\mathcal B:T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal B, \ \mu(T^{-1}(B))=\mu(B)\}.\] Then the semi-algebra \(\mathcal J\subseteq\mathcal J'\). The algebra generated by \(\mathcal J\) lies in \(\mathcal J'\). Moreover, \(\mathcal J'\) is a monotone class, because if \(A_i\nearrow A\), then \(T^{-1}(A_i)\nearrow T^{-1}(A)\); as \(\mu(T^{-1}(A_i))=\mu(A_i)\), we have \[\lim_{i\to\infty}\mu(T^{-1}(A_i))=\mu(T^{-1}(A))=\mu(A).\] Similarly, one deals with \(A_i\searrow A\). Thus \(\mathcal J'\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\mathcal J\), but \(\mathcal B\) is, by definition, the smallest such set of sets. Hence \(\mathcal J'=\mathcal B\), so \(T\) is \(\mu\)-invariant.

A good time to stop, breathe, and look at examples.

Example 1 — Measure-preserving systems

1.

Rotation: \((\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,m_{S^1},\mathcal B_{S^1},R_\alpha)\), where \(R_\alpha\colon\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) and \(R_\alpha(t)=t+\alpha\pmod1\).

2.

Doubling: \((\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,m_{S^1},\mathcal B_{S^1},T_2)\), where \(T_2\colon\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) and \(T_2(t)=2t\pmod1\).

3.

Bernoulli shift: \(\bigl(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\prod_{\mathbb N}\mu_{1/2},\mathcal B,\sigma\bigr)\), where \(\mu_{1/2}(\{0\})=\mu_{1/2}(\{1\})=1/2\), and \(\mu=\prod_{\mathbb N}\mu_{1/2}\) is the product measure, with \(\sigma(x_0,x_1,x_2,\ldots)=(x_1,x_2,\ldots)\).

Example 2 — Measurable isomorphism

Define \(\phi\colon\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) by \[\phi((x_0,x_1,\ldots)):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x_n}{2^{n+1}}.\] \(\phi^{-1}\) is not well-defined on rationals in base \(2\) (the dyadic rationals, \(\mathbb Z[1/2]\)), because they do not have a unique base-\(2\) representation. \(\mathbb Z[1/2]\) is countable in \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), hence has Lebesgue measure \(0\), so \(\phi^{-1}\) is invertible.

To prove \(\mu(\phi^{-1}((a,b)))=m_{S^1}((a,b))=b-a\), it is enough to prove it for \(a=0\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1)\), because, given any \((a,b)\subseteq[0,1)\), \[\begin{align*} \mu(\phi^{-1}((a,b))) &=\mu\bigl(\phi^{-1}((b,0)\setminus(a,0))\bigr)\\ &=\mu\bigl(\phi^{-1}((b,0))\setminus\phi^{-1}((a,0))\bigr)\\ &=\mu(\phi^{-1}((b,0)))-\mu(\phi^{-1}((a,0))). \end{align*}\]

Also, given any \((a,b)\subseteq[0,1]\), there exist \(p_n,q_n\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1)\) such that \((p_n,q_n)\nearrow(a,b)\).

Now note that \[\mu(\phi^{-1}((0,a)))=\mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_i\right),\] where, if \(a=0.10010011\), \[A_1=\{0\}\times\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad A_2=\{1,0,0,0\}\times\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad\ldots,\] and \(A_i=\{1,0,0,1,0,0,\ldots,\underset{i}{0}\}\times\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), where \(i\) is the position of the next \(1\) in the base-\(2\) expansion of \(a\). Thus \[\mu\left(\bigcup A_i\right)=\sum\mu(A_i) =\sum_{\substack{1\text{ in the}\\i\text{th place}}}\frac1{2^i}=a=a-0.\]

Also, \(\phi\circ\sigma=T_2\circ\phi\). Hence the Bernoulli system is measurably isomorphic to the circle-doubling system.

Our Goals and Motives

We have a means to measure, hence a way to compare, and we wish to compare \(E\) with its iterates \(T^{\circ n}(E)\). As \(T\) is measure-preserving, we are justified in asking how \(\{T^{\circ n}(E)\}_n\) behaves, because \(T\) preserves measure, so \(E\) and \(T(E)\) belong to the same structural space; hence comparison is natural.

With that in mind, we ask the following questions:

  • What happens to \(\{T^{\circ n}x\}\) as \(n\to\infty\)?

  • What happens to \(T^{\circ n}(E)\) as \(n\to\infty\), for \(E\in\mathcal B\)?

  • What happens to \(f\circ T^n\) as \(n\to\infty\), for measurable \(f\colon X\to\mathbb R\) (or \(\mathbb C\))?

We shall develop tools and techniques to understand the implications of these questions, and answer them to the extent we can, culminating in Furstenberg’s multiple recurrence theorem (FMRT).

Theorem 2 — Furstenberg’s multiple recurrence theorem (FMRT)

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system. Let \(E\in\mathcal B\) satisfy \(\mu(E)>0\), and let \(k\geq1\). Then there exists \(n\geq1\) such that \[E\cap T^n(E)\cap\cdots\cap T^{(k-1)n}(E)\neq\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there exist \(x\in X\) and \(n\geq1\) such that \(T^{\ell n}(x)\in E\) for every \(0\leq\ell<k\).

From this we get a combinatorial analogue:

Theorem 3 — Szemerédi’s theorem

Let \(E\subset\mathbb Z\) satisfy \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{|E\cap[-N,N]|}{2N+1}>0.\] Then \(E\) has arbitrarily large arithmetic progressions.

And declare victory!
