Consider \[f\colon S\longrightarrow S, \qquad f\in\operatorname{Hol}(S),\quad S\text{ a Riemann surface}.\] If one feels uncomfortable with that level of generality, then simply consider \(p\colon\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) (a polynomial), or \(S=\widehat{\mathbb C}\) (the Riemann sphere), forcing \(f\) to be a rational polynomial, \(f(z)=p(z)/q(z)\).

title: Recurrence and Three Views of Ergodicity
html:
Recurrence Theorems

Of all the impositions on a measure-preserving system, the one that is perhaps ill-motivated is the demand that \(\mu(X)<\infty\). Let’s look at why it matters.

Theorem 4 — Poincaré recurrence

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system and let \(E\in\mathcal B\). Then there exists \(F\subseteq E\), \(F\in\mathcal B\), such that \(\mu(F)=\mu(E)\) and, for every \(x\in F\), \(T^n(x)\in E\) for infinitely many \(n\geq1\).

Proof. Let us first look at sets that escape \(E\) in one go: \[B:=\{x\in E:T^nx\notin E\text{ for every }n\geq1\}.\] Note that \[\begin{align*} B&=E\cap T^{-1}(X\setminus E)\cap T^{-2}(X\setminus E)\cap\cdots,\\ T^{-n}(B)&=T^{-n}(E)\cap T^{-n-1}(X\setminus E) \cap T^{-n-2}(X\setminus E)\cap\cdots. \end{align*}\] If \(n>m\), then \[T^{-m}(B)=\left(\bigcap_{k\geq1}T^{-m-k}(X\setminus E)\right)\cap T^{-m}(E),\] and there exists \(k_0\)

such that \(n=m+k_0\). Thus \(T^{-m}(B)\subseteq T^{-m-k_0}(X\setminus E)=T^{-n}(X\setminus E)\), and we have \(T^{-n}(B)\subseteq T^{-n}(E)\). Hence \[T^{-n}(B)\cap T^{-m}(B)=\varnothing\qquad(n\neq m).\] As \(T\) is \(\mu\)-invariant and \(\mu(X)=1\), it follows that \(\mu(B)=0\). Consequently, for almost every \(x\in E\), \(T^{\circ n}(x)\in E\) for some \(n\). Thus there exists \(F_1\subseteq E\) with \(\mu(F_1)=\mu(E)\), where \[F_1=\{x\in E:T^{\circ n}(x)\in E\text{ for some }n\}.\] One can similarly get \(F_2,F_3,\ldots\), working with \(T^2,T^3,\ldots\). Since \(\mu(E\setminus F_i)=0\) for every \(i\), the set \(F=\bigcap_i F_i\subseteq E\) satisfies \(\mu(F)=\mu(E)\).

In \(F\), for every \(x\) and every \(n\), there exists \(k\) such that \(T^{nk}(x)\in E\). To prove that, for every \(x\in F\), \(T^nx\in E\) for infinitely many \(n\), note that \(x\in F\) implies \(x\in F_1\), so there is an \(n_1\) such that \(T^{n_1}(x)\in E\). Also, \(x\in F_{n_1+1}\) implies that there is an \(n_2>n_1\) such that \(T^{n_2}(x)\in E\), and so on. Hence \(T^nx\in E\) for infinitely many \(n\), for almost every \(x\in E\).

Remark

Notice that this implies the pigeonhole principle if \(X=\{1,2,3,\ldots,n\}\), \(\mu\) is the uniform probability measure on \(2^X\), and \(T\) is any bijective map. What we essentially did is lift the pigeonhole principle from the category of sets to that of measure-preserving systems. Here, we do not call such results PHP (pigeonhole principle); we call them recurrence theorems.

Remark

We crucially used the fact that \(\mu\) is a bounded measure. This turns out to be the right analogue of a compact metric-space structure on \(X\) in a topological dynamical system. Recurrence is an important feature, because recurrence is the first emergence of a pattern in a measure-preserving system. Thus \(\mu\) being a probability measure ensures that no information is lost under the transformation \(T\) of \(X\).

Remark

Define \(T\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(T(x):=x+1\). Then \(T\) is \(m\)-invariant, where \(m\) is Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^2\). But notice that the set \(T(\mathbb D)\) escapes to infinity. In such cases we have nothing in \(\mathbb R\) to compare \(\mathbb D\) with: \(\mathbb D\) runs off to infinity. But if you had a measure-preserving system, \(\mathbb D\) would return to itself, almost, and hence studying the orbit amounts to studying a finite set of sets that have almost-everywhere overlap, providing us with a means to compare!

Remark

Bounded measure need not mean that the set \(X\) is bounded, as shall be illustrated now.

Lemma 5 — Another litmus test for measure-preserving systems

\((X,T,\mu)\) is a measure-preserving system if and only if \[\int f\,d\mu=\int f\circ T\,d\mu \qquad\text{for every }f\in L^\infty(\mu).\]

Proof. Let \(f=\chi_B\). Then \[\mu(B)=\int\chi_B\,d\mu=\int\chi_B(T)\,d\mu =\int\chi_{T^{-1}(B)}\,d\mu=\mu(T^{-1}(B)),\] so \(T\) is \(\mu\)-invariant. Conversely, as \(\mu(X)<\infty\), \(L^1(\mu)\supset L^2(\mu)\supset\cdots\supset L^\infty(\mu)\), and we have \(\int f\,d\mu=\int f\circ T\,d\mu\) for all simple functions \(f\). Now let \(f\in L^1(\mu)\). There exist \(f_n\nearrow f\), so the dominated convergence theorem gives \[\int f\,d\mu=\int f\circ T\,d\mu \qquad\text{for every }f\in L^\infty(\mu).\]

Now define the following measure on \(\mathbb R\): \[\mu([a,b]):=\int_a^b\frac{dx}{\pi(1+x^2)}.\] Let \((\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,m_{S^1})\) be the usual \(S^1\) with Lebesgue measure. The map \(T\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) given by \[T(x)=\frac12\left(x-\frac1x\right),\qquad T(0)=0,\] is \(\mu\)-invariant, because, for \(f\in L^1(\mu)\), we have \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(T(x))\frac{dx}{\pi(1+x^2)} =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(T(x))\frac{dT(x)}{\pi(1+T(x)^2)}.\] Set \(y=T(x)\) to obtain \(\int f\circ T\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu\). It is now easy to check that \[\phi\colon(\mathbb R,\mathcal B_{\mathbb R},\mu,T) \longrightarrow(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,\mathcal B_{S^1},m_{S^1},T_2), \qquad \phi(x)=\frac1\pi\arctan(x)+\frac12,\] is an isomorphism.

But \(\mathbb R\) is by no means bounded. Thus a measure-preserving system ensures that transformations do not blow points off to infinity, and that is why it can accommodate unbounded sets in its realm as well.

Ergodicity

As far as the behaviour of orbits goes, we know that if \(E\) is measurable in \(X\), then, for almost every \(x\in E\), \(\{T^{\circ n}(x)\}_n\) returns to \(E\) infinitely often. Let us extend this madness further. Say \(x\in X\) and \(E\subset X\) is measurable: can we have some sort of recurrence for the orbit of \(x\), \(\{T^{\circ n}(x)\}_n\), if \(x\notin E\)?

There are some set-theoretic obstructions to such a recurrence, because if \(T^{-1}(E)=E\), the orbit of \(x\) shall not intersect \(E\). So let us replace \(X\) by \(E\) and \(E\) by some measurable \(F\subseteq E\). Notice immediately that we are looking for some sort of irreducibility criterion here.

Definition 5 — Ergodicity

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system. We say \(T\) is ergodic if, for every \(B\in\mathcal B\) such that \(T^{-1}(B)=B\), we have \(\mu(B)=0\) or \(\mu(B)=1\).

We shall now try to understand ergodicity from three essentially distinct perspectives, each revealing an interconnection.

Measure-Theoretic Ergodicity

Proposition 6

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system. The following are equivalent:

(1)

\(T\) is ergodic.

(2)

For \(B\in\mathcal B\), \(\mu(T^{-1}(B)\mathbin\triangle B)=0\) implies \(\mu(B)=0\) or \(\mu(B)=1\) (almost ergodic).

(3)

\(\mu(A)>0\) implies \(\mu\bigl(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}T^{-n}(A)\bigr)=1\) (recurrence theorem).

(4)

\(\mu(A)\mu(B)>0\) implies that there exists \(n\geq1\) such that \(\mu(T^{-n}A\cap B)>0\) (mixing criterion).

Proof. \((1)\Rightarrow(2)\). Set \[C=\bigcap_{N=0}^{\infty}\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}T^{-n}(B).\] The idea is to pick \(B\) such that \(T^{-1}(B)=B\) almost everywhere, i.e. \(\mu(T^{-1}(B)\mathbin\triangle B)=0\), and construct a \(C\) out of \(B\) such that \(T^{-1}C=C\) and \(\mu(C)=\mu(B)\). Note that \[B\mathbin\triangle\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}T^{-n}(B)\right) \subseteq\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\bigl(B\mathbin\triangle T^{-n}(B)\bigr).\] Now \[\begin{align*} \mu(T^{-1}(B)\mathbin\triangle B) &=\mu\bigl(T^{-1}(T^{-1}(B)\mathbin\triangle B)\bigr)\\ &=\mu(T^{-2}(B)\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}(B))\\ &=\cdots=\mu(T^{-i}B\mathbin\triangle T^{-i-1}(B))=0. \end{align*}\] Let \(x\in B\mathbin\triangle T^{-n}(B)\). Then either \(x\in B\setminus T^{-n}(B)\) or \(x\in T^{-n}(B)\setminus B\). If \(x\in B\setminus T^{-n}(B)\) and \(x\in T^{-i}(B)\) for every \(0\leq i\leq k\), then \(k\leq n\) and

\(x\in T^{-k}(B)\setminus T^{-k-1}(B)\). One can argue similarly for \(x\in T^{-n}(B)\setminus B\) to get \[B\mathbin\triangle T^{-n}(B) \subseteq\bigcup_{i=0}^{n-1}\bigl(T^{-i}(B)\mathbin\triangle T^{-i-1}(B)\bigr),\] so \(\mu(B\mathbin\triangle T^{-n}(B))=0\). Set \(C_N=\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}T^{-n}(B)\). Then, of course, \[C_0\supseteq C_1\supseteq C_2\supseteq C_3\supseteq C_4\supseteq\cdots, \qquad \mu(C_N\mathbin\triangle B)=0.\] Since \(C_N\searrow C\), we have \(\mu(C\mathbin\triangle B)=0\), and hence \(\mu(C)=\mu(B)\). Also, \[T^{-1}(C)=\bigcap_{N=0}^{\infty}\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}T^{-n-1}(B) =\bigcap_{N\geq1}C_N=\bigcap_{N\geq0}C_N=C.\] Therefore \(\mu(C)=\mu(B)\in\{0,1\}\), by the ergodicity of \(T\).

\((2)\Rightarrow(3)\). Let \(\mu(A)>0\) and set \(B=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}T^{-n}(A)\). Then \(T^{-1}(B)\subseteq B\). Since \(\mu\) is \(T\)-invariant, \(\mu(T^{-1}(B)\mathbin\triangle B)=0\). As \(T^{-1}(A)\subseteq B\), we have \(\mu(B)\neq0\), because \(\mu(T^{-1}(A))=\mu(A)>0\). Thus \[\mu\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}T^{-n}(A)\right)=1.\] Therefore, any point \(x\in X\) recurs on a given set of positive measure via an ergodic map.

\((3)\Rightarrow(4)\). If \(\mu(A)\mu(B)>0\), then \(\mu(A)>0\) and \(\mu(B)>0\), so \(\mu\bigl(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}T^{-n}(A)\bigr)=1\).

Since the \(T^{-n}(A)\) cover \(X\) almost everywhere, we have \[0<\mu(B)<\mu\left(B\cap\bigcup T^{-n}(A)\right) \leq\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu(B\cap T^{-n}(A)).\] Hence there exists \(n\geq1\) such that \(\mu(B\cap T^{-n}(A))>0\). We shall see the relevance of such statements when we introduce the notion of mixing systems.

\((4)\Rightarrow(1)\). If \(T^{-1}(A)=A\), then \[0=\mu(A\cap(X\setminus A)) =\mu(T^{-n}(A)\cap(X\setminus A))\qquad(n\geq1).\] Hence \(\mu(A)=0\) or \(\mu(X\setminus A)=0\), so \(\mu(A)\in\{0,1\}\) and \(T\) is ergodic.

Operator-Theoretic Ergodicity

Let us begin by associating an operator \(U_T\) to \(T\) as follows: \[U_T\colon L^2(\mu)\longrightarrow L^2(\mu),\qquad U_T(f):=f\circ T.\] Now \(L^2(\mu)\) is a Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). Let \(f_1,f_2\in L^2(\mu)\). Then \[\langle U_Tf_1,U_Tf_2\rangle =\int(f_1\circ T)\overline{(f_2\circ T)}\,d\mu =\int f_1\overline{f_2}\,d\mu=\langle f_1,f_2\rangle,\] by the second litmus test. From this we see \(\langle f_1,U_T^*U_Tf_2\rangle=\langle f_1,f_1\rangle\), so \[\langle f_1,(U_T^*U_T-\id)f_2\rangle=0 \qquad\text{for all }f_1,f_2\in L^2(\mu).\]

A standard argument

would tell you that \[\sup_{\substack{\|f_1\|\leq1\\\|f_2\|\leq1}} \left|\langle f_1,(U_T^*U_T-\id)f_2\rangle\right| =\|U_T^*U_T-\id\|=0.\] Thus \(U_T\) is a unitary operator, which goes by the name Koopman operator.

Proposition 7

\(T\) is ergodic if and only if the eigenvectors of \(U_T\) associated to \(1\) are constants in \(L^2_\mu(X)\).

Proof. If \(B\) is such that \(\mu(T^{-1}(B)\mathbin\triangle B)=0\), then \(\chi_B=\chi_B\circ T\) almost everywhere. Thus \(U_T\chi_B=\chi_B\), so \(\chi_B\) is a constant. Hence \(\mu(B)=0\) or \(\mu(B)=1\), and \(T\) is ergodic. If \(U_Tf=f\) implies \(f\equiv0\) almost everywhere, then \(T\) is ergodic.

Conversely, let \(f\colon X\to\mathbb R\) be measurable. Let \(k\in\mathbb Z\) and \(n\geq1\), and define \[A_n^k:=\left\{x:f(x)\in\left[\frac{k}{n},\frac{k+1}{n}\right)\right\}.\] Now we know that \[T^{-1}(A_n^k)\mathbin\triangle A_n^k \subseteq\{x:f\circ T(x)\neq f(x)\},\] which has measure zero if \(U_Tf=f\). The ergodicity of \(T\) implies \(\mu(A_n^k)\in\{0,1\}\), and we have \(X=\bigsqcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}A_n^k\). Thus there exists \(k(n)\in\mathbb Z\) such that \(\mu(A_n^{k(n)})=1\). For every \(n\), \[f(x)\in\left[\frac{k(n)}{n},\frac{k(n)+1}{n}\right) \quad\text{almost everywhere}.\] Letting \(n\to\infty\) shows that \(f\) is a constant almost everywhere.

Remark

Thus ergodicity can be rephrased in operator theory too. Properties possessing such translations are called unitary properties.

Fourier-Analytic Ergodicity

Here we impose a compact abelian group structure on \(X\). Then it has a unique translation-invariant measure \(m_X\), called the Haar measure of \(X\). We will not prove the existence of \(m_X\) here. We shall further assume that, given \(f\in L^2_{m_X}(X)\), we have the following character-theoretic expansion: \[f(x)=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat X}c_\chi\chi(x), \qquad \sum_{\chi\in\widehat X}|c_\chi|^2=\|f\|^2.\]

Proposition 8

In the setup above, a continuous surjective homomorphism \(T\colon X\to X\) is \(m_X\)-invariant if and only if, for a character \(\chi\in\widehat X\), \(\chi(T^n(x))=\chi(x)\) implies that \(\chi\) is trivial, i.e. \(\chi\equiv1\).

Proof. Suppose \(T\) is ergodic and let \(\chi\) be nontrivial such that \(\chi\circ T^n=\chi\), with \(n\) the least such integer. Set \[\widetilde\chi:=\chi+\chi\circ T+\cdots+\chi\circ T^{n-1}.\] Then \(\widetilde\chi\circ T=\widetilde\chi\), i.e. \(U_T\widetilde\chi=\widetilde\chi\). From the operator-theoretic setting, we see that \(\widetilde\chi\) is constant. But \(\langle\widetilde\chi,\chi\rangle_X\neq0\), so \(\widetilde\chi\) is not trivial. Hence \(\chi\) must be trivial.

Conversely, if \(U_Tf=f\), first write \(f\in L^2_{m_X}\) as \(f(x)=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat X}c_\chi\chi(x)\). Since \(U_Tf=f\), we have

\(c_\chi=c_{\chi\circ T}=c_{\chi\circ T^2}=\cdots\). Now, as \(\sum_{\chi\in\widehat X}|c_\chi|^2\) converges to \(\|f\|^2\), we must have \(c_\chi=0\), or \(\{c_{\chi\circ T^n}\}_n\) is periodic. But that would imply \(\chi\equiv1\). Hence \(f\) is a constant, so \(T\) is ergodic.

Remark

Having seen ergodicity, it is natural to ask whether we can reduce a measure-preserving system into “ergodic components”. Given any \(E\subset X\), one has a natural \(T\)-invariant set \(\{T^n(E)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\). Now \(X\) being ergodic assures us that \(\{T^n(E)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\) covers \(X\) almost everywhere. But if \(X\) were not ergodic, there is no apparent reason why a subset of \(X\) would exist such that \(\{T^n(F)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\) covers \(E\) almost everywhere, where \(F\subseteq E\). If we hope to use some form of Zorn’s lemma, the existence of an ergodic subsystem \((E,\mathcal B|_E,\mu|_E,T|_E)\) is required. Thus this problem of decomposing measure-preserving systems into ergodic components is natural. We shall deal with it later.

Remark

Using Proposition 8—I mean the ideas in it—one can prove that the circle-doubling map and the rotation map are ergodic. Finally, as the Bernoulli system is isomorphic to the circle-doubling system, the Bernoulli shift map is ergodic too. Thus almost all the examples we saw are ergodic transformations.
excerptHtml: Of all the impositions on a measure-preserving system, the one that is perhaps ill-motivated is the demand that \(\mu(X)<\infty\). Let’s look at why it matters.

title: Mean, Maximal, and Pointwise Ergodic Theorems
html:
In our attempt to get a hold on the nature of \(\{T^{\circ n}(x)\}_n\) or \(\{T^{\circ n}(E)\}_n\), we saw that \(\{T^{\circ n}(x)\}_n\) is recurrent. Further, if \(T\) is ergodic, then \(\{T^{\circ n}(x)\}_n\) is recurrent on all positive-measure subsets of \(X\) (for almost every \(x\in X\)). The next natural question to ask is: how recurrent are they? Mathematically speaking, we ask what happens, as \(N\to\infty\), to \[A_N^f:=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^n f \qquad\text{(the $T$-average of $f$).}\] Although we started off by asking about \(U_T^n f\) as \(n\to\infty\), we shall see that, as a consequence of the Koopman–Neumann lemma for positive bounded sequences, if \(A_N^f\to A\) as \(N\to\infty\), then \(U_T^n f\to A\) as \(n\to\infty\), \(n\notin J\), where \(J\) has “density” zero in \(\mathbb Z\).

In answering what happens to \(\frac1{N+1}\sum_{n=0}^{N}U_T^n f\) as \(N\to\infty\), ergodic theorems will, in some sense, establish a duality between space and time. We plan to prove the following.

Theorem 9 — Birkhoff

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system, with \(T\) ergodic. If \(f\in L^1_\mu\), then \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}U_T^j f=\int f\,d\mu.\]

The left-hand side is an average over time, and the right-hand side, being an integral, is an average over space. If \(f=\chi_B\), then the ergodic theorem is telling you that the probability of \(T^n(x)\in B\) is given by the size of \(B\) (or the measure of \(B\)). The independence of the theorem from \(x\in X\) is the remarkable thing to observe, and the imposition that \(T\) be ergodic is essential; otherwise, there may be \(x\in X\) such that \(T^n(x)\notin B\) for all \(n\geq1\). But as soon as you remove that set-theoretic hindrance, recurrence of orbits is governed by the sizes of sets. Now let me explain the duality.

Thus certain spatial information can be translated into temporal information, and vice versa.

In this lecture we shall give a complete proof of Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem (often also called the pointwise ergodic theorem). We must emphasise that ergodic theorems are unitary properties.

Theorem 10 — von Neumann’s mean ergodic theorem: \(L^2_\mu\) version

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system. Let \(P_T\) be the orthogonal projection of \(L^2_\mu\) onto \[I=\{g\in L^2_\mu:U_Tg=g\}.\] Then, for every \(f\in L^2_\mu\), \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^nf\longrightarrow P_Tf \quad\text{in the $L^2_\mu$ norm.}\]

Proof. Let us first begin by finding \(I^\perp\). Set \(B=\{U_Tg-g:g\in L^2_\mu\}\), and claim that \(B^\perp=I\). If \(f\in I\), then \(U_Tf=f\). Hence \[\langle f,U_Tg-g\rangle =\langle U_Tf,U_Tg\rangle-\langle f,g\rangle=0,\] so \(f\in B^\perp\). If \(f\in B^\perp\), then \[\langle U_Tg-g,f\rangle=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ \langle U_Tg,f\rangle=\langle g,f\rangle \ \Longrightarrow\ \langle g,(U_T^*-\id)f\rangle=0 \qquad(g\in L^2_\mu).\] Therefore \[\sup_{\|g\|\leq1}|\langle g,(U_T^*-\id)f\rangle| =0=\|(U_T^*-\id)f\|.\]

Thus \(U_T^*f=f\). Since \(U_T\) is unitary, \(U_Tf=f\), so \(f\in I\). Consequently, \(B^\perp=I\) and \(L^2_\mu(X)=I\oplus\overline B\). Write \(f=P_Tf+h\), with \(h\in\overline B\). It now suffices to prove \(\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^nh\to0\) in \(L^2_\mu\). For \(h=U_Tg-g\), with \(g\in L^2_\mu\), the telescoping series gives \[\left\|\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^n(U_Tg-g)\right\|_2 =\frac1N\|U_T^Ng-g\|_2 \leq\frac{\|U_T-\id\|\,\|g\|_2}{N} \leq\frac{2\|g\|_2}{N}.\]

Here \(U_T\), being an isometry, must have norm \(1\). Therefore \(\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^nh\to0\) in \(L^2_\mu\), since \(2\|g\|_2/N\to0\) as \(N\to\infty\).

Theorem 11 — von Neumann’s mean ergodic theorem: \(L^1_\mu\) version

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system. For every \(f\in L^1_\mu\), \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^nf\longrightarrow f'\in L^1_\mu \quad\text{in $L^1_\mu$,}\qquad U_Tf'=f'.\]

Proof. Note that \[\left(\int_X|f|\,d\mu\right)^2 \leq\left(\int_X|f|^2\,d\mu\right) \left(\int_X1^2\,d\mu\right), \qquad\text{so }\|\cdot\|_1\leq\|\cdot\|_2.\] If \(g\in L^\infty_\mu\subset L^2_\mu\), then \(\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_T^ng\to g'\) in \(L^1_\mu\). Now \(\|A_N^g\|_\infty\leq\|g\|_\infty\), and \(|\langle A_N^g,\chi_B\rangle|\leq\|g\|_\infty\mu(B)\). Since \(A_N^g\to g'\), the dominated convergence theorem gives \(|\langle g',\chi_B\rangle|\leq\|g\|_\infty\mu(B)\).

If \(g'\) does not have bounded essential supremum, one can find sets \(B_N\) such that \(\mu(B_N)>0\) and \(g'|_{B_N}>N\). Then \[N\mu(B_N)<|\langle g',\chi_{B_N}\rangle| \leq\|g\|_\infty\mu(B_N),\] a contradiction. Thus \(g'\in L^\infty_\mu\). As \(g\in L^2_\mu\), the \(L^2\) version of von Neumann’s ergodic theorem tells us that \(g'\) is \(T\)-invariant.

Now we exploit the fact that \(L^\infty_\mu\) is dense in \(L^2_\mu\).

Fix \(f\in L^1_\mu\) and \(\epsilon>0\). Let \(g\in L^\infty_\mu\) satisfy \(\|f-g\|_1<\epsilon\). Since \(T\) is \(\mu\)-invariant, \(\|A_N^f-A_N^g\|_1<\epsilon\). Also, there are \(g'\) and \(N_0\) such that \(\|A_N^g-g'\|_1<\epsilon\) for all \(N\geq N_0\). By the triangle inequality, \[\|A_N^f-A_{N'}^f\|_1<4\epsilon\qquad(N,N'\geq N_0).\] Thus \(A_N^f\) is Cauchy in \(L^1_\mu\). Since \(L^1_\mu\) is complete (the Riesz–Fischer theorem), \(A_N^f\to f'\).

It is now an elementary exercise to show that \(f'\) is \(T\)-invariant: \[U_TA_N^f=\frac{N+1}{N}A_{N+1}^f-\frac1Nf,\] and hence \[\|U_TA_N^f-A_N^f\|_1 =\left\|\frac{N+1}{N}A_{N+1}^f-A_N^f-\frac1Nf\right\|_1 \leq\|A_{N+1}^f-A_N^f\|_1+\frac2N\|f\|_1.\] As \(N\to\infty\), \(\|f'\circ T-f'\|_1=0\), so \(f'\circ T=f'\) almost everywhere.

Remark

If \(T\) is ergodic, then, for \(f=\chi_B\), we only know so far that the frequency of orbit visits of \(f\) is a fixed number, independent of \(x\).

Remark — Quantitative estimate

We have \(A_N^{\chi_B}=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\chi_B\circ T\).

As \(T\) is \(\mu\)-invariant, \[\int_X\chi_B\circ T\,d\mu=\int_X\chi_B\,d\mu=\mu(B) \qquad\text{(by Litmus Test 2).}\] Therefore \[\int_X A_N^{\chi_B}\,d\mu=\mu(B) \geq\sqrt{\mu(B)}\, \mu\bigl(\{x:A_N^{\chi_B}(x)>\sqrt{\mu(B)}\}\bigr),\] and hence \[\mu\bigl(\{x:A_N^{\chi_B}(x)>\sqrt{\mu(B)}\}\bigr) \leq\sqrt{\mu(B)}.\] Thus the measure of points in \(B\) that spend at least a proportion \(\sqrt{\mu(B)}\) of the time in \(B\) is at most \(\mu(B)^{1/2}\).

In light of the quantitative remark above, we have a more quantitative version of the ergodic theorem.

Theorem 12 — Maximal ergodic theorem

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be a measure-preserving system, and let \(g:X\to\mathbb R\), \(g\in L^1_\mu\). Define, for \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[E_\alpha:=\left\{x\in X: \sup_{n\geq1}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g(T^ix)>\alpha\right\}.\] Then \[\alpha\mu(E_\alpha)\leq\int_{E_\alpha}g\,d\mu\leq\|g\|_1, \qquad \alpha\mu(E_\alpha\cap A)\leq\int_{E_\alpha\cap A}g\,d\mu \quad\text{if }T^{-1}(A)=A.\]

We shall first prove a technical lemma and derive the theorem from it in a snap.

Lemma 13

Let \(U:L^1_\mu\to L^1_\mu\) be a positive linear operator with \(\|U\|\leq1\). Given \(f\in L^1_\mu\), set \[f_k=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}U^\ell f,\qquad f_0=0, \qquad F_N=\max\{f_n:0\leq n\leq N\}.\] Then \(\int_{\{x:F_N(x)>0\}}f\,d\mu\geq0\) for every \(N\geq1\).

Proof. We have \(F_N\in L^1_\mu\), since \(F_N\leq\sum_{n=0}^N|f_n|\). Also, \(F_N\geq f_n\) for \(0\leq n\leq N\), so positivity and linearity give \(UF_N+f\geq Uf_n+f=f_{n+1}\). Thus \(UF_N+f\geq\max_{1\leq n\leq N}f_n\). Set \(P=\{x:F_N(x)>0\}\). For \(x\in P\), \[F_N(x)=\max_{0\leq n\leq N}f_n(x) =\max_{1\leq n\leq N}f_n(x),\] since \(f_0=0\). Hence \(UF_N(x)+f(x)\geq F_N(x)\), or \(f(x)\geq F_N(x)-UF_N(x)\). By positivity, \(UF_N(x)\geq0\), as \(F_N(x)\geq0\). It follows that \[\int_P f\,d\mu \geq\int_P F_N\,d\mu-\int_P UF_N\,d\mu =\int_XF_N\,d\mu-\int_PUF_N\,d\mu,\]

because \(F_N(x)=0\) if \(x\notin P\). Therefore \[\int_Pf\,d\mu\geq\int_XF_N\,d\mu-\int_XUF_N\,d\mu =\|F_N\|_1-\|UF_N\|_1\geq0.\] Here the equality uses positivity, and the last inequality uses \(\|U\|\leq1\).

Proof of Theorem 12. Set \(f=g-\alpha\) and \(Uf:=f\circ T\). This is a unitary positive operator, so \(\|U\|\leq1\). We have \[E_\alpha=\bigcup_{N=0}^\infty\{x:F_N(x)>0\}.\] By the lemma, \(\int_{E_\alpha}f\,d\mu\geq0\), so \(\int_{E_\alpha}g\,d\mu\geq\alpha\mu(E_\alpha)\). To obtain the other inequality, look at \[\bigl(A,\mathcal B|_A,\mu(A)^{-1}\mu|_A,T|_A\bigr).\qedhere\]

Remark

This theorem has essentially removed the dependence on \(N\) in the statement made in the quantitative remark above.

Let us finally prove our desired theorem.

Theorem 14 — Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem

If \(f\in L^1_\mu\), then \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}f(T^j(x))=f^*(x).\] The function \(f^*\) is \(T\)-invariant, and \(\int f^*\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu\).

Proof. Of course, the measure-preserving system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is lurking in the background. Since the nature of the result is purely additive, we may assume without loss of generality that \(f:X\to\mathbb R\). Define \[f^*(x)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(T^i(x)), \qquad f_*(x)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(T^i(x)).\]

Trick (which we noticed before).

\[\frac{n+1}{n}\left(\frac1{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^nf(T^i(x))\right) =\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(T^i(T(x)))+\frac1nf(x) \leq f^*\circ T+\frac1nf(x).\]

Choose \(\{n_k\}_k\) such that \(A_{n+1}^f\to f^*\). Since \((n_k+1)/n_k\to1\), we obtain \(f^*\leq f^*\circ T\).

If we instead choose \(\{n_k\}_k\) such that \(A_n^f\) on the right-hand side converges to \(f^*\), then \[\limsup_{n_k}\frac{n+1}{n}A_{n+1}^f =f^*\circ T\leq\limsup_n A_{n+1}^f=f^*.\] Consequently, and similarly for \(f_*\), \[\begin{equation} f^*=f^*\circ T,\qquad f_*=f_*\circ T. \tag{$*$} \end{equation}\] Let \(\alpha>\beta\), with \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Q\), and set \[E_\alpha^\beta=\{x\in X:f_*(x)<\beta\text{ and }f^*(x)>\alpha\}.\]

By (*), \(T^{-1}(E_\alpha^\beta)=E_\alpha^\beta\). Also, \(E_\alpha\supseteq E_\alpha^\beta\), where \(E_\alpha\) is as in Theorem 12. That theorem gives \[\alpha\mu(E_\alpha\cap E_\alpha^\beta) \leq\int_{E_\alpha\cap E_\alpha^\beta}f\,d\mu,\] since \(T^{-1}(E_\alpha^\beta)=E_\alpha^\beta\). Similarly, applying it to \(-f\) gives \(\int_{E_\alpha^\beta}f\,d\mu\leq\beta\mu(E_\alpha^\beta)\). Combining these, \[\alpha\mu(E_\alpha^\beta) \leq\int_{E_\alpha^\beta}f\,d\mu \leq\beta\mu(E_\alpha^\beta).\] Since \(\alpha>\beta\), \(\mu(E_\alpha^\beta)=0\) for all rational \(\alpha>\beta\). By the density of \(\mathbb Q\) in \(\mathbb R\), \[\{x:f_*(x)<f^*(x)\} =\bigcup_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Q\\\alpha>\beta}}E_\alpha^\beta.\] The union has measure zero, so \(f_*=f^*\) almost everywhere. Thus \[A_n^f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(T^i(x))\longrightarrow f^*=f_* \qquad\text{almost everywhere.}\] By the \(L^1_\mu\) version of von Neumann’s ergodic theorem, \(A_n^f\to f'\in L^1_\mu\) in \(L^1_\mu\). A consequence of the

Borel–Cantelli lemma gives a sequence \(n_k\to\infty\) such that \[A_{n_k}^f(x)=:g_{n_k}(x)\longrightarrow f'(x) \qquad\text{almost everywhere.}\]

Hence \(f^*=f'=f_*\) in \(L^1_\mu\), and \(f^*\) is \(T\)-invariant because \(f'\) is. Now \(g_n\to f^*\) almost everywhere. By the dominated convergence theorem and \(T\)-invariance of \(\mu\), we also get \[\int f\,d\mu=\int g_n\,d\mu=\int f^*\,d\mu.\qedhere\]

Remark — Final remark

If \(T\) is ergodic, then \(f^*\) must be constant, since it is \(T\)-invariant (the eigenfunctions of \(U_T\) corresponding to \(1\) are only the constants). Thus \[\int f^*\,d\mu=f^*\mu(X)=f^*=\int f\,d\mu,\] and we finally get the link between space and time averages: \[\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(T^i(x)) =\int_Xf\,d\mu.}\]
excerptHtml: In answering what happens to \(\frac1{N+1}\sum_{n=0}^{N}U_T^n f\) as \(N\to\infty\), ergodic theorems will, in some sense, establish a duality between space and time. We plan to prove the following.

title: Mixing, Products, and Spectral Criteria
html:
Mixing

Ergodic theorems give you all the equidistribution theorems one would hope for, so let us now abandon the study of orbits. Recall that we studied ergodicity from three different perspectives:

  • Measure-theoretic: to obtain dynamical information.

  • Operator-theoretic: to obtain equidistribution theorems.

  • Fourier-analytic: for some examples.

Now let us focus on the study of “set-orbits” \(\{T^{\circ n}(E)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\). The measure-theoretic perspective gave us information about \(\{T^{\circ n}(x)\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\), namely recurrence theorems; the operator-theoretic perspective told us about \(\{f\circ T^n\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}\). Now it is time to give up these perspectives and look at it for what it is: a probability space. Let us view the system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) probabilistically. Before we jump into that, here is a small observation. We saw that \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f\circ T^n\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu \quad\text{in $L^2_\mu$, as $N\to\infty$.}\] One can restate this slightly to obtain a probabilistic interpretation

of ergodicity: \[T\text{ is ergodic} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A\cap T^{-n}(B)) \longrightarrow\mu(A)\mu(B).\]

  • If \(T\) is ergodic, then, by the dominated convergence theorem, \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\langle f\circ T^n,g\rangle \longrightarrow\left(\int f\,d\mu\right)\left(\int g\,d\mu\right).\] Set \(f=\chi_B\) and \(g=\chi_A\) to obtain the desired result.

  • Conversely, if \(T^{-1}(A)=A\), set \(B=X\setminus A\). We obtain \(\mu(A)\mu(X\setminus A)=0\), so \(\mu(A)\in\{0,1\}\).

Thus, on average, \(T\) pulls back an event and tries to make it independent of \(A\). If \(T^{-n}(B)\) and \(A\) were independent, then \[\mu(A\cap T^{-n}(B)) =\mu(A)\mu(T^{-n}(B))=\mu(A)\mu(B),\] and convergence would be assured. In general, however, an ergodic map just tries to separate events and is not always successful. Keeping this in mind, let us look at maps that asymptotically make \(T^{-n}(B)\) and \(A\) independent.

Definition 6 — Mixing

A system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is mixing if, for all \(A,B\in\mathcal B\), \[\mu(A\cap T^{-n}(B))\longrightarrow\mu(A)\mu(B) =\mu(A)\mu(T^{-n}(B))\qquad(n\to\infty).\]

Definition 7 — Weak mixing

A system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is weakly mixing if, for all \(A,B\in\mathcal B\), \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \bigl|\mu(A\cap T^{-n}(B))-\mu(A)\mu(B)\bigr| \longrightarrow0\qquad(N\to\infty).\]

Remark

For a sequence \(\{a_n\}_n\) (for example, \(a_n\) may be \(\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\)), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}|a_i|=0,\] but not conversely. Thus mixing implies weak mixing. Further, given a weakly mixing system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) and \(T^{-1}B=B\), we have \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|\mu(A\cap B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|\longrightarrow0.\] Set \(A=X\setminus B\). Then \(\mu(A)\mu(B)\to0\), so \(\mu(A)=0\) or \(\mu(B)=0\), and \(T\) is ergodic. Consequently, \[\text{Mixing}\ \subset\ \text{Weak mixing}\ \subset\ \text{Ergodicity}.\] Said differently:

  • \(T^{-1}\) makes \(A\) and \(B\) asymptotically independent: this is mixing.

  • \(T^{-1}\) makes \(A\) and \(B\) asymptotically independent except on a zero-density set: this is weak mixing.

  • \(T^{-1}\) tries to make \(A\) and \(B\) independent on average: this is ergodicity.

Remark

Since \(T^{-1}\) tries to separate events in whatever manner we prescribe, we say that the inverse of \(T^{-1}\), namely \(T\), mixes events. Hence we call such systems mixing or weakly mixing. It turns out that weak mixing (a formulation due to von Neumann) is quite a natural thing, as it has so many equivalent formulations. A generalisation of this concept will be crucial for us in establishing Szemerédi’s theorem.

Now let us see other equivalent formulations of weak mixing, to find

connections between the probabilistic interpretation and the others.

Theorem 15 — Mixing equivalences

Given a system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\), the following are equivalent:

(1)

\(T\) is weakly mixing.

(2)

\(T\times T\) is ergodic with respect to \(\mu\times\mu\).

(3)

\(T\times T\) is weakly mixing with respect to \(\mu\times\mu\).

(4)

If \((Y,\mathcal B',\nu,S)\) is ergodic, then \((X\times Y,\mathcal B\times\mathcal B',\mu\times\nu,T\times S)\) is ergodic.

(5)

\(U_T\) has continuous spectrum: its only eigenvalue is \(1\), and the corresponding eigenspace consists of constant functions.

This is a long proof, so hang tight. We will first prove an interesting technical lemma due to Koopman and von Neumann.

Lemma 16 — Koopman–Neumann

Let \(\{a_n\}\) be a sequence of bounded nonnegative real numbers. The following are equivalent:

(i)

\(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j=0\).

(ii)

There exists \(J\subseteq\mathbb N\) of density zero, where \[\operatorname{density}(J):= \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n|J\cap[1,n]|,\] such that \(a_n\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\) with \(n\notin J\).

(iii)

\(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j^2=0\).

Proof. Set \(J_k:=\{j\in\mathbb N:a_j>1/k\}\). This gives the natural inclusions \(J_1\subseteq J_2\subseteq J_3\subseteq\cdots\). By definition, \[\frac1k|J_k\cap[0,n)| <\sum_{\substack{0\leq i\leq n-1\\a_i>1/k}}a_i \leq\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i.\] Dividing by \(n\), \[\frac1n|J_k\cap[0,n)| <k\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i\right)\longrightarrow0,\] so \(\operatorname{density}(J_k)=0\) for all \(k\geq1\). Choose \(0<\ell_1<\ell_2<\cdots\) such that \(\frac1n|J_k\cap[0,n)|\leq1/k\) for all \(n\geq\ell_k\), and set \[J=\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty\bigl(J_k\cap[\ell_k,\ell_{k+1})\bigr).\]

Since \(J_k\subseteq J_{k+1}\), \(J_k\cap[\ell_{k+1},\ell_{k+2})\subseteq J_{k+1}\cap[\ell_{k+1},\ell_{k+2})\), so \(J_k\cap[\ell_k,\infty)\subseteq J\). If \(n\notin J\) and \(n\geq\ell_k\), then \(n\notin J_k\), and hence \(a_n\leq1/k\). Thus \(a_n\to0\) with \(n\notin J\). Let \(n\in[\ell_k,\ell_{k+1})\). Then \[\begin{aligned} J\cap[0,n) &=\left(\bigcup_{i=0}^\infty J_i\cap[\ell_i,\ell_{i+1})\right)\cap[0,n)\\ &\subseteq\left(\bigcup_{i=0}^{k}J_i\cap[\ell_i,\ell_{i+1})\right)\cap[0,n) \subseteq J_k\cap[0,n), \end{aligned}\] because \(J_i\subseteq J_{i+1}\) for all \(i\geq0\). Therefore \(\frac1n|J\cap[0,n)|\leq\frac1n|J_k\cap[0,n)|\leq1/k\), by our choice of \(\{\ell_k\}_{k\geq0}\). Thus \(J\) has density zero.

Now suppose \(a_n\to0\) with \(n\notin J\). Since \(\{a_n\}_n\) is bounded, there exists \(R>0\) such that \(a_n\leq R\) for every \(n\geq1\).

For each \(k\geq1\), choose \(N_k\) such that \(n\notin J\), \(n\geq N_k\) imply \(a_n<1/k\), and such that \(\frac1n|J\cap[0,n)|\leq1/k\). For all \(n\geq kN_k\), \[\begin{aligned} \frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i &=\frac1n\left(\sum_{i=0}^{N_k-1}a_i +\sum_{\substack{i\in J\\N_k\leq i<n}}a_i +\sum_{\substack{i\notin J\\N_k\leq i<n}}a_i\right)\\ &<\frac1n\left(RN_k+R|J\cap[0,n)|+\frac nk\right)\\ &\leq\frac{RN_k}{n}+R\frac{|J\cap[0,n)|}{n}+\frac1k \leq\frac Rk+\frac Rk+\frac1k =\frac{2R+1}{k}\longrightarrow0\qquad(k\to\infty). \end{aligned}\] Similarly, \[a_n\xrightarrow[n\notin J]{}0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_n^2\xrightarrow[n\notin J]{}0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i^2\longrightarrow0.\]

Proof of Theorem 15. We shall use the Koopman–Neumann lemma without mentioning it explicitly. Keep in mind henceforth that \[\begin{aligned} &\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|\longrightarrow0\\ &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} |\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|^2\longrightarrow0\\ &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\xrightarrow[n\notin J]{}\mu(A)\mu(B), \quad\text{where $J$ has density zero.} \end{aligned}\]

\((1)\Longrightarrow(3)\).

Given \(A_1,B_1,A_2,B_2\in\mathcal B\), there are density-zero sets

\(J_1,J_2\) such that \[\begin{equation} \mu(A_1\cap T^{-n}B_1)\xrightarrow[n\notin J_1]{}\mu(A_1)\mu(B_1), \qquad \mu(A_2\cap T^{-n}B_2)\xrightarrow[n\notin J_2]{}\mu(A_2)\mu(B_2). \tag{$*$} \end{equation}\]

Set \(J=J_1\cup J_2\). Clearly, \[\frac1n|J\cap[0,n)| \leq\frac1n|J_1\cap[0,n)|+\frac1n|J_2\cap[0,n)|\longrightarrow0,\] so \(J\) has density zero. Therefore \[\begin{aligned} &\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n\notin J}} \bigl|(\mu\times\mu)((A_1\times A_2)\cap(T\times T)^{-n}(B_1\times B_2))\\ & -(\mu\times\mu)(A_1\times A_2)(\mu\times\mu)(B_1\times B_2)\bigr|\\ &=\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n\notin J}} \bigl|\mu(A_1\cap T^{-n}B_1)\mu(A_2\cap T^{-n}B_2) -\mu(A_1)\mu(A_2)\mu(B_1)\mu(B_2)\bigr|=0, \end{aligned}\] by the definition and (*). The \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal B\times\mathcal B\) contains the algebra of rectangles \(\mathcal J'\). Let \(\widetilde\mu=\mu\times\mu\), and let \[\mathcal J:=\left\{A\in\mathcal B\times\mathcal B: \begin{array}{l} \text{for all }A_1,A_2\in\mathcal J,\\ \widetilde\mu(A_1\cap T^{-n}A_2) \xrightarrow[n\notin J_{A_1A_2}]{}\widetilde\mu(A_1)\mu(A_2),\\ \operatorname{density}(J_{A_1A_2})=0 \end{array}\right\}.\]

Clearly, \(\mathcal J'\subseteq\mathcal J\). It would now suffice to prove that \(\mathcal J\) is a monotone class. If \(A_i\nearrow A\), then \(\widetilde\mu(A_i\cap T^{-n}A_2) \to\widetilde\mu(A_i)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\) with \(n\notin J_{A_iA_2}\). We therefore have \[\widetilde\mu(A_i\cap T^{-n}A_2) -\widetilde\mu(A_i)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\longrightarrow0 \quad\left(n\notin\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}J_{A_iA_2},\quad1\leq i\leq n\right).\]

Let \(J_k=\bigcup_{i=1}^kJ_{A_iA_2}\), so \(J_1\subseteq J_2\subseteq\cdots\). Now mimic the proof of

Koopman–Neumann by finding \(0<\ell_1<\ell_2<\cdots\) such that \(\frac1n|J_k\cap[0,n)|\leq1/k\), and define \[J=\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty J_k\cap[\ell_k,\ell_{k+1}).\] Clearly, for any \(k\), \(J_k\cap[\ell_k,\infty)\subseteq J\). Thus, for \(n\notin J\) and \(n\geq\ell_k\), \[\widetilde\mu(A_i\cap T^{-n}A_2) -\widetilde\mu(A_i)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\longrightarrow0 \qquad(i\leq k).\] It follows that \[\widetilde\mu(A_i\cap T^{-n}A_2) -\widetilde\mu(A_i)\widetilde\mu(A_2) \xrightarrow[n\in J]{}0\qquad(i\geq1).\]

As \(A_i\nearrow A\), we know that \[\widetilde\mu(A_i\cap T^{-n}A_2)-\widetilde\mu(A_i)\widetilde\mu(A_2) \longrightarrow \widetilde\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A_2)-\widetilde\mu(A)\widetilde\mu(A_2),\] and \(\widetilde\mu(A\cap T^{-n}A_2)-\widetilde\mu(A)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\to0\). The exchange of limits can be justified by the fact that \[\lim_{(m,n)\to\infty} \bigl(\widetilde\mu(A_m\cap T^{-n}A_2) -\widetilde\mu(A_m)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\bigr)=0,\] and that, for every \(m\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\widetilde\mu(A_m\cap T^{-n}A_2) -\widetilde\mu(A_m)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\bigr)\) exists, while, for every \(n\), \(\lim_{m\to0}\bigl(\widetilde\mu(A_m\cap T^{-n}A_2) -\widetilde\mu(A_m)\widetilde\mu(A_2)\bigr)\) exists. Hence Fubini’s theorem, together with dominated convergence for counting measure on \((\mathbb N\setminus J)\times\mathbb N\), yields the result.

Thus \(\mathcal J\) is a monotone class, as the case \(A_i\searrow A\) can be handled similarly. Consequently, \(\mathcal J=\mathcal B\times\mathcal B\).

\((3)\Longrightarrow(1)\).

If \(T\times T\) is weakly mixing, then \[\begin{aligned} \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl|&(\mu\times\mu)((A\times X)\cap(T\times T)^{-n}(B\times X))\\ &-(\mu\times\mu)(A\times X)(\mu\times\mu)(B\times X)\bigr|=0. \end{aligned}\] Therefore \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} |\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)|=0,\] and \(T\) is weakly mixing.

\((1)\Longrightarrow(4)\).

Let \((Y,\mathcal B',\nu,S)\) be an ergodic system, and let \(T\) be weakly mixing. For \(A_1,B_1\in\mathcal B\) and \(A_2,B_2\in\mathcal B'\), \[\begin{aligned} &\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(\mu\times\nu) ((A_1\times A_2)\cap(T\times S)^{-n}(B_1\times B_2))\\ &=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A_1\cap T^{-n}B_1)\nu(A_2\cap S^{-n}B_2)\\ &=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A_1)\mu(B_1)\nu(A_2\cap S^{-n}B_2)\\ &\quad+\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} [\mu(A_1\cap T^{-n}B_1)-\mu(A_1)\mu(B_1)]\nu(A_2\cap S^{-n}B_2). \end{aligned}\] Since \(S\) is ergodic, \(\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\nu(A_2\cap S^{-n}B_2)\to\nu(A_2)\nu(B_2)\). Since \(T\) is weakly mixing, \(\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|\mu(A_1\cap T^{-n}B_1)-\mu(A_1)\mu(B_1)|\to0\).

Thus \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(\mu\times\nu) ((A_1\times A_2)\cap(T\times S)^{-n}(B_1\times B_2)) \longrightarrow\mu(A_1)\mu(B_1)\nu(A_2)\nu(B_2),\] and \(T\times S\) is ergodic. Again, one has to extend this result from the algebra of rectangles to the \(\sigma\)-algebra by exchanging limits.

\((4)\Longrightarrow(2)\).

Let \((Y,\mathcal B',\nu,S)\) be the ergodic system with \(Y=\{y\}\), \(T=\id\), and \(\nu(\{y\})=1\).

Then \[(X\times Y,\mathcal B\times\mathcal B',\mu\times\nu,T\times S) \cong(X,\mathcal B,\mu,T),\] so \(T\) is ergodic. Alternatively, as stated in the remark, weak mixing implies ergodicity. Applying (4) again, \(T\times T\) is ergodic.

\((2)\Longrightarrow(1)\).

Let \(\mu^2=\mu\times\mu\) be the product measure. Since \(T\times T\) is ergodic, we have \[\begin{aligned} \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B) &=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu^2((A\times X)\cap(T\times T)^{-n}(B\times X))\\ &\longrightarrow\mu^2(A\times X)\mu^2(B\times X)=\mu(A)\mu(B), \end{aligned}\] and \[\begin{aligned} \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)^2 &=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu^2((A\times A)\cap(T\times T)^{-n}(B\times B))\\ &\longrightarrow\mu^2(A\times A)\mu^2(B\times B)=\mu(A)^2\mu(B)^2. \end{aligned}\] Now we have

\[\begin{aligned} &\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)-\mu(A)\mu(B))^2\\ &=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)^2+\mu(A)^2\mu(B)^2 -2\mu(A)\mu(B)\left(\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mu(A\cap T^{-n}B)\right)\\ &\longrightarrow2\mu(A)^2\mu(B)^2-2\mu(A)\mu(B)\mu(A)\mu(B)=0. \end{aligned}\]

\((2)\Longrightarrow(5)\).

Suppose \(U_Tf=\lambda f\), where \(\lambda\in S^1\) because \(U_T\) is unitary. Define \(g(x_1,x_2)=f(x_1)\overline{f(x_2)}\). Then \[U_{T\times T}g(x,y)=g(Tx,Ty)=\lambda\overline\lambda\,g(x,y)=g(x,y).\] By ergodicity of \(T\times T\), \(g\) must be constant almost everywhere. Also, \(U_Tf=\lambda f\) gives \(f\circ T=\lambda f\), so \(\lambda=1\). Hence \(U_T\) has continuous spectrum.

\((5)\Longrightarrow(2)\).

Suppose \(T\times T\) is not ergodic. There exists a nonconstant \(f\in L^2_\mu(X\times X)\). We can assume without loss of generality that \(f(x,y)=\overline{f(y,x)}\). If both \(f(x,y)+\overline{f(y,x)}\) and \(i(f(x,y)-\overline{f(y,x)})\) were constant, then \(f(x,y)\) would also be constant. Thus we may either work with one of them or assume the symmetry \(f(x,y)=\overline{f(y,x)}\). Now subtract \(\int f\,d\mu^2\) from \(f\). Then \(\int(f-\int f\,d\mu^2)\,d\mu^2=0\), so we may also assume \(\int f\,d\mu^2=0\). Define the Hilbert–Schmidt operator \[(F(g))(x):=\int_X f(x,y)g(y)\,d\mu(y).\]

  • \(F\) is self-adjoint, by Fubini’s theorem.

  • \(F\) is nontrivial, because \(f\) is.

  • \(\|F\|_{\mathrm{HS}}=\|f\|_{\mu^2}<\infty\). The Hilbert–Schmidt norm is bounded, so \(F\) is compact.

  • Since \(F\) is self-adjoint, \(\sup_{\|x\|\leq1}|\langle Fx,x\rangle|=\|F\|\). Since \(F\) is nontrivial, this supremum is nonzero. Therefore \(\|F\|\) or \(-\|F\|\) is an eigenvalue of \(F\), again a consequence of \(F\) being a nontrivial compact self-adjoint operator.

  • There exists \(\lambda\ne0\) such that the nullspace of \(T-\lambda I\) is nontrivial. The closed subspace \(N_\lambda\) is Banach, and \(\lambda^{-1}T:N_\lambda\to N_\lambda\). Since \(T/\lambda\) is compact, \(N_\lambda\) is locally compact, equivalently finite-dimensional.

Thus \(F(g)=\lambda g\) for some \(g\), with \(\lambda\ne0\). Then \[\begin{aligned} \lambda g(Tx) &=\int_X f(Tx,y)g(y)\,d\mu(y)\\ &=\int_X f(Tx,Ty)g(Ty)\,d\mu(y) =\int_X f(x,y)g(Ty)\,d\mu(y). \end{aligned}\] The second equality uses the \(\mu\)-invariance of \(T\), and the last uses the \(T\times T\)-invariance of \(f\). Hence \(F(g\circ T)=\lambda(g\circ T)\), so \(g\in N_\lambda\) implies \(g\circ T\in N_\lambda\). Therefore \(U_T:N_\lambda\to N_\lambda\), and \(U_T\) has a nontrivial eigenvalue. If \(g\) is an eigenvector corresponding to it, then

\[\int_X\lambda(g\circ T)\,d\mu =\int_X\int_X f(g\circ T)\,d\mu^2.\] If \(g\) were constant, then \(\lambda=\int_{X^2}f\,d\mu^2=0\), a contradiction. Thus \(U_T\) has a nontrivial eigenvector and does not have continuous spectrum.

Let us stop this session by setting up the premise for the infamous Rokhlin problem.

Definition 8 — \(k\)-fold mixing

A system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is \(k\)-fold mixing if \[\mu(A_0\cap T^{-n_1}A_1\cap\cdots\cap T^{-n_k}A_k) \longrightarrow\mu(A_0)\cdots\mu(A_k)\] as \(n_1,n_2-n_1,n_3-n_2,\ldots,n_k-n_{k-1}\to\infty\), for all \(A_i\in\mathcal B\), \(0\leq i\leq k\).

Question — Rokhlin problem (open)

If \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) is mixing, is it \(k\)-fold mixing for every \(k\geq1\)?
excerptHtml: Ergodic theorems give you all the equidistribution theorems one would hope for, so let us now abandon the study of orbits. Recall that we studied ergodicity from three different perspectives:

title: Return Times, Kakutani Skyscrapers, and Rokhlin Towers
html:
There is a deep question concerning mixing systems called the Rokhlin problem. Here we shall see beautiful work of Rokhlin and Kakutani: Rokhlin towers and Kakutani skyscrapers.

Induced Transformations

Let us work with the system \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\), where \(T\) is invertible. The very first result that we proved—a result that revealed the first emergence of a pattern—was Poincaré’s recurrence theorem. It tells you that, given a set \(A\), almost all points of \(A\) under \(T\) keep hitting \(A\) ad infinitum. Now let us quantify the implication of that theorem by asking:

What is the expected return time to \(A\)? Assume \(\mu(A)>0\).

We shall address that question by looking at the first return time to \(A\). This shall suffice, for the second return time is the first for the iterated image of the starting point, and so on.

Define \[r_A(x):=\inf_{n\geq1}\{n\mid T^n(x)\in A\}.\]

This quantity \(r_A\) gives us a natural way of defining a transformation on \(A\).

Definition 9 — Induced transformation

Define \(T_A\colon A\to A\) by \(T_A(x):=T^{r_A(x)}(x)\). This is defined almost everywhere on \(A\), and is called the transformation induced by \(T\) on \(A\), or the induced transformation on \(A\).

  • \(r_A\colon X\to\mathbb N\) is measurable, because we have \[\begin{aligned} \text{``first return'':}\quad \{x\in A\mid r_A(x)=1\}&=A_1=A\cap T^{-1}(A),\\ \text{``second return'':}\quad \{x\in A\mid r_A(x)=2\}&=A_2=(A\cap T^{-2}(A))\setminus A_1,\\ &\ \vdots\\ \text{``$n$th return'':}\quad \{x\in A\mid r_A(x)=n\}&=A_n=(A\cap T^{-n}(A))\setminus\bigcup_{i<n}A_i. \end{aligned}\] As \(A_n\) is measurable for every \(n\geq1\), \(r_A\) is measurable, for the sets \(\{n\}\) generate the \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb N\).

  • \(T_A\colon A\to A\) is also measurable. Since \(T\) is invertible, for \(B\in\mathcal B\) with \(B\subseteq A\), clearly \(T_A^{-1}(B)=\widetilde B\) almost everywhere, so \(T_A\) is measurable. Here notice that \[\widetilde B=\bigcup_{n\geq1}T^{-n}(B\cap A_n) \quad\text{almost everywhere},\] as \(T^{-1}\) is defined almost everywhere.

  • \(\bigl(A,\mathcal B|_A,\mu_A=\frac1{\mu(A)}(\mu|_A),T_A\bigr)\) is a measure-preserving system.

  • As is to be naturally expected, if \(T\) is ergodic, then so is \(T_A\). Firstly, notice that \(A=\bigsqcup_{n\geq1}A_n\). Thus, if \(B\in\mathcal B|_A\), then \(B=\bigsqcup_{n\geq1}(B\cap A_n)\), so \[\mu_A(B)=\frac1{\mu(A)}\sum_{n\geq1}\mu(B\cap A_n), \qquad T_A(B)=\bigsqcup_{n\geq1}T_A(B\cap A_n) =\bigsqcup_{n\geq1}T^n(B\cap A_n).\] Hence \[\begin{aligned} \mu_A(T_A(B)) &=\frac1{\mu(A)}\sum_{n\geq1}\mu\bigl(T^n(B\cap A_n)\bigr)\\ &=\frac1{\mu(A)}\sum_{n\geq1}\mu(B\cap A_n) &&\text{($T$ is $\mu$-invariant)}\\ &=\mu(B). \end{aligned}\]

    If \(T_A\) is not ergodic, there exists \(B\) with \(T_A^{-1}(B)=B\) and \(0<\mu(B)<\mu(A)\), i.e. \(0<\mu_A(B)<1\). Then \[\bigcup_{n\geq1}\ \bigcup_{j=0}^{n-1}T^j(B\cap A_n)\] is \(T\)-invariant and has nonzero measure (check!).

Having addressed the nature of the induced transformation, let us introduce Kakutani skyscrapers and see how a simple construction can help us get two marvellous results, one of them addressing the question raised at the beginning of the lecture.

Kakutani Skyscrapers

Description.

The ground floor represents \(A\) as a disjoint union of sets \(\{A_k\}_{k\geq1}\). By definition, points in \(A_2\) travel to some set before returning to \(A\). The first floor consists of the sets \(A_2\) onwards lifted to a set beyond \(A\); the second floor is obtained similarly, and the \(n\)th floor inductively. \(T_A\) takes points in \(A_3\), for instance, on a ride to all the floors above it and lands on \(A\).

Remark

Poincaré recurrence is basically saying that the ground floor has \(\{A_k\}_{k\geq1}\) almost everywhere, and hence the tower above it. Ergodicity of \(T\) tells you that every point of \(X\) belongs to some floor of the skyscraper, as \(\mu(A)>0\).

Theorem 17 — Expected Return Time, due to Kac

Let \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) be an invertible ergodic system. If \(\mu(A)>0\), then \[\int_A r_A\,d\mu=1.\] In other words, the expected return time is \[\frac1{\mu(A)}\int_A r_A\,d\mu=\frac1{\mu(A)}.\]

Proof. Since \(T\) is invertible, ergodicity of \(T\) implies ergodicity of \(T^{-1}\). As we know, \(\mu\bigl(\bigcup_{n\geq1}T^n(A)\bigr)=1\), so the skyscraper contains almost all of \(X\). Thus, summing up tower-wise, \[\begin{aligned} 1=\mu(X) &=\sum_{n\geq1}\mu\bigl(A_n\sqcup T(A_n)\sqcup\cdots\sqcup T^{n-1}(A_n)\bigr)\\ &=\sum_{n\geq1}n\mu(A_n)=\int_A r_A\,d\mu, \end{aligned}\] as \(\sum_{k=1}^n k\chi_{A_k}\nearrow r_A\).

Therefore, the bigger the set, the sooner the points will return. In particular, if \(\mu(A)>\frac12\), then the expected return time is less than \(2\).

Theorem 18 — Rokhlin’s Tower Decomposition

In the setting of Theorem 17, suppose that \(\mu(\{x\})=0\) for all \(x\in X\), i.e. \(\mu\) is nonatomic. Then for every \(n\geq1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(B\in\mathcal B\) such that

  • \(B,T(B),\ldots,T^{n-1}(B)\) are disjoint;

  • \(\displaystyle\mu\left(\bigsqcup_{k=0}^{n-1}T^k(B)\right)>1-\varepsilon\).

Proof. Nonatomic measures are measures which have no “atoms”. In mathematical terms, given \(E\in\mathcal B\), there exists \(F\in\mathcal B\) such that \(0<\mu(F)<\mu(E)\). Then \(\mu(F)\) or \(\mu(E\setminus F)\) is less than \(\mu(E)/2\). Replacing \(F\) by \(E\), one can inductively construct measurable sets satisfying \[\mu(\widetilde F)<\frac{\mu(E)}{2^n}<\frac1{2^n}.\]

Now, given \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), select \(A\in\mathcal B\) such that \(0<\mu(A)<\varepsilon/n\). The skyscraper yields the decomposition of \(X\) into towers \[A_k\sqcup T(A_k)\sqcup\cdots\sqcup T^{k-1}(A_k).\] Set \[B=\bigsqcup_{k\geq n}\ \bigsqcup_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/n\rfloor-1}T^{jn}(A_k).\] Then \(B,T(B),T^2(B),\ldots,T^{n-1}(B)\) are disjoint; each belongs to a particular residue class modulo \(n\). The set \(\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}T^k(B)\) is all of \(X\) except those sets in the skyscraper comprising no more than \(n\) floors in each tower. Therefore \[\mu\left(\left(\bigsqcup_{k=0}^{n-1}T^k(B)\right)^c\right) \leq n\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\mu(A_k) \leq n\mu(A)<\varepsilon,\] which implies \(\mu\bigl(\bigsqcup_{k=0}^{n-1}T^k(B)\bigr)>1-\varepsilon\).

Pictorially speaking, this is what happened. Let us represent towers by numbers.

\[\def\arraystretch{1.25} \begin{array}{rcccccccc} B &=&1&1&1&1&\begin{gathered}[b]5\\1\end{gathered}&\begin{gathered}[b]5\\1\end{gathered}&\cdots\\ T(B) &=&2&2&2&2&\begin{gathered}[b]6\\2\end{gathered}&\begin{gathered}[b]6\\2\end{gathered}&\cdots\\ T^2(B) &=&3&3&3&3&\begin{gathered}[b]7\\3\end{gathered}&\begin{gathered}[b]7\\3\end{gathered}&\cdots\\ T^3(B) &=&4&4&4&4&\begin{gathered}[b]8\\4\end{gathered}&\begin{gathered}[b]8\\4\end{gathered}&\cdots \end{array}\] Since we are stopping at \(\lfloor k/n\rfloor-1\), all towers between \(A_4\) and \(A_8\) will have no means of reaching floors beyond \(4\). Similarly, towers between \(A_8\) and \(A_{12}\) will have no means of reaching beyond the eighth floor, and so on. Each tower will have some residual floors, unattended by iterates of \(B\), and there can be at most \(4\) in our case.

This decomposition is usually called a Rokhlin tower of height \(n\) with base \(B\) and residual set of size \(\varepsilon\).

This sort of brings us to the end of our discussion on measure-preserving systems. Let us stop by stating things to look forward to.

In our brief five lectures we have encountered two fundamental questions:

1.

The problem of decomposing the state space into ergodic components.

2.

The problem of classifying measure-preserving systems.

Soon we shall be dealing with these two, and the next thing to look forward to will be the proof of Szemerédi’s theorem!

title: Invariant Measures and the Geometry of Ergodicity
html:
Let’s put both a topological structure and a measure on our state space \(X\).

Let \((X,d)\) be a compact metric space and \(T\colon X\to X\) be a continuous map. This is the setup of a topological dynamical system. It turns out that, the moment you have this, there are some measures you can impose on \(X\) naturally, which is precisely why we studied measure-preserving systems first. We want our measures to capture the “size” of sets, so we require our measures to be positive. Riesz’s representation theorem tells you that all positive linear functionals in \(C(X)^*\) are in one-to-one correspondence with bounded Borel measures on \(X\): \[\boxed{\Lambda\in C(X)^*\ \sim\ \int_X d\mu, \qquad \mu\text{ a bounded Borel measure}.}\] Thus, the set of all possible Borel probability measures that one can impose on \(X\) can be naturally obtained from the structure imposed on \(X\), i.e. the structure of a compact metric space.

Denote by \(\mathcal M(X)\) the space of Borel probability measures on \(X\). Our

attempts at building a geometric perspective on ergodicity begin by endowing \(\mathcal M(X)\), again, with a natural metric-space structure.

Give \(C(X)^*\) the weak-\(*\) topology. Notice first that the set \[\mathcal M(X):=\left\{\mu\in C(X)^*\ \middle|\ \int_X1\,d\mu=1,\quad \int_Xf\,d\mu\geq0\text{ for every }f\in C(X),\ f\geq0\right\}\] is closed in \(C(X)^*\), under the natural identification, because we have:

  • If \(\mu_n\to\mu\), then \(\int_X f\,d\mu_n\to\int_X f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in C(X)\). Set \(f=1\) to get \(\int_X1\,d\mu=1\).

  • Since \(\int_Xf\,d\mu_n\geq0\) and \(\int_Xf\,d\mu_n\to\int_Xf\,d\mu\), we get \(\int_Xf\,d\mu\geq0\) for every \(f\in C(X)\) with \(f\geq0\).

Clearly, the norm of the operator \(\mu\) is \(\mu(X)\), for \[\left|\int_Xf\,d\mu\right|\leq\|f\|_\infty\int_X1\,d\mu\] (now set \(f=1\)). Thus \(\mathcal M(X)\) is compact in the weak-\(*\) topology: by the Banach–Alaoglu theorem, the unit ball in \(C(X)^*\), under the usual operator norm, is weak-\(*\) compact, and \(\mathcal M(X)\) is closed in the unit ball. Further, if \(\mu_1,\mu_2\in\mathcal M(X)\), then \(s\mu_1+(1-s)\mu_2\in\mathcal M(X)\), so \(\mathcal M(X)\) is a convex compact subspace of \(C(X)^*\).

Remark

\(\mathcal M(X)\) can also be metrizable, but that aspect of it is not relevant

to us as of now.

Given a topological dynamical system \((X,d,T)\), we have a way to associate probability measures on \(X\) using the topological structure imposed on \(X\). Of these, let us now look at those measures \(\mu\in\mathcal M(X)\) such that \(\mu\) is \(T\)-invariant. Then we shall have a measure-preserving system to which we can export our knowledge developed so far.

The map \(T\) induces a continuous map \(T_*\colon\mathcal M(X)\to\mathcal M(X)\), defined by \[T_*(\mu)(A):=\mu(T^{-1}(A)).\] It is continuous because \(\int_Xf\,d(T_*\mu)=\int_Xf\circ T\,d\mu\). If \(\mu_n\xrightarrow{*}\mu\), then \(\int_Xf\circ T\,d\mu_n\to\int_Xf\circ T\,d\mu\), so \[\int_Xf\,d(T_*\mu_n)\longrightarrow\int_Xf\circ T\,d\mu =\int_Xf\,d(T_*\mu) \qquad\text{for every }f\in C(X).\] Hence \(T_*\mu_n\to T_*\mu\).

If \(\mathcal M^T(X):=\{\mu\in\mathcal M(X)\mid\mu\text{ is $T$-invariant}\}\), the continuity of \(T_*\) implies that \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) is closed, hence compact, in \(\mathcal M(X)\). Also, \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) is convex. Therefore \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) is also a convex compact subspace of \(C(X)^*\).

Theorem 19 — Krylov–Bogolyubov

We can do ergodic theory on \((X,d,T)\): given a topological dynamical system \((X,d,T)\), we have \(\mathcal M^T(X)\neq\varnothing\).

Proof. We have \(\mathcal M(X)\neq\varnothing\) because \(\delta_x\in\mathcal M(X)\), where, for every Borel set \(A\subseteq X\), \[\delta_x(A):=\begin{cases}1,&x\in A,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] The measures \(\delta_x\) can be identified with points in \(X\). As \(\mathcal M(X)\) is convex, if \(X\) has at least two points then \(\mathcal M(X)\) will be uncountable.

Now let \(\nu_n\in\mathcal M(X)\) and set \(\mu_n:=\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}T_*^j(\nu_n)\). Since \(\mathcal M(X)\) is compact, there exists \(\mu_{n(j)}\to\mu\). Let \(f\in C(X)\). Then \[\begin{aligned} \left|\int f\circ T\,d\mu_{n(j)}-\int f\,d\mu_{n(j)}\right| &=\frac1{n(j)}\left|\int\sum_{i=0}^{n(j)-1} (f\circ T^{i+1}-f\circ T^i)\,d\nu_{n(j)}\right|\\ &=\frac1{n(j)}\left|\int(f\circ T^{n(j)+1}-f)\,d\nu_{n(j)}\right|\\ &\leq\frac2{n(j)}\|f\|_\infty\longrightarrow0 \qquad(j\to\infty). \end{aligned}\]

Thus \(\int f\circ T\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in C(X)\), implying that \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\). Hence \(\mathcal M^T(X)\neq\varnothing\).

Remark

Replace \((X,d,T)\) with \((\mathcal M(X),\widetilde d,T_*)\), where \(\widetilde d\) is the metric that generates its weak-\(*\) topology. By the

previous theorem, \(\mathcal M^{T_*}(\mathcal M(X))\neq\varnothing\), so there exists a \(T_*\)-invariant measure on \(\mathcal M(X)\). Birkhoff’s theorem tells us that, given almost every \(\nu\in\mathcal M(X)\), \[\widetilde\mu_n=A_n^\nu:=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}U_{T_*}^i f(\nu) \longrightarrow f'(\nu),\] where \(f'\) is \(T_*\)-invariant. Since \(\{\nu\}\) is a Borel set in the metric space \(\mathcal M(X)\), set \(f=\chi_{\{\nu\}}\). Now \[\int_{\mathcal M(X)}f'\,d\widetilde\nu =\int_{\mathcal M(X)}f\,d\widetilde\nu =\widetilde\nu(\{\nu\}),\] where \(\widetilde\nu\) is the \(T_*\)-invariant measure. Hence \(f'=\chi_{\{\nu\}}\) almost everywhere (only if \(f'\geq0\)).

Therefore, we have this dual notion in play here: consider the fact that \(\mathcal M(X)\) in some sense also contains \(X\). \[\boxed{\begin{gathered}\text{Equidistribution theorems}\\\text{in }\mathcal M(X)\end{gathered} \quad\approx\quad \begin{gathered}\text{Invariant measures}\\\text{on }X\end{gathered}}\]

Now recall that \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) is convex, so one can talk about its extreme points: points in \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) which cannot be further broken down into linear, convex combinations of other elements in \(\mathcal M^T(X)\). Denote the set of extreme points by \(\mathcal E^T(X)\). For measures in \(\mathcal E^T(X)\), we have the following lemma.

Lemma 20

If \(\mu_1,\mu_2\in\mathcal E^T(X)\) with \(\mu_1\neq\mu_2\), then \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are mutually singular, if \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are ergodic. That is, there exist measurable sets \(A,B\) such that \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), \(A\cup B=X\), and \(\mu_1(B)=\mu_2(A)=0\).

Proof. This is a very simple consequence of the ergodic theorem.

For every \(f\in C(X)\), by the pointwise ergodic theorem, \[A_n^f(x)\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu_1\quad(*) \qquad\text{and}\qquad A_n^f(x)\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu_2\quad(\star).\] Now choose \(f\in C(X)\) such that \(\int f\,d\mu_1\neq\int f\,d\mu_2\). If \(A=\{x\mid(*)\text{ holds}\}\) and \(B=\{x\mid(\star)\text{ holds}\}\), then \(\mu_1(A)=\mu_2(B)=1\).

Remark

One can generalize this to \(n\) ergodic measures by induction. All you need is a function \(f\in C(X)\) such that \(\{\int f\,d\mu_i\}_{i=1}^n\) is a sequence of distinct elements. Since linear functionals on a topological vector space are open maps, if \(\Lambda_i\) represents \(\int d\mu_i\), then \[E_{ij}:=\{f\mid\Lambda_i f\neq\Lambda_j f\}\] is open and dense in \(C(X)\). Thus \(\bigcap_{i,j}E_{ij}\) is nonempty, as \(C(X)\) is a Baire space. Therefore, if \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) were pictorially a convex hull of finitely many ergodic extreme points, then the state space \(X\) would have a finite decomposition into ergodic components.

The following theorem ensures that such a geometric decomposition of the space can always be done.

Theorem 21 — Extremal Ergodicity

The ergodic elements of \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) are precisely \(\mathcal E^T(X)\).

Proof. If \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\) is not ergodic, then there exists \(B\) such that \(0<\mu(B)<1\) and \(T^{-1}B=B\). Thus \(\mu(B)^{-1}\mu|_B\) and \(\mu(X\setminus B)^{-1}\mu|_{X\setminus B}\) are \(T\)-invariant, and \[\mu=\mu(B)\bigl(\mu(B)^{-1}\mu|_B\bigr) +\mu(X\setminus B)\bigl(\mu(X\setminus B)^{-1}\mu|_{X\setminus B}\bigr),\] a convex linear combination.

If \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\) is ergodic and \(\mu=s\nu_1+(1-s)\nu_2\), then, since \(s,1-s>0\), clearly \(\nu_1\ll\mu\) and \(\nu_2\ll\mu\). One of these would suffice. The Radon–Nikodym theorem tells you that there exists \(f\in L_\mu^1\) such that \(f=d\nu_1/d\mu\), implying \(\nu_1(A)=\int_Af\,d\mu\).

Here is the cheeky part of the proof. Set \(B:=\{x\mid f(x)<1\}\). Then \[\begin{aligned} \int_{B\cap T^{-1}B}f\,d\mu+\int_{B\setminus T^{-1}B}f\,d\mu &=\nu_1(B)=\nu_1(T^{-1}B)\\ &=\int_{B\cap T^{-1}B}f\,d\mu+\int_{T^{-1}B\setminus B}f\,d\mu, \end{aligned}\] so \(\int_{B\setminus T^{-1}B}f\,d\mu=\int_{T^{-1}B\setminus B}f\,d\mu\).

Also, \[\begin{aligned} \mu(T^{-1}B\setminus B) &=\mu(T^{-1}B)-\mu(T^{-1}B\cap B)\\ &=\mu(B)-\mu(T^{-1}B\cap B)=\mu(B\setminus T^{-1}B). \end{aligned}\] Now we further have \[\mu(B\setminus T^{-1}B) >\int_{B\setminus T^{-1}B}f\,d\mu =\int_{T^{-1}B\setminus B}f\,d\mu \geq\mu(T^{-1}B\setminus B).\] This implies \(\mu(B\mathbin\triangle T^{-1}B)=0\), so \(\mu(B)\in\{0,1\}\). If \(\mu(B)=1\), then \[1=\nu_1(X)=\int_Xf\,d\mu<\mu(B)=1,\] a contradiction. Hence \(\mu(B)=0\). Similarly, \(\mu(\{x\mid f(x)>1\})=0\), so \(f(x)=1\) almost everywhere. Thus \(\nu_1=\mu\), implying \(\mu\in\mathcal E^T(X)\): it is an extreme point.

The argument made in the remark above can be extended to a countable collection of elements in \(\mathcal E^T(X)\). In such cases, using the ergodic theorem, one can get an explicit decomposition of the state space. But a more interesting question is: what about the case when \(\mathcal E^T(X)\) is a continuum? How is one supposed to get down to the minimal dynamical nuts and bolts of a given measure-preserving topological dynamical system? In that case, Choquet’s representation theorem

comes in handy to yield ergodic components of the state space as infinitesimal components of an integral representation!

Theorem 22 — Ergodic Decomposition

Given a topological dynamical system \((X,T)\) and any \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\), there exists a unique probability measure \(\lambda\) on the Borel sets of \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) such that \[\lambda(\mathcal E^T(X))=1, \qquad \int_Xf\,d\mu=\int_{\mathcal E^T(X)}\left(\int_Xf\,d\nu\right)d\lambda(\nu) \quad\text{for all }f\in C(X).\] These correspond, respectively, to the finite expressions \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i=1\) and \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\nu_i\).

Remark

Notice also that the uniqueness of \(\lambda\) tells you that the decomposition is unique!

title: Unique Ergodicity and Equidistribution
html:
Let’s explore the interplay between equidistribution and ergodicity. Birkhoff’s theorem told us that, if a system is ergodic, then its orbits are all equidistributed. Now we are looking for a converse of this statement, and it turns out that the converse is pretty surprising indeed. Without any further delay, let’s reveal it.

Theorem 23 — Unique ergodicity

The convergence \[A_N^f(x):=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(T^nx)\longrightarrow C_f, \qquad f\in C(X),\] where \(C_f\) is independent of \(x\), is equivalent to \(\lvert\mathcal M^T(X)\rvert=1\).

How did that happen!

Proof.

\((\Downarrow)\) Choose some \(\delta_x\in\mathcal M(X)\). Then, by a theorem we proved in the previous post, \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\delta_{T^nx}\overset{*}{\longrightarrow}\mu,\] for there cannot be more than one accumulation point, as \(\lvert\mathcal M^T(X)\rvert=1\). Now, by the ergodic theorem, we have \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(T^nx)\longrightarrow\int_X f\,d\mu,\] independently of \(x\).

\((\Uparrow)\) Let \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\). As \(\mu\) is \(T\)-invariant, we have \(\int_X f(T^nx)\,d\mu=\int_X f\,d\mu\). By the dominated convergence theorem, \[\int_X f\,d\mu =\int_X\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(T^nx)\,d\mu =\int_X C_f\,d\mu=C_f.\] Thus \(\int_X f\,d\mu=C_f\) for all \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\), and hence \(\lvert\mathcal M^T(X)\rvert=1\).

Remark — 1

Notice that Choquet’s theorem implies that \(\lvert\mathcal M^T(X)\rvert=1\) if \(\lvert\mathcal E^T(X)\rvert=1\), for \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) consists of “convex linear combinations” of elements of \(\mathcal E^T(X)\).

Remark — 2

When \((X,T)\) is uniquely ergodic, the convergence in the theorem above is uniform. Otherwise, there exists \(x\), for a given \(\varepsilon\), such that \[\left|\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}g(T^nx)-C_g\right|\geq\varepsilon.\] Set \(\mu_N=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\delta_{T^nx}\). By weak-\(*\) compactness, we have \(\mu_{N(k)}\to\nu\), and therefore \(\left|\int_X g\,d\nu-C_g\right|\geq\varepsilon\). Now \(C_g=\int_X g\,d\mu\), where \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\), so \(\nu\ne\mu\). A contradiction!

Thus the convergence is independent of both \(x\) and \(n\); it is really well-distributed!

This therefore leads us to the right definition of equidistribution of a given sequence \((x_j)_j\). This can help us visually and mathematically understand ergodic orbits.

Definition 10 — Equidistribution

We say that \((x_n)_n\), with \(x_n\in X\), is equidistributed in \((X,T)\) if, for every \(f\in C(X)\), we have \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n f(x_j) =\int_X f(x)\,d\mu(x).\]

Remark

The discussion of unique ergodicity yields another startling duality between equidistribution and invariance of measures. It shows that the spaces \(X\) and \(\mathcal M(X)\) are intricately connected.

Definition 11 — Generic point

We say that \(x\in X\) is generic if either of two equivalent conditions holds:

(i)

Invariant measure in \(\mathcal M(X)\): \(\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{T^jx}\overset{*}{\longrightarrow}\mu\).

(ii)

Equidistribution in \(X\):

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}f(T^jx) \longrightarrow\int_X f\,d\mu \qquad\bigl(\forall f\in C(X)\bigr).\]

Let us see one easy consequence of the ergodic theorem before moving on to the probabilistic interpretation of equidistribution.

Proposition 24

If \(\mu\in\mathcal M^T(X)\) is ergodic, then almost every \(x\in X\) is generic.

Proof. By the Stone–Weierstrass theorem, \((C(X),\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty)\) is separable. Let

\((f_n)_n\) be dense in \(C(X)\). The reason we are going for a dense subset is that

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n f(T^nx) =\int_X f\,d\mu\qquad(\forall x\in X_f),\qquad\mu(X_f)=1.\] But \(X_f\) depends on \(f\); we now need to drop that dependence.

For each \(f_n\), one obtains a set \(X_{f_n}\), and \(\mu\bigl(\bigcap_nX_{f_n}\bigr)=1\). Set \(X'=\bigcap_nX_{f_n}\). By the ergodic theorem, for all \(x\in X'\) and \(i\geq1\), \[\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f_i(T^nx)\longrightarrow\int_X f_i\,d\mu.\]

As \((f_i)_i\) is dense in \((C(X),\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty)\), it is dense uniformly, and \[|f(x)-f_i(x)|<\varepsilon\qquad\forall i\geq N_0.\] Now, for a sufficiently large \(N\geq N_0\), given \(\varepsilon>0\), we have (with \(A_N^f\) denoting the average) \[\begin{align*} &\left|\int f\,d\mu-\limsup_{N\to\infty} \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(T^nx)\right| =\left|\int f\,d\mu-\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^f\right|\\ &\quad=\left|\int f\,d\mu-\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^f -\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^{f_i} +\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^{f_i} -\int f_i\,d\mu+\int f_i\,d\mu\right|\\ &\quad\leq\left|\int f\,d\mu-\int f_i\,d\mu\right| +\left|\limsup_{N\to\infty}(A_N^f-A_N^{f_i})\right| +\left|\int f_i\,d\mu-\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^{f_i}\right|\\ &\quad<\varepsilon. \end{align*}\] One can similarly estimate \(\liminf_{N\to\infty}A_N^f\) to obtain that, for all \(x\in X'\), \(\lim_{N\to\infty}A_N^f(x)=\int_X f\,d\mu\).

To see what equidistribution means probabilistically, one must go to \([0,1]\). There we have the following.

Lemma 25

Let \([0,1]\), equipped with Lebesgue measure, be our setting. If \((x_n)_{n\geq1}\) is equidistributed, then \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n \bigl|\{j:1\leq j\leq n,\ x_j\in[a,b]\}\bigr|=b-a.\]

In other words, equidistribution means being uniformly distributed over \([0,1]\). We have the same for ergodic orbits in the more general setting of a probability measure space, but those are special sequences regardless of how general the setting is: notice that \(\mathcal E^T(X)\) is merely the set of extremal points of \(\mathcal M^T(X)\).

Proof.

Let \(f^-\) and \(f^+\) be as shown in the figure. Note that \(f^-\leq\chi_{[a,b]}\leq f^+\), and one can arrange \(f^\pm\) so that \[\int_0^1(f^+-f^-)(x)\,dx\leq2\varepsilon.\]

Putting them together as we did in the proposition above, \[\begin{align*} b-a-2\varepsilon &\leq\int_0^1f^-\,dx \leq\liminf_{N\to\infty}A_N^{\chi_{[a,b]}} \leq\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^{\chi_{[a,b]}}\\ &\leq\int_0^1f^+\,dx\leq b-a+2\varepsilon. \end{align*}\] Thus \(\liminf_{N\to\infty}A_N^{\chi_{[a,b]}} =\limsup_{N\to\infty}A_N^{\chi_{[a,b]}}=b-a\).

Remark

Therefore, all equidistribution theorems can be consequences of ergodic theory, provided one finds the right transformation that is uniquely ergodic. For instance, rotation, namely \(P(x)=x+\alpha\) with \(\alpha\notin\mathbb Q\), is equidistributed in \([0,1]\), for \(R_\alpha\) is uniquely ergodic. There is a general theorem due to Weyl which talks about equidistribution of a degree-\(n\) polynomial \(P(n)\) where at least one coefficient is irrational.

Theorem 26 — Jewett–Krieger

\[\begin{gathered} \text{Ergodic system on a}\\ \text{Lebesgue space}\\ (X,\mathcal B,\mu,T) \end{gathered} \quad\cong\quad \begin{gathered} \text{Minimal uniquely ergodic}\\ \text{topological dynamical system} \end{gathered}\] Here minimal means that, for every \(x\), the orbit of \(x\) is dense in \(X\).

Note that measurable isomorphisms only preserve sizes of sets. If

our \((X,\mathcal B,\mu,T)\) were an ergodic topological dynamical system, then the isomorphism does not preserve any structure on \(\mathcal M^T(X)\), because, in the image, \(\lvert\mathcal M^T(X)\rvert=1\) regardless of what \(\mathcal M^T(X)\) is.

Thus invariance of measures is entirely a topological attribute of a system, not a measurable one!

We have dealt with one of the problems raised in Lecture 5, that of ergodic decomposition. In the next few lectures, let us deal with the problem of classifying systems up to measurable isomorphisms.
