Lemma 101 — Zsigmondy’s theorem

If \(a,b,n\) are positive integers with \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), then \(a^n-b^n\) has a prime factor dividing none of \(a^k-b^k\) for \(k<n\), with the exceptions \(2^6-1^6\), and \(n=2\) when \(a+b\) is a power of \(2\). If \(a>b\) and \(n\geq2\), then

\(a^n+b^n\) has a prime factor dividing none of \(a^k+b^k\) for \(k<n\), except \(2^3+1^3\).

Application: IMO shortlist (2000).

Find positive integer triples \((a,m,n)\) with \(a^m+1\mid(a+1)^n\). The obvious solution is \((2,3,n)\), since \(2^3+1\mid3^n\) for all \(n\). Prove this! For \((a,m)\ne(2,3)\), Zsigmondy’s theorem supplies a prime factor of \(a^m+1\) not dividing \(a+1\), so it does not divide \((a+1)^n\). Hence there are no other solutions. Quite quickly done. “Is it seriously an IMO-shortlisted problem?” is the usual reaction.

Solve the following using Zsigmondy.

Round 1: Fight. Japanese MO (2011).

Find all positive integer quintuples \((a,n,p,q,r)\) such that \(a^n-1=(a^p-1)(a^q-1)(a^r-1)\).

Round 2: Fight.

Prove Fermat’s last theorem, asserting that \(x^n+y^n=z^n\) has no solutions with \(xyz\ne0\). Take \(z\) to be prime!

Final round: Fight. Balkan MO (2009).

Solve \(5^x-3^y=z^2\) for \(x,y,z\in\mathbb N\).

You used calculus in that!

If \(a^n+n\) is a multiple of \(b^n+n\) for every positive integer \(n\), prove that \(a=b\), where \(a,b\in\mathbb N\). Suppose there exists such an \(n\) and seek \((a,b)\), with \(a\geq b\). Let \(f(a)=a^n+n\) and \(f(b)=b^n+n\), with \(f(a)=kf(b)\), \(k\in\mathbb N\). Then the notes differentiate: \[\frac{df(a)}{da}=\frac{d[kf(b)]}{db} \Longrightarrow na^{n-1}=nkb^{n-1} \Longrightarrow k=(a/b)^{n-1}.\] Also \(k=(a^n+n)/(b^n+n)=a^{n-1}/b^{n-1}\), so \(n=\dfrac{a^{n-1}b^{n-1}(a-b)}{a^{n-1}-b^{n-1}}\). A contradiction follows from Zsigmondy’s theorem!

We have proved a stronger case: “\(b^n+n\nmid a^n+n\) for \(a>b\), with the exception \(1^2+1\mid2^2+2\).” Can you guess where that exception came from?

Challenge: Kiran S. Kedlaya, Crux Mathematicorum.

For positive integers \(x,y,z\), prove that \((xy+1)(yz+1)(zx+1)\) is a perfect square if and only if \(xy+1\), \(yz+1\), and \(zx+1\) are each perfect squares. Soumik Ghosh communicated a solution that seems deceptively correct. Hats off to the ingenious use of infinite descent. Dangerous!

Call \((x,y,z)\) good if \((xy+1)(yz+1)(zx+1)\) is a perfect square. The claim is that every three-element subset of \((x,y,z,t)\) is good, where \[t=x+y+z+2xyz-2\sqrt{(xy+1)(yz+1)(zx+1)}.\] This \(t\) is a root of \[x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2-2(xy+yz+zx+xt+yt+zt)-4xyzt-4=0,\] which may be rewritten as \[(x+y-z-t)^2=4(xy+1)(zt+1),\quad (y+z-x-t)^2=4(yz+1)(xt+1),\quad (z+x-y-t)^2=4(zx+1)(yt+1).\] Wow! This is equivalent to a Ramanujan move. Multiply \(4(xy+1)(zt+1)\), \(4(yz+1)(xt+1)\), and \((xy+1)^2\), then divide by \((xy+1)(yz+1)(zx+1)\) to obtain that \((xy+1)(yt+1)(zt+1)\) is a perfect square. Similarly, \((yz+1)(yt+1)(zt+1)\) and \((xz+1)(xt+1)(zt+1)\) are perfect squares. Thus every three-element subset is good. Now, without loss of generality, let \(z\geq x,y\). Then \(z\geq t\), so replace \((z,y,x)\) by \((t,y,x)\). At every step the maximal element decreases, until eventually \(t=0\). It follows, by arguing correspondingly, that \(xy+1\), \(yz+1\), and \(zx+1\) are perfect squares. Quite dangerously done.

I recently created another problem for you!

Challenge.

For \(a_1,\ldots,a_n,x,y\in\mathbb N\), prove the following system has solutions if and only if \(x=y\):

\[a_1^x+\cdots+a_n^x=b^x,\qquad a_1^y+\cdots+a_n^y=b^y,\] where \(b\) is a natural number.

Calculus—oh, not again!

IMO (1997).

Solve \(a^{b^2}=b^a\) in positive integers. Let \(a\geq b\). The source takes \((a,b)=b\), so \(a=bk\). Then \(b^{b^2}k^{b^2}=b^{bk}\) and \(k^{b^2}=b^{bk-b^2}\). Put \(k=b^x\). This gives \[xb^2=b^{x+1}-b^2 \Longrightarrow b^2(x+1)=b^{x+1} \Longrightarrow x+1=b^{x-1}.\] Set \(y=x+1\). Then \(y=b^{y-2}\), \(k=b^{y-1}\), \(a=b^y\), and \(b=\sqrt[y-2]{y}\). The pairs \((b,y)\) are \((1,1),(3,3),(2,4)\). Since \(2^{y-2}-y\) is increasing, the difference grows exponentially. Thus the only pairs \((a,b)\) are \((1,1),(27,3),(16,2)\).

Number-theoretic inequalities

Here is a legendary problem due to Paul Erdős. Each positive integer \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) is less than \(1951\), and the least common multiple of any two exceeds \(1951\). Show \(1/a_1+\cdots+1/a_n<1+n/1951\). The solution is magical! The number of multiples of \(a_i\) in \(\{1,\ldots,1951\}\) is \(\lfloor1951/a_i\rfloor\), so \(\sum_i\lfloor1951/a_i\rfloor\leq1951\). Since \(x-1<\lfloor x\rfloor\), we obtain \(\sum_i(1951/a_i-1)<1951\), proving the claim.

Only Paul Erdős could pose these problems! Here is another.

Magical solution: Erdős–Straus problem.

Given \(3\mid n+1\), prove that there are integers \(x,y,z\) with \(4xyz=n(xy+yz+zx)\). Take \(x=n\), \(y=(n-2)/3+1\), and \(z=n(n+1)/3\). The source celebrates with “\((\text{Q.E.D.})^\infty\)!” Solve the problem when \(4\mid n+1\). Homework!

Let me show more problems with magical solutions. I hope you have understood what that means.

Problem 1.

Given \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z^+\) and primes \(p_1,\ldots,p_n,q\), show that, for every \(\alpha\), there exists an \(n\) such that \(p_1^\alpha+p_2^\alpha+\cdots+p_n^\alpha=q^\beta\).

Problem 2.

Find infinitely many families of solutions in nine distinct integers \(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z_1,z_2,z_3\) of \[(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)+(y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2)=z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2,\] even if no three of the numbers form a Pythagorean triple. I posed these two problems long ago, and both have magical solutions. I will not spoil the eagerness and curiosity by revealing them now; perhaps in a later volume. Try them!
excerptHtml: Find the largest positive integer \(n\) such that \(n+10\mid n^3+100\). Since \(n+10\equiv0\pmod{n+10}\), we have \(n\equiv-10\pmod{n+10}\). Thus \(n^3+100\equiv-900\equiv0\pmod{n+10}\), so \(n+10\mid900\). The maximum value is \(n=890\).

title: Standard Inequalities and Ingenious Cauchy–Schwarz Applications
html:
Challenge

Let \(a,b,c>0\) satisfy \(0<\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c\leq3\sqrt2\). Establish \[\frac{a^2+2a-2}{a\sqrt b}+\frac{b^2+2b-2}{b\sqrt c} +\frac{c^2+2c-2}{c\sqrt a}\leq3\sqrt2+\ln8.\] The second box in the source records \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\dfrac{a^2+2a-2}{a\sqrt b}<6\sqrt2\).

Lemma 71 — Arithmetic–geometric mean inequality

For all positive reals \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\), \[\frac{a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n}{n}\geq\sqrt[n]{a_1a_2\cdots a_n},\] with equality if \(a_1=a_2=\cdots=a_n\).

\((1,0,0,\ldots,0)\succ(1/n,1/n,\ldots,1/n)\): direct Muirhead! Alternatively, consider the constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=S\) and employ Lagrange’s method to prove it.

Application: Nesbitt’s inequality.

\[\frac a{b+c}+\frac b{c+a}+\frac c{a+b}\geq\frac32.\] Set \[S=\frac a{b+c}+\frac b{c+a}+\frac c{a+b},\quad M=\frac b{b+c}+\frac c{c+a}+\frac a{a+b},\quad N=\frac c{b+c}+\frac a{c+a}+\frac b{a+b}.\] We are aware that \(M+N=3\). By AM–GM, \[M+S=\frac{a+b}{b+c}+\frac{b+c}{c+a}+\frac{c+a}{a+b}\geq3,\qquad N+S=\frac{a+c}{b+c}+\frac{a+b}{c+a}+\frac{b+c}{a+b}\geq3.\] Thus \(M+N+2S\geq6\), so \(2S\geq3\) and \(S\geq3/2\). Q.E.D.!

Lemma 72 — Weighted AM–GM inequality

\[\frac{a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n}{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n} \geq\sqrt[x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n]{a_1^{x_1}a_2^{x_2}\cdots a_n^{x_n}}.\]

Application: RMO (1989).

Let \(a,b,c\) be the side lengths of a triangle. Prove that \[(a+b-c)^a(b+c-a)^b(c+a-b)^c\leq a^ab^bc^c.\] Indeed, \[\begin{aligned} \left(\frac{a+b-c}{a}\right)^a \left(\frac{b+c-a}{b}\right)^b \left(\frac{c+a-b}{c}\right)^c &\leq\left(\frac{a\frac{a+b-c}{a}+b\frac{b+c-a}{b}+c\frac{c+a-b}{c}}{a+b+c}\right)^{a+b+c}\\ &=\left(\frac{2(a+b+c)-(a+b+c)}{a+b+c}\right)^{a+b+c} =\left(\frac{a+b+c}{a+b+c}\right)^{a+b+c}=1. \end{aligned}\] Q.E.D.

An ingenious application of AM–GM: AMTI Junior, finals (2014).

\[\frac{x^4}{(y-1)^2}+\frac{y^4}{(z-1)^2}+\frac{z^4}{(x-1)^2}\geq48.\] We have \(x^2/(x-1)\geq4\Longleftrightarrow(x-2)^2\geq0\). Hence \[\frac13\left(\frac{x^4}{(y-1)^2}+\frac{y^4}{(z-1)^2}+\frac{z^4}{(x-1)^2}\right) \geq\sqrt[3]{\left(\frac{x^2}{x-1}\right)^2 \left(\frac{y^2}{y-1}\right)^2\left(\frac{z^2}{z-1}\right)^2} =\sqrt[3]{4^2\cdot4^2\cdot4^2}.\] Therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}x^4/(y^2-2y+1)\geq3\cdot4^2=48\). Q.E.D.! This solution was communicated to me by Vedant. “Thanks to him!”

Standard inequalities

There are some standard inequalities that one can take down as standard lemmas.

Lemma 73 — Standard inequalities

1.

\((x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\geq8xyz\).

2.

\(x^2+y^2+z^2\geq xy+yz+zx\).

3.

\(xy+yz+zx\geq\sqrt{3xyz(x+y+z)}\). Important.

4.

\(x^3+y^3+z^3+5xyz\geq(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\).

5.

\(x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2\geq xyz(x+y+z)\). Important.

6.

\(xy^3+yz^3+zx^3\geq xyz(x+y+z)\).

Also important: \(x^2+y^2+z^2\geq x+y+z\) when \(xyz=1\).

Problems.
1.

\(x^2/y^2+y^2/z^2+z^2/x^2\geq x/y+y/z+z/x\) (SAT, 2000).

2.

Find all real triples \((x,y,z)\) satisfying \[3(x^2+y^2+z^2)=1,\qquad x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2=xyz(x+y+z)^3\] (AMTI Inter, final, 2014).

3.

\((1+a)^8+(1+b)^8\geq128ab(a+b)^2\) (IMOTC, 2014).

4.

\(R/r\geq b/c+c/b\) (favourite problem at CSL!).

I will present the solution to problem 3 (IMOTC, 2014): \[(1+a)^8+(1+b)^8\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}128ab(a+b)^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left(\frac{1+a}{2}\right)^8+\left(\frac{1+b}{2}\right)^8 \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}\frac{ab(a+b)^2}{2}.\] Now \[\left(\frac{1+a}{2}\right)^8+\left(\frac{1+b}{2}\right)^8 \geq a^4+b^4\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}\frac{ab(a+b)^2}{2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{a^4+b^4}{2}\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}ab\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2.\] Since \((a^2+b^2)/2\geq((a+b)/2)^2\) and \(ab\leq(a^2+b^2)/2\), \[\left(\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}\right)^2\geq ab\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2, \qquad \frac{a^4+b^4}{2}\geq\left(\frac{a^2+b^2}{2}\right)^2 \geq ab\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2.\] The last step uses RMS \(\geq\) AM. W\(^5\); Q.E.D.

We talked about the power-mean inequality a few pages ago, but let us still declare it a “lemma” in public.

Lemma 74 — Power-mean inequality

\[\left(\frac{a_1^m+a_2^m+\cdots+a_n^m}{n}\right)^{1/m} \geq\left(\frac{a_1^n+a_2^n+\cdots+a_n^n}{n}\right)^{1/n} \qquad\text{if }m\geq n.\]

This is the power-mean inequality. We already dealt with one special case, the “square-root heuristic”; here is another: \[\sqrt{\frac{a_1^2+a_2^2+\cdots+a_n^2}{n}}\geq\frac{a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n}{n}.\] RMS (root mean square) \(\geq\) AM (arithmetic mean). We have already seen an application of the previous lemma! Let us look at another lemma and its application.

Lemma 75 — A sum and its reciprocal sum

If \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\) are positive reals, then \[(a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n)\left(\frac1{a_1}+\frac1{a_2}+\cdots+\frac1{a_n}\right)\geq n^2.\]

To prove it, use AM \(\geq\) HM.

An ingenious application, posed by P. K. Hung.

Let \(a,b,c,d\) be positive real numbers. Prove that \[\left(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c+\frac1d\right)^2 \geq\frac1{a^2}+\frac4{a^2+b^2}+\frac9{a^2+b^2+c^2} +\frac{16}{a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2}.\] We have \[\frac1{a^2}\geq\frac1{a^2},\qquad \frac2{ab}\geq\frac4{a^2+b^2},\qquad \frac2{ac}+\frac2{bc}\geq\frac8{ac+bc},\qquad \frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\geq\frac4{b^2+c^2},\] and \[\frac2{ad}+\frac2{bd}+\frac2{cd} \geq\frac{18}{ad+bd+cd}\geq\frac{16}{a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2}.\]

Also, \[\frac8{bc+ac}\geq\frac8{a^2+b^2+c^2},\qquad \frac4{b^2+c^2}\geq\frac1{b^2+c^2+a^2}.\] Now add the results to finish the proof.

Corollary 76 — To the reciprocal-sum lemma

\[\frac x{a_1}+\frac x{a_2}+\cdots+\frac x{a_n} \geq\frac{xn^2}{a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_n}.\] This is a form of the modern Cauchy inequality.

In fact, P. K. Hung thought of a generalization and conjectured that \[\left(\frac1{a_1}+\frac1{a_2}+\cdots+\frac1{a_n}\right)^2 \geq\frac1{a_1^2}+\frac4{a_1^2+a_2^2}+\cdots+ \frac{n^2}{a_1^2+a_2^2+\cdots+a_n^2}.\]

Q.E.D.s using Cauchy–Schwarz

Iran (1998).

Prove that if \(x,y,z>0\) satisfy \(1/x+1/y+1/z=2\), then \[\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\leq\sqrt{x+y+z}.\] If you shout “square-root heuristics” at this, then pat yourself: that is an immeasurably wrong path to take! You have no reason to believe me; try it for yourself. In fact, if we make the following adjustment, there is some hope: \[\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1} &=\sqrt a\sqrt{\frac{x-1}{a}}+\sqrt b\sqrt{\frac{y-1}{b}}+\sqrt c\sqrt{\frac{z-1}{c}}\\ &\leq\sqrt{(a+b+c)\left(\frac{x-1}{a}+\frac{y-1}{b}+\frac{z-1}{c}\right)}. \end{aligned}\] Now comes the crucial move: take \(a=x\), \(b=y\), \(c=z\). Q.E.D.!

Kvant: Vasile Cîrtoaje.

Prove that for any real numbers \(a,b,c,x,y,z\), \[ax+by+cz+\sqrt{(a^2+b^2+c^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2)} \geq\frac23(a+b+c)(x+y+z).\] The usual temptation is to apply Cauchy to the big square-root term, but that is just a wild-goose chase. Rather, as usual, let us do something unusual. \[\begin{aligned} \frac23(a+b+c)(x+y+z)-(ax+by+cz) &=\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}a\left(\frac{2y+2z-x}{3}\right)\\ &\leq\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\, \sqrt{\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\left(\frac{2y+2z-x}{3}\right)^2}. \end{aligned}\] You know what? We have thus reached an unusual fact. Look below! \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\left(\frac{2x+2y-z}{3}\right)^2=\sum x^2.\] Wow! A.T.: always true. Q.E.D.!

A problem that took Titu Andreescu several weeks to resolve.

For positive reals \(x,y,z,a,b,c\) such that \(xy+yz+zx=3\), prove that \[\frac a{b+c}(y+z)+\frac b{c+a}(z+x)+\frac c{a+b}(x+y)\geq3.\] It is sufficient to establish

\[\frac a{b+c}(y+z)+\frac b{c+a}(z+x)+\frac c{a+b}(x+y) \geq\sqrt{3(xy+yz+zx)}.\] Now we may assume that \(x+y+z=1\). How? Our inequality takes the form \[\frac a{b+c}+\frac b{c+a}+\frac c{a+b} \geq\sqrt{3(xy+yz+zx)}+\frac a{b+c}x+\frac b{c+a}y+\frac c{a+b}z.\] By Cauchy, \[\frac a{b+c}x+\frac b{c+a}y+\frac c{a+b}z \leq\sqrt{\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\left(\frac a{b+c}\right)^2\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}x^2}.\] We must now prove \[\sqrt{\sum\left(\frac a{b+c}\right)^2\sum x^2} +\sqrt{3(xy+yz+zx)}\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\leq}}\sum\frac a{b+c}.\] Since \(\sqrt{12ABC}\leq(3B+4AC)/2\), we get \[\begin{aligned} \sqrt{12ABC}+AB+3C&\leq\frac{3B}{2}+2AC+AB+3C,\\ (\sqrt{AB}+\sqrt{3C})^2&\leq\frac32B+2AC+AB+3C =\left(\frac32+A\right)(B+2C). \end{aligned}\] Put \(A=\sum(a/(b+c))^2\), \(B=\sum x^2\), and \(C=\sum xy\). Then \[\sqrt{\sum\left(\frac a{b+c}\right)^2\sum x^2}+\sqrt{3(xy+yz+zx)} \leq\sqrt{\left(\frac32+\sum\left(\frac a{b+c}\right)^2\right) \left(\sum x^2+2\sum xy\right)}.\] Thus it remains to prove \[\sqrt{\frac32+\sum\left(\frac a{b+c}\right)^2} \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\leq}}\sum\frac a{b+c} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac32+\sum\left(\frac a{b+c}\right)^2 \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\leq}}\left(\sum\frac a{b+c}\right)^2.\] Expanding the right-hand side reduces this to \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{ab}{(b+c)(c+a)}\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}\frac34.\] In full, \[\frac{ab}{(b+c)(c+a)}+\frac{bc}{(c+a)(a+b)}+\frac{ca}{(a+b)(b+c)} \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}\frac34 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)+ca(a+c)}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)} \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}\frac34.\] Therefore we need \[4\sum ab(a+b)\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}3\sum ab(a+b)+6abc \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum ab(a+b)\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}6abc,\] and hence \((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\geq9abc\). True! W\(^5\); Q.E.D.

“Did you notice that if \(x+y+z=1\), then \((x+y+z)^2=1\)? Thus \(x^2+y^2+z^2+2(xy+yz+zx)=1\), so \(x^2+y^2+z^2=-5\), but \(\sum x^2>0\). Therefore we conclude that Titu lost his mind!” Or…

A close inspection reveals the genius in that move. We have \(xy+yz+zx=3\). Let \(x+y+z=k\), so \(x/k+y/k+z/k=1\). Take \(X=x/k\), \(Y=y/k\), and \(Z=z/k\). We wanted to prove \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac a{b+c}(y+z)\geq\sqrt{3(xy+yz+zx)}\). Divide by \(k\) to obtain \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac a{b+c}\left(\frac yk+\frac zk\right) \geq\sqrt{\frac{3(xy+yz+zx)}{k^2}} =\sqrt{3\left(\frac xk\frac yk+\frac yk\frac zk+\frac zk\frac xk\right)}.\] That is, \[\frac a{b+c}(Y+Z)+\frac b{c+a}(Z+X)+\frac c{a+b}(X+Y) \geq\sqrt{3(XY+YZ+ZX)}.\] We have \(X+Y+Z=1\). It does not matter whether you use capital or small letters: finally, we intend to eliminate them all. So his move is perfectly justified! Nowhere in his proof does he use both \(x+y+z=1\) and \(xy+yz+zx=3\). Thus our first contradictory argument is invalid. “So sorry, Titu!”

Usefulness of square-root heuristics (Lemma 66 in the manuscript): China (1982).

Let \(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\) be positive numbers such that \(a_1+\cdots+a_n=1\). Prove that \[\frac{a_1}{\sqrt{1-a_1}}+\cdots+\frac{a_n}{\sqrt{1-a_n}} \geq\frac1{\sqrt{n-1}}(\sqrt{a_1}+\cdots+\sqrt{a_n}).\] By square-root heuristics, \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{a_i}\leq\sqrt{n\sum a_i}=\sqrt n, \qquad\frac1{\sqrt{n-1}}\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{a_i}\leq\sqrt{\frac n{n-1}}.\] We seek \(\sum a_i/\sqrt{1-a_i}\geq\sqrt{n/(n-1)}\). Chebyshev’s inequality gives \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{a_i}{\sqrt{1-a_i}} \geq\frac1n\sum a_i\sum\frac1{\sqrt{1-a_i}} =\frac1n\sum\frac1{\sqrt{1-a_i}}.\] Therefore it is sufficient to prove \(\frac1n\sum1/\sqrt{1-a_i}\geq\sqrt{n/(n-1)}\). By Cauchy–Schwarz, \[\sum\frac1{\sqrt{1-a_i}}\geq\frac{n^2}{\sum\sqrt{1-a_i}} \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}\frac{n\sqrt n}{\sqrt{n-1}}.\] The latter reduces to \(\sqrt{n(n-1)}\geq\sum\sqrt{1-a_i}\). By square-root heuristics, \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{1-a_i}\leq\sqrt{n\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1-a_i)}=\sqrt{n(n-1)}.\] W\(^5\). Q.E.D.

What an amazing argument (WAAA!!!).

For \(x,y,z\in\mathbb R\), \[x^2+y^2+z^2\geq x\sqrt{y^2+z^2}+y\sqrt{x^2+z^2}.\] Indeed, AM \(\geq\) GM gives \[\begin{aligned} x^2+y^2+z^2&=x^2+\left(\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\right)^2 \geq2x\sqrt{y^2+z^2}, &&\text{I},\\ x^2+y^2+z^2&=y^2+\left(\sqrt{x^2+z^2}\right)^2 \geq2y\sqrt{x^2+z^2}, &&\text{II}. \end{aligned}\] If \(x\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\geq y\sqrt{x^2+z^2}\), substitute in I and the result follows. But that inequality need not hold: if \(y\sqrt{x^2+z^2}\geq x\sqrt{y^2+z^2}\), substitute in II. Aha! WAAA. Conclusion follows…

Vedant and I created the following problem. Define \(x_k=(a^k+b^k+c^k)/3\), where \(a,b,c>0\). Given \(abc\geq3\sqrt3\), prove that \[x_1^6\left(\frac{x_1^2-x_1+1}{x_1^2+1}\right) +x_2^3\left(\frac{x_2^2-x_2+1}{x_2^2+1}\right) +x_3^2\left(\frac{x_3^2-x_3+1}{x_3^2+1}\right)>\frac32.\] The problem is really nice from an application point of view. Take it as a challenge from my side!

I recently made an inequality that is really awesome. Take this as another challenge!

Mission impossible.

Define \(x_k=a^k+b^k+c^k\) for positive \(a,b,c\). Given \(abc\geq e/\pi\), prove that \(x_2^3+x_3^2+x_6\geq10^4/1999\). Dangerous stuff. Oops, a little misprint: the inequality is strict. Can you find why equality cannot be achieved? Anyway, it is very difficult. It is beautiful because my date of birth is 10-4-1999; also, \(abc\geq e/\pi\) has nothing to do with \(e\), \(\pi\), or any of their high-tech properties. Just chill!

Vedant had another history period today, and guess what? That crazy boy created another problem! Given \(2a^2+4b^3+8c^4=1\) and \(a,b,c>0\), prove \[\frac{2+64a^4c^4+2a^4}{a^4+1} +\frac{1+32b^8+b^4}{1+b^4}\leq\frac{10}{3}.\] He did not stop there; he created another classical inequality. This one is obvious! Let \(A,B,C\in[0,\pi/2)\) satisfy \(\tan^2A+\tan^2B+\tan^2C=9\). If \(A,B,C\) are the angles of a triangle, prove that it is equilateral. This is too obvious, so add a restriction: use only RMS \(\geq\) AM \(\geq\) HM.

It is time to reveal another secret: a lemma giving a solution in two lines! Leave it for a moment and try these two challenges created by me.

Mission impossible.
1.

Given \(x,y,z\in[0,1]\) with \(x+y+z=2\), prove \(\sqrt{(1-x)/x}+\sqrt{(1-y)/y}+\sqrt{(1-z)/z}>\sqrt3\).

2.

Given positive \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) with sum \(n\), prove \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\dfrac{a_i^2}{a_i^4+1}>\dfrac{n}{n^3+1}\).

The first is not difficult compared with the magical second one!

Clever AM–GM: AMTI inter-final.

Let \(a,b,c,d>0\) satisfy \(\dfrac1{1+a^4}+\dfrac1{1+b^4}+\dfrac1{1+c^4}+\dfrac1{1+d^4}=1\). Prove \(abcd\geq3\).

Solution 1, due to Pranjal Warade.

\[\frac1{1+a^4}+\frac1{1+b^4}+\frac1{1+c^4} =1-\frac1{1+d^4}=\frac{d^4}{1+d^4} \geq3\sqrt[3]{\frac1{(1+a^4)(1+b^4)(1+c^4)}}.\] Obtain analogous inequalities for \(a,b,c\) and multiply them to get \((abcd)^4\geq3^4\), hence \(abcd\geq3\).

Solution 2, due to the author.

Put \(A=1/(1+a^4)\), \(B=1/(1+b^4)\), \(C=1/(1+c^4)\), \(D=1/(1+d^4)\). Then \(a^4=(1-A)/A\), and similarly for the others. Using \(A+B+C+D=1\), \[\begin{align*} \frac{1-A}{A}\frac{1-B}{B}\frac{1-C}{C}\frac{1-D}{D} &=\frac{B+C+D}{A}\frac{A+C+D}{B}\frac{A+B+D}{C}\frac{A+B+C}{D}\\ &\geq\frac{3(BCD)^{1/3}\,3(ACD)^{1/3}\,3(ABD)^{1/3}\,3(ABC)^{1/3}}{ABCD} =3^4. \end{align*}\] Thus \(abcd\geq3\).

Right or wrong: who cares!

For positive \(a,b,c\), prove \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(a^4+b^2)/(c^3+a^2b)\geq3\). First claim that the minimum of the left-hand side is \(k\). Now \(\max(k)\) is the minimum of the left-hand side, so let us compute \(\max(k)\): \[\begin{align*} \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{a^4+b^2}{c^3+a^2b} &\geq\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{2a^2b}{c^3+a^2b} =\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac1{c^3/(2a^2b)+1/2}\\ &\geq\frac{18/2}{\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}c^3/(2a^2b)+3/2}\geq k. \end{align*}\] Hence \(18/k-3\geq\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}c^3/(a^2b)\geq3\), so \(k\leq3\) and \(\max(k)=3\). Therefore the required sum is at least \(3\), with equality if and only if \(a=b=c=1\). Was that correct!

An inequality from the constraint.

For real \(a,b,c\) satisfying \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}ab/c^2=3\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}1/a^2=3\), prove \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}a^2/(b^2c^2)\geq11/8\). First focus on the cleavage of the constraint! \[\begin{align*} \sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{ab}{c^2}=3 &\Longrightarrow\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(ab)^3-3(abc)^2=0\\ &\Longrightarrow\frac12\left(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}ab\right) \left(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(ab-bc)^2\right)=0\\ &\Longrightarrow\frac{a^3b^3c^3}2 \left(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac1a\right) \left(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\left(\frac1a-\frac1b\right)^2\right)=0. \end{align*}\] We are mature enough to see that \(a,b,c\) are distinct (not necessarily pairwise!), so \(\sum1/a=0\). This also follows from \(\det\begin{pmatrix}bc&ca&ab\\ca&ab&bc\\ab&bc&ca\end{pmatrix}=0\). We also have \(\sum1/a^2=1\). Put \(x=1/a\), \(y=1/b\), \(z=1/c\). Let us do some childish computations. \(x^2=y^2+z^2+2yz\) implies \(y^2+z^2+yz=1/2\geq3yz\), so \(y^2z^2\leq1/36\). Also \(2x^2=1+2yz\leq1+1/3\), whence \(x^2\leq2/3\) and \(x^2y^2z^2\leq1/54\). Since \((\sum x)^2=\sum x^2+2\sum xy\), we have \(\sum xy=-1/2\). Moreover, \[\sum x^2y^2=(\sum xy)^2-2xyz\sum x=(\sum xy)^2=\frac14.\] We further peep to note that \((\sum x^2y^2)^2=\sum x^4y^4+2x^2y^2z^2\sum x^2 =\sum x^4y^4+2x^2y^2z^2\). Hence \((1/16-\sum x^4y^4)/2=(xyz)^2\leq1/54\), giving \(\sum x^4y^4\geq11/(16\cdot27)\).

Now \(a^2b^2c^2\geq54\) and \(\sum1/(a^4b^4)\geq11/(16\cdot27)\), so \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{a^2b^2c^2}{a^4b^4} \geq\frac{11\cdot54}{16\cdot27} \Longrightarrow\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{a^2}{b^2c^2}\geq\frac{11}8.\] That is what I am talking about! Q.E.D.!
excerptHtml: Let \(a,b,c>0\) satisfy \(0<\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c\leq3\sqrt2\). Establish \[\frac{a^2+2a-2}{a\sqrt b}+\frac{b^2+2b-2}{b\sqrt c} +\frac{c^2+2c-2}{c\sqrt a}\leq3\sqrt2+\ln8.\] The second box in the source records \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\dfrac{a^2+2a-2}{a\sqrt b}<6\sqrt2\).

title: An Inequality Toolkit: Jensen, Muirhead, and Schur
html:
Prove that \(\dfrac a{1+bc}+\dfrac b{1+ca}+\dfrac c{1+ab}\leq2\) if \(0\leq a,b,c\leq1\). Without loss of generality, let \(a\geq b\geq c\). Since \((1-a)(1-b)\geq0\), we have \(1+ab\geq a+b\), so \(1+2ab\geq a+b\).

Now \(a+b+c\leq1+1+2ab=2(1+ab)\), and hence \[\frac a{1+bc}+\frac b{1+ca}+\frac c{1+ab} \leq\frac a{1+ab}+\frac b{1+ab}+\frac c{1+ab}\leq2.\]

Lemma 15 — Cauchy’s inequality application

\(\dfrac{x^4}{(y-1)^2}+\dfrac{y^4}{(z-1)^2}+\dfrac{z^4}{(x-1)^2}\geq48\).

Cauchy’s inequality reduces the desired assertion to \[\left(\frac{x^2}{y-1}+\frac{y^2}{z-1}+\frac{z^2}{x-1}\right)^2\geq144, \quad\text{and then to}\quad \frac{x^2}{y-1}+\frac{y^2}{z-1}+\frac{z^2}{x-1}\geq12.\] It remains to show \(\dfrac{(x+y+z)^2}{x+y+z-3}\geq12\). Writing \(a=x+y+z\), this becomes \(a^2\geq12a-36\), or \((a-6)^2\geq0\).

Lemma 22 — Catalan’s identity

\(1-\frac12+\frac13-\frac14+\cdots+\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n} =\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{n+k}\).

Application.

Prove that \[\frac1{n+1}\left(1+\frac13+\frac15+\cdots+\frac1{2n-1}\right) >\frac1n\left(\frac12+\frac14+\cdots+\frac1{2n}\right).\] Multiplying through, the desired inequality becomes \[1+\frac13+\cdots+\frac1{2n-1} >\left(1+\frac1n\right)\left(\frac12+\frac14+\cdots+\frac1{2n}\right),\] or \[1-\frac12+\frac13-\frac14+\cdots+\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n} >\frac1{2n}+\frac1{4n}+\frac1{6n}+\cdots+\frac1{2n^2}.\] By the identity, it is enough to compare \(\frac1{n+1}+\cdots+\frac1{2n}\) with \(\frac1{2n}+\frac1{4n}+\cdots+\frac1{2n^2}\). Add the inequalities \(\frac1{2n}\geq\frac1{2n}\), \(\frac1{2n-1}>\frac1{4n}\), \(\ldots\), \(\frac1{n+1}>\frac1{2n^2}\) to finish.

Lemma 23 — Homogenization

Homogenization is a useful technique for solving problems: apply the technique of “jugaad” to make the degrees the same.

Application.

Let \(a,b,c>0\) and \(abc=1\). Prove that \(a+b+c\leq a^2+b^2+c^2\).

There are expressions of three different degrees, \(3\), \(2\), and \(1\). To homogenize the inequality, multiply by \(\sqrt[3]{abc}\): \[\sqrt[3]{abc}(a+b+c)\leq a^2+b^2+c^2, \quad\text{or}\quad a^{4/3}b^{1/3}c^{1/3}+a^{1/3}b^{4/3}c^{1/3}+a^{1/3}b^{1/3}c^{4/3} \leq a^2+b^2+c^2.\] Since \((4/3,1/3,1/3)\prec(2,0,0)\), the notes invoke Muirhead’s theorem to obtain \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}a^{4/3}b^{1/3}c^{1/3}\leq\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}a^2\).

Lemma 24 — Second-derivative test

The best test for convexity or concavity is the second-derivative test: if \(f''(x)\geq0\), then \(f\) is convex; otherwise \(f\) is concave.

This technique, combined with Jensen’s inequality or a maxima-minima argument, yields many beautiful and elegant solutions.

Lemma 25 — Jensen’s inequality

Let \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) be convex. For any \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in I\) and nonnegative reals \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n\), \[\omega_1f(x_1)+\cdots+\omega_nf(x_n) \geq\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\omega_i\right) f\left(\frac{\sum_i\omega_ix_i}{\sum_i\omega_i}\right).\] If \(f\) is concave, reverse the sign.

Application: IMO 1995, problem 2.

If \(a,b,c>0\) and \(abc=1\), prove that \[\frac1{a^3(b+c)}+\frac1{b^3(c+a)}+\frac1{c^3(a+b)}\geq\frac32.\]

Substitute \(x=1/a\), \(y=1/b\), \(z=1/c\). For \(f(x)=1/x\), we have \(f''(x)=2/x^3>0\), so \(f\) is convex. Now Jensen’s inequality gives \[\begin{align*} \frac1{a^3(b+c)}+\frac1{b^3(c+a)}+\frac1{c^3(a+b)} &=\frac{x^2}{y+z}+\frac{y^2}{z+x}+\frac{z^2}{x+y}\\ &=xf\left(\frac{y+z}{x}\right)+yf\left(\frac{z+x}{y}\right)+zf\left(\frac{x+y}{z}\right)\\ &\geq(x+y+z)f\left(\frac{(y+z)+(z+x)+(x+y)}{x+y+z}\right)\\ &=\frac{x+y+z}{2}\geq\frac{3\sqrt[3]{xyz}}2 =\frac{3\sqrt[3]{1/(abc)}}2=\frac32. \end{align*}\]

Lemma 26 — Muirhead and majorization

Muirhead’s theorem and majorization techniques are analogues of each other. If \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\succ(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\), then for positive \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \[\sum_{\mathrm{sym}}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n} \geq\sum_{\mathrm{sym}}x_1^{b_1}\cdots x_n^{b_n}.\] For majorization, let \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) be convex and suppose \((x_n)\succ(y_n)\). Then \(\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\geq\sum_{i=1}^n f(y_i)\) (Karamata’s inequality).

Warning: Like Jensen’s, do not flip the sign if \(f\) is concave!

Let me show some beautiful applications of these ideas.

Prove that, for positive reals \(a,b,c\), \((a^2b+b^2c+c^2a)(ab^2+bc^2+ca^2)\geq9a^2b^2c^2\). Let us expand this “dumbass” to obtain another “dumbass”: \[\begin{align*} (a^2b+b^2c+c^2a)(ab^2+bc^2+ca^2) ={}&a^3b^3+b^3c^3+c^3a^3+3a^2b^2c^2\\ &+a^4bc+ab^4c+abc^4. \end{align*}\] Notice \((3,3,0)\succ(2,2,2)\) and \((4,1,1)\succ(2,2,2)\). Thus Muirhead gives \[\sum_{\mathrm{sym}}a^3b^3c^0\geq\sum_{\mathrm{sym}}a^2b^2c^2, \qquad \sum_{\mathrm{sym}}a^4bc^0\geq\sum_{\mathrm{sym}}a^2b^2c^2.\] The conclusion follows.

Lemma 53 — Sum-of-squares strategy

If none of the standard techniques proves an inequality, try expressing it as a sum of squares greater than or equal to zero.

Application: V. Cîrtoaje.

For real \(a,b,c\), prove \((a^2+b^2+c^2)^2\geq3(a^3b+b^3c+c^3a)\). The solution is like magic! Have a look.

\[(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2-3(a^3b+b^3c+c^3a) =\frac12\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(a^2-2ab+bc-c^2+ca)^2\geq0.\] The source celebrates this with “\((\text{Q.E.D.})^\infty\).”

Lemma 60 — Schur’s inequality

Define \(T(a_1,\ldots,a_n)=\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}\). For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) and \(\beta>0\), the following inequalities hold: \[\begin{align*} T(\alpha+2\beta,0,0)+T(\alpha,\beta,\beta)&\geq2T(\alpha+\beta,0,0),&&\text{first form},\\ T(\alpha+\beta,\alpha+\beta,0)+T(2\alpha,\beta,\beta)&\geq2T(\alpha+\beta,\beta,\alpha),&&\text{second form}. \end{align*}\]

Important.

Applications.

Prove that \(a^4+b^4+c^4+a^2bc+b^2ca+c^2ab\geq2(a^3b+b^3c+c^3a)\). First realize that standard Muirhead fails; with Schur, the solution is two lines: \[T(2+2\cdot1,0,0)+T(2,1,1)\geq2T(3,0,0),\] which follows by setting \(\alpha=2\), \(\beta=1\).

Prove \(3(x^2y+y^2z+z^2x)(xy^2+yz^2+zx^2)\geq xyz(x+y+z)^3\). First try all the nonsense tricks and conclude that the problem is impenetrable. Then gather courage to expand that big bull, obtaining \[2T(4,1,1)+3T(3,3,0)+T(2,2,2)\geq6T(3,2,1).\] We have \[\begin{align*} [3,3,0]+[2,2,2]&\geq2[3,2,1],&&\text{I},\\ 2[4,1,1]&\geq2[3,2,1],&&\text{II},\\ 2[3,3,0]&\geq2[3,2,1],&&\text{III}. \end{align*}\] I follows from Schur’s second form with \(\alpha=2\), \(\beta=1\). Add I, II, and III to finish.

There are true villains on the IMO jury who pose problems like this one. Prove \[x^4+y^4+z^4+3(x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2) \geq2\bigl(x^3(y+z)+y^3(z+x)+z^3(x+y)\bigr).\] It is homogeneous and symmetric, but none of the standard techniques works. Recall Lemma 53, where we learned that magical spell. Write \([4,0,0]+3[2,2,0]\geq4[3,1,0]\). Bring everything to the left and rearrange to obtain \((x-y)^4+(y-z)^4+(z-x)^4\geq0\).

Lemma 61 — Square-root heuristic: Stanley Rabinowitz

If \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}f(x)\) has three terms, then \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{f(x)}\leq\sqrt{3\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}f(x)}\).

Use the power-mean inequality: if \(m\leq n\), then \[\left(\frac{a^m+b^m+c^m}{3}\right)^{1/m} \leq\left(\frac{a^n+b^n+c^n}{3}\right)^{1/n}.\] Set \(m=1/2\), \(n=1\), obtaining \(\bigl(\sum\sqrt{f(x)}\bigr)^2/9\leq\sum f(x)/3\). An alternative proof writes \(3=1+1+1\) and applies Cauchy.

Lemma 62 — Extension of the root heuristic

If \(\sum f(x)\) has \(n\) terms, then \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt[m]{f(x)}\leq\sqrt[m]{n^{m-1}\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}f(x)}.\] This is analogous to the power-mean inequality.

Application.

Prove \(\sqrt x+\sqrt y+\sqrt z\leq\sqrt{3(x+y+z)}\). Apply the square-root heuristic with \(f(a)=a\).

What was that! P. K. Hung.

For positive \(a,b,c\) with \(a+b+c=1\), prove \(1/a+1/b+1/c\geq25/(1+48abc)\). Here is the magical one-liner: \[\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c-\frac{25}{1+48abc} =\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{(a+b-3c)^2(a-b)^2}{ab(1+48abc)}\geq0.\]
excerptHtml: Prove that \(\dfrac a{1+bc}+\dfrac b{1+ca}+\dfrac c{1+ab}\leq2\) if \(0\leq a,b,c\leq1\). Without loss of generality, let \(a\geq b\geq c\). Since \((1-a)(1-b)\geq0\), we have \(1+ab\geq a+b\), so \(1+2ab\geq a+b\).

title: Rearrangement, Convexity, and Power Means
html:
Lemma 55 — Popoviciu’s theorem

Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be convex on an interval \(I\), and let \(x_1,x_2,x_3\in I\). Then \[\begin{align*} f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)+3f\left(\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3}{3}\right) \geq{}&2f\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)+2f\left(\frac{x_2+x_3}{2}\right)\\ &+2f\left(\frac{x_3+x_1}{2}\right). \end{align*}\]

This classic was formulated by the Romanian mathematician Tiberiu Popoviciu.

Application.

For real \(x,y,z\), prove \(|x|+|y|+|z|-|x+y|-|y+z|-|z+x|+|x+y+z|\geq0\). Let \(f(a)=|a|\), convex on \((-\infty,\infty)\). By Popoviciu’s theorem, \[|x|+|y|+|z|+3\left|\frac{x+y+z}{3}\right| \geq2\left|\frac{x+y}{2}\right|+2\left|\frac{y+z}{2}\right|+2\left|\frac{z+x}{2}\right|.\] This is exactly the desired inequality.

Rearrangement and convexity

Lemma 85 — Rearrangement inequality

Consider two collections of real numbers in increasing order, \(a_1\leq a_2\leq\cdots\leq a_n\) and \(b_1\leq b_2\leq\cdots\leq b_n\). For any permutation \((a'_1,\ldots,a'_n)\) of \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\), \[a_1b_1+a_2b_2+\cdots+a_nb_n\geq a'_1b_1+a'_2b_2+\cdots+a'_nb_n.\]

Application.

Let \(a,b,c\) be positive numbers with \(abc=1\). Prove that \[\frac ab+\frac bc+\frac ca\geq a+b+c.\]

Solution 1.

Apply the rearrangement inequality to \[(a_1,a_2,a_3)=\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac ab},\sqrt[3]{\frac bc},\sqrt[3]{\frac ca}\right), \quad(b_1,b_2,b_3)=\left(\sqrt[3]{\left(\frac ab\right)^2},\sqrt[3]{\left(\frac bc\right)^2},\sqrt[3]{\left(\frac ca\right)^2}\right),\] and the permutation \((a'_1,b'_1,c'_1)=(\sqrt[3]{b/c},\sqrt[3]{c/a},\sqrt[3]{a/b})\), to derive \[\frac ab+\frac bc+\frac ca\geq\sqrt[3]{\frac{a^2}{bc}} +\sqrt[3]{\frac{b^2}{ca}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{c^2}{ab}}=a+b+c,\] since \(abc=1\). Q.E.D.! There are two more possible Q.E.D.s for this problem; the next is an ingenious application of AM–GM.

Solution 2.

\[\begin{aligned} \frac13\left(\frac ab+\frac ab+\frac bc\right)&\geq\sqrt[3]{\frac{a\cdot a\cdot b}{b\cdot b\cdot c}}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{a^2}{bc}}=a,\\ \frac13\left(\frac bc+\frac bc+\frac ca\right)&\geq\sqrt[3]{\frac{b\cdot b\cdot c}{c\cdot c\cdot a}}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{b^2}{ca}}=b,\\ \frac13\left(\frac ca+\frac ca+\frac ab\right)&\geq\sqrt[3]{\frac{c\cdot c\cdot a}{a\cdot a\cdot b}}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{c^2}{ab}}=c. \end{aligned}\] Add all three to obtain \(a/b+b/c+c/a\geq a+b+c\). The third solution follows from Muirhead’s theorem.

Solution 3.

\[\frac ab+\frac bc+\frac ca=a^2c+b^2a+c^2b \mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}(abc)^{2/3}(a+b+c) =\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}a^{5/3}b^{2/3}c^{2/3}.\] Since \((2,1,0)\succ(5/3,2/3,2/3)\), the result follows. Q.E.D.!

A two-line proof of the AM–GM inequality.

We have \(x_i^{t_i}=e^{t_i\log x_i}\). Since \(e^x\) is convex, we can deduce \[x_1^{t_1}x_2^{t_2}\cdots x_n^{t_n} =e^{t_1\log x_1+\cdots+t_n\log x_n} \leq t_1e^{\log x_1}+\cdots+t_ne^{\log x_n}=t_1x_1+\cdots+t_nx_n.\] Now put \(t_1=t_2=\cdots=t_n=1/n\) to obtain, by Jensen’s inequality, \[\frac{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n}{n}\geq\sqrt[n]{x_1x_2\cdots x_n}.\] Q.E.D.!

Challenge.

Define \(x_k=(a^k+b^k+c^k)/3\) for \(a,b,c>0\). Prove the following inequality: \[\frac13\left(\frac{x_1^5}{x_2x_3}+\frac{x_2^2}{x_1x_3}+\frac{x_3}{x_1x_2}\right)>1.\] P.S. This problem has a two-line solution, so don’t think that it is complicated!

Now let us proceed on our eternal journey. Let me show you the magic of convexity–concavity arguments: problems get resolved in seconds!!

So far, so good. By the way, did you figure out how to resolve the challenge we came across two pages ago? Hold on: here comes that two-line solution! \[\begin{aligned} x_3^2\geq x_2^3\geq x_1^6 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac13(x_3^2+x_2^3+x_1^6)\left(\frac12+\frac13+\frac16\right) >\frac{x_3^2}{2}+\frac{x_2^3}{3}+\frac{x_1^6}{6}\geq x_1x_2x_3,\\ \frac{x_3^2+x_2^3+x_1^6}{x_1x_2x_3}>3 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{x_1^5}{x_2x_3}+\frac{x_2^2}{x_1x_3}+\frac{x_3}{x_1x_2}>3. \end{aligned}\] W\(^5\). Q.E.D.! You see, we are done in just two steps!

For \(a,b,c>0\) with \(abc=1\), prove \(\sqrt{a+3}+\sqrt{b+3}+\sqrt{c+3}\geq6\). The source also annotates \(ab+bc+ca=3\). \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{a+3} \geq3\sqrt[6]{28+3(ab+bc+ca)+9(a+b+c)} \geq3\sqrt[6]{28+9+27}=6.\]

For positive \(x,y,z\), prove \(\sqrt{x+y+z}\left(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\dfrac{\sqrt y}{z+x}\right)\geq3\sqrt3/2\). Normalize \(x+y+z=1\), and set \(f:(0,1)\to\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=\sqrt x/(1-x)\). Since \(f\) is convex, \(f(x)+f(y)+f(z)\geq3f(1/3)\), which gives the result.
excerptHtml: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be convex on an interval \(I\), and let \(x_1,x_2,x_3\in I\). Then \[\begin{align*} f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)+3f\left(\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3}{3}\right) \geq{}&2f\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)+2f\left(\frac{x_2+x_3}{2}\right)\\ &+2f\left(\frac{x_3+x_1}{2}\right). \end{align*}\]

title: Lagrange Multipliers and Boundary Analysis
html:
Lagrange multipliers

Lemma 39 — Lagrange multipliers

This is a powerful technique employed by Lagrange to resolve geometric maxima-minima problems. To understand this divine technique completely, do not get scared by the following lines. Get acquainted with partial derivatives before proceeding.

Suppose one is given the multivariable function \(f(x,y,z)=x^2+x+2y^2+3z^2\) and \(x^2+y^2+z^2=1\), and is asked to prove that \(x^2+x+2y^2+3z^2\leq25/8\). This should blow your mind: “Where did that \(25/8\) come from?” “That is not homogeneous!” “What should I do with that \(x\)?” Lagrange observed that the partial derivatives of \(f\) can be equated to \(\lambda\) times the partial derivatives of \(x^2+y^2+z^2\). Here \(\lambda\) is the Lagrange multiplier. This is like writing \(\vec a=\lambda\vec b\). \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\lambda\frac{\partial(x^2+y^2+z^2)}{\partial x},\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\lambda\frac{\partial(x^2+y^2+z^2)}{\partial y},\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=\lambda\frac{\partial(x^2+y^2+z^2)}{\partial z}.\] Thus we solve \[2x+1=2\lambda x,\qquad4y=2\lambda y,\qquad6z=2\lambda z, \qquad x^2+y^2+z^2=1.\] We now have four variables and four equations. Determine those variables; the resulting \((x,y,z)\), substituted into \(f\), yields an extremal point. This statement is sometimes called Lagrange’s theorem.

The following example should give you confidence to use it. Prove that \((x+y+z)/3\geq\sqrt[3]{xyz}\). Find the maximum of \(f(x,y,z)=xyz\) with \(g(x,y,z)=x+y+z=S\). The three equations \(\partial f/\partial x=\lambda\partial g/\partial x\), \(\partial f/\partial y=\lambda\partial g/\partial y\), \(\partial f/\partial z=\lambda\partial g/\partial z\) give \(yz=\lambda\), \(zx=\lambda\), \(xy=\lambda\). Thus \(xy=yz=zx\), so \(x=y=z=S/3\). Plugging this into \(f\) gives \[f(S/3,S/3,S/3)\geq f(x,y,z) \Longrightarrow(S/3)^3\geq xyz \Longrightarrow\frac{x+y+z}{3}\geq\sqrt[3]{xyz}.\] Introduce the notation “gradient of a function \(f\),” written \(\nabla f\): \[\nabla f(x_1,x_2,x_3)= \left(\frac{\partial f(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{\partial x_2}, \frac{\partial f(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{\partial x_3}\right).\]

Instead of the first three equations in the previous problem, it suffices to write \(\nabla f(x,y,z)=\lambda\nabla g(x,y,z)\).

USAMO.

Let \(a,b,c\geq0\) and \(a^2+b^2+c^2+abc=4\). Prove that \(0\leq ab+bc+ca-abc\leq2\). Put \(f(a,b,c)=ab+bc+ca-abc\). We are to find its maximum and minimum under the given condition, called a constraint. Let us call Lagrange to rescue us: \[\nabla f=\lambda\nabla(a^2+b^2+c^2+abc), \quad (b+c-bc,a+c-ac,a+b-ab)=\lambda(2a+bc,2b+ac,2c+ab).\] Equivalently, \[\begin{cases} b+c-bc=\lambda(2a+bc),\\ a+c-ac=\lambda(2b+ac),\\ a+b-ab=\lambda(2c+ab),\\ a^2+b^2+c^2+abc=4. \end{cases}\] Solving gives the two solutions \((1,1,1)\) and \((0,\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\), with \(f(1,1,1)=2\) and \(f(0,\sqrt2,\sqrt2)=2\); hence \(f(a,b,c)\leq2\). We also notice that \((2,0,0)\) is a solution and \(f(2,0,0)=0\), so \(0\leq f(a,b,c)\). Thus \(0\leq f(a,b,c)\leq2\).

IMO (1984).

With \(x+y+z=1\), prove that \(0<xy+yz+zx-2xyz\leq7/27\). The technique of Lagrange multipliers is frequently a victim of hostile review. Before equating gradients, it is essential to show that the gradients are continuous. Let \(f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+zx-2xyz\) and \(g(x,y,z)=x+y+z=1\). Both are polynomials and have continuous first-order partial derivatives. Then \[\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g \Longrightarrow(y+z-2yz,x+z-2xz,x+y-2xy)=(\lambda,\lambda,\lambda).\] From \(y+z-2yz=x+z-2xz\) we get \(y-x=2z(y-x)\), so \(y=x\) or \(z=1/2\). Similarly, \[x=y\ \text{or}\ z=\tfrac12,\qquad y=z\ \text{or}\ x=\tfrac12,\qquad z=x\ \text{or}\ y=\tfrac12,\qquad x+y+z=1.\] The resulting solutions, up to permutation, are \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\) and \((1/2,1/2,0)\). Since \(f(1/3,1/3,1/3)=7/27>f(1/2,1/2,0)=1/4\), these are its extreme values. Therefore \(0<1/4\leq xy+yz+zx-2xyz\leq7/27\).

Lemma 40 — Warning about Lagrange multipliers

Lagrange multipliers could prove lethal. These stunts on the previous pages are performed only by experts. Please do not imitate them in the RMO or INMO; if left with no other option, perform them at your own risk!

There is a strong reason for this warning. Consider the following problem. If \(a,b,c\) are the sides of a triangle of perimeter \(2\), prove that \(a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc<2\). Our constraint is \(g(a,b,c)=a+b+c=2\), and we seek the maximum of \(f(a,b,c)=a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc\). Before proceeding, let me write another lemma.

Lemma 41 — The multiplier procedure

In a problem where Lagrange multipliers are applied, search for a constraint on the variables. Under this constraint, determine the extreme values of the desired function by equating the gradient of one to \(\lambda\) times the gradient of the other: \(\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g\). Then plug the solutions back into \(f\): the smallest resulting value is its minimum and the largest is its maximum.

For example, the preceding IMO problem gave \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\) and \((1/2,1/2,0)\). Substituting, we get \(7/27\) and \(1/4\), so \(1/4\leq f(x,y,z)\leq7/27\).

Lemma 41 explains the steps. Apply them now: \[\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g \Longrightarrow(2(a+bc),2(b+ac),2(c+ab))=(\lambda,\lambda,\lambda).\] Thus \(a+bc=b+ac=c+ab\), with \(a+b+c=2\). From \(a+bc=b+ac\), we get \(a-b=c(a-b)\), so \(a=b\) or \(c=1\). Similarly, \(b=c\) or \(a=1\), and \(c=a\) or \(b=1\). Case analysis yields \((2/3,2/3,2/3)\) and \((1,1,0)\), for which \(f(2/3,2/3,2/3)=52/27\) and \(f(1,1,0)=2\). The notes say “\(52/27\) is largest and \(2\) is smallest,” and conclude \[2\leq f(a,b,c)\leq52/27 \Longrightarrow2\leq a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc.\] “!! Bullshit!!” Think where we might have gone wrong. Meanwhile, here is a simple, clever solution using elementary algebra. We have \(a+b+c=p=2\), so \(s=(a+b+c)/2=1\). The desired inequality can be rewritten successively as \[\begin{align*} (a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ac)+2abc&<2,\\ 2-2(ab+bc+ac)+2abc&<0,\\ 1-ab-bc-ac+abc&<0,\\ -(-1+ab+bc+ac-abc)&<0,\\ -(1-2+ab+bc+ac-abc)&<0,\\ -(1-a-b-c+ab+bc+ac-abc)&<0,\\ -(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)&<0,\\ -(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)&<0. \end{align*}\] This proves \(a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc<2\).

The error is hidden. Did you notice that \(a,b,c\) were given as sides of a triangle? Thus \(a+b>c\) when \(c=\max(a,b,c)\). This constraint was overlooked, so the checker will not notice your solution: “Tit for tat!” The sides of a triangle are nonzero. This technique is so powerful that it proves some interesting results. Look at the following.

Prove the law of reflection.

First reaction: “Are you kidding? Come on, be serious!”

It suffices to show \(\angle APA'=\angle BPB'\). We additionally use the fact that light travels along the shortest path. The constraint is \(g(x,y)=x+y=A'B'\), and \(f(x,y)=AP+BP\). Since \(AP=\sqrt{x^2+(AA')^2}\) and \(BP=\sqrt{y^2+(BB')^2}\), \[f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+(AA')^2}+\sqrt{y^2+(BB')^2},\qquad \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g.\] Thus \[\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+(AA')^2}},\frac{y}{\sqrt{y^2+(BB')^2}}\right) =(\lambda,\lambda),\qquad \frac{A'P}{AP}=\frac{B'P}{BP}.\] Also \(\angle AA'P=\angle BB'P\).

Therefore \(\triangle APA'\sim\triangle BPB'\), giving \(\angle APA'=\angle BPB'\).

Vedant’s enigma.

Given three positive reals \(x\geq y\geq z\) such that \(x^2+y^2+z^2+2xyz=1\), prove that \[2xz+y^2\leq\frac34.\] I asked him for a hint, to which he responded by saying that

we have \(2xz=xz+xz\). I was like, “Are you serious?!” He makes the following threatening move: \[2xz+y^2=xz+y^2+zx=x\cdot z+y\cdot y+z\cdot x.\] Since \(x\geq y\geq z\), we have \[xz+yy+zx\leq\frac13(x+y+z)(x+y+z)=\frac{(x+y+z)^2}{3}.\] Now substitute \(x=\cos A\), \(y=\cos B\), and \(z=\cos C\). (Don’t ask me why!!) Then \[\cos A+\cos B+\cos C\leq3\cos\left(\frac{A+B+C}{3}\right) =3\cos60^\circ,\qquad x+y+z\leq\frac32.\] Thus \((x+y+z)^2/3=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac94=\tfrac34\), giving \(xz+y^2+zx\leq3/4\), and therefore \(2xz+y^2\leq3/4\). (Q.E.D.)–1.

I gave him the following solution: “Lagrange! Lagrange! Help!” Let’s leave it to the expert now. Let \(g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2+2xyz=1\) be the constraint function, and maximize \(f(x,y,z)=2xz+y^2\). The condition \(\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g\) gives \[(2z,2y,2x)=\lambda(2x+2yz,2y+2zx,2z+2xy).\] Therefore \(2z=\lambda(2x+2yz)\), \(2y=\lambda(2y+2zx)\), and \(2x=\lambda(2z+2xy)\), so \[\frac{x+yz}{z}=\frac{y+zx}{y}=\frac{z+xy}{x}=\frac1\lambda.\] It follows that \(x/z+y=z/x+y\), hence \(z=x\). Also \(x/z+y=1+zx/y\), so \(x+y=x+x^2/y\), giving \(x=y\) and thus \(x=y=z=1/2\). Consequently \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\) is the only solution, and \[f(x,y,z)\leq f(1/2,1/2,1/2) =2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12+\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac34.\]

Thus \(f(x,y,z)\leq3/4\), giving \(2xz+y^2\leq3/4\). (Q.E.D.)–2.

Lemma 81 — Normalization

Given a homogeneous inequality, such as \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{(a+b)^2+(b+c)^2}{(a+b)(a+b+c)}>\frac{2014}{1024},\] you can assume \(a+b+c\) equals any number you feel like! Surprised?

Don’t expect me to explain the reason for this, since we crossed these things a few pages ago.

Application.

“What do you think? Every time I’ll write applications for you? Go find one for yourself!” \(\longrightarrow\) “Shu, shu…!” Sorry! I am not that rude; I did this just for a change. Anyway, I have already applied this in this book. Go search!

Magic of 3.

Find the maximum value of \(x(1-x^3)\) for \(0\leq x\leq1\). We cannot do much with the product unless you have a nice command of calculus; then you can use methods such as second-derivative analysis, blah, blah, blah… But can we think of something else? Yes! Of course. Let \(y=x(1-x^3)\). Then \(3y^3=3x^3(1-x^3)(1-x^3)(1-x^3)\). Did you notice that our magic worked? \[3y^3\leq\left(\frac{3x^3+(1-x^3)+(1-x^3)+(1-x^3)}4\right)^4 =\left(\frac34\right)^4.\] Thus \(y\leq3/(4\sqrt[3]4)\); the maximum value is \(3/(4\sqrt[3]4)\). It is attained when \(3x^3=1-x^3\), that is, \(x=1/\sqrt[3]4\). Q.E.D.!

The blah, blah, blah that I mentioned was actually the following: \(f(x)=x-x^4\), so \(f'(x)=1-4x^3=0\) gives \(x=1/\sqrt[3]4\). Thus \(f'(1/\sqrt[3]4)\) is either a minimum or a maximum, that is, an extreme value. We also have \(f''(x)=-12x^2<0\), so \(f'(1/\sqrt[3]4)\) is indeed the maximum value. Therefore \(f'(1/\sqrt[3]4)=3/(4\sqrt[3]4)\). Another Q.E.D.!

Now let me present a surprising inequality that can be resolved using normalization.

Application.

If \(x,y,z\) are real numbers, show that \[(x^2+y^2+z^2)^3\geq(x^3+y^3+z^3)^2.\] It is equivalent to prove \(\sqrt[3]{x^3+y^3+z^3}\leq\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\). Observe that the inequality is homogeneous. Assume \(x^2+y^2+z^2=1\), because if \(x^2+y^2+z^2=k^2\) with \(k\in\mathbb R_+\), then \((x/k)^2+(y/k)^2+(z/k)^2=1\), or \(X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\) (where \(x\mapsto X\)). Now, to normalize the situation, divide by \(k\): \[\frac{\sqrt[3]{x^3+y^3+z^3}}k\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\leq}} \frac{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}k.\] This is equivalent to \[\sqrt[3]{\left(\frac xk\right)^3+\left(\frac yk\right)^3+\left(\frac zk\right)^3} \leq\sqrt{\left(\frac xk\right)^2+\left(\frac yk\right)^2+\left(\frac zk\right)^2},\] that is, \(\sqrt[3]{X^3+Y^3+Z^3}\leq1\). It is not important to have capitals in your solution, so let \(x^2+y^2+z^2=1\). Let us prove \(x^3+y^3+z^3\leq1\) using Lagrange multipliers. Set \(G(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2=1\) and \(F(x,y,z)=x^3+y^3+z^3\). Then \(\nabla G=(2x,2y,2z)\) and \(\nabla F=(3x^2,3y^2,3z^2)\). Thus \(\nabla F=\lambda\nabla G\) gives \[\begin{aligned} 3x^2=2\lambda x&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0\text{ or }x=2\lambda/3,\\ 3y^2=2\lambda y&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=0\text{ or }y=2\lambda/3,\\ 3z^2=2\lambda z&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=0\text{ or }z=2\lambda/3. \end{aligned}\] We obtain \((x,y,z)=(1,0,0)\), \((1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3)\), and \((1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0)\). Since \[F(1,0,0)\geq F(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,0)\geq F(1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3),\] we have \(1/\sqrt3\leq x^3+y^3+z^3\leq1\). Q.E.D.!

Boundary-analysis techniques

To master boundary-analysis techniques, you must gather some boundary-analysis lemmas (BALLs). I wrote two Ls because there are two basic lemmas.

Lemma 86 — Boundary-analysis lemma I

Given any linear function, its maximum or minimum is attained at the boundary of its domain.

Lemma 87 — Boundary-analysis lemma II

Given a convex function, its maximum is attained at an endpoint of its domain.

Weierstrass’s theorem.

Now let us look at some convexity–concavity arguments that will give you an idea of how things are done!

Problem 1: Romanian team selection test.

For a given positive number \(a\), find the maximum of \[\sum_{k=1}^n(a-a_1)(a-a_2)\cdots(a-a_{k-1})a_k(a-a_{k+1})\cdots(a-a_n),\] where \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) range independently over \([0,a]\). Pick any one variable, say \(a_k\), and consider all other \(a_i\) to be constant. You get a linear function in \(a_k\), which ranges over \([0,a]\). By BALL I, the maximum is attained at an endpoint, that is, \(a_k=0\) or \(a\). Argue similarly for all \(a_i\). Therefore the sum reaches its maximum for a certain choice of \(a_k=0\) or \(a\), \(k=1,\ldots,n\).

If all \(a_k=0\), the sum is zero. If two or more \(a_k=a\), the sum is zero. If one \(a_k=a\) and the others are zero, the sum is \(a^n\). Thus the maximum value is \(a^n\). BAT I.

Problem 2: Titu Andreescu.

Let \(0\leq a,b,c,d\leq1\). Prove that \[(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)(1-d)+a+b+c+d\geq1.\] Choose any one variable and let the others be constant. It is a linear function, so it attains its maximum when the chosen variable is either zero or one. Argue similarly for all four variables, giving \((a,b,c,d)=0\) or \(1\). If one variable is zero, the value is \(3\); if all equal one, the value is \(4\). If two variables are zero, the value is \(2\); if three or all of them are zero, the value is \(1\). We observe that \(1\) is the smallest of all the values obtained, so the minimum of the function is \(1\). The conclusion follows. BAT I.

These are some standard techniques, but there are one or two more problems with quite a different way of sorting things.

Problem 3: W. L. Putnam Mathematical Competition.

Let \(n\) be a natural number and \(x_i\in[0,1]\) for \(i=1,2,\ldots,n\). Find the maximum of \(\sum_{i<j}|x_i-x_j|\).

I am assuming that you are capable enough to argue and conclude that the maximum of the sum is attained when all \(x_i\) equal zero or one. Now let us proceed from here. Let \(p\) of them be zero and \(n-p\) of them be one. Then the sum is \(p(n-p)\); look below the summation sign carefully to realize why! Now maximize \(p(n-p)\) for yourself. Q.E.D.! BALL II; BAT II.

Problem 4: USAMO.

If \(a,b,c,d,e\in[p,q]\) with \(p>0\), prove that \[(a+b+c+d+e)\left(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c+\frac1d+\frac1e\right) \leq25+6\left(\sqrt{\frac pq}-\sqrt{\frac qp}\right)^2.\] Fix \(a,b,c,d\) to be constants. The left-hand side is now of the form \(\widehat a x+\widehat b/x+\widehat c\), where \(\widehat a,\widehat b,\widehat c>0\) and \(x\in[p,q]\). This is a convex function, so it attains its maximum at an endpoint. Thus \((a,b,c,d,e)=p\) or \(q\). If \(n\) of them equal \(p\) and \(5-n\) equal \(q\), then the left-hand side has the form \[n^2+(5-n^2)+n(5-n)\left(\frac pq+\frac qp\right) =25+n(5-n)\left(\sqrt{\frac pq}-\sqrt{\frac qp}\right)^2.\] W\(^5\). Q.E.D. BAT II.

So now you have two bats and two balls. What are you waiting for? Go play with some problems and enjoy yourself. Okay, I’ll give you problems to throw away… here they come!

Game 1, round 1: fight!

The nonnegative numbers \(a,b,c,A,B,C,k\) satisfy \(a+A=b+B=c+C=k\). Prove that \(aB+bC+cA\leq k^2\).

Round 2: fight!

Prove that for \(a,b,c\in[0,1]\), \[\frac a{b+c+1}+\frac b{c+a+1}+\frac c{a+b+1}+(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)\leq1.\]

Final round: fight!

Prove that if \(1\leq x_k\leq2\) for all \(k=1,2,\ldots,n\), then \[\left(\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{x_k}\right)^2\leq n^3.\] I know you might have hit a K.O. in the first two and got your ass kicked in the last one. I know it is comparatively difficult. Let us solve the last one. \[\sqrt[3]{\left(\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{x_k}\right)^2} \leq\frac13\left(\sum_{k=1}^n x_k+\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{x_k}+\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1{x_k}\right) =\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{x_k+2/x_k}{3}.\] The function \(x+2/x\) is convex, with its maximum at an endpoint of the interval, that is, \(x_k=1\) or \(2\). In both cases we end up with \(3\), so \((x_k+2/x_k)/3\leq1\). Thus \(\sum_{k=1}^n(x_k+2/x_k)/3\leq n\). W\(^5\) \(\longrightarrow\) K.O. \(\longrightarrow\) You win!!

When finding the maximum or minimum area of a triangle, one may use the deadly move of coordinate bashing. Carry the following lemma in your pocket.

Lemma 102 — Hadamard’s inequality

If \(A=(a_{ij})\) is an \(n\times n\) matrix, then \(|\det A|^2\leq\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^n|a_{ij}|^2\bigr)\). Equality holds if and only if the rows are orthogonal.

Application: Mathematical Reflections, issue 1 (2014).

In triangle \(ABC\), a point \(P\) is at distances \(R_1=1\), \(R_2=2\), \(R_3=3\) from \(A,B,C\). Find the maximum area of \(ABC\). Place \(P\) at the origin, with \(A=(x_1,y_1)\), \(B=(x_2,y_2)\), \(C=(x_3,y_3)\). Then \(x_i^2+y_i^2=R_i^2\) and \[[ABC]=\frac12\begin{vmatrix}1&x_1&y_1\\1&x_2&y_2\\1&x_3&y_3\end{vmatrix},\qquad \begin{vmatrix}1&x_1&y_1\\1&x_2&y_2\\1&x_3&y_3\end{vmatrix}^{\!2} \leq(R_1^2+1)(R_2^2+1)(R_3^2+1).\] The source concludes \([ABC]\leq\sqrt{(R_1^2+1)(R_2^2+1)(R_3^2+1)}\). AWD: “And we’re done!”
excerptHtml: This is a powerful technique employed by Lagrange to resolve geometric maxima-minima problems. To understand this divine technique completely, do not get scared by the following lines. Get acquainted with partial derivatives before proceeding.

title: Circle Geometry: Inversion, Radical Axes, and Special Circles
html:
Geometry and problem-solving strategies

Lemma 30 — Inversion

Inversion is a powerful technique for geometry problems. It is a magical spell that converts a complex geometry problem into an obvious fact, if one gets lucky. Refer to BMC or Kiran Kedlaya’s notes.

Let \(C_1,C_2,C_3,C_4\) be four circles in the plane. Suppose \(C_1,C_2\) meet at \(P_1,Q_1\); \(C_2,C_3\) at \(P_2,Q_2\); \(C_3,C_4\) at \(P_3,Q_3\); and \(C_4,C_1\) at \(P_4,Q_4\). Show that, if \(P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4\) lie on a line or circle, then \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4\) also lie on a line or circle.

This can be resolved using coordinates! Now let us perform the magic; say with me these words: “Problema invertó!”

Apply \(I(P_1,R)\).

Our magic worked! It remains to prove that \(Q_1Q_2Q_3Q_4\) is concyclic. Since \(P_1P_2P_3P_4\) is concyclic, it inverts into a straight line; now \(P_2,P_3,P_4\) are collinear. It remains to chase three angles: \[\angle Q_3Q_4Q_1=\angle Q_3P_3P_4=\angle Q_3Q_2P_2 \Longrightarrow\angle Q_1Q_4Q_3=\angle Q_3Q_2P_2.\] This implies that \(Q_1Q_2Q_3Q_4\) is concyclic. “Finished!”

Lemma 31 — Distance formula for inversion

If segment \(AB\) inverts to \(A_1B_1\) under \(I(O,r)\), then \(A_1B_1=\dfrac{AB\,r^2}{OA\cdot OB}\).

This is helpful: it gives a two-line proof of Ptolemy’s theorem.

I thought the proof would fit on the previous page, but it did not. Overconfidence is lethal! From \(A_1C_1=A_1B_1+B_1C_1\), inversion about \(D\) gives \[\frac{AB\,r^2}{DA\cdot DB}+\frac{BC\,r^2}{DB\cdot DC} =\frac{AC\,r^2}{DA\cdot DC}.\] Cancelling \(r^2\) and multiplying through, \[\frac{AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD}{DA\cdot DB\cdot DC} =\frac{AC}{DA\cdot DC} \Longrightarrow AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD=AC\cdot BD.\]

Lemma 32 — Similar triangles and concyclicity

If triangles \(ABC\) and \(AB'C'\) are similar, then \(BB'CC'\) is concyclic.

This is an obvious geometric fact; a simple angle chase yields the result.

Lemma 33 — Converse of the alternate-segment theorem

An Olympiad student knows the alternate-segment theorem, but its converse is a powerful tool: the “CAST lemma”.

The IMO jury loves posing problems where one is expected to show that a segment is tangent to a circle. Instead of drawing the circle, if a simple angle chase establishes the converse of the alternate-segment theorem, “that would be it!” Let me show a lovely IMO problem resolved by a clever application of the above two lemmas. In fact, I checked the competition papers: more than a dozen problems are of this type, and one appeared in IMO 2014!

Two circles intersect at \(A\) and \(B\). An arbitrary line through \(B\) meets the first circle at \(C\) and the second at \(D\). The tangents to \(\omega_1\) at \(C\) and to \(\omega_2\) at \(D\) meet at \(M\). Let \(AM\cap CD=X\). Through \(X\), a line parallel to \(CM\) meets \(AC\) at \(K\). Prove that \(BK\) is tangent to the second circle.

We have \(\angle BCM=\angle CAB\) and \(\angle BDM=\angle BAD\). Hence \(\angle CAD=\angle BCM+\angle BDM=180^\circ-\angle CMD\), so \(ACMD\) is concyclic. Also \(\angle DXL=\angle DCM=\angle CAB=\angle KXB\), giving \(\triangle ABC\sim\triangle XKC\) (AAA). By Lemma 32, \(KBXA\) is cyclic. Further, \(\angle XCM=\angle KAB\) and \(\angle CXM=\angle BKA\), so \(\triangle BKA\sim\triangle MXC\) (AAA). Thus \(\angle CMX=\angle KBA=\angle BDA\), and the CAST lemma gives the result.

Radical-axis theorem

Let us begin by defining what is meant by the power of a point. The idea was first discovered by ancient Greeks; Euclid wrote it in his Elements. The name “power of a point” (P.O.P.) was given by the world-renowned geometer Jacob Steiner.

Lemma 82 — Power of a point

Given a circle and a point \(P\), draw a line through \(P\) intersecting the circle at \(A\) and \(B\). Then the product \(PA\cdot PB\) stays constant.

Lemma 83 — Radical-axis theorem I

The locus of points whose powers with respect to two nonconcentric circles are equal is a line perpendicular to the line of centres of the two circles.

Lemma 84 — Radical-axis theorem II

If there are three circles \(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3\), then their radical axes are concurrent. That point of concurrence is called the radical centre.

Application 2 of Lemma 49 in the manuscript is immediate once you are aware of such a thing!

Application: USAMO (1997), problem 2.

Let \(ABC\) be a triangle, and draw isosceles triangles \(DBC\), \(AEC\), and \(ABF\) external to \(ABC\), with \(BC\), \(CA\), and \(AB\) as their respective bases. Prove that the lines through \(A,B,C\) perpendicular to \(EF,FD,DE\), respectively, are concurrent. (There are 25 solutions to this problem!)

It must be clear that we should somehow show \(X\) to be the radical centre of three circles. But where are the circles? Okay, be patient! We have \(\ell\perp EF\). In order for \(\ell\) to be a radical axis, we must prove—no, not prove: construct—circles with centres \(F,E\). So let’s exploit the fact that \(FA=FB\) and \(EA=EC\) by erecting circles with centres \(F,E\) and radii \(FA,EA\), respectively. Argue similarly for point \(D\), and don’t forget to write Q.E.D.!

W.A.L.L.: What a Lovely Locus problem (I. F. Sharygin).

Given a point \(A\) inside a circle, construct a chord \(XY\) passing through \(A\). Draw tangents at \(X,Y\), and let their intersection be \(P\). Find the locus of \(P\). (Rephrased.) Let \(\omega\) be our circle, with centre \(O\) and radius \(r\), and let \(A\) be a point inside it. Construct a circle with diameter \(AO\).

Given any chord \(XY\) passing through \(A\), its midpoint lies on this circle, since \(\angle OBA=\angle OBX=90^\circ\) and \(O\) is the centre.

Our point \(P\) is nothing but the midpoint of the chord inverted with respect to \(I(O,r)\). Since a circle inverts back to a line, that line is precisely the locus—W.A.L.L.—of \(P\). Q.E.D.!

Lemma 89 — Simson’s line

The feet of the perpendiculars drawn from any point on the circumcircle of a triangle to its sides are collinear. The converse is also true.

Application.

The sides \(AB,BC,AC\) of \(\triangle ABC\) are cut by a transversal at \(Q,R,S\), respectively. The circumcircles of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle SCR\) intersect at \(P\). Prove that \(ASPQ\) is cyclic.

Draw \(PX,PY,PZ,PW\) perpendicular to \(AB,AC,QR,BC\), respectively, as shown in the figure. Since \(P\) is on the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\), the points \(X,Y,W\) are collinear. Since \(P\) is on the circumcircle of \(\triangle SCR\), the points \(Y,Z,W\) are collinear. It follows that \(X,Y,Z\) are collinear. Thus \(P\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle AQS\), and \(APQS\) is cyclic. Q.E.D.

Lemma 90 — Nine-point circle

The midpoints of the sides, the feet of the altitudes, and the midpoints of the segments joining the orthocentre to the vertices all lie on a circle, called the nine-point circle.

Application: Proofathon geometry contest (2014).

In \(\triangle ABC\), with orthocentre \(H\), let \(BH,CH\) intersect \(AC,AB\) at \(E,F\), respectively. The tangent to the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\) at \(A\) intersects \(BC\) at \(P\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AH\), and let \(EF\) intersect \(BC\) at \(G\). Prove that \(PM\parallel GH\). (Draw that bullshit figure for yourself!)

By the nine-point-circle theorem, \(DFME\) is cyclic, so \(FX\cdot XE=DX\cdot MX\). Also \(HEAF\) is cyclic, since \(\angle AFC=\angle AEH=90^\circ\), so \(FX\cdot XE=XH\cdot XA\). Therefore \[\frac{FX\cdot XE}{FX\cdot XE}=\frac{DX\cdot MX}{XH\cdot HA} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{DX}{XA}=\frac{XH}{MX} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{HD+HX}{AM+MX}=\frac{HX}{MX}.\] Thus \(HD/AM=HX/MX\), and \(HD/MH=HX/MX=DX/XA\), since \(AM=MH\). We have \(PA^2=PB\cdot PC\) because \(PA\) is tangent to the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\). Hence \(PA/PB=PC/PA\), so \(\triangle PAB\sim\triangle PCA\), and \(\angle PBA=\angle PCA=\angle BFC+\angle FCB\). It follows that \(\angle PBA=\angle BEC+\angle FEB=\angle GEC\), since \(BFEC\) is cyclic. Now \(\angle PAC=\angle GEC\), so \(GE\parallel PA\), and \[\frac{GD}{PG}=\frac{DX}{XA}=\frac{HX}{MX}=\frac{HD}{MH}, \qquad\frac{GD}{PG}=\frac{HD}{MH},\] giving \(GH\parallel PM\). Q.B.D.: Quite Boringly Done!

Lemma 91 — Excentre

The external bisectors of two angles and the internal bisector of the third concur at a point, called the excentre.

Application.

In a triangle \(ABC\), the lines formed by reflecting \(BC\) across \(AB\) and \(AC\) intersect at \(D\). Prove that the circumcentre of \(\triangle ABC\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle BCD\). There is one more problem: take this one as an application of Ravi substitutions. The bisector of \(\angle A\) intersects \(BC\) and the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\) at \(D,E\). Show that \(\triangle BDE\) and \(\triangle CDE\) have the same circumradius.

Proofathon, problem 3.

The incentre of \(\triangle BCD\) lies on the circumcentre of \(\triangle ABC\). Claim: try to prove this!

Solution. Join \(AD\), and let it intersect the circumcircle of \(\triangle BCD\) at \(O\). Now \(BOCD\) is cyclic, so \(\angle BOC=180^\circ-\angle BDC=180^\circ-x\). Observe that \(AB,AC\) are external angle bisectors of \(\angle B,\angle C\) of \(\triangle BCD\). External bisectors of two angles and the internal bisector of the third are always concurrent. Hence \(AD\) is an angle bisector. Call this I. From I, \(\angle BDO=\angle CDO=x/2\), so \(\angle OBC=\angle ODC=x/2\) and \(\angle OCB=\angle ODB=x/2\). Thus \(\triangle BOC\) is isosceles, and \(BO=OC\).

Crucial angle chase.

We have \(\angle ABC=90^\circ-\angle DBC/2\) and \(\angle ACB=90^\circ-\angle DCB/2\). Therefore \[\angle BAC=180^\circ-\left(180^\circ-\frac{\angle DBC+\angle DCB}{2}\right) =\frac{\angle DBC+\angle DCB}{2}=\frac{180^\circ-x}{2}=90^\circ-\frac x2.\] Call this II. From II, \(\angle BAC=90^\circ-x/2\), so \(\angle BOC=2\angle BAC\), and also \(OB=OC\). Therefore \(O\) is the circumcentre of \(\triangle ABC\). Q.E.D.

Proofathon, problem 4.

We have \(ABEC\) cyclic. Thus \(A/2=\angle BCE=\angle BAD\), and \(\angle CBE=\angle CAD=A/2\). Since \(AD\) bisects \(\angle A\), we get \(\angle BCE=\angle CBE=A/2\). Hence \(\triangle BEC\) is isosceles, so \(BE=CE\); call this \(\star\).

Facts.

\(R=abc/(4\Delta)\), where \(\Delta\) is the area; \(\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)\); and \([ABC]=\tfrac12ab\sin\angle A\). We have \[R(\triangle BDE)=\frac{BD\cdot DE\cdot BE}{4[BDE]}, \qquad R(\triangle CDE)=\frac{DE\cdot CE\cdot DC}{4[CDE]}.\] We seek \(BD\cdot DE\cdot BE/(4[BDE])=DE\cdot CE\cdot DC/(4[CDE])\); call this I. Since \(BE=CE\), this reduces to \(BD/[BDE]=CD/[CDE]\), or \(BD/CD=[BDE]/[CDE]\). Now \[[BDE]=\tfrac12BD\cdot DE\sin\angle BDE, \qquad[CDE]=\tfrac12DE\cdot CD\sin\angle CDE.\] Consequently \[\frac{[BDE]}{[CDE]}= \frac{\tfrac12BD\cdot DE\sin\angle BDE}{\tfrac12DE\cdot CD\sin\angle CDE} =\frac{BD}{CD},\] because \(\angle BDE=180^\circ-\angle CDE\). This establishes I, hence \(R(\triangle BDE)=R(\triangle CDE)\). GeoGebra.

Magic of the nine-point circle: INMO (2012).

Let \(ABC\) be acute, and take \(D,E,F\) on \(BC,CA,AB\) so that \(AD\) is a median, \(BE\) is the internal angle bisector, and \(CF\) is an altitude. Suppose \(\angle FDE=\angle C\), \(\angle DEF=\angle A\), and \(\angle EFD=\angle B\). Prove that \(ABC\) is equilateral. Try it first!

Step 1.

Since \(\angle AFD=\angle B+\angle FDB\), we obtain \(\angle AFE+\angle B=\angle B+\angle FDB\), so \(\angle AFE=\angle FDB\). Similarly \(\angle AFE=\angle FDB=\angle DEC\). Construct \(FF'\parallel BC\). Then \(\angle F'FD=\angle FDB=\angle DEC\), so \(FF'ED\) is cyclic.

Step 2.

A similar argument puts \(F,F',E,E',D,D'\) on a circle. Since \(D\) is the midpoint of \(BC\), \(D'\) the midpoint of \(AB\), and \(F\) a perpendicular foot, this is the nine-point circle. Wow! The nine-point circle meets \(AC\) at the perpendicular foot and the midpoint. Thus \(E\) is one of those two. Since \(BE\) bisects the angle, this forces \(AB=BC\); hence \(E'\) and \(D\) coincide. Now \(DE\parallel AB\), so \(\angle DEC=\angle A\). Step 1 gives \(\angle FDB=\angle DEC=\angle A\). Also \(BD=CD\) and \(\angle BFC=90^\circ\), so \(FD=BD\) and \(\angle DFB=\angle B\).

Step 3.

In triangle \(FDB\), \(\angle B+\angle B+\angle A=180^\circ\). In triangle \(ABC\), \(\angle B+\angle A+\angle A=180^\circ\). Thus \(2\angle B+\angle A=2\angle A+\angle B\) and \(A=B=C=60^\circ\).

Here is another problem. In triangle \(ABC\), altitudes \(BE,CF\) meet at \(H\). Let \(AM\) be a median and \(HP\perp AM\). Prove that \(EF,PH,BC\), extended as necessary, are concurrent.

This has a magical one-line solution. Try it and return! Construct \(AH\perp BC\) at \(D\). The sets \(AFHPE\), \(HPDM\), and \(FEMD\) are each concyclic. \(EF\) is the radical axis of the first circle and the nine-point circle; \(HP\) is the radical axis of the first and second circles; \(DM\) is the radical axis of the second and the nine-point circle. The radical-axis theorem gives the conclusion.

Lemma 107 — The arc midpoint and the incentre

In the configuration of Figure LB2.14, \(MI=MB=MC\).

Application: IMO 2006.

Let \(ABC\) have incentre \(I\), and let \(P\) be an interior point satisfying \(\angle PBA+\angle PCA=\angle PBC+\angle PCB\). Show that \(AP\geq AI\), with equality if and only if \(P=I\). This can be taken as an exercise: it is trivial once you notice that \(BPIC\) is cyclic!
