title: Working Backwards, Area Ratios, and Geometric Constructions
html:
Lemma 34 — A working-backwards strategy

Another major lemma is the strategy of working backwards, in a slightly different version used here to resolve problems. First read the statement. If it asks to prove that “\(A\) holds if and only if \(B\) is true,” then, for this type of problem, just show that if \(A\) holds, \(B\) follows.

Consider the following geometry problem from IMO 1994, problem 2. Let \(ABC\) be an isosceles triangle with \(AB=AC\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(BC\), and let \(O\) lie on line \(AM\) with \(OB\perp AB\). Let \(Q\) be on segment \(BC\), distinct from \(B,C\). Let \(E\) lie on line \(AB\) and \(F\) on line \(AC\), with \(E,Q,F\) distinct and collinear. Prove that \(OQ\perp EF\) if and only if \(QE=QF\).

Trailer.

Let \(E\) and \(F\) lie on the same side of \(Q\), as shown.

Write \(\angle EQM=x+z\) and \(\angle OQM=y+w\). Then \(\angle EQO=(x+y)+(z+w)=\pi/2+k\). For \(OQ\perp EQ\), \(k=0\), so \(z=w=0\). But this requires \(Q=B\) or \(Q=C\), contrary to the assumption. Thus \(E,F\) cannot both lie on the same side of \(Q\).

Movie.

According to Lemma 34, we intend to show that \(OQ\perp EF\) implies \(QE=QF\).

\(OQBE\) is cyclic, so \(\angle QOE=\angle QBA=x\), say. Then \(\angle MBA=\angle BOM=x\). By symmetry of the figure, \(\angle BOM=\angle MOC=x\). Also \(\angle MBA=\angle MCA=x\), so \(\angle MCO=\pi/2-\angle MOC=\pi/2-x\). Thus \(\angle ACO=(\pi/2-x)+x=90^\circ\). Consequently \(QOCF\) is cyclic, and \(\angle QCF=\angle QOF=x=\angle QOE\). This establishes \(QE=QF\).

To finish, argue as follows. Suppose the contrary of the result were true, that there were a point \(Q\) for which \(QE\ne QF\) even though \(OQ\perp EF\). But we proved that \(OQ\perp EF\) implies \(QE=QF\), establishing the nonexistence of such a point.

Lemma 35 — Caution with the strategy

Lemma 34 cannot be applied very easily. Since it is a new technique, it can lead to a major error if the final argument is not formed correctly. Here we exploited the fact that a statement \(B\) in mathematical logic has only two truth values, true or false. There are statements with more than two truth values; anyway, for Olympiad business it is well and good.

Many combinatorial geometry problems are based on very elementary geometry. To excel in the IMO, at least give a glance to lesser theorems.

Lemma 36 — Pascal’s theorem

If \(A,X,A'\) and \(B,Y,B'\) are collinear in the two-circle configuration, then \(AB\parallel A'B'\).

This simple theorem is often neglected by Olympiad students; as a result, they have difficulty solving the following problem.

Two circles intersect at \(X,Y\). Draw a chord \(AB\) in the first circle. Extend \(AX,BY\) to meet the second circle at \(A',B'\). Construct a circle through \(A',B'\), and extend \(XA',YB'\) to meet the third circle at \(A^2,B^2\). Iterate this \(2014\) times. Determine the number of trapeziums in the resulting configuration. Edit in the source: “parallelograms” is replaced by “trapeziums.”

Lemma 37 — Express side ratios as area ratios

In a geometry problem, expressing ratios of sides as ratios of areas is often a nice, clean technique.

Application: British Mathematical Olympiad.

Suppose the cevians \(AP,BQ,CR\) meet at \(T\). Prove that \(\dfrac{TP}{AP}+\dfrac{TQ}{BQ}+\dfrac{TR}{CR}=1\).

Using brackets for areas, \[\frac{TP}{AP}=\frac{[BTP]}{[ABP]}=\frac{[TPC]}{[APC]} =\frac{[BTP]+[TPC]}{[ABP]+[APC]}=\frac{[BTC]}{[ABC]}.\] Similarly, \(\dfrac{TP}{AP}+\dfrac{TQ}{BQ}+\dfrac{TR}{CR} =\dfrac{[ATB]+[BTC]+[CTA]}{[ABC]}=1\).

There is yet another application of this lemma.

BAMO (2007).

In triangle \(ABC\), \(D,E\) are interior points of side \(BC\) with \(BD=CE\) and \(\angle BAD=\angle CAE\). Prove that \(ABC\) is isosceles. We use two elementary facts: triangles with equal bases and the same height have equal areas, and \([ABC]=\frac12ab\sin A\).

Since \([ABD]=[AEC]\), we have \(\frac12\sin x\,AB\cdot AD=\frac12\sin x\,AC\cdot AE\), so \(AB/AC=AE/AD\). Also \(BE=CD\) and \(\angle BAE=\angle DAC\), whence \([ABE]=[ADC]\). Thus \[\frac12\sin(x+z)\,AB\cdot AE=\frac12\sin(x+z)\,AC\cdot AD \Longrightarrow\frac{AB}{AC}=\frac{AD}{AE}.\] It follows that \(AD/AE=AE/AD\), so \(AD=AE\) and \(AB/AC=1\). Therefore \(ABC\) is isosceles.

Remark

Another major approach to geometry problems assigns masses to points and is sometimes called “mass-point geometry.” In my opinion, problems solved using these elementary operations on masses can be resolved using Ceva’s theorem or Menelaus’s theorem.

The following is a nice application of Menelaus’s theorem and can itself be considered a lemma.

Lemma 38 — Two concurrency conditions

Let \(ABC\) be a triangle, and let \(D,E,F\) lie on \(BC,CA,AB\), respectively, with \(AD,BE,CF\) concurrent. If \(M,N,P\) lie on \(EF,FD,DE\), then \(AM,BN,CP\) concur if and only if \(DM,EN,FP\) concur.

I used GeoGebra to draw a nice, neat figure of this problem. Do not forget Lemma 34 for if-and-only-if problems.

“The secret of resolving any difficult geometric problem is drawing a clean figure.” The original figure is headed “Good application of Menelaus” and signed Viswanathan.

Innovative solution.

Let \(D,E,F\) lie on the sides \(BC,CA,AB\) of triangle \(ABC\), respectively, with \(BD=CE=AF\) and \(\angle BDF=\angle CED=\angle AFE\). Prove that \(ABC\) is equilateral.

Triangles \(AFE,BFD,CED\) have equal bases and an equal angle. If \(A\geq B\geq C\), then \(FE\geq FD\geq DE\). Inside triangle \(DEF\), \(FD\geq DE\geq EF\). Together these imply \(FD=DE=EF\), hence \(AB=BC=AC\).

Strategy: the poet’s way.

If you are expected to prove something, assume that the statement to be proved is true. Deduce all possibilities, and then try to prove any one of those deductions independently, that is, without assuming the statement to be true.

Let us look at an example of the previous strategy!

Application: RMO (1995).

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(K,L\) are points on \(BC\) such that \(BC\cdot KL=BK\cdot CL\), and \(AL\) bisects \(\angle KAC\). Prove that \(AL\perp AB\).

(Apologies for such a mind-blowing figure!) Let us assume the result is true: \(AL\perp AB\). Now perform a little angle chase, because that is the only thing we are capable of doing! Since \(AL\) bisects \(\angle KAC\), let \(\angle LAK=\angle LAC=\alpha\). Then \(\angle KAB=90^\circ-\alpha\) and \(\angle BAD=180^\circ-(90^\circ-\alpha+\alpha+\alpha)=90^\circ-\alpha\). Aha! Thus \(\angle KAB=\angle BAD=90^\circ-\alpha\), so \(AB\) is an exterior angle bisector of \(\triangle KAC\). Let us prove this fact independently. How should we proceed? You know what? That is a stupid question to ask; rather, you should be asking, “Did I use all the data?” The answer is an obvious no! We are given \(BC\cdot KL=BK\cdot CL\), so \(BC/BK=CL/KL\): a fact! What can we possibly do with \(CL/KL\)? We immediately notice that \(AL\) bisects \(\angle KAC\), giving \(CL/KL=AC/AK\). Thus \(BC/BK=AC/AK\), another fact! This should immediately tell you that \(AB\) is an exterior angle bisector of \(\angle KAC\) in \(\triangle KAC\). W\(^5\): which was what we wanted!

Employ the same strategy to resolve the following problem! In \(\triangle ABC\), \(AM\) is a median that divides \(\angle BAC\) in the ratio \(1:2\). Extend \(AM\) through \(M\) to \(D\) so that \(\angle DBA=90^\circ\). Prove that \(AC=\tfrac12 AD\).

Solving geometry problems using scissors rather than theorems

C.A.P.: Cut and Paste problem (IMO, 1996).

Let \(P\) be a point inside \(\triangle ABC\) such that \[\angle APB-\angle C=\angle APC-\angle B.\] Let \(D,E\) be the incentres of \(\triangle APB,\triangle APC\), respectively. Show that \(AP,BE,CD\) concur.

Multiply the sides of triangle I by \(z\), those of II by \(x\), and those of III by \(y\). Anybody got some glue?! Okay, let’s repaste.

The angle condition on \(P\) gives \(\alpha+\theta=\beta+\gamma\), so \(cz=by\). Thus \(c/b=y/z\), giving \(AB/AC=BP/CP\), and hence \(AB/BP=AC/CP\). W\(^5\). Q.E.D.!

Two magical constructions

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A=120^\circ\). Express the length of the internal angle bisector of \(\angle A\) in terms of the two adjacent sides. (With any trigonometry, of course!)

What a superb figure! \(X,A,C\) are collinear; \(Y,A,B\) are collinear; and \(XB\parallel AM\parallel YC\). The construction we made might have been clear. The figure itself represents the situation so nicely that it leaves me speechless. Okay! Let us not exaggerate too much. Now the solution is two lines: \[\frac1{BX}+\frac1{CY}=\frac1{AM} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac1{AB}+\frac1{AC}=\frac1{AM} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad AM=\frac{AB\cdot AC}{AB+AC}.\] Q.E.D.!

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(CD\) is the altitude to \(AB\), and \(P\) is a point on \(DC\). \(AP\) meets \(CB\) at \(Q\), and \(BP\) meets \(CA\) at \(R\). Prove that \(\angle RDC=\angle QDC\) using Ceva’s theorem.

Since \(\triangle GRC\sim\triangle DRA\), we have \(CR/RA=GC/AD\). Also \(\triangle CQH\sim\triangle BQD\), giving \(BQ/CQ=BD/CH\). Now Ceva’s theorem yields \[\frac{CR}{RA}\frac{AD}{DB}\frac{BQ}{QC}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{GC}{AD}\frac{AD}{DB}\frac{BD}{CH}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad CG=CH.\] In \(\triangle GCD\) and \(\triangle HCD\), we have \(GC=CH\) and \(\angle GCD=\angle HCD=90^\circ\). Thus \(\triangle GDC\cong\triangle HDC\), so \(\angle RDC=\angle QDC\). Q.E.D.!
excerptHtml: Another major lemma is the strategy of working backwards, in a slightly different version used here to resolve problems. First read the statement. If it asks to prove that “\(A\) holds if and only if \(B\) is true,” then, for this type of problem, just show that if \(A\) holds, \(B\) follows.

title: Triangle Inequalities and Trigonometric Substitutions
html:
Lemma 42 — Triangle inequality

If \(ABC\) is a triangle, then \(a+b>c\), where \(c=\max(a,b,c)\).

This elegant inequality has two nontrivial applications.

Classical application.

Let \(A,B\) be two points on the same side of a line \(XY\). Find \(M\) on that line such that \(AM+MB\) is minimal. This gives an alternative proof of the law of reflection. How?

The figure itself is the solution: \(A'M'+M'B\geq A'B\). I like the following explanation. Since \(AM+MB\) must be the shortest path, light sent from \(A\) to \(B\) after reflection must meet the line at the required \(M\). It should satisfy the law of reflection, which we proved. Thus choose \(M\) so that \(\angle AMX=\angle BMY\). “Finished!”

The second application is the following lemma.

Lemma 43 — Triangle-side substitution

If \(a,b,c\) are the sides of a triangle, then \(a=x+y\), \(b=y+z\), and \(c=z+x\).

Application.

For the sides \(a,b,c\) of a triangle, prove that \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}a(b^2+c^2-a^2)\leq3abc\). The desired inequality becomes \[\begin{align*} a(b^2+c^2-a^2)+b(c^2+a^2-b^2)+c(a^2+b^2-c^2)&\leq3abc,\\ a^2(b+c-a)+b^2(c+a-b)+c^2(a+b-c)&\leq3abc. \end{align*}\] Substituting gives \[\begin{align*} (x+y)^2(2z)+(y+z)^2(2x)+(z+x)^2(2y) &\leq3(x+y)(y+z)(z+x),\\ 2\bigl((x^2+2xy+y^2)z+(y^2+2yz+z^2)x+(z^2+2zx+x^2)y\bigr) &\leq3(x+y)(y+z)(z+x),\\ 2\bigl(x^2(y+z)+y^2(z+x)+z^2(x+y)+6xyz\bigr) &\leq3(x+y)(y+z)(z+x),\\ 2\bigl((x+y)(y+z)(z+x)+4xyz\bigr) &\leq3(x+y)(y+z)(z+x). \end{align*}\] This reduces to \(8xyz\leq(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\).

Remark

The cosine formula also proves the inequality. Put \(b^2+c^2-a^2=2bc\cos A\). Then \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}2abc\cos A\leq3abc\) becomes \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\cos A\leq3/2\), obvious after applying Jensen’s inequality. This is the intuitive way to solve it!

I will soon write an extensive explanation of trigonometric substitution. Have a look at the trailer.

Lemma 52 — Trigonometric substitution

If \(x^2+y^2=1\), then \(x=\sin\theta\) and \(y=\cos\theta\).

This elementary idea resolves a deceptively difficult IMOTC 2014 problem. Let \(x,y\) be rational and \(x^5+y^5=2x^2y^2\). Prove that \(1-xy\) is a rational square. Then \[\frac{x^3}{2y^2}+\frac{y^3}{2x^2}=1, \quad\frac{x^3}{y^2}=2\sin^2\theta, \quad\frac{y^3}{x^2}=2\cos^2\theta.\] Consequently \[xy=\frac{x^3}{y^2}\frac{y^3}{x^2}=4\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta=\sin^22\theta, \quad1-xy=\cos^22\theta=(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)^2.\]

I do not encourage bombarding students with formulas. The following should be analyzed, not memorized.

Ravi substitution

\(s=x+y+z\) \(\displaystyle\sin\frac A2=\sqrt{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}}\)
\(\Delta=\sqrt{xyz(x+y+z)}\) \(\displaystyle\sin\frac B2=\sqrt{\frac{(s-c)(s-a)}{ac}}\)
\(\displaystyle r=\sqrt{\frac{xyz}{x+y+z}}\) \(\displaystyle\sin\frac C2=\sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-b)}{ab}}\)
\(\displaystyle R=\frac{(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)}{4\sqrt{xyz(x+y+z)}}\) \(\displaystyle\cos\frac A2=\sqrt{\frac{s(s-a)}{bc}}\)
\(\displaystyle r_a=\frac{\sqrt{xyz(x+y+z)}}x\) \(\displaystyle\cos\frac B2=\sqrt{\frac{s(s-b)}{ac}}\)
\(\displaystyle r_b=\frac{\sqrt{xyz(x+y+z)}}y\) \(\displaystyle\cos\frac C2=\sqrt{\frac{s(s-c)}{ba}}\)
\(\displaystyle r_c=\frac{\sqrt{xyz(x+y+z)}}z\)

Lemma 66 — Substitutions to kill problems

The following substitutions are useful:

1.

If \(xyz=x+y+z+2\), use \(x=(a+b)/c\), \(y=(b+c)/a\), \(z=(c+a)/b\). Apply \((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=ab(a+b)+bc(b+c)+ca(c+a)+2abc\).

2.

If \(xy+yz+zx+2xyz=1\), use \(x=a/(b+c)\), \(y=b/(a+c)\), \(z=c/(a+b)\). Divide by \(xyz\) and convince yourself of its validity!

3.

If \(x^2+y^2+z^2-xyz=4\), use \(x=a+1/a\), \(y=b+1/b\), \(z=c+1/c\). Expand \(xyz=(a+1/a)(b+1/b)(c+1/c)\) and verify it yourself.

4.

If \(x^2+y^2+z^2+xyz=4\), use \(x=2\cos A\), \(y=2\cos B\), \(z=2\cos C\). Equivalently, if \(x^2+y^2+z^2+2xyz=1\), use \(x=\cos A\), \(y=\cos B\), \(z=\cos C\). Apply \(\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C+2\cos A\cos B\cos C=1\).

Application.

Find all positive real triples satisfying \(x^2+y^2+z^2=xyz+4\) and \(xy+yz+zx=x+y+z+6\). Put \(x=a+1/a\), \(y=b+1/b\), \(z=c+1/c\), with \(abc=1\). Then \[xy+yz+zx=(a+1/a)(b+1/b)+(b+1/b)(c+1/c)+(c+1/c)(a+1/a) =x+y+z+\sum\left(\frac ab+\frac ba\right).\] Thus \(a/b+b/a+b/c+c/b+a/c+c/a=6\), so \(a=b=c=1\) and \(x=y=z=2\).

Two ingenious trigonometric substitutions.

\[a^2+b^2+c^2\geq4\Delta\sqrt3 \qquad\text{(IMO 1961; Weitzenb\"ock's inequality).}\] Put \(\Delta=\tfrac12 ab\sin C\), so \(4\sqrt3\Delta=2\sqrt3ab\sin C\). The desired inequality is equivalent to \[\frac ab+\frac ba+\frac{c^2}{ab}\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}2\sqrt3\sin C.\] Apply the cosine rule \(c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C\). Then \[\frac{2a}{b}+\frac{2b}{a}\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}}2(\sqrt3\sin C+\cos C) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{a^2+b^2}{2ab}\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\geq}} \sin C\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\cos C\frac12=\sin(C+30^\circ).\] We have \((a^2+b^2)/(2ab)\geq1\geq\sin(C+30^\circ)\). Q.E.D.! This can also be resolved using Ravi substitutions. Do it! (There are 12 more solutions to the above problem; refer to P.S.T.)

Romania (2002).

If \(a,b,c\in(0,1)\), prove that \[\sqrt{abc}+\sqrt{(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)}<1.\] Let \(a=\cos^2 A\), \(b=\cos^2 B\), \(c=\cos^2 C\). We have \[\cos A\cos B\cos C+\sin A\sin B\sin C <\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B=\cos(A-B)\leq1.\] Q.E.D.!

Recall the application of Lemma 30 in the manuscript: it can be resolved without Schur’s inequality. For positive reals \(a,b,c\), prove that \[(a+b-c)(b+c-a)(a+c-b)\leq abc.\] Let \(x=a+b-c\), \(y=b+c-a\), and \(z=a+c-b\). Then \(a=(x+z)/2\), \(b=(x+y)/2\), and \(c=(y+z)/2\). The inequality reduces to \[xyz\mathrel{\stackrel{?}{\leq}}\frac{x+y}{2}\frac{y+z}{2}\frac{z+x}{2}, \qquad (x+y)(y+z)(z+x)\geq8xyz.\] A.W.D.! And we are done!

Clever AM–GM.

If \(a,b,c\) are positive reals satisfying \(a+b+c=1\), prove that \[\sqrt{a+bc}+\sqrt{b+ca}+\sqrt{c+ab}\leq2.\] We cannot do much with the nonhomogeneous expression inside the radical. So let’s homogenize!

\[\sqrt{a+bc}=\sqrt{a(a+b+c)+bc}=\sqrt{(a+b)(a+c)}\leq\frac{2a+b+c}{2}.\] Add the three similar inequalities to obtain \(\sum\sqrt{a+bc}\leq4(a+b+c)/2=2\). Q.E.D.!

Lemma 95 — Erdős–Mordell inequality

Let \(P\) be an arbitrary point in or on \(\triangle ABC\). If \(p_a,p_b,p_c\) are its distances from the sides, then \[PA+PB+PC\geq2(p_a+p_b+p_c),\] with equality if and only if \(AB=BC=CA\) and \(P\) is the circumcentre.

Application: IMO (1991).

Let \(P\) be a point inside \(\triangle ABC\). Prove that at least one of \(\angle PAB,\angle PBC,\angle PCA\) is at most \(30^\circ\).

Project \(P\) onto \(AB,BC,AC\). We have \(PA+PB+PC\geq2(PA'+PB'+PC')\), so at least one of \(PA\geq2PC'\), \(PB\geq2PA'\), or \(PC\geq2PB'\) holds. Without loss of generality, take \(PA\geq2PC'\). Then \(1/2\geq PC'/PA=\sin\angle PAB\), giving \(\angle PAB\leq30^\circ\) or \(\angle PAB\geq150^\circ\). If \(\angle PAB\geq150^\circ\), then \(\angle PBC<30^\circ\). Q.E.D.!

Pull the trigger

There are some trigonometric identities you should be aware of. Take them as standard lemmas.

Lemma 96 — Trigonometric identities

1.

\(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\).

2.

\(1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x\).

3.

\(1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x\).

4.

\(\sin(a\pm b)=\sin a\cos b\pm\cos a\sin b\).

5.

\(\cos(a\pm b)=\cos a\cos b\mp\sin a\sin b\).

6.

\(\tan(a\pm b)=(\tan a\pm\tan b)/(1\mp\tan a\tan b)\).

7.

\(\sin2a=2\sin a\cos a=2\tan a/(1+\tan^2a)\).

8.

\(\cos2a=\cos^2a-\sin^2a=(1-\tan^2a)/(1+\tan^2a)\).

9.

\(\sin3a=3\sin a-4\sin^3a\).

10.

\(\cos3a=4\cos^3a-3\cos a\).

11.

\(\sin(a/2)=\sqrt{(1-\cos a)/2}\).

12.

\(\cos(a/2)=\sqrt{(1+\cos a)/2}\).

13.

\(\sin a+\sin b=2\sin((a+b)/2)\cos((a-b)/2)\).

14.

\(\cos a+\cos b=2\cos((a+b)/2)\cos((a-b)/2)\).

15.

\(\cos a-\cos b=-2\sin((a-b)/2)\sin((a+b)/2)\).

16.

\(2\sin a\cos b=\sin(a+b)+\sin(a-b)\).

17.

\(2\cos a\cos b=\cos(a+b)+\cos(a-b)\).

18.

\(2\sin a\sin b=\cos(a-b)-\cos(a+b)\).

19.

\(\cos A=(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc)\).

20.

\(a/\sin A=b/\sin B=c/\sin C=2R\).

Lemma 97 — Trigonometric substitutions and inequalities

Here \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi\).

1.

\(ab+bc+ca=1\Longrightarrow a=\tan(\alpha/2),\ b=\tan(\beta/2),\ c=\tan(\gamma/2)\).

2.

\(a+b+c=abc\Longrightarrow a=\tan\alpha,\ b=\tan\beta,\ c=\tan\gamma\).

3.

\(a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc=1\Longrightarrow a=\sin(\alpha/2),\ b=\sin(\beta/2),\ c=\sin(\gamma/2)\).

4.

\(\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma\leq3\sqrt3/8\).

5.

\(\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma\leq1/8\).

6.

\(\sin(\alpha/2)\sin(\beta/2)\sin(\gamma/2)\leq1/8\).

7.

\(\cos(\alpha/2)\cos(\beta/2)\cos(\gamma/2)\leq3\sqrt3/8\).

8.

\(\tan(\alpha/2)+\tan(\beta/2)+\tan(\gamma/2)\geq\sqrt3\).

9.

\(a^2+b^2+c^2+2abc=1\) is equivalent to \(x^2+y^2+z^2+xyz=4\).

Let \(x,y,z>1\) be real numbers such that \(1/x+1/y+1/z=2\). Prove that \(\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\leq\sqrt{x+y+z}\). Let \(x=a+1\), \(y=b+1\), and \(z=c+1\). Then \(1/(a+1)+1/(b+1)+1/(c+1)=2\), that is, \(ab+bc+ca+2abc=1\). Substitute \(ab=\sin^2(\alpha/2)\), \(bc=\sin^2(\beta/2)\), and \(ac=\sin^2(\gamma/2)\). We require \(\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{bc}+\sqrt{ca}\leq3/2\), which follows by squaring the original inequality \(\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c\leq\sqrt{a+b+c+3}\) and cancelling terms. It becomes \(\sin(\alpha/2)+\sin(\beta/2)+\sin(\gamma/2)\leq3/2\), which follows from Jensen’s inequality. Q.E.D.!

Ingenious trigonometric substitution!

Let \(a,b,c\) be positive reals with \(a+b+c=1\). Prove that \[\sqrt{\frac{ab}{c+ab}}+\sqrt{\frac{bc}{a+bc}}+\sqrt{\frac{ca}{b+ca}}\leq\frac32.\] Once you get that sparkling idea, the solution is two lines! \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{\frac{ab}{c+ab}} =\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{\frac{ab}{c(a+b+c)+ab}} =\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\sqrt{\frac{ab}{(c+a)(c+b)}}.\] We know that \(a+b,b+c,c+a\) are the sides of a triangle. Therefore the last sum is \(\sin(\alpha/2)+\sin(\beta/2)+\sin(\gamma/2)\leq3/2\). Q.E.D.!

Let’s bash that system!

Find all triples \((x,y,z)\) of real numbers satisfying \[3(x+1/x)=4(y+1/y)=5(z+1/z)\tag{1}\] and \[xy+yz+zx=1.\tag{2}\] From (1), \[\frac{x}{3(1+x^2)}=\frac{y}{4(1+y^2)}=\frac{z}{5(1+z^2)}.\] Let \(x=\tan(\alpha/2)\), \(y=\tan(\beta/2)\), and \(z=\tan(\gamma/2)\). Now \(\sin\alpha=2x/(1+x^2)\), \(\sin\beta=2y/(1+y^2)\), and \(\sin\gamma=2z/(1+z^2)\), so \[\frac{\sin\alpha}{3}=\frac{\sin\beta}{4}=\frac{\sin\gamma}{5}.\] From (2), \(1/z=(x+y)/(1-xy)\), giving \(\cot(\gamma/2)=\tan((\alpha+\beta)/2)\). Hence \((\alpha+\beta)/2=\pi/2-\gamma/2\), and \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi\). Thus \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are the angles of a triangle, and the opposite sides are in the ratio \(3:4:5\). We have a right triangle with \(\gamma=\pi/2\), \(\sin\alpha=3/5\), and \(\sin\beta=4/5\). Therefore \(x=\tan(\alpha/2)=1/3\), \(y=\tan(\beta/2)=1/2\), and \(z=\tan(\gamma/2)=1\). So \((x,y,z)=(1/3,1/2,1)\) or \((-1/3,-1/2,-1)\). Q.E.D.!

Pull the trigger

Problem 1.

Triangle \(ABC\) is isosceles with \(AB=AC\) and \(\angle BAC=20^\circ\). Point \(P\) is on \(AC\) such that \(AP=BC\). Find \(\angle PBA\).

Let’s pull the trigger! The sine rule for \(\triangle ABP\) and \(\triangle BPC\) yields the following (angles in the calculations below are measured in degrees): \[\frac{BP}{\sin80}=\frac{BC}{\sin(x+20)},\qquad \frac{BP}{\sin20}=\frac{AP}{\sin x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\sin20}{\sin80}=\frac{\sin x}{\sin(x+20)}.\]

Consequently, \[\begin{align*} \frac1{4\cos20\cos40} &=\frac1{\sin(x+20)/\sin x},& \frac1{2\cos60+2\cos20}&=\frac{\sin x}{\sin(x+20)},\\ 1+2\cos20 &=\frac{\sin x\cos20+\cos x\sin20}{\sin x} =\cos20+\cot x\sin20. \end{align*}\] Hence \[\frac1{\sin20}=\cot x-\cot20 =\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}-\frac{\cos20}{\sin20} =\frac{\cos x\sin20-\sin x\cos20}{\sin x\sin20},\] and therefore \(\sin x=\sin20\cos x-\sin x\cos20=\sin(20-x)\). Now we obtain \(\sin x=\sin(20-x)\Rightarrow x=20-x\Rightarrow x=10^\circ\); or we could also have \(x=180k-(20-x)\Rightarrow x=180k-20+x\Rightarrow180k=20^\circ\), which is equivalent to the solution \(x=10\). Therefore \(\angle PBA=10^\circ\). Q.E.D.!

P.S. A gifted ninth grader by the name of Sergey Yusin proposed [unclear: the continuation is cut off at the bottom of the scan].

Problem 2.

Let the incircle of \(\triangle ABC\) touch \(BC,CA,AB\) at \(D,E,F\), respectively. If \(DI\) extended meets \(EF\) at \(K\), where \(I\) is the incentre of \(\triangle ABC\), prove that \(A,K,M\) are collinear, where \(M\) is the midpoint of \(BC\).

It suffices to show that \(AK\) extended meets \(BC\) at \(M\), where \(BM=MC\). Let’s proceed! Let’s pull the trigger!

The sine rule for \(\triangle FIK\) and \(\triangle KIE\) gives \[\frac{KE}{\sin B}=\frac{IK}{\sin(A/2)},\qquad \frac{KF}{\sin C}=\frac{IK}{\sin(A/2)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{KE}{KF}=\frac{\sin B}{\sin C}.\] Now apply the sine rule to \(\triangle AFK\) and \(\triangle AKE\) to obtain \[\frac{KE}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{AE}{\sin\angle AKE},\qquad \frac{KF}{\sin\beta}=\frac{AF}{\sin\angle AKF} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{KE}{KF}=\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\beta}.\] Thus \(\sin\alpha/\sin\beta=\sin B/\sin C\). Applying the sine rule again to \(\triangle ABC\) gives \[\frac{AB}{\sin C}=\frac{AC}{\sin B} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{AB}{AC}=\frac{\sin C}{\sin B}=\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\alpha}.\] Now we get \(AB\sin\alpha=AC\sin\beta\), and hence \(\frac12 AB\sin\alpha\cdot AM=\frac12 AC\sin\beta\cdot AM\). This implies \([ABM]=[ACM]\Rightarrow BM=MC\).

Ingenious trigonometric substitution.

Let \(x,y,z>0\) satisfy \(xy+yz+zx=3xyz\). Prove \((2y+2z+x)^2>12xyz\).

Let us pull the trigger! From the condition, \(1/(3x)+1/(3y)+1/(3z)=1\), hence \(1/(3x)+(y+z)/(3yz)=1\). Put \(1/(3x)=\cos^2\theta\) and \((y+z)/(3yz)=\sin^2\theta\). Then \(\cos\theta=1/\sqrt{3x}\) and \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{(y+z)/(3yz)}\). Using the obvious fact \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta>1\), we obtain \[\begin{align*} \frac1{\sqrt{3x}}+\frac{\sqrt{y+z}}{\sqrt{3yz}}>1 &\Longrightarrow \sqrt{3yz}+\sqrt{3x(y+z)}>3\sqrt{xyz}\\ &\Longrightarrow\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{x(y+z)}>\sqrt{3xyz}. \end{align*}\] Since \(\sqrt{yz}\leq(y+z)/2\) and \(\sqrt{x(y+z)}\leq(x+y+z)/2\), we get \(y+z+x/2>\sqrt{3xyz}\), proving the result. Quite innovatively done.

That inequality using trigonometric substitution was all pure dumbass; sorry I did not realize it. Pranjal pointed out that one should substitute \(12xyz=4xy+4yz+4zx\) and prove it directly. It was that obvious! Let me rephrase it. Let \(x,y,z\) be positive integers satisfying \(xy+yz+zx=3xyz\). Prove \(27xyz>8(x+y+z)\) in two different ways.

It was obvious!

Let \(a,b,c\) be sides of a triangle similar to \(ABC\). Prove \(2c^3+ab+bc+ca>a^3+b^3+c^3+3abc\). One may prove \((a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)+c^3>a^3+b^3+3abc\) by using \[a^3+b^3-c^3+3abc-\left(\sum ab\right)\left(\sum a\right) =\left(\sum a\right)\left(\sum a^2-2\sum ab\right)<0.\] Now, because it is homogeneous, assume \(a+b+c=1\). This also exploits the fact that \(a,b,c\) are the sides of a triangle similar to \(ABC\). The actual problem was to find the range of the area, given that \(ABC\) is equilateral. Try it!

APMO 1996: a wonder.

For the side lengths \(a,b,c\) of a triangle, prove \(\sqrt{a+b-c}+\sqrt{b+c-a}+\sqrt{c+a-b}\leq\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c\).

Write the left-hand side as \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(\sqrt{c+a-b}+\sqrt{a+b-c})/2\). Now use \((\sqrt x+\sqrt y)/2\leq\sqrt{(x+y)/2}\) to obtain \[\frac{\sqrt{c+a-b}+\sqrt{a+b-c}}2\leq\sqrt a,\qquad \frac{\sqrt{a+b-c}+\sqrt{b+c-a}}2\leq\sqrt b,\qquad \frac{\sqrt{b+c-a}+\sqrt{c+a-b}}2\leq\sqrt c.\] Now what? Q.E.D.!
excerptHtml: Let \(A,B\) be two points on the same side of a line \(XY\). Find \(M\) on that line such that \(AM+MB\) is minimal. This gives an alternative proof of the law of reflection. How?

title: Isogonal Conjugates and Pole–Polar Geometry
html:
Isogonal conjugates

I am back with a tantalizing, appetizing feast of mathematical insight! Let us begin with the intriguing concept of isogonal conjugates.

Lemma 98 — Isogonal conjugates

Given a point \(P\) inside triangle \(ABC\), reflect \(AP,BP,CP\) in the angle bisectors of \(A,B,C\). The resulting lines are concurrent. Their point of concurrence is the isogonal conjugate of \(P\) in triangle \(ABC\).

The circumcentre and orthocentre are isogonal conjugates of each other, while the incentre is its own isogonal conjugate.

Application.

Remember the IMO 1996 problem with a cut-and-paste solution discussed in Volume 1? For those who did not read Volume 1—how dare you!—here is the problem.

IMO (1996).

In triangle \(ABC\), an interior point \(P\) satisfies \(\angle APB-\angle C=\angle APC-\angle B\). Prove that the bisectors of \(\angle PBA\) and \(\angle PCA\), together with \(AP\), concur.

The angle condition on \(P\) gives \(\alpha+\delta=\beta+\gamma\). Angle bisectors concur to give the incentre; therefore \(AP\) and the bisectors of \(\angle ABP\) and \(\angle ACP\) are concurrent. “Game’s over.” The two points shown on \(AP\) need not coincide.

Guess that! Pythagoras Olympiad (1980).

In triangle \(ABC\), a point \(D\) satisfies \(\angle DCA=\angle DCB=\angle DBC=10^\circ\) and \(\angle DBA=20^\circ\). Find \(\angle CAD\).

“Sometimes we get lucky!” Apply trigonometric Ceva: \[\frac{\sin x}{\sin(130^\circ-x)}\frac{\sin20^\circ}{\sin10^\circ} \frac{\sin10^\circ}{\sin10^\circ}=1 \Longrightarrow\frac{\sin x}{\sin(130^\circ-x)} =\frac{\sin10^\circ}{\sin20^\circ}=\frac1{2\cos10^\circ}.\] Quickly guess \(x=30^\circ\). To write it formally, note \[\frac12\frac1{\cos10^\circ} =\sin30^\circ\frac1{\sin100^\circ}, \quad\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin100^\circ} =\frac{\sin x}{\sin(130^\circ-x)} \Longrightarrow x=30^\circ.\] It is still not fully general; anyway, it is a novel but nonsense method!

Lemma 99 — Concurrent perpendiculars

Let \(A,B,C\) form a triangle and \(P,Q,R\) be three points in the plane. The lines through \(P,Q,R\) perpendicular to \(BC,CA,AB\), respectively, are concurrent if and only if \(BP^2-PC^2+CQ^2-QA^2+AR^2-RB^2=0\).

This has quite a crispy application. Have a look!

IMOTC: Indian Team Selection Test 3 (2014).

For \(i=1,2,3\), let \(x_i,y_i\) be nonzero real numbers, and put \(v_i=x_i+y_i\). Suppose \[x_1x_2x_3=-y_1y_2y_3,\qquad x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2,\] and both \((v_1,v_2,v_3)\) and \((v_1^2,v_2^2,v_3^2)\) satisfy the triangle inequalities. Prove that exactly one of \(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3\) is negative. Let \(ABC\) have \(|BC|=v_1\), \(|CA|=v_2\), \(|AB|=v_3\). The triangle inequalities for the squares imply that \(ABC\) is acute. Take \(D,E,F\) on the extended sides \(BC,CA,AB\), respectively, with \(|BD|=x_1\), \(|CE|=x_2\), \(|AF|=x_3\), considering directed segments. The product condition and Menelaus’s theorem imply that \(D,E,F\) are collinear. The squared-sum condition implies that the perpendiculars at \(D,E,F\) to \(BC,CA,AB\) concur. Thus \(D,E,F\) form a Simson line, and their perpendiculars concur on the circumcircle. Since \(ABC\) is acute, exactly one lies outside the corresponding side segment, proving that exactly one number is negative. Quite intelligently done.

Lemma 103 — Trigonometric Ceva

In triangle \(ABC\), the lines \(AD,BE,CF\) are concurrent if and only if \(\sin\angle BAD\sin\angle ACF\sin\angle CBE =\sin\angle DAC\sin\angle BCF\sin\angle ABE\).

This powerful lemma proves not only concurrency but also collinearity!

Application: British MO 2013–14, round 2.

The point \(P\) lies inside \(ABC\) with \(\angle ABP=\angle PCA\). Choose \(Q\) so that \(PBQC\) is a parallelogram. Prove \(\angle QAB=\angle CAP\).

Solution due to Pranjal Warade. It is equivalent to proving that the isogonal conjugate \(P'\) of \(P\) lies on \(AQ\); in other words, that \(A,P',Q\) are collinear, or that \(AQ,BB',CC'\) concur. The source writes \[\frac{\sin\angle QAB}{\sin\angle QAC} \frac{\sin\angle ACC'}{\sin\angle BCC'} \frac{\sin\angle BB'}{\sin\angle ABB'} =\frac{\sin\angle QAB}{\sin\angle QAC} \frac{\sin\angle PCB}{\sin\angle PBC} =\frac{BQ}{QC}\frac{BP}{PC}=1.\] The marked points in the original drawing are not necessarily coincident.

Pole and polar argument

To master PAPA techniques, begin with the standard definitions.

In the drawing, \(P\) is the pole of \(XY\) and the line \(p=XY\) is the polar of \(P\). Here are three magical properties of PAPA. Draw the figures yourself for a better picture!

Lemma 104 — La Hire’s theorem: PAPA I

Let \(x,y\) be the polars of \(X,Y\), respectively. Then \(X\) lies on \(y\) if and only if \(Y\) lies on \(x\).

Lemma 105 — Intersection of polars: PAPA II

Let \(x,y,z\) be the polars of \(X,Y,Z\). Then \(Z=x\cap y\) if and only if \(z=XY\).

Lemma 106 — Complete quadrilateral: PAPA III

Let \(W,X,Y,Z\) lie on a circle. If \(P=XY\cap WZ\), \(Q=WX\cap ZY\), and \(R=XZ\cap YW\), then the polar of \(P\) is \(QR\). Similarly, the polar of \(Q\) is \(PR\).

I was amazed by Akopyan’s presentation of geometry theorems. His book, Geometry in Figures, is probably one of the best on Olympiad geometry. Let us adopt his style for some PAPA applications!

Problem 1.

Prove \(RS\perp UV\).

\(K\) lies on \(r\), so \(R\) lies on \(k\) by PAPA I, La Hire’s theorem. \(S\) lies on \(k\) by PAPA III, so \(k=RS\) and \(RS\perp UV\). Quite quickly done. Imagine the source: it appeared in the Chinese Mathematical Olympiad!

Problem 2.

Prove that \(P,E,F\) are collinear.

By definition, \(q=EF\). By PAPA III, \(P\) lies on \(q\). Therefore \(P,E,F\) are collinear. Quite quickly done. This also appeared in the Chinese Mathematical Olympiad, in 1997!

Challenge.

Solve the fourth geometry problem of the IMO Shortlist 2009 using PAPA.

title: Transformations: Rotating, Reflecting, and Cutting Figures
html:
Transformations

Lemma 92 — Transformation techniques

We can rotate figures, reflect figures, and invert figures. Let’s see some examples. Transformation techniques are a powerful tool that you must have in your arsenal.

Transformation I.

\(AB=BC=CA\), \(PA=3\), \(PB=4\), and \(PC=5\). Find \([ABC]\).

Rotate \(\triangle APB\) by \(60^\circ\) to \(AP'C\). Similarly obtain \(BP''C\) and \(BP'''A\). Now \([APB]=[AP'C]\), \([BPC]=[BP'''A]\), and \([APC]=[BP''C]\). Thus \([\text{hexagon}]=2[ABC]\). That hexagon consists of three quadrilaterals, each consisting of a \(3\)–\(4\)–\(5\) right triangle and an equilateral triangle. Hence \[[\text{hexagon}]=3\left(\frac12\cdot3\cdot4\right) +\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(3^2+4^2+5^2), \qquad[ABC]=9+\frac{25\sqrt3}{4}.\]

Transformation II: Pompeiu’s theorem.

Given a point \(P\) inside \(\triangle ABC\), the lengths \(PA,PB,PC\) always form the sides of a triangle. Rotate \(\triangle ABC\) through \(60^\circ\) about \(C\) to \(A'AC\). Then \(\triangle PP'C\) is equilateral, so \(PP'=PC\). Now notice \(\triangle APP'\): its sides are \(PA,PB,PC\). W\(^5\).

There is another beautiful extension: if \(P\) lies along arc \(BC\) of the circumcircle of the equilateral triangle \(ABC\), then \(PA=PB+PC\).

Transformation III.

Choose one point on each side of a unit square. Let the quadrilateral formed by those points have sides \(a,b,c,d\). Prove that \(a+b+c+d\geq2\sqrt2\).

Use multiple reflections in the sides to obtain a solution. The solution I like most is the following. The perimeter of \(ABCD\) is minimal if it is a closed light path. All those light polygons have perimeter \(2\sqrt2\): when you join the midpoints of the sides, you get a light polygon with perimeter \(2\sqrt2\). Therefore \(a+b+c+d\geq2\sqrt2\). Q.E.D.!

Transformation IV.

Let us solve the Cut and Paste IMO problem using inversion.

Perform inversion of the inside triangle with respect to \(I(P,r)\). The angle condition on \(P\) implies \(\alpha+\theta=\beta+\gamma\), so \(\triangle A'B'C'\) is isosceles. Thus \(A'B'=A'C'\). Using the distance relation, \[\frac{AB\cdot r^2}{PA\cdot PB}=\frac{AC\cdot r^2}{PC\cdot PA} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{AB}{BP}=\frac{AC}{PC}.\] W\(^5\). Q.E.D.

Recall the application of Lemma 98 and the cut-and-paste solution. That was my hundredth lemma; here is an application to complete the formality!

Tournament of Towns (2002).

In triangle \(ABC\), a point \(P\) satisfies \(\angle ABP=\angle ACP\) and \(\angle PBC=\angle PAC\). Prove using pure geometry that \(P\) is the orthocentre.

This is obvious using trigonometric Ceva, but they expect a purely geometric solution. Give me those scissors!

I hope the figure is not looking like Greek and Latin to you! Anybody got some glue? Let us repaste it. The rearranged pieces give \(\angle PAB=\angle PCB=z\), and then \(2(x+y+z)=180^\circ\). Thus \(x+y+z=90^\circ\), so \(P\) is the orthocentre of \(ABC\). This was my hundredth lemma with an application. What was yours?
excerptHtml: We can rotate figures, reflect figures, and invert figures. Let’s see some examples. Transformation techniques are a powerful tool that you must have in your arsenal.

title: Puzzles, Surprises, and Marvellous Methods of Multiplication
html:
Lemma 45 — ASA lemma

Always stay alert, always stay awake.

Do not take me for a fool: I mean what I state. Let me show examples where an Olympiad student solves without presence of mind. Find \(a^2+b^2+c^2\) where \(a^2+2b=6\), \(b^2+4c=-7\), and \(c^2+6a=-13\). Adding gives \[\begin{align*} (a^2+2b)+(b^2+4c)+(c^2+6a)&=-14,\\ (a^2+6a)+(b^2+2b)+(c^2+4c)&=-14,\\ (a^2+6a+9)+(b^2+2b+1)+(c^2+4c+4)&=0,\\ (a+3)^2+(b+1)^2+(c+2)^2&=0. \end{align*}\] Thus \(a=-3,b=-1,c=-2\), and \(a^2+b^2+c^2=9+1+4=14\). If this sounds perfect, “slap yourself and wake up!” Notice that \(a=-3,b=-1,c=-2\) do not satisfy the first and last equations. Where did we go wrong? “We blindly assumed \(a,b,c\) to be real numbers!” Here is another example.

Leningrad Mathematical Olympiad.

In triangle \(ABC\), \(\angle B=60^\circ\), \(AD\perp BC\), and \(CE\perp AB\). Prove that the circumcentre of \(ABC\) lies on the common bisector of \(\angle AOE\) and \(\angle COD\). Let us begin by drawing a neat figure.

Let \(\omega\) be the circumcircle of triangle \(AOC\), meeting the common bisector \(\ell\) at \(X\). Then \(AOXC\) is cyclic. Drop the perpendicular from \(X\) to \(AC\) at \(M\). We have \[\begin{align*} \angle DOE&=120^\circ=\angle AOC=\angle AXC,\\ \angle DOC&=\angle ABC=60^\circ=2\angle XOC, \quad\text{so }\angle XOC=30^\circ,\\ \angle XOC&=\angle XAM=30^\circ=\pi/2-\angle AXM, \quad\text{so }\angle AXM=60^\circ. \end{align*}\] Thus \(\angle MXC=60^\circ=\angle AXM\), giving \(\triangle AXM\cong\triangle BXM\) and \(MA=MC\). Therefore \(XM\) is a perpendicular bisector. Since \(\angle AXC=120^\circ=2\angle ABC\), \(X\) is the circumcentre, so the circumcentre lies on \(\ell\).

Did you notice something missing here too? Turn the page to find out! There are more such examples.

Average speed.

A plane travels from \(A\) to \(B\) at \(160\) mph and returns from \(B\) to \(A\) at \(240\) mph. Find its average speed. The usual temptation is \((160+240)/2=200\) mph, giving a wrong answer. The two trips do not take the same time. If their common distance is \(L\), then \(T_1=L/160\) and \(T_2=L/240\). The average time is \((T_1+T_2)/2\), while total time is \(T_1+T_2=L/160+L/240=L/96\). Total distance is \(2L\), so average speed is \(2L/(L/96)=192\) mph.

“Here one completely forgets the possibility that the point \(X\) may even coincide with \(O\).”

Ramanujan’s problem.

Find \(\sqrt{1+2\sqrt{1+3\sqrt{1+4\sqrt{1+5\sqrt{1+\cdots}}}}}\). Use \[x+1=\sqrt{1+x(x+2)} =\sqrt{1+x\sqrt{1+(x+1)(x+3)}} =\sqrt{1+x\sqrt{1+(x+1)\sqrt{1+\cdots}}}.\] Put \(x=2\).

Without calculating \(\sqrt2\), show that \(7/5\) is closer to it than \(3/2\). We do not know \(\sqrt2\), but we do know \((\sqrt2)^2\).

Magic of coordinate geometry.

Given \(\vec P(t)=A(\hat\imath\cos(kt)-\hat\jmath\sin(kt))\), determine the angle between \(\vec P(t)\) and \(\vec F(t)\), where \(P(t)\) and \(F(t)\) are momentum and force. We have \[\vec F(t)=\frac{dP(t)}{dt}=-Ak\sin(kt)\hat\imath-Ak\cos(kt)\hat\jmath =\frac{\partial(A\cos(kt))}{\partial t}\hat\imath -\frac{\partial(A\sin(kt))}{\partial t}\hat\jmath.\] Now let us throw this bunch of information onto our coordinate plane.

\[\begin{aligned} FO&=\sqrt{A^2k^2\sin^2(kt)+A^2k^2\cos^2(kt)}=Ak,\\ PO&=\sqrt{A^2\cos^2(kt)+A^2\sin^2(kt)}=A,\\ FP&=\sqrt{A^2(\cos(kt)+k\sin(kt))^2+A^2(k\cos(kt)-\sin(kt))^2} =A\sqrt{k^2+1}. \end{aligned}\] We have \(OF^2+OP^2=FP^2\), so \(\angle FOP=\pi/2=90^\circ\). Q.E.D.!

You are not supposed to do these bullshits: just put \(t=0\) in \(P(t)\) and \(F(t)\). This gives \(P(t)=A\hat\imath\) and \(F(t)=-Ak\hat\jmath\). \(P\) is along \(X\), and \(F\) is along \(-Y\), so \(\angle FOP=\pi/2\). Q.E.D.!

You know what? You are not even supposed to play those dirty tricks. In two-dimensional motion, \(\vec a\cdot\vec v=0\), \(\vec F=m\vec a\), and \(\vec P=m\vec v\). Thus \(\vec F\cdot\vec P=\vec a\cdot\vec v=0\), giving \(\vec F\perp\vec P\). Another Q.E.D.! Enough!

Source note. PDF page 41 repeats the two notebook pages on PDF page 40, including the normalization lemma and the momentum–force diagram. That repeated spread is transcribed once above.

British mathematical problem (2014).

Prove that it is impossible to have a cuboid whose volume, surface area, and perimeter are numerically equal. We have \(V=lbh\), \(S=2(lb+bh+hl)\), and \(P=4(l+b+h)\). It follows that \[\frac1l+\frac1b+\frac1h=\frac12, \qquad\frac1{lb}+\frac1{bh}+\frac1{hl}=\frac14.\] Now \[\left(\frac1l+\frac1b+\frac1h\right)^2 =\frac1{l^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{h^2} +2\left(\frac1{lb}+\frac1{bh}+\frac1{hl}\right).\] Thus \(1/4-1/2=-1/2=1/l^2+1/b^2+1/h^2<0\), a contradiction! Q.E.D.! Find another way to solve it!

Was it that simple?

Ten Indians were blindfolded and dressed in caps, each of one of two colours. Their blindfolds were removed. They stood so that the tenth could see nine people in front, the ninth could see eight, and so on. A person who could guess his cap’s colour would be saved; otherwise he would be executed. Can they have a strategy that saves the maximum number of Indians?

The tenth should say red if he sees an even number of red caps, and green otherwise. If the tenth is shot, the ninth can be sure of the tenth person’s cap colour and that caps of that colour are odd in number. He would count the caps of that colour; if he finds an even number, then… or otherwise he can guess his colour, and so on. I bet you did not understand the solution. Even I want that to happen:

it was pretty hard to write down the solution, but it is still not a solution being a solution! Try that!

Common sense is like a deodorant: those who need it the most lack it!

1. Proportional angles.

Is \(\triangle ABC\sim\triangle PQR\)? You might be wondering: if the sides are proportional, the triangles are similar, but what if the angles are proportional? To tell you the reality, it’s all a big dumbass! Since \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^\circ\) and \(\alpha k+\beta k+\gamma k=180^\circ\), we have \(k=1\). Thus the angles of \(\triangle PQR\) are also \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\), so \(\triangle ABC\sim\triangle PQR\). Q.E.D.!

2. Solve the puzzle.

\(1=5\), \(2=25\), \(3=325\), \(4=4325\). Then \(5={}?\)

3. Two digits.

Construct the smallest possible integer using just two digits. You know what? You can create a number as small as possible! But how?!

Answers.

2. If \(1=5\), then \(5=1\). Q.E.D.!

3. \(-\bigl[(9!!!!\cdots!)^{(9!!!!\cdots!)}\bigr]\). This is how it should be done!

Mission impossible

1. Compass-only midpoint.

Construct the midpoint of a line segment without using a ruler, but only a compass! I will not tell you exactly what I did. Go figure it out for yourself!

2. Equilateral triangle.

Inscribe an equilateral triangle inside an arbitrary triangle \(ABC\). Challenge!

Marvellous methods of multiplication: triple M

The way Egyptian nerds did it!

Suppose you want to multiply \(11\times17\). They do the following:

Half sequence \(\boxed{11}\) \(\boxed5\) \(2\) \(\boxed1\) \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) in general
Double it \(17\) \(34\) \(68\) \(136\) \(2n\) in general

Identify the odd entries in the half sequence, and add the corresponding numbers from the double sequence. We have \(11\mapsto17\), \(5\mapsto34\), and \(1\mapsto136\), so the sum is \(17+34+136=187=11\times17\). Why does that bullshit work? Let’s find out. Suppose we are interested in the product \(N\times M\).

Half \(N\) \(N/2\) \(N/4\) \(N/8\) \(N/16\) \(\cdots\) \(1\)
Double \(M\) \(2M\) \(4M\) \(8M\) \(16M\) \(\cdots\) \(2^kM\)

Express \(N\) in binary: \(N=2^{\alpha_1}+2^{\alpha_2}+\cdots+2^{\alpha_n}\). For example, \(11=2^3+2^1+2^0\). Our product \(N\times M\) is nothing but \(2^{\alpha_1}M+\cdots+2^{\alpha_n}M\). Each and every term \(2^{\alpha_1}M,\ldots,2^{\alpha_n}M\) must have occurred somewhere in the double sequence. If we find where it occurred, then a mere addition of those terms gives the product \(N\times M\).

Now notice the half sequence: a general entry is of the form \(N/2^n\). If \(2^n\) is a part of the decomposition of \(N\), then \[\begin{aligned} \frac N{2^n} &=\frac{2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_j}+2^n+2^{b_1}+\cdots+2^{b_k}}{2^n}\\ &=\frac{2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_j}}{2^n}+\frac{2^n}{2^n} +\frac{2^{b_1}+\cdots+2^{b_k}}{2^n} =\text{even}+1+\text{decimal}=\text{odd}, \end{aligned}\] where \(a_i>n\) for all \(i\), and \(b_i<n\) for all \(i\). We have \((2^{b_1}+\cdots+2^{b_k})/2^n<1\), because \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}1/2^k=1\). Now we claim that \(2^{\alpha_i}\) is a part of the decomposition of \(N\) if and only if \(N/2^{\alpha_i}\) is odd. The corresponding double-sequence entry is \(2^{\alpha_i}M\). Adding all such terms gives \(2^{\alpha_1}M+\cdots+2^{\alpha_n}M=N\times M\). W\(^5\): Which Was What We Wanted! Q.E.D.!

Parabolic multiplication.

Suppose you want \(4\times3\). Take \(A(4,16)\) and \(B(-3,9)\). Join \(AB\): its intersection with the \(Y\)-axis gives the product! Why does this happen? Use your knowledge of coordinates to find out why.

A geometry problem leads to a continued fraction.

\(T_1\) is an isosceles triangle with circumcircle \(K\). Let \(T_2\) be another isosceles triangle inscribed in \(K\), whose base is one of the equal sides of \(T_1\), and which overlaps the interior of \(T_1\). Similarly create \(T_3\), and so on. Do the triangles \(T_n\) approach an equilateral triangle as \(n\to\infty\)?

The figure explains the vertex angles of \(T_1,T_2,T_3,T_4\). We claim that the vertex angle of the \(T_n\) triangle is \(x\): \[x=\cfrac{180^\circ-\cfrac{180^\circ-\cfrac{180^\circ-\alpha}{2}}{2}}{2} \quad\cdots\quad=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{90(-1)^k}{2^k}.\] Now, as \(n\to\infty\), we have \(x=(\pi/2)/(1+1/2)=\pi/3=60^\circ\). W\(^5\). Q.E.D.!

Out of the box.

Place one of \(+,-,\times,\div\) in each blank of \(8\ \underline{\kern .5cm}\ 8\ \underline{\kern .5cm}\ 8=6\). The answer, due to Shovan, is \((8\div8)+8=6\). Think it is wrong? Turn the page upside down, then decide!

A trivial trick!

Solve in real numbers: \(x=\sqrt{x+2\sqrt{x+2\sqrt{x+2\sqrt{x+2\sqrt{3x}}}}}\). The source replaces \(3x\) by \(x+2x\), continues the nested radical indefinitely, and writes \(x=\sqrt{x+2x}\). Thus \(x^2=3x\), giving \(x=0\) or \(x=3\). Q.E.D.!

I remember asking this question; why do not you fiddle with it too? Is \((-1)^\pi\) positive or negative? I hear you saying “WTF!!!”

The answer was quite unexpected! \(e^{i\pi}=-1\) gives \(e^{i\pi^2}=(-1)^\pi=\cos(\pi^2)+i\sin(\pi^2)\). Since \(\pi^2\) is not a root of \(\sin\theta\), this is complex, so \((-1)^\pi\) is complex too! There is another proof. Represent \(\pi=a/b\), where \(a,b\) are not necessarily finite: \(\pi=(31415925\ldots)/10^\infty\). Since we cannot determine the last digit of \(\pi\), we are done! Q.E.D.!

Find \(a^2+b^2+c^2\) where \(a^2+2b=6\), \(b^2+4c=-7\), and \(c^2+6a=-13\). Adding gives \[\begin{align*} (a^2+2b)+(b^2+4c)+(c^2+6a)&=-14,\\ (a^2+6a)+(b^2+2b)+(c^2+4c)&=-14,\\ (a^2+6a+9)+(b^2+2b+1)+(c^2+4c+4)&=0,\\ (a+3)^2+(b+1)^2+(c+2)^2&=0. \end{align*}\] Thus \(a=-3,b=-1,c=-2\), and \(a^2+b^2+c^2=9+1+4=14\). title: Problems Proposed by S. Ramanujan
html:
Problems proposed by S. Ramanujan

Let us compile some problems proposed by the mathematical god, S. Ramanujan.

1.

Prove without calculus that \(\frac32\log2=1+\frac2{4^3-4}+\frac2{8^3-8}+\frac2{12^3-12}+\cdots\).

2.

Show that it is possible to solve the equations \[\begin{array}{ll} x+y+z=a,&px+qy+rz=b,\\ p^2x+q^2y+r^2z=c,&p^3x+q^3y+r^3z=d,\\ p^4x+q^4y+r^4z=e,&p^5x+q^5y+r^5z=f. \end{array}\]

3.

Find \(\sqrt{1+2\sqrt{1+3\sqrt{1+4\sqrt{1+\cdots}}}}\) and \(\sqrt{6+2\sqrt{7+3\sqrt{8+\cdots}}}\).

4.

If \(\alpha\beta=\pi\), show that \(\sqrt\alpha\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}/\cosh(\alpha x)\,dx =\sqrt\beta\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}/\cosh(\beta x)\,dx\).

5.

Show that Euler’s constant \(\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+1/2+\cdots+1/n-\log n)\) equals \[\log2-1\left(\frac2{3^3-3}\right) -2\left(\frac2{6^3-6}+\frac2{9^3-9}+\frac2{12^3-12}\right)-\cdots,\] the first term in the \(n\)th group being \(2/\bigl(((3^n+3)/2)^3-(3^n+3)/2\bigr)\).

6.

Show that \[\prod_{n=1}^\infty\left(1+\frac1{n^3}\right)=\frac1\pi\cosh\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad \prod_{n=2}^\infty\left(1-\frac1{n^3}\right)=\frac1{3\pi}\cosh\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{2}.\]

7.

For any odd positive integer \(n\), show that \(\int_0^\infty\sin(nx)/\bigl((\cosh x+\cos x)x\bigr)\,dx=\pi/4\), and hence prove \[\frac\pi8=\frac1{\cosh(\pi/(2n))+\cos(\pi/(2n))} -\frac1{3\bigl(\cosh(3\pi/(2n))+\cos(3\pi/(2n))\bigr)}+\cdots.\]

8.

If \(\sin(x+y)=2\sin((x-y)/2)\) and \(\sin(y+z)=2\sin((y-z)/2)\), prove \[\sqrt[4]{\tfrac12\sin x\cos z}+\sqrt[4]{\tfrac12\cos x\sin z} =\sqrt[12]{\sin2y}.\] Verify this when \(\sin2x=(\sqrt5-2)^3(4+\sqrt{15})^2\), \(\sin2y=\sqrt5-2\), and \(\sin2z=(\sqrt5-2)^3(4-\sqrt{15})^2\).

9.

Show that \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty n/(e^{2n\pi}-1)=1/24-1/(8\pi)\).

10.

Show that \[\begin{align*} (6a^2-4ab+4b^2)^3 &=(3a^2+5ab-8b^2)^3+(4a^2-4ab+6b^2)^3\\ &\quad +(5a^2-5ab-3b^2)^3, \end{align*}\] and find other quadratic expressions.

11.

\(2^n-7\) is a perfect square for \(n=3,4,5,7,15\). Find other values.

12.

Show that \[\prod_{j=0}^\infty\bigl(1+e^{-(2j+1)\pi\sqrt{55}}\bigr) =\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3+2\sqrt5}}{\sqrt2}\right) \bigl(e^{-\pi\sqrt{55}}\bigr)^{1/24}.\]
excerptHtml: Prove without calculus that \(\frac32\log2=1+\frac2{4^3-4}+\frac2{8^3-8}+\frac2{12^3-12}+\cdots\).

title: Problems for Anant Mudgal
html:
Problems for Anant Mudgal

\(\mathrm{P1}^{***}\).

Let \(a,b,c\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\min(a,b,c)=1/2\) and \(a+b+c=3\), and let \(v^2-3v+1=0\). Prove \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(a^2-bc+1)/(bc+va-1)\geq0\). Inequality.

\(\mathrm{P2}^{*}\).

Prove the continued-fraction identity \[\left(\displaystyle 1+\dfrac{1+\dfrac{1+\dfrac{1+\dfrac{1+\cdots}{4}}{3}}{2}}{1}\right)^2 =\displaystyle 2+\dfrac{4+\dfrac{8+\dfrac{16+\dfrac{32+\cdots}{4}}{3}}{2}}{1}.\]

Algebra.

P3.

Find all continuous \(f:(1,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) such that \(f(x+y)f(x)f(y)=f(x+y)(f(x)+f(y))-f(x)f(y)\). Functional equation.

P4.

Prove that \(\{\pi\}=\sqrt{32+\sqrt{512+\sqrt{8192+\cdots}}} (1/15+1/63+1/143)-1\). Computations.

P5.

Among the numbers in \([100000,200000]\), there exists a prime gap \(\ll12\). Number theory.

P6.

Given any set of \(n\) points, \(n\geq3\), define a \(k\)-rich line to be one containing exactly \(k\) points. Prove that the number of \(2\)-rich and \(3\)-rich lines counted together is more than “\(2\) or \(3\)”. Geometry.

P7.

Given \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty1/n^2=\pi^2/6\), compute the probability that a number \(n\) is square-free, meaning that it has no square divisor other than \(1\). Probability theory.

P8.

For positive \(a,b,c\) with \(\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}1/(a+b+1)=1\), prove \(\sqrt[4]{\prod_{\mathrm{cyc}}(a^2-ab+b^2)}+abc\geq2\). Open!

P9.

Under the same constraint, prove \[\sqrt[4]{\prod_{\mathrm{cyc}}(a^2-ab+b^2)} +\frac{2abc}{\sqrt{a+b+c+1}}\geq\sqrt{a+b+c+1}.\] I forgot the solution!

title: Thrilling Thirty: The Surviving Problems
html:
A note to the reader

This is not the end of our journey; there is a lot more to come. I decided not to write the 100th lemma. Rather, I have given you, the reader, the option to choose one of the best ideas and title that the 100th lemma! Anyway, I myself formed a thrilling thirty problems. Take that as a sweet dessert after such a memorable feast.

Happy Problem Solving!

Do not forget: I’ll be back. Ba Bum Bum Bum…

Thrilling Thirty

1.

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(M\) is the midpoint of the base \(BC\). The triangle is dissected into two parts of equal area. Find a way to dissect one piece into as few pieces as possible so that their rearrangement tiles the other exactly.

2.

Given a triangle \(ABC\) in a plane \(R\), construct a geometrical entity \(\Psi\) in the plane so that a suitable isometry with respect to \(\Psi\) transforms the base \(BC\) to \(B_1C_1\), where the perimeter of \(ABC\) equals the perimeter of \(AB_1C_1\).

3.

A cylinder fits a complete sphere exactly. Another sphere of maximum radius is introduced into the cylinder so that it fits in exactly. Find its radius if the radius of the first sphere is \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\).

4.

Determine the number of ways to arrange circles subject to the following conditions:

  • Each circle touches at least one other circle.

  • No two circles intersect at more than one point.

  • Two configurations are distinct if they have a point of differentiation other than distance or size.

Challenge: Generalize to \(n\) circles.

5.

Let \(f\) be a function such that \(f(1)=y_0\) and \(f(n)=h(f(n-1))\), where \(h\) is a function of \(x\). If \[\psi(f(n-1))-\frac1{f(n-1)}=\frac{\psi(f(n))}{f(n-1)},\] determine \(\psi(x)\) in terms of \(x\).

6.

There are infinitely many boxes, numbered \(1,2,3,\ldots\). Put balls in each box so that the GCD of the numbers of balls in any two boxes equals the GCD of their box numbers. Pick the box numbered with your year of birth and find the number of balls in it.

7.

Find all pairs \((n,x)\), where \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(0\leq x\leq2\), such that \(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\arcsin(x/2^k)=\pi\).

8.

Prove that for every \(n\) there exists an \(m\) such that \(m^4\equiv406\pmod{3^n}\).

9.

Given two circles intersecting at \(X\) and \(Y\), draw a chord \(AB\) in the first circle. Extend \(AX\) and \(BY\) to intersect the second circle at \(A^1,B^1\); construct a circle passing through \(A^1,B^1\). Extend \(XA^1\) and \(YB^1\) to intersect the third circle at \(A^2,B^2\). Iterate this 2014 times. Determine the number of trapeziums in the resulting configuration.

10.

Suppose \(1/2014=1/x_1+1/x_2+\cdots+1/x_n\), where \(x_n>x_{n-1}>\cdots>x_2>x_1>1\) are positive integers. Find \(n\) and the \(x_i\) satisfying this equation. Are there infinitely many solutions?

11.

Prove the following binomial identity: \[\frac{\binom n0}{3}-\frac{\binom n1}{4}+\frac{\binom n2}{5} -\frac{\binom n3}{6}+\cdots\infty =\frac2{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}.\]

12.

Compute the following ascending fraction: \[1+\cfrac{1+\cfrac{1+\cfrac{1+\cfrac{1+\cfrac{1+\cdots}{4870847}}{2207}}{47}}{7}}{3}.\] Here \(7=3^2-2\), \(47=7^2-2\), \(2207=47^2-2\), \(4870847=2207^2-2\), and so on.

13.

If \(\Psi(x)\) is a function of \(x\) defined by \(\Psi(\alpha)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom\alpha k\), prove the recursion relation \[\sum_{k=0}^{\alpha}\Psi[\alpha-(k+1)]\Psi(\alpha) =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^{\alpha+1}}{n!}.\]

14.

If \(a,b,c\) are positive reals such that \(\sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt c=3\sqrt2\)…

[unclear: the remainder of Problem 14 is absent from the supplied scan].

15–17.

[unclear: these problems are absent from the supplied scan].

18.

[unclear: the beginning of Problem 18 is absent; only the following closing fragment survives].

And he told me, “We can write \((2xz=xz+xz)\)!!” to which I responded, “Are you serious!”

19.

Given positive reals \(a,b,c,d\) satisfying \(ac-bd=\sqrt{(1-a^2)(1-c^2)}-\sqrt{(1-b^2)(1-d^2)}\), prove that \(ad+bc\leq0\). Further prove that the inequality is also satisfied if \[abc-d=\sqrt{1-c^2}\left[\sqrt{(1-a^2)(1-b^2)} +\sqrt{b^2(1-a^2)}+\sqrt{a^2(1-b^2)}\right].\] An inspiration from Vedant’s problem!

20.

Triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral, \(P\) is a point on its circumcircle, and \(Q\) is any point outside the circle such that \(PB=PQ=5\,\mathrm m\). Vedant and Rahul start running along \(PA\) and \(PB\), respectively, with the same speed \(v\). I start running along \(QP\) with speed \(u\); after reaching \(P\), I decide to run with speed \(v\) towards \(C\).

It is found that Vedant and I take the same time to reach our respective destinations. Vedant says that we all run uniformly on our paths. Is Vedant a genius to point that out, or was he just out of his mind!

Furthermore, Rahul and I inform Vedant that it took us 5 and 10 seconds, respectively, to reach our destinations. Vedant responds that if \(BC=BQ\), then \(\triangle BQC\) is equilateral. Is Vedant a brainbox, or are we dumbasses?

21.

Imagine a frictionless rectangular billiard table with dimensions \((503\times p)\) metres, where \(p\) is prime. A ball is hit from a corner of the table with velocity \(\sqrt{2p^2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), making an angle of \(45^\circ\) with the rails. The ball rolls on the table for about 503 seconds before falling into a pocket. Vedant miscounts the number of times the ball hits a wall of the table, getting four more than the actual number. What number does Vedant obtain if the ball lands in the pocket from which it was originally shot?

22.

Vedant discovers a new particle. To respect his contribution, let us name it “VEDU” in his honour! It has a weird property: two particles brought close together bind to form a single particle.

There are three mutually intersecting unit circles such that the system of circles is symmetric about the lines \(PP^*,QQ^*,RR^*\), where these are their respective common chords. Let \(A,B,C\) be the midpoints of arcs \(PR,RQ,PQ\), respectively, such that the area of \(\triangle ABC\) is maximum. Six VEDUs are launched simultaneously with the same velocity along the circular paths \(AP,AR,BQ,BR,CQ,CP\). If the length of arc \(PR\) is \(x\), determine the velocity of each particle so that exactly after 2014 seconds all that remains is one VEDU.

23.

Prove that one cannot dissect a regular pentagon into exactly 2014 triangular pieces by a series of consecutive cuts. Furthermore, prove that one can always divide it into 2013 triangular pieces.

A cut is a straight line segment connecting two vertices. A new vertex is formed where two or more cuts intersect. A cut may connect two new vertices, two original vertices, or an original vertex and a new vertex.

24.

Obama and Osama are separated by some distance. A mirror starts moving from Obama to Osama along a certain path such that they can see each other. They spend time teasing each other (of course, by making those bullshit faces). Throughout the mirror’s journey, the sum of the angles of incidence and reflection of the light rays emanating from Obama equals the total angle of rotation of the mirror about the point of incidence \(P\). During the journey, there is a stage at which \(P\) is equidistant from Obama and Osama. If that distance is \(20\sqrt7\) metres, find the distance between Obama and Osama.

25.

Given positive reals \(a,b,c\), prove \[\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}\frac{(a+1)^2+(b+1)^2}{(a+b)(a+b+c)}>\frac{2014}{1024}.\]

26.

Given nine distinct integers satisfying \((x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)+(y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2)=z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2\), prove that there are infinitely many families of solutions of this Diophantine equation, even if no three of the nine integers \((x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z_1,z_2,z_3)\) form a Pythagorean triplet.

Open problem: Can one find all families of solutions of this Diophantine equation?

27.

Elementary puzzle:

  • If you take away my last two digits and place them in any order in front of me, I am an \(x\)-digit number, where \(x\) is my first digit.

  • If you take the first digit raised to the reciprocal of the number of sevens in me, you get my seventh digit.

  • Take the difference of my seventh and eighth digits: you get the number of zeroes in me. If you take the sum, you get back my first digit.

  • If you remove my first digit, my number of digits equals my seventh digit from the last. I behave the same way if you remove my first two digits.

28.

For every nonzero integer \(n\), there exists a pair of primes \((p,q)\) such that \(n\mid(p-q)\). Such pairs also occur infinitely often.

29.

Let \((x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)\in\mathbb R\). Prove that the following inequality holds if and only if \(n\geq m\): \[\sqrt[m]{\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{x_i^m}{m^m}} \geq\sqrt[n]{\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{x_i^n}{n^n}}.\] Equality holds if and only if \(n=m\).

30.

Define \(x_k=(a^k+b^k+c^k)/3\), where \(a,b,c\) are positive reals. Prove \[\frac{x_1^5}{x_2x_3}+\frac{x_2^2}{x_1x_3}+\frac{x_3}{x_1x_2}>3.\]

THE END??

title: The Language of Category Theory (in Algebraic Topology)
html:
Philosophy in Action

Definition 1 — Category

A category \(\mathcal C\) consists of a class of objects, denoted by \(\Ob(\mathcal C)\), and a class of composable morphisms, denoted by \(\Mor(\mathcal C)\).

Example 1

\(\cat{Sets}\), \(\cat{Grps}\), \(\cat{Rings}\), \(\cat{Top}\), \(k\text{-}\cat{Top}\), \(\cat{Top}_*\), \(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*\), \(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*/{\sim}\), \(\cat{CRings}\), \(\cat{Man}\), \(\ldots\).

Definition 2 — Functor

For categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), a functor \(F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) gives maps \(F\colon\Ob(\mathcal C)\to\Ob(\mathcal D)\) and \(F\colon\Mor(\mathcal C)\to\Mor(\mathcal D)\) such that \[F(*\xrightarrow{f}*)=\bigl(F(*)\xrightarrow{F(f)}F(*)\bigr),\qquad F(\id_*)=\id_{F(*)},\qquad F(f\circ g)=F(f)\circ F(g).\]

Example 2

Let \(\cat{PCTop}\) be the category of path-connected topological spaces. The assignments \(X\mapsto\pi_1(X)\) (the fundamental group of \(X\)) and \[(h\colon X\to Y)\longmapsto \bigl([f]\xmapsto{h_*}[h\circ f]\colon\pi_1(X)\to\pi_1(Y)\bigr)\] give a functor from \(\cat{CTop}\) to \(\cat{Grps}\). Moreover, \(\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\mapsto\mathbb Z\), \(\partial\mathbb D\mapsto\mathbb Z\), and \(z\mapsto z^2\) maps to \(n\mapsto2n\).

Functors give us ways to understand certain relations in a category better by translating them to a different category. Given two such translations, is there a way not to get lost in translation?

Definition 3 — Natural transformation

Let \(F,G\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) be two functors. A natural transformation is a collection of morphisms \(\{\nu_A\}_{A\in\Ob(\mathcal C)}\) such that the following square commutes.

We say that \(\{\nu_A\}_{A\in\Ob(\mathcal C)}\) is a natural isomorphism if \(\nu_A\) is an isomorphism for every \(A\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\).

Principle.

Every statement in category theory has a dual statement obtained by replacing \(f\circ g\) with \(g\circ f\) and domain with codomain, essentially flipping the arrows of the morphisms.

Let us now look at some examples to gather some context. But before that, a small digression. In set theory, certain sets, such as the set of all groups or the set of all singletons, cannot exist. Hence the need to write a new set of axioms to create what are called classes, whose elements are sets that satisfy given properties. But for our purposes, let us stick to small or locally small categories, thereby avoiding the set-versus-class conundrum.

Some Pillars of Category Theory

Functor Categories

Let \(\mathcal C=\Fun(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)\), where \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) are categories. Its objects are functors \(F\colon\mathcal A\to\mathcal B\), and its morphisms are natural transformations. We say \(\mathcal C\cong\mathcal D\) if there exist \(F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) and \(G\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) such that \(F\circ G=\id_{\mathcal D}\) and \(G\circ F=\id_{\mathcal C}\). We say \(\mathcal C\sim\mathcal D\) if \(F\circ G\sim\id_{\mathcal D}\) and \(G\circ F\sim\id_{\mathcal C}\), via natural isomorphisms.

Representable Functors

For \(X,C\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\), define \(h_X\colon\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\cat{Sets}\) by

\[h_X(C)=\Hom(C,X),\qquad h_X(f\colon C\to C')\colon\Hom(C,X)\to\Hom(C',X),\quad g\mapsto g\circ f.\]

We say that a functor \(F\colon\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\cat{Sets}\) is representable if there exists \(C\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\) such that \(F\cong h_C\).

Everything in category theory can be studied via appropriate representable functors. This is akin to studying the category \(\mathcal C\) by acting it on \(\mathcal C\), where the action is given by \(\Hom_{\mathcal C}(-,-)\).

Final and Initial Objects

Let \(F\colon\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\cat{Sets}\) be given by \(F(C)=*\) (a singleton) and \(F(f)=\id_*\). We say \(I\) is an initial object of \(\mathcal C\) if \(h_I\cong F\), where \(\cong\) denotes natural isomorphism.

Construction of \(I\).

Let \(I\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\) be such that, for every \(C\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\), there is a unique \(f\in\Mor(\mathcal C)\) with \(I\xrightarrow{f}C\).

Claim

\(h_I\cong F\).

For every \(C\in\mathcal C\), the sets \(h_I(C)\) and \(F(C)\) are isomorphic, as they both have a single element. A final object is the dual notion of an initial object. Therefore final objects are representable functors; categories with no final object yield standard examples of non-representable functors.

Limits and Colimits

Let \(\chi\colon J\to\mathcal C\) be a functor, where \(J\) is often called the index category. Let \(C_A\colon J\to\mathcal C\) be given by \(C_A(j)=A\) for every \(j\in\Ob(J)\) and \(C_A(\theta)=\id_A\) for every \(\theta\in\Mor(J)\). Define \[F_\chi\colon\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\cat{Sets},\qquad F_\chi(A):=\Nat(C_A,\chi),\] where \(\Nat\) stands for natural transformations, and \[\begin{aligned} F_\chi(f\colon A\to B)&\colon\Nat(C_A,\chi)\to\Nat(C_B,\chi),\\ \{\nu_B\}_{B\in\Ob(\mathcal C)}&\longmapsto \{f\circ\nu_B\}_{B\in\Ob(\mathcal C)}. \end{aligned}\]

If \(F_\chi\cong h_C\), then \(C=\lim(\chi)\) is called the limit of \(\chi\).

Construction of \(C\).

Define the category \(\mathcal C:=\Cone(\chi)\), with \[\Ob(\Cone(\chi))= \left(C,\{f_i\colon C\to\chi(i)\}_{i\in J}\right),\qquad C\in\Ob(\mathcal C),\] where the \(f_i\) are such that, if \(\alpha\colon i\to j\), then the following diagram commutes.

The morphisms are \[\Mor(\Cone(\chi))= \left(f\colon(C,\{f_i\}_i)\longrightarrow(C',\{f_i'\}_i)\right),\] where \(f\) is such that the following diagram commutes for every \(i\in\Ob(J)\).

\(\mathcal C\) is called the cone category of \(\chi\). A final object of \(\mathcal C\) is called the limit of \(\chi\). Let \(\lim(\chi)\) be the final object. Then it is easy to see that \(h_{\lim(\chi)}\cong F_\chi\), namely, \[\Hom(D,\lim(\chi))\cong\Nat(C_D,\chi)\qquad\text{(as sets)}.\] Given \(f\colon D\to\lim(\chi)\), we obtain \(\bigl(D,\{f\circ\chi_i\}_{i\in\Ob(J)}\bigr)\)

in \(\Ob(\Cone(\chi))\), where \(\chi_i\colon\lim(\chi)\to\chi(i)\). By definition, \(f\) must be unique, so we have the natural map \(f\mapsto\{f\circ\chi_i\}_{i\in\Ob(J)}\).

A colimit is the dual notion of a limit in \(\mathcal C\).

Adjunctions (or Adjoints)

Let \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\) be two categories, and let \(F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) be a functor. An adjoint to \(F\) is a functor \(G\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) such that \[\Hom_{\mathcal C}(C,G(D))\cong\Hom_{\mathcal D}(F(C),D).\] This can be given the coating of a representable functor. Define \[\overline F\colon\mathcal C\to\cat{Sets},\qquad C\longmapsto\Hom_{\mathcal D}(F(C),D),\]

and send \(f\colon C\to C'\) to the map \[\bigl(g\colon F(C)\to D\bigr)\longmapsto \bigl(g\circ F(f)\colon F(C')\to D\bigr).\]

Suppose \(\overline F\) is representable. Then there exists \(\overline D\) such that \[\Hom_{\mathcal C}(C,\overline D)\cong\Hom_{\mathcal D}(F(C),D).\] Set \(G(D):=\overline D\). It is easy to see how \(G\) should behave on morphisms \(f\colon D\to D'\).

Constructing New Categories from Old

Cone Category

We already saw this being done for a different purpose. Objects in a cone category generalize the notion of a morphism. A morphism relates a particular object to another, but a cone object relates to a bunch of objects already related

to each other.

Subcategory

The definition is obvious.

Quotient Category

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a category. For every \(X,Y\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\), an equivalence relation \(\sim\) is set up on \(\Hom_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)\) such that \[\left.\begin{gathered} f_1\sim f_2\quad\text{in }\Hom_{\mathcal C}(X,Y),\\ g_1\sim g_2\quad\text{in }\Hom_{\mathcal C}(Z,X) \end{gathered}\right\} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_1\circ g_1\sim f_2\circ g_2.\] Also, \(X\sim Y\) if there exist \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to X\) such that \(f\circ g\sim\id_Y\) and \(g\circ f=\id_X\).

Then \(\mathcal C/{\sim}\) is the quotient category.

Example 3

\(\Fun(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)/{\sim}\), for natural isomorphism; \(\cat{Top}/{\sim}\), for homotopy equivalence.

Comma Category

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a given category and \(B\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\). Write \(\mathcal C\downarrow B\) for the comma category over \(B\). Its objects are maps in \(\mathcal C\), of the form \(X\xrightarrow{\pi}B\) (a “\(B\)-parametrized family of objects in \(\mathcal C\)”). The set \[\Hom_{\mathcal C\downarrow B} \bigl((X\xrightarrow{\pi}B),(X'\xrightarrow{\pi'}B)\bigr)\] consists of the maps \(f\colon X\to X'\) for which the following diagram commutes.

The dual notion is \(B\downarrow\mathcal C\).

Example 4

If \(\mathcal C=\cat{Top}\) and \(B=\{*\}\), then \(B\downarrow\mathcal C=\cat{Top}_*\) (based spaces).

Finally, \(A\downarrow\mathcal C\downarrow B:=A\downarrow(\mathcal C\downarrow B)\) demands that the following diagram commute.

Category of Presheaves

Given a category \(\mathcal C\), define \(\PSh(\mathcal C)\) by taking functors \(F\colon\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\cat{Sets}\) as objects and natural transformations as morphisms. Thus \(\PSh(\mathcal C)=\Fun(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\cat{Sets})\).

Standard Instances

Morphisms as Functors

Let \(f\colon A\to B\) be a morphism, with \(A,B\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\). Let \(J\) be some index category and let \(\chi_A\colon J\to\mathcal C\) be the functor given by \[\chi_A(i)=A\quad(i\in\Ob(J)),\qquad \chi_A(f\colon i\to j)=\id_A.\] Then \(\Nat(\chi_A,\chi_B)\) captures the morphism from \(A\) to \(B\), and \(\Nat(\chi_A,\chi_B)\) is a functor in \(\Fun(J,\mathcal C)\).

Objects as Morphisms

Let \(X\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\). The points of \(X\) can be thought

of as \(\Hom_{\mathcal C}(*,X)\), where \(*\) is a final object in \(\mathcal C\). “Generalized points” can be thought of as \(\Hom_{\mathcal C}(A,X)\). We are simply generalizing these notions from \(\mathcal C=\cat{Sets}\), where \(*\) is a singleton set, and morphisms from \(*\) to \(X\) in \(\cat{Sets}\) give a correspondence with points of \(X\). Similarly, morphisms can be treated as objects once realized as functors in the functor category.

Groups as Categories

Given a group \(G\), define a category \(\mathcal BG\) as follows: \[\Ob(\mathcal BG):=\{*\}\quad\text{(a singleton)},\qquad \Mor(\mathcal BG):=G,\] where \(g\in G\) is a morphism \(*\to*\) and multiplication is composition.

Remark

\(\mathcal BG\) has no final object.

Forgetful Functors

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a category of certain sets with a particular

structure imposed. The forgetful functor is \[U\colon\mathcal C\to\cat{Sets},\qquad U(C)=C\quad\text{(the underlying set)},\qquad U(f\colon C\to D)=f\colon C\to D\quad\text{(the set map)}.\]

Exponentials

Let \(C,B\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\). The exponential is an object \(C^B\) such that, for any \(f\colon A\times B\to C\), there exists a unique \(\overline f\colon A\times B\to C^B\) for which the following diagram commutes.

We say \(\mathcal C\) is Cartesian closed if it contains exponentials and products (which you shall encounter soon).

Group Objects in Categories

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a category closed under finite products, and let \(G\in\mathcal C\) be an object. The structure of a group on \(G\) is the data of morphisms \[\mu\colon G\times G\to G,\qquad \nu\colon G\to G,\qquad e\colon *\to G,\] where \(*\) is a final product, such that the following diagrams commute.

Example 5

In \(\cat{Sets}\), a group object is a group; in \(\cat{Top}\), it is a topological group; in \(\cat{Man}\), it is a Lie group. In \(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*/{\sim}\), we shall call it an \(H\)-space. This category shall be explained soon.

Certain Limit Constructions in Algebraic Topology

Products and Coproducts

Let \(\{X_i\}_{i\in I}\) be objects in \(\mathcal C\). Consider the discrete category \(X\), with \(\Ob(X)=X_i\) and \(\Mor(X)=\id_{X_i}\), and let \(\chi\colon X\hookrightarrow\mathcal C\) be the inclusion. The limit and colimit of \(\chi\), if they exist, are products and coproducts. In \(\cat{Top}\), the product is \(\prod_{i\in I}X_i\), with the product topology, and the coproduct is \(\coprod_{i\in I}X_i\). In \(*\downarrow\cat{Top}\sim\cat{Top}_*\), the product of the \((X_i,x_i)\) is \(\bigl(\prod_{i\in I}X_i,\{x_i\}_{i\in I}\bigr)\) and the coproduct is \(\bigvee_{i\in I}(X_i,x_i)\).

Joins (\(\mathcal C=\cat{Top}\))

Given \(X,Y\in\mathcal C\), the join of \(X\) and \(Y\), denoted \(X*Y\), is the colimit of the following diagram.

Here \(\pi_1(x,y)=x\), \(i_1(x,y)=(x,y,0)\), \(i_2(x,y)=(x,y,1)\), and \(\pi_2(x,y)=y\). Explicitly, \[X*Y=(X\times Y\times[0,1])/{\sim},\qquad \begin{cases} (x,y,0)\sim(x',y,0),\\ (x,y,1)\sim(x,y',0), \end{cases}\] which is essentially all the line segments joining points in \(X\) and \(Y\).

The special cases are \[\begin{aligned} X*\{\mathrm{pt}\}&=: \Cone(X)\cong(X\times I)/(X\times\{0\}) &&\text{(denoted $CX$)},\\ X*S^0&=: \operatorname{Suspension}(X) \cong(X\times I)/(X\times\{0\},\,X\times\{1\}) &&\text{(denoted $\Sigma X$)}. \end{aligned}\] Also \(\Sigma S^n\cong S^{n+1}\). Therefore a purely category-theoretic way of constructing an \(n\)-sphere would be to take \(S^n=\underbrace{S^0*\cdots*S^0}_{n+1\text{ times}}\).

Pushouts and Pullbacks

A pushout is a colimit of the first diagram below (sometimes also called fibre products). The second gives the example \(\Cone(f):=(X\amalg CA)/{\sim}\), where \((a,1)\sim f(a)\).

The dual notion is a pullback.

Remark

The limit and colimit of a diagram are essentially two ways of putting objects together such that the relations between them are preserved.

In abelian groups, putting together \(G_0\xrightarrow{f_0}G_1\xrightarrow{f_1}G_2\xrightarrow{f_2}\cdots\) would mean looking at \((x_0,x_1,\ldots)\in\prod_{i=0}^{\infty}G_i\) such that \(f_i(x_i)=x_{i+1}\) (the direct product). In \(\cat{Top}\), putting together \(A\xrightarrow{f}X\) and \(A\xrightarrow{g}Y\) would give \((X\amalg Y)/\{f(x)\sim g(x):x\in A\}\). In \(\cat{Grps}\), putting together the same diagram would give \[(X*Y)/N\bigl(f(a)g(a)^{-1}:a\in A\bigr),\] the amalgamated product. Essentially, given \(\mathcal C\), one has to look for appropriate analogues of \(\prod\) and \(\coprod\), and then put objects together preserving the relations in the diagram.

Having seen all this, let us (sort of) look at the only lemma in category theory.

Lemma 1 — Yoneda’s lemma

Let \(F\in\PSh(\mathcal C)\). For any \(X\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\), there is an isomorphism of sets \[\Hom_{\PSh(\mathcal C)}(h_X,F)\cong F(X)\] that is natural in both \(X\) and \(F\).

Sketch of proof. Suppose \(\theta\in\Hom_{\PSh(\mathcal C)}(h_X,F)\), i.e. \(\{\theta_A\colon h_X(A)\to F(A)\}_{A\in\Ob(\mathcal C)}\). Define \[\Phi\colon\Hom_{\PSh(\mathcal C)}(h_X,F)\to F(X),\qquad \Phi\bigl(\{\theta_A\}_{A\in\Ob(\mathcal C)}\bigr)=\theta_X(\id_X).\] Let \(a\in F(X)\). Then \(\Psi(a)\in\Hom_{\PSh(\mathcal C)}(h_X,F)\) is given by \[\Psi(a)_A(f):=F(f)(a)\qquad(f\in h_X(A)),\] the natural evaluation. Verify the rest.

We shall conclude by giving two applications of Yoneda’s lemma.

Application 1

If \(\mathcal C\) is Cartesian closed, then for any three objects \(X,Y,Z\), \[\Hom_{\mathcal C}(X,\Hom_{\mathcal C}(Y,Z)) \cong\Hom_{\mathcal C}(X\times Y,Z),\] often written as \(Z^{X\times Y}\cong(Z^Y)^X\). It turns out that \(\cat{Top}\) is not Cartesian closed. Hence one considers \(k\text{-}\cat{Top}\), a full subcategory of \(\cat{Top}\) consisting of compactly generated spaces. Using this, in \(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*/{\sim}\cong(*\downarrow k\text{-}\cat{Top})/{\sim}\), one can prove that

\[\begin{aligned} \Hom_{(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*)/{\sim}}(X,\Omega_{y_0}Y) &:=\pi_b(X,\Omega_{y_0}Y)\\ &\cong\pi_b(\Sigma X,Y) =\Hom_{(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*)/{\sim}}(\Sigma X,Y). \end{aligned}\] Here \(\pi_b\) denotes the collection of based continuous maps \(X\to\Omega_{y_0}Y\), up to homotopy, sending the base point to the base point. The homotopy sets are \[\begin{aligned} \text{zeroth homotopy set}&:=\pi_b(*,Y),\\ \text{first homotopy set}&:=\pi_b(*,\Omega_{y_0}Y),\\ &\ \vdots\\ \text{$n$th homotopy set}&:=\pi_b(*,\Omega[\Omega^{n-1}(Y)]) \cong\pi_b(\Sigma^n*,Y)\cong\pi_b(S^n,Y). \end{aligned}\]

Application 2

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a category and \(X\in\Ob(\mathcal C)\). Then \(X\) is a group object if and only if \(h_X\colon\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\cat{Sets}\) lifts to groups, i.e. there exists \(\widetilde h_X\) making the following diagram commute; \(U\) is the forgetful functor.

Now \(\Omega_{y_0}Y\) can be made into a group object in \((k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*)/{\sim}\), i.e. an \(H\)-space. By Yoneda’s lemma, one can give a group structure to \[\Hom_{(k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*)/{\sim}}(A,\Omega_{y_0}Y) =\pi_b(A,\Omega_{y_0}Y)\] for every \(A\in\Ob((k\text{-}\cat{Top}_*)/{\sim})\), since the functor \(\pi_b(-,\Omega_{y_0}Y)\) lifts to \(\cat{Grps}\). This way one can give homotopy sets, homology sets, and cohomology sets a group structure!
