title: Erdős Distance Problem
html:
S. Viswanathan

According to Paul Erdős, his most important contribution to geometry is his distance conjecture. The formulation of the problem is quite innocuous and recreational in nature. Let me begin by stating the problem explicitly.

Let \(P\) be a set of \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^2\), and let \(\Delta(P):=\{|p-p'|:p,p'\in P,\ p\ne p'\}\). Thus \(\Delta(P)\) is essentially the set of possible distinct distances between distinct points. For instance, if \(P\) is the set described pictorially below, then \(\Delta(P)=\{10,2\}\).

But wait! What about \(|p_2-p_4|\)? Is there a way to salvage this blunder? Is there a configuration of four points such that three of them form an equilateral triangle and the fourth one is at a distance \(10\)? If you think about it for a minute, it is immediate that such a configuration is impossible, for the fourth point \(p_4\) must be the

centroid of \(\triangle p_1p_2p_3\), so \(|p_4-p_i|<2\) for every \(1\le i\le3\). If you think about it a bit more, you will realise that all configurations of four points in \(\mathbb R^2\) must have at least two distinct distances. Why? Set \(P=\{p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4\}\).

Given four points \(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4\), we have \(\binom42=6\) nonzero distances. By the pigeonhole principle, if \(|\Delta(P)|=1\), there must either be a square or an equilateral triangle in the configuration, and in either case \(|\Delta(P)|\ge2\).

This argument just showed us that the plane is rigid: it does not allow points on it to float around with an arbitrary set of distinct distances. As interesting as it may be to ask which sets of distances can be realised in \(\mathbb R^2\), let us begin by asking the following.

Question

What is \(\inf_{|P|=n}|\Delta(P)|\)? If \(g(n):=\inf_{|P|=n}|\Delta(P)|\) is the minimum number of possible distances, describe \(g(n)\).

We know \(g(0)=0\), \(g(1)=0\), \(g(2)=1\), \(g(3)=1\) (an equilateral triangle), \(g(4)=2\), \(g(5)=2\) (a pentagon), and so on. Erdős was particularly interested in trying to find bounds for \(g(n)\), both upper and lower bounds; he was not optimistic enough to look for asymptotes.

He believed that \(g(n)\) must roughly behave like \(n\) for large \(n\). It is firstly easy to see that, mostly, \(|\Delta(P)|\) will be like \(|P|^2\), because we can consider the following function (let \(|P|=n\)): \[F\colon\underbrace{\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^2}_{n\text{ times}} \longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad F(p_1,\ldots,p_n):=\prod_{1\le\ell\le i<j<k\le n} \bigl(|p_i-p_j|-|p_k-p_\ell|\bigr).\]

\(F\) is nonzero on a dense open set in \(\mathbb R^{2n}\). On that dense open set, some sets of points \(\{p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n\}\) need not all be distinct. Regardless, for all configurations \(P\) such that \(|P|\le n\), \(|\Delta(P)|=\binom{|P|}{2}\).

Forget those, because we are interested in \(g(n)\). The reason Erdős believed that \(g(n)\) is roughly linear is that he was able to come up with a configuration of \(n\) points, for every \(n\), such that \(|\Delta(P)|\sim n\). Indeed, if \(P=\{(0,1),(1,1),\ldots,(n-1,1)\}\), then \(|\Delta(P)|=n\). Thus \(g(n)\le n\) trivially, but Erdős was able to beat \(n\) by considering the following clever arrangement.

He considered an integer grid of size \(\sqrt N\times\sqrt N\), as shown below: \([0,\sqrt N]\times[0,\sqrt N]\cap\mathbb Z^2\).

We have \[\Delta(P)=\{\sqrt A:A=x^2+y^2,\ 0\le x,y\le\sqrt N\} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0\le A\le2N.\] Notice that \(|\Delta(P)|=|\{0\le n\le2N:n\text{ is a sum of two squares}\}|\). Therefore \[g(n)\le\bigl|\{0\le k\le2n:k\text{ is a sum of two squares}\}\bigr|.\] The expression on the right is usually denoted by \(\pi_2(2n)\). Let us give a rough heuristic for \(\pi_2(2n)\) using very elementary number theory.

Theorem 2 — Two Squares Theorem

\(n\) is a sum of two squares if and only if, for every prime \(p\mid n\) such that \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), we have \(2\mid\nu_p(n)\).

We shall not digress and give a proof, for it can be found in many standard texts in number theory. Instead, we shall use the theorem to roughly sketch an estimate for \(r_2(m)\).

Note that, for \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), if \(2\mid\nu_p(m)\), then \(p<\sqrt m\) (because \(p^2\mid m\)). From the integers up to \(m\), we must remove all odd powers of \(p\) and their multiples, where \(p\equiv-1\pmod4\). Note that this is equivalent to combining all the even powers of \(p\) and their multiples, where \(p\equiv-1\pmod4\). Let us do that via inclusion–exclusion!

Given a prime \(p\le m\), the quantity \(m(1-1/p)\) is roughly the number of integers at most \(m\) not divisible by \(p\). Similarly, \(m/p^2\) is the number of multiples of \(p^2\) at most \(m\). Hence the number of \(k\) such that \(p\nmid k\) or \(p^2\mid k\) is \[m\left(1-\frac1p\right)\left(1+\frac1{p^2}\right)+\frac m{p^3}, \qquad m\left(1-\frac1p\right)\left(1+\frac1{p^2}\right) =m-\frac mp+\frac m{p^2}-\frac m{p^3}.\]

One extends the inclusion–exclusion principle and ends up with \[m-\frac mp+\frac m{p^2}-\frac m{p^3}+\frac m{p^4}-\frac m{p^5}+\cdots \approx m\left(1-\frac1p\right)\left(1+\frac1{p^2}\right) \left(1-\frac1{p^3}\right)\left(1+\frac1{p^4}\right)\cdots.\] The correction sum will be something of the form \(\sum_{2\nmid k}P(k)/p^k\), where \(P(k)\) is the partition function. But let us ignore that, for \(P(k)<k^2\) and \(\sum_k k^2/p^k\) converges.

Now, if \(p\mid m\) and \(2\mid\nu_p(m)\), then \(p\le\sqrt m\). Thus \[r_2(m)\approx m\prod_{\substack{p\le\sqrt m\\p\equiv-1\ (4)}}\left(1-\frac1p\right) \prod_{\substack{p^2\le\sqrt m\\p\equiv-1\ (4)}}\left(1+\frac1{p^2}\right) \cdots.\] Each product after the first converges, so \(r_2(m)\approx m\prod_{p\le\sqrt m,\ p\equiv-1\ (4)}(1-1/p)\). One can now prove that \[\prod_{\substack{p\le\sqrt m\\p\equiv-1\ (4)}}\left(1-\frac1p\right) \approx\frac1{\sqrt{\log m}}.\] Again, refer to any standard text in analytic number theory for a proof. The reason we have \(1/2\) in the exponent of \(\log m\) can roughly be explained by the following, again vague, argument. The expression \(m\prod_{p\le\sqrt m}(1-1/p)\) counts the non-composite numbers and is approximately \(m/\log m\). Hence, by the Prime Number Theorem, \(\prod_{p\le\sqrt m}(1-1/p)\approx1/\log m\). Now, as primes are equidistributed modulo \(4\) between \(1\) and \(-1\), \[\prod_{\substack{p\le\sqrt m\\p\equiv1\ (4)}}\left(1-\frac1p\right) \approx \prod_{\substack{p\le\sqrt m\\p\equiv-1\ (4)}}\left(1-\frac1p\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \prod_{\substack{p\le\sqrt m\\p\equiv-1\ (4)}}\left(1-\frac1p\right) \approx\frac1{\sqrt{\log m}}.\]

Anyway, coming back to our problem, we now roughly know that \[g(n)\le r_2(2n)\approx\frac{2n}{\sqrt{\log(2n)}} \approx\frac n{\sqrt{\log n}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(n)=O\left(\frac n{\sqrt{\log n}}\right).\] Erdős was thus able to get this neat bound from an observation purely number-theoretic in nature. We now have a strong reason to believe that a lower bound roughly of order \(O(n^{1-\varepsilon})\) must exist for every \(\varepsilon>0\). This conviction led him to conjecture the following.

Conjecture 3 — Erdős Distance Conjecture

For every \(c<1\), \(g(n)=\Omega(n^c)\). This means that \[\limsup_{x\to\infty}|g(x)/x^c|>0.\]

A colloquial way of saying it is that \(g(n)\) is roughly \(n\), up to a logarithmic decay.

Remark

This slick observation of Erdős fails when you go to, say, \(\mathbb R^4\), for, by Lagrange’s Four-Square Theorem, every number is a sum of four squares. There number theory will not give you a logarithmic decay.

Getting an upper bound is easy; we just did it: \(g(n)\le cn/\sqrt{\log n}\). What proved to be extremely difficult was to get a lower bound, because that must use the dimension of the manifold one is dealing with very crucially: \(g(4)=1\) in \(\mathbb R^3\) (a tetrahedron).

The arguments must crucially use the fact that the dimension is \(2\) and the manifold is \(\mathbb R^2\), for even on a sphere a tetrahedron can be arranged, forcing \(g(4)=1\). We must use the fact that the points are not only in a two-dimensional manifold: they are in \(\mathbb R^2\).

The best lower bound one expects for \(g(n)\) is \(cn/\sqrt{\log n}\) for some \(c\) and large \(n\). People do not try to prove \(g(n)=\Omega(n^c)\), for the arguments are not yet structural. What they instead do is get better and better lower bounds. Here is Erdős’s conjecture rephrased.

Conjecture 4 — Lower bound

For some \(c>0\) and large \(n\), \(g(n)\ge cn/\sqrt{\log n}\).

Erdős did quite poorly in trying to come up with lower bounds, and perhaps he did not care enough at that point to announce prize money for this problem. I guess one can imagine him being content with just this much.

Theorem 5 — Erdős, 1946

\(g(n)\ge c\sqrt n\).

Proof. Let \(P\) be a configuration such that \(|P|=n\), and let \(p_0\in P\). Draw \(t\) circles centred at \(p_0\) such that every point in \(P\) belongs to one such circle and each circle has at least one point of \(P\).

By the pigeonhole principle, at least one circle must have at least \(n/t\) points of \(P\). Again by the pigeonhole principle, at least one of the hemispheres must have \(n/(2t)\) points. Pick the rightmost point to see that it will have at least \(n/(2t)\) distinct distances to points of \(P\) on that hemisphere. Therefore \[|\Delta(P)|\ge\max\left(t,\frac n{2t}\right) \ge\sqrt{t\left(\frac n{2t}\right)}=\sqrt{\frac n2}, \qquad g(n)\ge\sqrt{\frac n2}.\] Thus the constant \(c\) here is \(1/\sqrt2\).

Remark

This argument can be generalised to \(\mathbb R^d\) via induction to get \(g(n)\ge cn^{1/d}\), but the conjecture for \(\mathbb R^d\) is that \(g(n)\ge cn^{2/d}\), so even there this bound is quite bad!

Let us now look at a slight improvement of Erdős’s lazy result.

Theorem 6 — Moser, 1952

\(g(n)\ge cn^{2/3}\) for some \(c>0\).

Proof. Let \(P\) be a configuration such that \(|P|=n\). Choose \(x,y\in P\) such that \(|x-y|\) is minimal. Let \(O\) be the midpoint; centred at \(O\), draw annuli of

thickness \(|x-y|\). Call these annuli \(\widetilde A_1,\widetilde A_2,\ldots, \widetilde A_\ell\), as illustrated below.

Let \(L\) be the line joining \(x,y\). By the pigeonhole principle, half of \(P\) is, without loss of generality, on or above the line \(L\). Henceforth \(\widetilde A_i\) denotes the annuli on or above \(L\). Partition \(\{\widetilde A_i\}_{i=1}^{\ell}\) into \(\{\widetilde A_i\}_{i\equiv0\ (3)}\), \(\{\widetilde A_i\}_{i\equiv1\ (3)}\), and \(\{\widetilde A_i\}_{i\equiv-1\ (3)}\). By the pigeonhole principle, one of these parts must contain at least one third of \(P\), so that part contains one sixth of \(P\) above \(L\). Without loss of generality, let \(\{\widetilde A_i\}_{i\equiv0\ (3)}\) be that part. Let \(\widetilde A_{3j}\) be the \(j\)th annulus in this part, and let \[\{|p-x|:p\in\widetilde A_{3j}\}\cup \{|p-y|:p\in\widetilde A_{3j}\}=\{d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_k\}, \qquad 3k'\le\ell.\]

If we draw circles from \(x,y\) touching all points in \(\widetilde A_{3j}\), there will be \(k\) of them. Let \[A_i:=\{p\in\widetilde A_{3j}:|p-x|=d_i\},\qquad B_i:=\{p\in\widetilde A_{3j}:|p-y|=d_i\}.\] Then \(A_i=\bigcup_{k'}(A_i\cap B_{k'})\), since every point in \(A_{3j}\) at distance \(d_i\) from \(x\) is at some distance from \(y\).

Consequently \(\bigcup_i A_i=\bigcup_{i,k'}(A_i\cap B_{k'})\). Let \(|\bigcup_{i=1}^kA_i|=n_j\). We have \[\left|\bigcup_{i,k'}(A_i\cap B_{k'})\right| \le k^2\max_{i,k'}|A_i\cap B_{k'}|.\] Note that \(A_i\) and \(B_{k'}\) are points on the circles above \(L\), so \(|A_i\cap B_{k'}|\le1\), giving \(k\ge\sqrt{n_j}\). In the \(j\)th annulus \(\widetilde A_{3j}\) there are therefore at least \(\sqrt{n_j}\) distinct distances to \(x\). Notice that \(\widetilde A_{3j}\) and \(\widetilde A_{3j+3}\) can never have two points at the same distance, so we can sum them together to obtain \(|\Delta(P)|\ge\sum_j\sqrt{n_j}\).

Since each \(n_j\) denotes the number of points in \(\widetilde A_{3j}\) above \(L\), we have \(n/6\le\sum_jn_j\). Thus \[\frac n6\le\sum_jn_j \le\sum_j(\sqrt{n_j})(\sqrt{n_j}) \le\sqrt{\max_j n_j}\sum_j\sqrt{n_j} \le\sqrt{\max_j n_j}\,|\Delta(P)|.\] Also, \(|\Delta(P)|\ge\max_j n_j\). To see this, pick the annulus \(\widetilde A_{3j}\) in which \(n_j\) is maximum, and in it pick the rightmost point, just as we did in the proof of Erdős’s theorem. We obtain \[|\Delta(P)|\ge\max_j n_j,\qquad |\Delta(P)|\ge\frac n{6\sqrt{\max_j n_j}}.\]

It follows that \[|\Delta(P)|^2\,|\Delta(P)| \ge\frac{n^2}{36\max_j n_j}\max_j n_j=\frac{n^2}{36}, \qquad |\Delta(P)|\ge\frac{n^{2/3}}{36^{1/3}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(n)\ge\frac1{\sqrt[3]{36}}n^{2/3}.\] The constant here is \(1/\sqrt[3]{36}\).

Since Moser enhanced Erdős’s argument with quite a clever construction of foliated annuli, many joined the race to get to the bound \(cn/\sqrt{\log n}\).

Tools from Fourier analysis, number theory, graph theory, and even information theory have gone into the formulation and resolution of this conjecture, culminating in Guth’s near-optimal result! We are just \(1/\sqrt{\log n}\) away from Erdős’s conjecture. The future certainly shall bring hope.

title: Small Gaps between Primes
html:
S. Viswanathan

Let \(\mathbb P\) denote the set of primes. Enumerate them in increasing order as \(p_1,p_2,p_3,\ldots,p_n,\ldots\), where \(p_n\) denotes the \(n\)th prime. We ask a very basic question about the additive distribution of \(\mathbb P\). Fix a width parameter \(h\). How many primes can you find in the interval \([x,x+h]\), and how often?

Let us begin by making the question concrete. If there are \(k\) primes in \([x,x+h]\), of which \(p_n\) is the smallest, then \(p_{n+k}-p_n\le h\). It would suffice to study \(H_m:=\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+m}-p_n)\). Set \(\widehat H_m:=\{p_{n+m}-p_n:p_n\in\mathbb P\}\). If \(\widehat H_m\) is bounded, then, by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, so is \(H_m\). Further, one can say that in infinitely many intervals of size \(H_m\) there are at least \(m\) primes.

Studying \(\{H_m\}_m\), assuming that its terms are indeed numbers, is extremely hard because of the additive nature of the problem. Primes appear naturally only as factors, so they are suited for multiplicative studies. Regardless, there are deep conjectures about this. Of them all, the

famous, perhaps even mythical, one is the Twin Prime Conjecture.

Conjecture 18 — Twin Prime Conjecture

\(H_1=2\), or equivalently, there are infinitely many twin primes.

Recently, by deploying advanced sieve-theoretic tools, highly nontrivial bounds for \(H_m\) have been found, establishing that they are indeed numbers! The first breakthrough came from Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım, who developed a sieve technique to find at least two primes in an interval \([a,b]\).

2005: Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım.

They proved \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}=0.\] In fact, they proved the stronger version \(p_{n+1}-p_n\le(\log p_n)^{1/2+\varepsilon}\) infinitely often.

2013: Yitang Zhang.

\(\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n)=H_1\le70{,}000{,}000\).

2013: Polymath.

\(H_1\le4{,}680\). Tao organised a Polymath project, inviting mathematicians from all over to optimise Zhang’s technique. It turns out that Zhang, and subsequently the Polymath group, used Deligne’s theorem, which proves the Riemann hypothesis for finite fields.

A postdoc named James Maynard found a shortcut and surprised everyone. He used elementary sieve methods.

2013: J. Maynard, independently.

\(H_1\le600\). Subsequently, Maynard and Tao’s group joined forces.

2014: Maynard and Polymath.

\(H_1\le246\). They were also able to prove the following bound for \(H_m\).

2015: Maynard and Tao’s group.

\(H_m\ll m^3e^{4m}\), asserting for the first time that \(\{H_m\}_m\) is a sequence of integers.

This talk is about the 2005 work of Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım. Let us heuristically motivate \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log p_n=0\) and then see the technique that went into its proof. Since the problem is additive and the role of primes as factors does not seem to be to the fore, we shall model \(\mathbb P\) by a sequence just as sparse as \(\mathbb P\). Collect the numbers \(\{1,2,3,\ldots,n\}\). In this set there are \(n/\log n\) primes.

The probability of \(n\) being prime is therefore \(1/\log n\).

Remark — Caution

These arguments must be taken with a pinch of salt. Firstly, the probability of \(n\) being prime in \(\{1,2,\ldots,n+1\}\) is \(1/\log(n+1)\), and in \(\{1,2,\ldots,n+k\}\) it is \(1/\log(n+k)\), yet we choose \(1/\log n\). Secondly, if a number \(p>2\) is prime, then \(p+1\) is certainly not prime, since \(2\mid p+1\). Thus the probability that \(p+1\) is prime is \(0\), but according to our model it has nonzero probability \(1/\log(p+1)>0\).

We model primes as follows: \(\widehat{\mathbb P}:=\{p:X(p)=1\}\), where \(X(p)\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\mathbb P(X(p)=1)=1/\log p\). This is Cramér’s model of primes. Let us use it to count primes in \((p+\alpha\log p,p+\beta\log p)\) for a large prime \(p\). For some \(h\in(\alpha\log p,\beta\log p)\), the probability \[\mathbb P\bigl(X(p+i)=0,\ 1\le i\le h-1,\ \text{and }X(p+h)=0\bigr)\] is \[\begin{aligned} &\left(1-\frac1{\log(p+1)}\right) \left(1-\frac1{\log(p+2)}\right)\cdots \left(1-\frac1{\log(p+h-1)}\right)\frac1{\log(p+h)}\\ & \sim \left(1-\frac1{\log p}\right)^{h-1}\frac1{\log p}, \end{aligned}\] if \(h\) is small compared with \(p\).

By Taylor expansion, \(e^{-1/\log p}\sim1-1/\log p\). Combining these approximations, according to the random

model, the probability that the next prime lies in \((p+\alpha\log p,p+\beta\log p)\) is \[\begin{aligned} &\sum_{\alpha\log p<h<\beta\log p} \mathbb P\bigl(X(p+i)=0,\ 1\le i\le h-1,\ X(p+h)=0\bigr)\\ &\qquad\sim \sum_{\alpha\log p<h<\beta\log p} e^{-(h-1)/\log p}\frac1{\log p} \approx\int_\alpha^\beta e^{-t}\,dt. \end{aligned}\] Thus the probability that \((p_{\mathrm{next}}-p)/\log p\) lies between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is \(\int_\alpha^\beta e^{-t}\,dt=e^{-\alpha}-e^{-\beta}\). Set \(\alpha=0\) and take \(\beta\) very small. With positive probability, \((p_{\mathrm{next}}-p)/\log p\in[0,\varepsilon)\) for any \(\varepsilon>0\). This suggests the following.

Conjecture 19

\(\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}=0\).

Erdős was the first to make nontrivial progress. He proved \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log p_n\le1\). This was improved to \(0.24\). Finally, in 2005, Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım proved the following.

Theorem 20 — Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım

\(\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}=0\).

The quantity \(\log p\) is usually called the average gap because, according to the Prime Number Theorem, there is at least one prime on average in each interval \((k\log n,(k+1)\log n)\), where \(0\le k\le n/\log n\). With Theorem 20, one can ask whether \(\liminf_{p\to\infty}(p_{\mathrm{next}}-p)<\infty\), that is, whether bounded gaps between primes exist.

The Prime Number Theorem tells us that if \(p_{n+1}-p_n\not<\log p_n\) infinitely often, then eventually the intervals \((k\log n,(k+1)\log n)\) would not have primes, so the prime count for large \(n\) would be off. But one can ask what the largest possible gap is, infinitely often. We have a powerful conjecture, again a consequence of Cramér’s model.

Conjecture 21

\(\displaystyle\limsup_{p\to\infty} \frac{p_{\mathrm{next}}-p}{(\log p)^2}=1\).

Consider the sequence of consecutive numbers \(m!+2,m!+3,\ldots,m!+m\). If \(m!\sim x\), then the length of \((m!+2,m!+m)\) is \(\sim\log x/\log\log x\), which is far less than \((\log x)^2\). In fact, it is dominated even by the average gap.

Regardless, one must be ambitious. Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım were! They wanted to prove \(\boxed{H_1\le16}\). Their idea is rather benign. Let \(\mathcal H=\{h_1,h_2,\ldots,h_k\}\), where \(h_1<h_2<\cdots<h_k\). It is called an admissible \(k\)-tuple if \(\mathcal H\) has minimal diameter and misses one congruence class modulo every prime.

Given an admissible \(k\)-tuple, it makes sense to ask whether there can be two primes in \(\{n+h_1,n+h_2,\ldots,n+h_k\}\), since \(\mathcal H\) misses one congruence class, so the iterates can be primes. Suppose one can find a sequence \(\{a(n)\}_n\) of nonnegative numbers such that, for every \(j=1,2,\ldots,k\), \[\begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\n+h_j\in\mathbb P}}a(n) >\frac1k\sum_{x\le n\le2x}a(n). \tag{$\star$} \end{equation}\] Then \[\sum_{j=1}^k\left(\sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\n+h_j\in\mathbb P}}a(n)\right) =\sum_{x\le n\le2x}\#\{1\le j\le k:n+h_j\in\mathbb P\}\,a(n) >\sum_{x\le n\le2x}a(n).\] Hence \(\#\{1\le j\le k:n+h_j\in\mathbb P\}\ge2\), giving \(p_{n+1}-p_n\le\diam(\{h_j\}_{j=1}^k)\). Inspired by Selberg, their choice of \(\{a(n)\}_n\) is as follows. The idea is to choose \(a(n)=1\) if the numbers \(\{n+h_j\}_{j=1}^k\) are all prime, because, even without \((\star)\), we would at least have an upper bound on the number of prime \(k\)-tuples.

Let \(\{\lambda_d\}_d\) be a sequence of real numbers such that \(\lambda_1=1\) and \(\lambda_d=0\) for all \(d>R\). Set \[a(n):=\left(\sum_{d\mid(n+h_1)\cdots(n+h_k)}\lambda_d\right)^2.\] If \(R<x\le n\) and all the \(n+h_j\) are prime, then \(a(n)=1\). Expanding the square, one has \[\sum_{d_1,d_2}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2} \left(\sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\ d_1\mid(n+h_1)\cdots(n+h_k)\\d_2\mid(n+h_1)\cdots(n+h_k)}}1\right) = \sum_{d_1,d_2}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2} \left(\sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\{}[d_1,d_2]\mid(n+h_1)\cdots(n+h_k)}}1\right),\] since \([d_1,d_2]\mid m\) if and only if \(d_1\mid m\) and \(d_2\mid m\). Thus \(\sum_{x\le n\le2x,\ n+h_j\in\mathbb P}a(n)\) and \(\sum_{x\le n\le2x}a(n)\) are quadratic forms with coefficients \(\sum_{x\le n\le2x,\ [d_1,d_2]\mid\prod_{i=1}^k(n+h_i)}1\). One needs to choose \(\{\lambda_d\}_d\) to maximise \[\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\n+h_j\in\mathbb P}}a(n)} {\displaystyle\sum_{x\le n\le2x}a(n)}, \qquad\text{preferably making it greater than }1/k.\] The two quadratic forms need not commute and hence cannot be simultaneously diagonalised. Also, the coefficients are too complicated for Lagrange multipliers. Somehow, they narrowed the choice down to \[\lambda_d=\mu(d)P\left(\frac{\log(R/d)}{\log R}\right)\] for some polynomial \(P\). Perhaps the motivation lies in Selberg’s sieve.

With that choice of \(\lambda_d\), they were able to obtain \[\sum_{x\le n\le2x}a(n)\sim \frac{x}{(\log R)^k}\mathfrak S(\mathcal H) \int_0^1\frac{y^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}\bigl(P^{(k)}(1-y)\bigr)^2\,dy.\] For the numerator in the ratio, however, they have to evaluate \[\sum_{d_1,d_2\le R}\lambda_{d_1}\lambda_{d_2} \left(\sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\ [d_1,d_2]\mid\prod_{i=1}^k(n+h_i)\\n+h_j\in\mathbb P}}1\right).\] This amounts to evaluating the inner sum \(\sum_{x\le n\le2x,\ [d_1,d_2]\mid\prod_{i=1}^k(n+h_i),\ n+h_j\in\mathbb P}1\). We have \([d_1,d_2]\mid(n+h_1)\cdots(n+h_k)\Longrightarrow n\equiv-h_i\pmod{[d_1,d_2]}\). Of the congruence classes modulo \([d_1,d_2]\), let \(g([d_1,d_2])\) count those that are coprime. For each, we have to calculate the number of \(n\) such that \(n+h_j\) is prime. Here is where we need really strong equidistribution theorems.

We know \[\#\{p\in\mathbb P:p\le x,\ p\equiv a\pmod q\} \sim\frac{x}{\varphi(q)\log x},\] but this is for \(x\gg q\); here \([d_1,d_2]\sim R^2\sim x^{1/2}\)!

Assuming the strongest such equidistribution result,1 they obtained an asymptote for the numerator: \[\sum_{\substack{x\le n\le2x\\ [d_1,d_2]\mid\prod_{i=1}^k(n+h_i)\\n+h_j\in\mathbb P}}a(n) \sim \frac{x}{(\log x)(\log R)^{k-1}}\mathfrak S(\mathcal H) \int_0^1\frac{y^{k-2}}{(k-2)!}\bigl(P^{(k-1)}(1-y)\bigr)^2\,dy.\] But unfortunately this ratio is less than \(1/k\). Disappointing! They had to use the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture, perhaps the strongest equidistribution statement, to prove the following.

Theorem 22 — Assuming the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture

\(H_1\le16\).

Unconditionally, they were only able to retrieve an average result, Theorem 20. In estimating \(\{p\in\mathbb P:p\le x,\ p\equiv a\pmod q\}\), the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem allows \(q\) to be as large as \(\sqrt x\) while still giving equidistribution. It goes to show how immaculate primes are! In fact, the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture says that the exponent \(1/2\) in the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem can be improved to \(1-\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

This failed attempt to get \(H_1\le16\) led to decades of fascinating progress, leading up to the following state-of-the-art theorems.

Theorem 23 — Polymath

\(H_1\le246\).

Theorem 24 — Assuming the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture

\(H_1\le6\).

It was argued that one cannot beat \(6\) using sieve-theoretic tools because of something called the parity obstruction. Thus this theory is, at the moment, stagnant. Tao remarks that progress is one or two clever ideas away!

  1. Bombieri–Vinogradov’s theorem (as strong as the Riemann hypothesis).↩︎
excerptHtml: Let \(\mathbb P\) denote the set of primes. Enumerate them in increasing order as \(p_1,p_2,p_3,\ldots,p_n,\ldots\), where \(p_n\) denotes the \(n\)th prime. We ask a very basic question about the additive distribution of \(\mathbb P\). Fix a width parameter \(h\). How many primes can you find in the interval \([x,x+h]\), and how often?
